# Acknowledgments

With this being our fourth edition, we find ourselves used to saying this. It always needs to be said, though: Books are not created by authors alone. They are shepherded into existence by a community of collaborators, risk-takers, and other supporters, without whom the burden of comprehending and writing all this material would be overwhelming.

*   Brian Hardy, who, along with Bill Phillips, had the gusto to bring the very first edition of this book into the world.

*   Eric Maxwell, for single-handedly writing the For the More Curious section on dependency injection, for improving our coverage of notification channels, and for addressing numerous editor remarks that touched so many pages of this book.

*   David Greenhalgh and Josh Skeen, for lending their expertise as we “Kotlinified” this book and learned how to be Android developers in a Kotlin world.

*   Jeremy Sherman for being a surprise Android expert just when we needed him most. Thank you, Jeremy, for your detailed, thoughtful reviews and for letting us use some of your words directly in Loopers, Handlers, and HandlerThread.

*   Bryan Lindsey, our resident <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> expert (and expert in so many other Android-related things). Thanks for the special attention you gave to BeatBox and PhotoGallery.

*   Andrew Bailey, the most intelligent rubber duck we have ever met. Thank you for offering a listening ear many times over and for helping us talk through some tough conceptual decisions. Also, thank you for adding Oreo updates to our discussion on broadcast intents.

*   Jamie Lee, our intern-turned-developer-writer-editor extraordinaire. Thank you for editing slides, reviewing solutions, and addressing remarks. Your attention to detail is unparalleled and greatly appreciated.

*   Andrew Marshall, for proactively pushing improvements to the book, for leading one of our classes in a pinch, and for jumping in and finishing up slide edits during crunch time.

*   Zack Simon, our fantastically talented and soft-spoken Big Nerd Ranch designer, who beautified the nifty cheat sheet attached to this book. If you enjoy that sheet, you should find Zack and tell him so yourself. But we will also thank Zack right here: Thanks, Zack!

*   Our editor, Elizabeth Holaday. The famous beat author William S. Burroughs sometimes wrote by cutting up his work into little pieces, throwing them in the air, and publishing the rearrangement. Without a strong editor like Liz, our confusion and simpleminded excitement may have caused us to resort to such techniques. We are thankful that she was there to impose focus, precision, and clarity on our drafts.

*   Ellie Volckhausen, who designed our cover.

*   Anna Bentley, our copyeditor and proofreader. Thank you for sanding away the remaining rough edges of this book.

*   Chris Loper at IntelligentEnglish.com, who designed and produced the print and eBook versions of the book. His DocBook toolchain made life much easier, too.

*   Thanks to Aaron Hillegass, Stacy Henry, and Emily Herman. As a practical matter, it is not possible to do this work without Big Nerd Ranch, the company Aaron founded and that Stacy (CEO) and Emily (COO) now fearlessly lead. Thank you.

Finally, thanks to our students. There is a feedback loop between us and our students: We teach them out of these materials, and they respond to it. Without that loop, this book could never have existed, nor could it be maintained. If Big Nerd Ranch books are special (and we hope they are), it is that feedback loop that makes them so. Thank you.

# Learning Android

As a beginning Android programmer, you face a steep learning curve. Learning Android is like moving to a foreign city. Even if you speak the language, it will not feel like home at first. Everyone around you seems to understand things that you are missing. Things you already knew turn out to be dead wrong in this new context.

Android has a culture. That culture speaks Kotlin or Java (or a bit of both), but knowing Kotlin or Java is not enough. Getting your head around Android requires learning many new ideas and techniques. It helps to have a guide through unfamiliar territory.

That’s where we come in. At Big Nerd Ranch, we believe that to be an Android programmer, you must:

*   <samp class="emphasis">write</samp> Android applications

*   <samp class="emphasis">understand</samp> what you are writing

This guide will help you do both. We have trained thousands of professional Android programmers using it. We will lead you through writing several Android applications, introducing concepts and techniques as needed. When there are rough spots, or when some things are tricky or obscure, you will face them head on, and we will do our best to explain why things are the way they are.

This approach allows you to put what you have learned into practice in a working app right away rather than learning a lot of theory and then having to figure out how to apply it all later. You will come away with the experience and understanding you need to get going as an Android developer.

## Prerequisites

To use this book, you need to be familiar with Kotlin, including classes and objects, interfaces, listeners, packages, inner classes, object expressions, and generic classes.

If these concepts do not ring a bell, you will be in the weeds by page 2\. Start instead with an introductory Kotlin book and return to this book afterward. There are many excellent introductory books available, so you can choose one based on your programming experience and learning style. May we recommend <samp class="emphasis">Kotlin Programming: The Big Nerd Ranch Guide</samp>?

If you are comfortable with object-oriented programming concepts, but your Kotlin is a little shaky, you will probably be OK. We will provide some brief explanations about Kotlin specifics throughout the book. But keep a Kotlin reference handy in case you need more support as you go through the book.

## What’s New in the Fourth Edition?

This edition involved a major overhaul – every chapter was altered. The biggest change in this version is that the apps are written using Kotlin instead of Java. Because of this, our unofficial working name for this edition has been “Android 4K.”

Another sweeping change is the inclusion of Android Jetpack component libraries. We now use Jetpack (sometimes called AndroidX) libraries in place of the Support Library. Additionally, we incorporated new Jetpack APIs when applicable. For example, we use <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> to persist UI state across rotation. We use Room and <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> to implement a database and to query data from it. And we use WorkManager to schedule background work. These are just a few examples; you will find Jetpack components woven into all the projects in this book.

To focus on how modern Android applications are developed, this book now uses third-party libraries instead of just the APIs within the framework or within Jetpack. One example is dropping <samp class="classname">HttpURLConnection</samp> and other lower-level networking APIs in favor of using Retrofit and the suite of libraries it depends on. This is a big departure from our previous books, and we believe that this will better prepare you to dive into professional application development after reading our book. The libraries we chose to use are libraries we use in our daily lives as Android developers for our clients.

### Kotlin vs Java

Official support for Kotlin for Android development was announced at Google I/O in 2017\. Before that, there was an underground movement of Android developers using Kotlin even though it was not officially supported. Since 2017, Kotlin has become widely adopted, and it is most developer’s preferred language for Android development. At Big Nerd Ranch, we use Kotlin for all our app development projects – even legacy projects that are mostly Java.

The tide has continued to turn toward Kotlin in a very big way. The Android framework team has started adding `@nullable` annotations to legacy platform code. They have also released more and more Kotlin extensions for Android. And, as of this writing, Google is in the process of adding Kotlin examples and support to the official Android documentation.

The Android framework was originally written in Java. This means most of the Android classes you interact with are Java. Luckily, Kotlin is interoperable with Java, so you should not run into any issues.

We have chosen to display API listings in Kotlin, even if they are implemented behind the scenes in Java. You can see the Java API listings by browsing for the class you are interested in at [<samp class="uri">developer.android.com/​reference</samp>](https://developer.android.com/reference/).

Whether you prefer Kotlin or Java, this book teaches you how to write Android apps. The knowledge and experience you gain in developing apps for the Android platform will translate to either language.

## How to Use This Book

This book is not a reference book. Its goal is to get you over the initial hump to where you can get the most out of the reference and recipe books available. It is based on our five-day class at Big Nerd Ranch. As such, it is meant to be worked through from the beginning. Chapters build on each other, and skipping around is unproductive.

In our classes, students work through these materials, but they also benefit from the right environment – a dedicated classroom, good food and comfortable board, a group of motivated peers, and an instructor to answer questions.

As a reader, you want your environment to be similar. That means getting a good night’s rest and finding a quiet place to work. These things can help, too:

*   Start a reading group with your friends or coworkers.

*   Arrange to have blocks of focused time to work on chapters.

*   Participate in the forum for this book at [<samp class="uri">forums.bignerdranch.com</samp>](https://forums.bignerdranch.com).

*   Find someone who knows Android to help you out.

## How This Book Is Organized

As you work through this book, you will write seven Android apps. A couple are very simple and take only a chapter to create. Others are more complex. The longest app spans 11 chapters. All are designed to teach you important concepts and techniques and give you direct experience using them.

| <samp class="emphasis">GeoQuiz</samp> |
| <samp class="emphasis">CriminalIntent</samp> |
| <samp class="emphasis">BeatBox</samp> |
| <samp class="emphasis">NerdLauncher</samp> |
| <samp class="emphasis">PhotoGallery</samp> |
| <samp class="emphasis">DragAndDraw</samp> |
| <samp class="emphasis">Sunset</samp> |

### Challenges

Most chapters have a section at the end with exercises for you to work through. This is your opportunity to use what you have learned, explore the documentation, and do some problem-solving on your own.

We strongly recommend that you do the challenges. Going off the beaten path and finding your way will solidify your learning and give you confidence with your own projects.

If you get lost, you can always visit [<samp class="uri">forums.bignerdranch.com</samp>](https://forums.bignerdranch.com) for some assistance.

### Are you more curious?

There are also sections at the ends of many chapters labeled “For the More Curious.” These sections offer deeper explanations or additional information about topics presented in the chapter. The information in these sections is not absolutely essential, but we hope you will find it interesting and useful.

## Typographical Conventions

All code and XML listings are in a fixed-width font. Code or XML that you need to type in is always bold. Code or XML that should be deleted is struck through. For example, in the following function implementation, you are deleting the call to <samp class="methodname">Toast.makeText(…).show()</samp> and adding the call to <samp class="methodname">checkAnswer(true)</samp>.

```
trueButton.setOnClickListener { view: View ->
    Toast.makeText(
        this,
        R.string.correct_toast,
        Toast.LENGTH_SHORT
    )
        .show()
    checkAnswer(true)
}
```

## Using an eBook

If you are reading this book on an eReader, we want to point out that reading the code may be tricky at times. Longer lines of code may wrap to a second line, depending on your selected font size.

The longest lines of code in this book are 86 monospace characters, like this one.

```
<string name="question_text">Melbourne was the previous capital of Australia.</string>
```

You can play with your eReader’s settings to find the best for viewing long code lines.

If you are reading on an iPad with iBooks, we recommend you go to the Settings app, select iBooks, and set <samp class="guilabel">Full Justification OFF</samp> and <samp class="guilabel">Auto-hyphenation OFF</samp>.

When you get to the point where you are actually typing in code, we suggest opening the book on your PC or Mac in Adobe Digital Editions. (Adobe Digital Editions is a free eReader application you can download from [<samp class="uri">adobe.com/​products/​digitaleditions</samp>](https://adobe.com/products/digitaleditions).) Make the application window large enough so that you can see the code with no wrapping lines. You will also be able to see the figures in full detail.

## Android Versions

This book teaches Android development for the versions of Android in wide use at the time of writing. For this edition, that is Android 5.0 (Lollipop, API level 21) - Android 9.0 (Pie, API level 28). While there is still limited use of older versions of Android, we find that for most developers the amount of effort required to support those versions is not worth the reward.

If you would like information on supporting versions of Android earlier than 5.0, see earlier editions of this book. The third edition targeted Android 4.4 and up, the second edition targeted Android 4.1 and up, and the first edition targeted Android 2.3 and up.

As Android releases new versions, the techniques you learn in this book will continue to work, thanks to Android’s backward compatibility support (discussed in [Chapter 7](../Text/ch07.xhtml "7 Android SDK Versions and Compatibility")). We will keep track of changes at [<samp class="uri">forums.bignerdranch.com</samp>](https://forums.bignerdranch.com) and offer notes on using this book with the latest version.

# The Necessary Tools

To get started with this book, you will need Android Studio. Android Studio is an integrated development environment used for Android development that is based on the popular IntelliJ IDEA.

An install of Android Studio includes:

<samp class="emphasis">Android SDK</samp>

the latest version of the Android SDK

<samp class="emphasis">Android SDK tools and platform tools</samp>

tools for debugging and testing your apps

<samp class="emphasis">A system image for the Android emulator</samp>

a tool for creating and testing your apps on different virtual devices

As of this writing, Android Studio is under active development and is frequently updated. Be aware that you may find differences between your version of Android Studio and what you see in this book. Visit [<samp class="uri">forums.bignerdranch.com</samp>](https://forums.bignerdranch.com) for help with these differences.

## Downloading and Installing Android Studio

Android Studio is available from Android’s developer site at [<samp class="uri">developer.android.com/​studio</samp>](https://developer.android.com/studio).

If you do not already have it installed, you will also need to install the Java Development Kit (JDK 8), which you can download from [<samp class="uri">www.oracle.com</samp>](https://www.oracle.com).

If you are having problems, return to [<samp class="uri">developer.android.com/​studio</samp>](https://developer.android.com/studio) for more information.

## Downloading Earlier SDK Versions

Android Studio provides the SDK and the emulator system image from the latest platform. However, you may want to test your apps on earlier versions of Android.

You can get components for each platform using the Android SDK Manager. In Android Studio, select <samp class="guimenu">Tools</samp> → <samp class="guimenuitem">SDK Manager</samp>. (You will only see the <samp class="guilabel">Tools</samp> menu if you have a project open. If you have not created a project yet, you can instead access the SDK Manager from the Android Welcome dialog. Select <samp class="guimenu">Configure</samp> → <samp class="guimenuitem">SDK Manager</samp>.)

The SDK Manager is shown in [Figure 1](#pr04s02.xhtml_sdk_manager "Figure 1  Android SDK Manager").

**Figure 1  Android SDK Manager**

![Android SDK Manager](Images/tools_sdk_manager.png)

Select and install each version of Android that you want to test with. Note that downloading these components may take a while.

The Android SDK Manager is also how you can get Android’s latest releases, like a new platform or an update of the tools.

## A Hardware Device

The emulator is useful for testing apps. However, it is no substitute for an actual Android device when measuring performance. If you have a hardware device, we recommend using it at times when working through this book.

# <samp class="chapter_number">1</samp>
<samp class="chapter_name">Your First Android Application</samp>

This first chapter is full of new concepts and moving parts required to build an Android application. It is OK if you do not understand everything by the end of this chapter. You will be revisiting these ideas in greater detail as you proceed through the book.

The application you are going to create is called GeoQuiz. GeoQuiz tests the user’s knowledge of geography. The user presses <samp class="guibutton">TRUE</samp> or <samp class="guibutton">FALSE</samp> to answer the question onscreen, and GeoQuiz provides instant feedback.

[Figure 1.1](#ch01.xhtml_fig_tf_first_chapter "Figure 1.1  Do you come from a land down under?") shows the result of a user pressing the <samp class="guibutton">TRUE</samp> button.

**Figure 1.1  Do you come from a land down under?**

![Do you come from a land down under?](Images/tf_first_chapter.png)

## App Basics

Your GeoQuiz application will consist of an <samp class="firstterm">activity</samp> and a <samp class="firstterm">layout</samp>:

*   An activity is an instance of <samp class="classname">Activity</samp>, a class in the Android SDK. An activity is responsible for managing user interaction with a screen of information.

    You write subclasses of <samp class="classname">Activity</samp> to implement the functionality that your app requires. A simple application may need only one subclass; a complex application can have many.

    GeoQuiz is a simple app and will start off with a single <samp class="classname">Activity</samp> subclass named <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>. <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> will manage the user interface, or UI, shown in [Figure 1.1](#ch01.xhtml_fig_tf_first_chapter "Figure 1.1  Do you come from a land down under?").

*   A layout defines a set of UI objects and the objects’ positions on the screen. A layout is made up of definitions written in XML. Each definition is used to create an object that appears onscreen, like a button or some text.

    GeoQuiz will include a layout file named <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp>. The XML in this file will define the UI shown in [Figure 1.1](#ch01.xhtml_fig_tf_first_chapter "Figure 1.1  Do you come from a land down under?").

The relationship between <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> and <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp> is diagrammed in [Figure 1.2](#ch01s01.xhtml_fig_tf_first_design "Figure 1.2  MainActivity manages what activity_main.xml defines").

**Figure 1.2  `MainActivity` manages what `activity_main.xml` defines**

![MainActivity manages what activity_main.xml defines](Images/tf_design.png)

With those ideas in mind, let’s build an app.

## Creating an Android Project

The first step is to create an Android <samp class="firstterm">project</samp>. An Android project contains the files that make up an application. To create a new project, first open Android Studio.

If this is your first time running Android Studio, you will see the Welcome dialog, as in [Figure 1.3](#ch01s02.xhtml_fig_tf_welcome_dialog "Figure 1.3  Welcome to Android Studio").

**Figure 1.3  Welcome to Android Studio**

![Welcome to Android Studio](Images/Android-Studio-Welcome-Dialog.png)

Before you begin your project, take a moment to turn off a feature that could interfere with your work. Instant Run is designed to streamline development by allowing you to push code changes without building a new APK. Unfortunately, it does not always work as intended, so we recommend that you disable it while working through this book.

At the bottom of the Welcome dialog, click <samp class="guilabel">Configure</samp>, then choose <samp class="guilabel">Settings</samp>. On the lefthand side of the Preferences for New Projects screen ([Figure 1.4](#ch01s02.xhtml_fig_tf_preferences "Figure 1.4  Preferences for New Projects")), expand <samp class="guilabel">Build, Execution, Deployment</samp> and choose <samp class="guilabel">Instant Run</samp>. Uncheck the box next to <samp class="guilabel">Enable Instant Run to hot swap code/resource changes on deploy (default enabled)</samp> and click <samp class="guibutton">OK</samp>.

(If you have used Android Studio before and do not see the Welcome dialog when you start up, go to <samp class="guimenu">Android Studio</samp> → <samp class="guimenuitem">Preferences</samp>, then expand <samp class="guilabel">Build, Execution, Deployment</samp> and continue as above.)

**Figure 1.4  Preferences for New Projects**

![Preferences for New Projects](Images/Android-Studio-Preferences-Dialog.png)

Back at the Welcome dialog, choose <samp class="guilabel">Start a new Android Studio project</samp>. If you do not see the dialog, choose <samp class="guimenu">File</samp> → <samp class="guisubmenu">New</samp> → <samp class="guimenuitem">New Project...</samp>.

Welcome to the Create New Project wizard ([Figure 1.5](#ch01s02.xhtml_fig_tf_new_project_0 "Figure 1.5  Choosing a project template")). Make sure the <samp class="guilabel">Phone and Tablet</samp> tab is selected, pick <samp class="guilabel">Empty Activity</samp>, and click <samp class="guibutton">Next</samp>.

**Figure 1.5  Choosing a project template**

![Choosing a project template](Images/Android-Studio-Choose-Your-Project-Dialog.png)

You should now see the <samp class="guilabel">Configure your project</samp> screen ([Figure 1.6](#ch01s02.xhtml_fig_tf_new_project_1 "Figure 1.6  Configuring your new project")). Enter <samp class="guilabel">GeoQuiz</samp> as the application name. For package name, enter <samp class="guilabel">com.bignerdranch.android.geoquiz</samp>. For the project location, use any location on your filesystem that you want.

Select <samp class="guilabel">Kotlin</samp> from the <samp class="guibutton">Language</samp> drop-down menu. Select a <samp class="guilabel">Minimum API level</samp> of <samp class="guilabel">API 21: Android 5.0 (Lollipop)</samp>. You will learn about the different versions of Android in [Chapter 7](../Text/ch07.xhtml "7 Android SDK Versions and Compatibility"). Last, make sure the checkbox next to <samp class="guilabel">Use AndroidX artifacts</samp> is checked. Your screen should look like [Figure 1.6](#ch01s02.xhtml_fig_tf_new_project_1 "Figure 1.6  Configuring your new project").

**Figure 1.6  Configuring your new project**

![Configuring your new project](Images/Android-Studio-New-Project-Dialog.png)

Notice that the package name uses a “reverse DNS” convention: The domain name of your organization is reversed and suffixed with further identifiers. This convention keeps package names unique and distinguishes applications from each other on a device and on the Google Play Store.

As of this writing, new projects generated by Android Studio are in Java by default. Selecting <samp class="guilabel">Kotlin</samp> as the language tells Android Studio to include the dependencies, such as Kotlin build tools, necessary to write and build Kotlin code for your app.

Java was the only development language officially supported until May 2017, when the Android team announced official support for Kotlin for Android development at Google I/O. These days, Kotlin is preferred by most developers, ourselves included, which is why this book uses Kotlin. But if you choose to use Java in your projects outside of this book, the Android concepts and content you will learn here will still be applicable.

Google used to provide a monolithic “support” library of helpers and compatibility shims. AndroidX explodes this single library into many independently developed and versioned libraries, collectively called “Jetpack.” Selecting <samp class="guilabel">Use AndroidX artifacts</samp> makes your project ready to use these newly independent tools. You will learn more about Jetpack and AndroidX in [Chapter 4](../Text/ch04.xhtml "4 Persisting UI State"), and you will use various Jetpack libraries throughout this book.

(Android Studio updates regularly, so your wizard may look slightly different from what we are showing you. This is usually not a problem; the choices should be similar. If your wizard looks very different, then the tools have changed more drastically. Do not panic. Head to this book’s forum at [<samp class="uri">forums.bignerdranch.com</samp>](https://forums.bignerdranch.com) and we will help you navigate the latest version.)

Click <samp class="guibutton">Finish</samp>. Android Studio will create and open your new project.

## Navigating in Android Studio

Android Studio opens your project in a window like the one shown in [Figure 1.7](#ch01s03.xhtml_fig_tf_default_project_window "Figure 1.7  A fresh project window"). If you have launched Android Studio before, your window configuration might look a little different.

**Figure 1.7  A fresh project window**

![A fresh project window](Images/Android-Studio-GeoQuiz-initial-project-annotated.png)

The different panes of the project window are called <samp class="firstterm">tool windows</samp>.

The lefthand view is the <samp class="firstterm">project tool window</samp>. From here, you can view and manage the files associated with your project.

The view across the bottom is the <samp class="firstterm">build tool window</samp>. Here you can view details about the compilation process and the status of the build. When you created the project, Android Studio automatically built it. You should see in the build tool window that the process completed successfully.

In the project tool window, click the disclosure arrow next to <samp class="guilabel">app</samp>. Android Studio automatically opens the files <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp> and <samp class="filename">MainActivity.kt</samp> in the main view, called the <samp class="firstterm">editor tool window</samp> or just the <samp class="firstterm">editor</samp> ([Figure 1.8](#ch01s03.xhtml_fig_tf_default_project_window_files_open "Figure 1.8  Editor engaged")). If this is not your first time opening Android Studio, the editor tool window may have opened automatically when you created the project.

**Figure 1.8  Editor engaged**

![Editor engaged](Images/Android-Studio-GeoQuiz-After-Expanding-App-annotated.png)

Notice the `Activity` suffix on the class name. This is not required, but it is an excellent convention to follow.

You can toggle the visibility of the various tool windows by clicking on their names in the strips of tool buttons on the left, right, and bottom of the screen. There are keyboard shortcuts for many of these as well. If you do not see the tool button strips, click the gray square button in the lower-left corner of the main window or choose <samp class="guimenu">View</samp> → <samp class="guimenuitem">Tool Buttons</samp>.

## Laying Out the UI

Click the tab for the layout file, <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp>. This will open the layout editor in the editor tool window ([Figure 1.9](#ch01s04.xhtml_fig_tf_layout_editor "Figure 1.9  Layout editor")). If you do not see a tab for <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp>, do not worry. Expand <samp class="filename">app/res/layout/</samp> in the project tool window. Double-click <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp> to open the file. If <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp> opens but shows XML instead of the layout editor, click the <samp class="guilabel">Design</samp> tab at the bottom of the editor tool window.

**Figure 1.9  Layout editor**

![Layout editor](Images/Android-Studio-Layout-Editor.png)

By convention, a layout file is named based on the activity it is associated with: Its name begins with `activity_`, and the rest of the activity name follows in all lowercase, using underscores to separate words (a style called “snake_case”). So, for example, your layout file’s name is <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp>, and the layout file for an activity called <samp class="classname">SplashScreenActivity</samp> would be named <samp class="filename">activity_splash_screen</samp>. This naming style is recommended for layouts as well as other resources that you will learn about later.

The layout editor shows a graphical preview of the file. Select the <samp class="guilabel">Text</samp> tab at the bottom to see the backing XML.

Currently, <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp> holds the default activity layout template. The template changes frequently, but the XML will look something like [Listing 1.1](#ch01s04.xhtml_pl_os_default_layout "Listing 1.1  Default activity layout (res/layout/activity_main.xml)").

**Listing 1.1  Default activity layout (`res/layout/activity_main.xml`)**

```
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<androidx.constraintlayout.widget.ConstraintLayout
        xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
        xmlns:tools="http://schemas.android.com/tools"
        xmlns:app="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res-auto"
        android:layout_width="match_parent"
        android:layout_height="match_parent"
        tools:context=".MainActivity">

    <TextView
            android:layout_width="wrap_content"
            android:layout_height="wrap_content"
            android:text="Hello World!"
            app:layout_constraintBottom_toBottomOf="parent"
            app:layout_constraintLeft_toLeftOf="parent"
            app:layout_constraintRight_toRightOf="parent"
            app:layout_constraintTop_toTopOf="parent"/>

</androidx.constraintlayout.widget.ConstraintLayout>
```

The default activity layout defines two <samp class="classname">View</samp><samp class="firstterm">s</samp>: a <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp> and a <samp class="classname">TextView</samp>.

Views are the building blocks you use to compose a UI. Everything you see on the screen is a view. Views that the user can see or interact with are called <samp class="firstterm">widgets</samp>. Some widgets show text. Some widgets show graphics. Others, like buttons, do things when touched.

The Android SDK includes many widgets that you can configure to get the appearance and behavior you want. Every widget is an instance of the <samp class="classname">View</samp> class or one of its subclasses (such as <samp class="classname">TextView</samp> or <samp class="classname">Button</samp>).

Something has to tell the widgets where they belong onscreen. A <samp class="classname">ViewGroup</samp> is a kind of <samp class="classname">View</samp> that contains and arranges other views. A <samp class="classname">ViewGroup</samp> does not display content itself. Rather, it orchestrates where other views’ content is displayed. <samp class="classname">ViewGroup</samp>s are often referred to as layouts.

In the default activity layout, <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp> is the <samp class="classname">ViewGroup</samp> responsible for laying out its sole child, a <samp class="classname">TextView</samp> widget. You will learn more about layouts and widgets and about using <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp> in [Chapter 10](../Text/ch10.xhtml "10 Creating User Interfaces with Layouts and Widgets").

[Figure 1.10](#ch01s04.xhtml_fig_tf_default_layout_demarcated "Figure 1.10  Default views as seen onscreen") shows how the <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp> and <samp class="classname">TextView</samp> defined in [Listing 1.1](#ch01s04.xhtml_pl_os_default_layout "Listing 1.1  Default activity layout (res/layout/activity_main.xml)") would appear onscreen.

**Figure 1.10  Default views as seen onscreen**

![Default views as seen onscreen](Images/tf_default_layout_demarcated.png)

But these are not the widgets you are looking for. The interface for <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> requires five widgets:

*   a vertical <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp>

*   a <samp class="classname">TextView</samp>

*   a horizontal <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp>

*   two <samp class="classname">Button</samp>s

[Figure 1.11](#ch01s04.xhtml_fig_tf_first_chapter_with_widget_lines "Figure 1.11  Planned widgets as seen onscreen") shows how these widgets compose <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>’s interface.

**Figure 1.11  Planned widgets as seen onscreen**

![Planned widgets as seen onscreen](Images/tf_first_chapter_with_widget_lines.png)

Now you need to define these widgets in your layout XML. Edit the text contents of <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp> to match [Listing 1.2](#ch01s04.xhtml_pl_tf_first_chapter_layout_xml "Listing 1.2  Defining widgets in XML (res/layout/activity_main.xml)"). The XML that you need to delete is struck through, and the XML that you need to add is in bold font. This is the pattern we will use throughout this book.

Do not worry about understanding what you are typing; you will learn how it works next. However, do be careful. Layout XML is not validated, and typos will cause problems sooner or later.

You will see errors on the three lines that start with `android:text`. Ignore these errors for now; you will fix them soon.

**Listing 1.2  Defining widgets in XML (`res/layout/activity_main.xml`)**

```
<androidx.constraintlayout.widget.ConstraintLayout
        xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
        xmlns:tools="http://schemas.android.com/tools"
        xmlns:app="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res-auto"
        android:layout_width="match_parent"
        android:layout_height="match_parent"
        tools:context=".MainActivity">

    <TextView
            android:layout_width="wrap_content"
            android:layout_height="wrap_content"
            android:text="Hello World!"
            app:layout_constraintBottom_toBottomOf="parent"
            app:layout_constraintLeft_toLeftOf="parent"
            app:layout_constraintRight_toRightOf="parent"
            app:layout_constraintTop_toTopOf="parent"/>

</androidx.constraintlayout.widget.ConstraintLayout>

<LinearLayout xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="match_parent"
    android:gravity="center"
    android:orientation="vertical">

    <TextView
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:padding="24dp"
        android:text="@string/question_text" />

    <LinearLayout
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:orientation="horizontal">

        <Button
            android:layout_width="wrap_content"
            android:layout_height="wrap_content"
            android:text="@string/true_button" />

        <Button
            android:layout_width="wrap_content"
            android:layout_height="wrap_content"
            android:text="@string/false_button" />

    </LinearLayout>

</LinearLayout>
```

Compare your XML with the UI shown in [Figure 1.11](#ch01s04.xhtml_fig_tf_first_chapter_with_widget_lines "Figure 1.11  Planned widgets as seen onscreen"). Every widget has a corresponding XML element, and the name of the element is the type of the widget.

Each element has a set of XML <samp class="firstterm">attributes</samp>. Each attribute is an instruction about how the widget should be configured.

To understand how the elements and attributes work, it helps to look at the layout from a hierarchical perspective.

### The view hierarchy

Your widgets exist in a hierarchy of <samp class="classname">View</samp> objects called the <samp class="firstterm">view hierarchy</samp>. [Figure 1.12](#ch01s04.xhtml_fig_tf_initial_layout "Figure 1.12  Hierarchical layout of widgets and attributes") shows the view hierarchy that corresponds to the XML in [Listing 1.2](#ch01s04.xhtml_pl_tf_first_chapter_layout_xml "Listing 1.2  Defining widgets in XML (res/layout/activity_main.xml)").

**Figure 1.12  Hierarchical layout of widgets and attributes**

![Hierarchical layout of widgets and attributes](Images/activity_main_layout_no_id_no_tools.png)

The root element of this layout’s view hierarchy is a <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp>. As the root element, the <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp> must specify the Android resource XML namespace at <samp class="literal">http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android</samp>.

<samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp> inherits from <samp class="classname">ViewGroup</samp>, which, as we said earlier, is a subclass of <samp class="classname">View</samp> that contains and arranges other views. You use a <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp> when you want views arranged in a single column or row. Other <samp class="classname">ViewGroup</samp> subclasses that you will meet later include <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp> and <samp class="classname">FrameLayout</samp>.

When a view is contained by a <samp class="classname">ViewGroup</samp>, that view is said to be a <samp class="firstterm">child</samp> of the <samp class="classname">ViewGroup</samp>. The root <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp> has two children: a <samp class="classname">TextView</samp> and another <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp>. The child <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp> has two <samp class="classname">Button</samp> children of its own.

### Widget attributes

Let’s go over some of the attributes that you have used to configure your widgets.

#### android:layout_width and android:layout_height

The `android:layout_width` and `android:layout_height` attributes are required for almost every type of widget. They are typically set to either <samp class="constant">match_parent</samp> or <samp class="constant">wrap_content</samp>:

| <samp class="constant">match_parent</samp> |
| <samp class="literal">wrap_content</samp> |

For the root <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp>, the value of both the height and width attributes is <samp class="constant">match_parent</samp>. The <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp> is the root element, but it still has a parent – the view that Android provides for your app’s view hierarchy to live in.

The other widgets in your layout have their widths and heights set to `wrap_content`. You can see in [Figure 1.11](#ch01s04.xhtml_fig_tf_first_chapter_with_widget_lines "Figure 1.11  Planned widgets as seen onscreen") how this determines their sizes.

The <samp class="classname">TextView</samp> is slightly larger than the text it contains due to its `android:padding="24dp"` attribute. This attribute tells the widget to add the specified amount of space to its contents when determining its size. You are using it to get a little breathing room between the question and the buttons. (Wondering about the `dp` units? These are density-independent pixels, which you will learn about in [Chapter 10](../Text/ch10.xhtml "10 Creating User Interfaces with Layouts and Widgets").)

#### android:orientation

The `android:orientation` attribute on the two <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp> widgets determines whether their children will appear vertically or horizontally. The root <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp> is vertical; its child <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp> is horizontal.

The order in which children are defined determines the order in which they appear onscreen. In a vertical <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp>, the first child defined will appear topmost. In a horizontal <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp>, the first child defined will be leftmost. (Unless the device is set to a language that runs right to left, such as Arabic or Hebrew. In that case, the first child will be rightmost.)

#### android:text

The <samp class="classname">TextView</samp> and <samp class="classname">Button</samp> widgets have `android:text` attributes. This attribute tells the widget what text to display.

Notice that the values of these attributes are not literal strings. They are references to <samp class="firstterm">string resources</samp>, as denoted by the `@string/` syntax.

A string resource is a string that lives in a separate XML file called a <samp class="firstterm">strings file</samp>. You can give a widget a hardcoded string, like `android:text="True"`, but it is usually not a good idea. Placing strings into a separate file and then referencing them is better because it makes localization (which you will learn about in [Chapter 17](../Text/ch17.xhtml "17 Localization")) easy.

The string resources you are referencing in <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp> do not exist yet. Let’s fix that.

### Creating string resources

Every project includes a default strings file named <samp class="filename">res/values/strings.xml</samp>.

Open <samp class="filename">res/values/strings.xml</samp>. The template has already added one string resource for you. Add the three new strings that your layout requires.

**Listing 1.3  Adding string resources (`res/values/strings.xml`)**

```
<resources>
    <string name="app_name">GeoQuiz</string>
    <string name="question_text">Canberra is the capital of Australia.</string>
    <string name="true_button">True</string>
    <string name="false_button">False</string>
</resources>
```

(Depending on your version of Android Studio, you may have additional strings. Do not delete them. Deleting them could cause cascading errors in other files.)

Now, whenever you refer to <samp class="literal">@string/false_button</samp> in any XML file in the GeoQuiz project, you will get the literal string “False” at runtime.

The errors in <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp> about the missing string resources should now be gone. (If you still have errors, check both files for typos.)

Although the default strings file is named <samp class="filename">strings.xml</samp>, you can name a strings file anything you want. You can also have multiple strings files in a project. As long as the file is located in <samp class="filename">res/values/</samp>, has a `resources` root element, and contains child `string` elements, your strings will be found and used.

### Previewing the layout

Your layout is now complete. Switch back to <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp> and preview the layout in the <samp class="guilabel">Design</samp> pane by clicking the tab at the bottom of the editor tool window ([Figure 1.13](#ch01s04.xhtml_fig_tf_preview_pane "Figure 1.13  Previewing activity_main.xml in the Design pane")).

**Figure 1.13  Previewing `activity_main.xml` in the Design pane**

![Previewing activity_main.xml in the Design pane](Images/Android-Studio-GeoQuiz-Layout-Preview-Pane.png)

[Figure 1.13](#ch01s04.xhtml_fig_tf_preview_pane "Figure 1.13  Previewing activity_main.xml in the Design pane") shows the two kinds of preview available. You can select from the preview types using a menu that drops down from the blue diamond button leftmost in the top toolbar. You can show either kind of preview individually or both together, as shown here.

The preview on the left is the <samp class="firstterm">Design</samp> preview. This shows how the layout would look on a device, including theming.

The preview on the right is the <samp class="firstterm">Blueprint</samp> preview. This preview focuses on the size of widgets and the relationships between them.

The <samp class="guilabel">Design</samp> pane also allows you to see how your layout looks on different device configurations. At the top of the pane, you can specify the type of device, the version of Android to simulate, the device theme, and the locale to use when rendering your layout. You can even pretend your current locale uses right-to-left text.

In addition to previewing, you can also build your layouts using the layout editor. On the left there is a palette that contains all of the built-in widgets ([Figure 1.14](#ch01s04.xhtml_fig_tf_first_preview "Figure 1.14  Graphical layout editor")). You can drag these widgets from the palette and drop them into your view. You can also drop them into the component tree in the bottom left to have more control over where the widget is placed.

[Figure 1.14](#ch01s04.xhtml_fig_tf_first_preview "Figure 1.14  Graphical layout editor") shows the preview with <samp class="firstterm">layout decorations</samp> – the device status bar, app bar with GeoQuiz label, and virtual device button bar. To see these decorations, click the eyeball button in the toolbar just above the preview and select <samp class="guilabel">Show Layout Decorations</samp>.

**Figure 1.14  Graphical layout editor**

![Graphical layout editor](Images/Android-Studio-GeoQuiz-Layout-Design-Preview.png)

You will find this graphical editor especially valuable when working with <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp>, as you will see for yourself in [Chapter 10](../Text/ch10.xhtml "10 Creating User Interfaces with Layouts and Widgets").

## From Layout XML to View Objects

How do XML elements in <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp> become <samp class="classname">View</samp> objects? The answer starts in the <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> class.

When you created the GeoQuiz project, a subclass of <samp class="classname">Activity</samp> named <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> was created for you. The class file for <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> is in the <samp class="filename">app/java</samp> directory of your project.

A quick aside about the directory name before we get into how layouts become views: This directory is called <samp class="filename">java</samp> because Android originally supported only Java code. In your project, because you configured it to use Kotlin (and Kotlin is fully interoperable with Java), the <samp class="filename">java</samp> directory is where the Kotlin code lives. You could create a <samp class="filename">kotlin</samp> directory and place your Kotlin files there, but you would have to tell Android that the new folder includes source files so they would be included in your project. In most cases, separating your source files based on their language provides no benefit, so most projects just place their Kotlin files in the <samp class="filename">java</samp> directory.

<samp class="filename">MainActivity.kt</samp> may already be open in a tab in the editor tool window. If it is not, locate the <samp class="filename">app/java</samp> directory in the project tool window and click on it to reveal its contents, then click to reveal the contents of the com.bignerdranch.android.geoquiz package. (Not one of the packages with the name shaded green – those are the test packages. The production package is unshaded.) Open the <samp class="filename">MainActivity.kt</samp> file and take a look at its contents.

**Listing 1.4  Default class file for `MainActivity` (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
package com.bignerdranch.android.geoquiz

import androidx.appcompat.app.AppCompatActivity
import android.os.Bundle

class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContentView(R.layout.activity_main)
    }
}
```

(Wondering what <samp class="classname">AppCompatActivity</samp> is? It is a subclass of Android’s <samp class="classname">Activity</samp> class that provides compatibility support for older versions of Android. You will learn much more about <samp class="classname">AppCompatActivity</samp> in [Chapter 14](../Text/ch14.xhtml "14 The App Bar").)

If you are not seeing all of the import statements, click the <samp class="guilabel">+</samp> symbol to the left of the first import statement to reveal the others.

This file has one <samp class="classname">Activity</samp> function: <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp>.

The <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp> function is called when an instance of the activity subclass is created. When an activity is created, it needs a UI to manage. To give the activity its UI, you call <samp class="methodname">Activity.setContentView(layoutResID: Int)</samp>.

This function <samp class="firstterm">inflates</samp> a layout and puts it onscreen. When a layout is inflated, each widget in the layout file is instantiated as defined by its attributes. You specify which layout to inflate by passing in the layout’s <samp class="firstterm">resource ID</samp>.

### Resources and resource IDs

A layout is a <samp class="firstterm">resource</samp>. A resource is a piece of your application that is not code – things like image files, audio files, and XML files.

Resources for your project live in a subdirectory of the <samp class="filename">app/res</samp> directory. In the project tool window, you can see that <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp> lives in <samp class="filename">res/layout/</samp>. Your strings file, which contains string resources, lives in <samp class="filename">res/values/</samp>.

To access a resource in code, you use its resource ID. The resource ID for your layout is `R.layout.activity_main`.

To see the current resource IDs for GeoQuiz, you must bravely explore into the world of auto-generated code – code that the Android build tool writes on your behalf. First, run the build tool by clicking the green hammer icon in the toolbar at the top of the Android Studio window.

By default, Android Studio displays the <samp class="guilabel">Android</samp> project view in the project tool window. This view hides the true directory structure of your Android project so that you can focus on the files and folders that you need most often. To see the files and folders in your project as they actually are, locate the dropdown at the top of the project tool window and change from the <samp class="guilabel">Android</samp> view to the <samp class="guilabel">Project</samp> view ([Figure 1.15](#ch01s05.xhtml_ss_tf_toggle_android_studio_project_view "Figure 1.15  Project tool window: Android view vs Project view")).

**Figure 1.15  Project tool window: Android view vs Project view**

![Project tool window: Android view vs Project view](Images/tf_toggle_android_studio_project_view.png)

In the <samp class="guilabel">Project</samp> view, expand the <samp class="filename">GeoQuiz</samp> directory and keep going until you can see the contents of <samp class="filename">GeoQuiz/app/build/generated/not_namespaced_r_class_sources/debug/processDebugResources/r/</samp>. In this directory, find your project’s package name and drill down until you find <samp class="filename">R.java</samp> within that package ([Figure 1.16](#ch01s05.xhtml_fig_tf_explore_generatedJava "Figure 1.16  Viewing R.java")).

**Figure 1.16  Viewing `R.java`**

![Viewing R.java](Images/Android-Studio-explore-generatedJava.png)

Double-click on the file to open it. Because <samp class="filename">R.java</samp> is generated by the Android build process, you should not change it, as you are subtly warned at the top of the file ([Listing 1.5](#ch01s05.xhtml_pl_r_java "Listing 1.5  Current GeoQuiz resource IDs (R.java)")).

**Listing 1.5  Current GeoQuiz resource IDs (`R.java`)**

```
/* AUTO-GENERATED FILE.  DO NOT MODIFY.
 *
 * This class was automatically generated by the
 * aapt tool from the resource data it found.  It
 * should not be modified by hand.
 */

package com.bignerdranch.android.geoquiz;

public final class R {
    public static final class anim {
        ...
    }
    ...
    public static final class id {
        ...
    }
    public static final class layout {
        ...
        public static final Int activity_main=0x7f030017;
    }
    public static final class mipmap {
        public static final Int ic_launcher=0x7f030000;
    }
    public static final class string {
        ...
        public static final Int app_name=0x7f0a0010;
        public static final Int false_button=0x7f0a0012;
        public static final Int question_text=0x7f0a0014;
        public static final Int true_button=0x7f0a0015;
    }
}
```

By the way, you may not see this file instantly update after making a change to your resources. Android Studio maintains a hidden <samp class="filename">R.java</samp> file that your code builds against. The <samp class="filename">R.java</samp> file in [Listing 1.5](#ch01s05.xhtml_pl_r_java "Listing 1.5  Current GeoQuiz resource IDs (R.java)") is the one that is generated for your app just before it is installed on a device or emulator. You will see this file update when you run your app.

The <samp class="filename">R.java</samp> file can be large, and much of this file is omitted from [Listing 1.5](#ch01s05.xhtml_pl_r_java "Listing 1.5  Current GeoQuiz resource IDs (R.java)").

This is where the `R.layout.activity_main` comes from – it is an integer constant named <samp class="varname">activity_main</samp> within the <samp class="classname">layout</samp> inner class of <samp class="classname">R</samp>.

Your strings also have resource IDs. You have not yet referred to a string in code, but if you did, it would look like this:

```
 setTitle(R.string.app_name)
```

Android generated a resource ID for the entire layout and for each string, but it did not generate resource IDs for the individual widgets in <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp>. Not every widget needs a resource ID. In this chapter, you will only interact with the two buttons in code, so only they need resource IDs.

To generate a resource ID for a widget, you include an `android:id` attribute in the widget’s definition. In <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp>, add an `android:id` attribute to each button. (You will need to switch to the <samp class="guilabel">Text</samp> tab to do this.)

**Listing 1.6  Adding IDs to `Button`s (`res/layout/activity_main.xml`)**

```
<LinearLayout ... >

    <TextView
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:padding="24dp"
        android:text="@string/question_text" />

    <LinearLayout
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:orientation="horizontal">

        <Button
            android:id="@+id/true_button"
            android:layout_width="wrap_content"
            android:layout_height="wrap_content"
            android:text="@string/true_button" />

        <Button
            android:id="@+id/false_button"
            android:layout_width="wrap_content"
            android:layout_height="wrap_content"
            android:text="@string/false_button" />

    </LinearLayout>

</LinearLayout> 
```

Notice that there is a `+` sign in the values for `android:id` but not in the values for `android:text`. This is because you are <samp class="emphasis">creating</samp> the resource IDs and only <samp class="emphasis">referencing</samp> the strings.

Before moving on, change the project tool window from the <samp class="guilabel">Project</samp> view to the <samp class="guilabel">Android</samp> view. Throughout this book, the <samp class="guilabel">Android</samp> view will be used – but feel free to use the <samp class="guilabel">Project</samp> version if you prefer. Also, close <samp class="filename">R.java</samp> by clicking the <samp class="guilabel">x</samp> in its editor tab.

## Wiring Up Widgets

You are ready to wire up your button widgets. This is a two-step process:

*   get references to the inflated <samp class="classname">View</samp> objects

*   set listeners on those objects to respond to user actions

### Getting references to widgets

Now that the buttons have resource IDs, you can access them in <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>. Type the following code into <samp class="filename">MainActivity.kt</samp> ([Listing 1.7](#ch01s06.xhtml_pl_tf_add_button_variables "Listing 1.7  Accessing view objects by ID (MainActivity.kt)")). (Do not use code completion; type it in yourself.) After you save the file, it will report two errors. You will fix the errors in just a second.

**Listing 1.7  Accessing view objects by ID (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {

    private lateinit var trueButton: Button
    private lateinit var falseButton: Button

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContentView(R.layout.activity_main)

        trueButton = findViewById(R.id.true_button)
        falseButton = findViewById(R.id.false_button)
    }
}
```

In an activity, you can get a reference to an inflated widget by calling <samp class="methodname">Activity.findViewById(Int)</samp>. This function returns the corresponding view. Rather than return it as a <samp class="classname">View</samp>, it is cast to the expected subtype of <samp class="classname">View</samp>. Here, that type is <samp class="classname">Button</samp>.

In the code above, you use the resource IDs of your buttons to retrieve the inflated objects and assign them to your view properties. Since the view objects are not inflated into and available in memory until after <samp class="methodname">setContentView(…)</samp> is called in <samp class="methodname">onCreate(…)</samp>, you use `lateinit` on your property declarations to indicate to the compiler that you will provide a non-null <samp class="classname">View</samp> value before you attempt to use the contents of the property. Then, in <samp class="methodname">onCreate(…)</samp>, you look up and assign the view objects the appropriate properties. You will learn more about <samp class="methodname">onCreate(…)</samp> and the activity lifecycle in [Chapter 3](../Text/ch03.xhtml "3 The Activity Lifecycle").

Now let’s get rid of those pesky errors. Mouse over the red error indicators. They both report the same problem: <samp class="guilabel">Unresolved reference: Button</samp>.

These errors are telling you that you need to import the <samp class="classname">android.widget.Button</samp> class into <samp class="filename">MainActivity.kt</samp>. You could type the following import statement at the top of the file:

```
 import android.widget.Button
```

Or you can do it the easy way and let Android Studio do it for you. Just press Option-Return (or Alt-Enter) to let the IntelliJ magic under the hood amaze you. The new import statement now appears with the others at the top of the file. This shortcut is generally useful when something is not correct with your code. Try it often!

This should get rid of the errors. (If you still have errors, check for typos in your code and XML.) Once your code is error free, it is time to make your app interactive.

### Setting listeners

Android applications are typically <samp class="firstterm">event driven</samp>. Unlike command-line programs or scripts, event-driven applications start and then wait for an event, such as the user pressing a button. (Events can also be initiated by the OS or another application, but user-initiated events are the most obvious.)

When your application is waiting for a specific event, we say that it is “listening for” that event. The object that you create to respond to an event is called a <samp class="firstterm">listener</samp>, and the listener implements a <samp class="firstterm">listener interface</samp> for that event.

The Android SDK comes with listener interfaces for various events, so you do not have to write your own. In this case, the event you want to listen for is a button being pressed (or “clicked”), so your listener will implement the <samp class="interfacename">View.OnClickListener</samp> interface.

Start with the <samp class="guibutton">TRUE</samp> button. In <samp class="filename">MainActivity.kt</samp>, add the following code to <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp> just after the variable assignments.

**Listing 1.8  Setting a listener for the TRUE button (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    setContentView(R.layout.activity_main)

    trueButton = findViewById(R.id.true_button)
    falseButton = findViewById(R.id.false_button)

    trueButton.setOnClickListener { view: View ->
        // Do something in response to the click here
    }
}
```

(If you have an <samp class="guilabel">Unresolved reference: View</samp> error, try using Option-Return [Alt-Enter] to import the <samp class="classname">View</samp> class.)

In [Listing 1.8](#ch01s06.xhtml_pl_tf_set_true_listener "Listing 1.8  Setting a listener for the TRUE button (MainActivity.kt)"), you set a listener to inform you when the <samp class="classname">Button</samp> known as <samp class="varname">trueButton</samp> has been pressed. The Android framework defines <samp class="classname">View.OnClickListener</samp> as a Java interface with a single method, <samp class="methodname">onClick(View)</samp>. Interfaces with a <samp class="emphasis">single abstract method</samp> are common enough in Java that the pattern has a pet name, <samp class="firstterm">SAM</samp>.

Kotlin has special support for this pattern as part of its Java interoperability layer. It lets you write a function literal, and it takes care of turning that into an object implementing the interface. This behind-the-scenes process is called <samp class="firstterm">SAM conversion</samp>.

Your on-click listener is implemented using a lambda expression. Set a similar listener for the <samp class="guibutton">FALSE</samp> button.

**Listing 1.9  Setting a listener for the FALSE button (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    ...
    trueButton.setOnClickListener { view: View ->
        // Do something in response to the click here
    }

    falseButton.setOnClickListener { view: View ->
        // Do something in response to the click here
    }
}
```

## Making Toasts

Now to make the buttons fully armed and operational. You are going to have a press of each button trigger a pop-up message called a <samp class="firstterm">toast</samp>. A toast is a short message that informs the user of something but does not require any input or action. You are going to make toasts that announce whether the user answered correctly or incorrectly ([Figure 1.17](#ch01s07.xhtml_fig_tf_run_with_toast "Figure 1.17  A toast providing feedback")).

**Figure 1.17  A toast providing feedback**

![A toast providing feedback](Images/tf_first_chapter.png)

First, return to <samp class="filename">strings.xml</samp> and add the string resources that your toasts will display.

**Listing 1.10  Adding toast strings (`res/values/strings.xml`)**

```
<resources>
    <string name="app_name">GeoQuiz</string>
    <string name="question_text">Canberra is the capital of Australia.</string>
    <string name="true_button">True</string>
    <string name="false_button">False</string>
    <string name="correct_toast">Correct!</string>
    <string name="incorrect_toast">Incorrect!</string>
</resources>
```

Next, update your click listeners to create and show a toast. Use code completion to help you fill in the listener code. Code completion can save you a lot of time, so it is good to become familiar with it early.

Start typing the code shown in [Listing 1.11](#ch01s07.xhtml_pl_os_activity_toast "Listing 1.11  Making toasts (MainActivity.kt)") in <samp class="filename">MainActivity.kt</samp>. When you get to the period after the <samp class="classname">Toast</samp> class, a pop-up window will appear with a list of suggested functions and constants from the <samp class="classname">Toast</samp> class.

To choose one of the suggestions, use the up and down arrow keys to select it. (If you wanted to ignore code completion, you could just keep typing. It will not complete anything for you if you do not press the Tab key, press the Return key, or click on the pop-up window.)

From the list of suggestions, select <samp class="methodname">makeText(context: Context, resId: Int, duration: Int)</samp>. Code completion will add the complete function call for you.

Fill in the parameters for the <samp class="methodname">makeText(…)</samp> function until you have added the code shown in [Listing 1.11](#ch01s07.xhtml_pl_os_activity_toast "Listing 1.11  Making toasts (MainActivity.kt)").

**Listing 1.11  Making toasts (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    ...
    trueButton.setOnClickListener { view: View ->
        // Do something in response to the click here
        Toast.makeText(
                this,
                R.string.correct_toast,
                Toast.LENGTH_SHORT)
                .show()
    }

    false.setOnClickListener { view: View ->
        // Do something in response to the click here
        Toast.makeText(
                this,
                R.string.incorrect_toast,
                Toast.LENGTH_SHORT)
                .show()
    }
}
```

To create a toast, you call the static function <samp class="methodname">Toast.makeText(Context!, Int, Int)</samp>. This function creates and configures a <samp class="classname">Toast</samp> object. The <samp class="classname">Context</samp> parameter is typically an instance of <samp class="classname">Activity</samp> (and <samp class="classname">Activity</samp> is a subclass of <samp class="classname">Context</samp>). Here you pass the instance of <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> as the <samp class="classname">Context</samp> argument.

The second parameter is the resource ID of the string that the toast should display. The <samp class="classname">Context</samp> is needed by the <samp class="classname">Toast</samp> class to be able to find and use the string’s resource ID. The third parameter is one of two <samp class="classname">Toast</samp> constants that specify how long the toast should be visible.

After you have created a toast, you call <samp class="methodname">Toast.show()</samp> on it to get it onscreen.

Because you used code completion, you do not have to do anything to import the <samp class="classname">Toast</samp> class. When you accept a code completion suggestion, the necessary classes are imported automatically.

Now, let’s see your app in action.

## Running on the Emulator

To run an Android application, you need a device – either a hardware device or a <samp class="firstterm">virtual device</samp>. Virtual devices are powered by the Android emulator, which ships with the developer tools.

To create an Android virtual device (or AVD), choose <samp class="guimenu">Tools</samp> → <samp class="guimenuitem">AVD Manager</samp>. When the AVD Manager appears, click the <samp class="guilabel">+Create Virtual Device...</samp> button in the lower-left corner of the window.

In the dialog that appears, you are offered many options for configuring a virtual device. For your first AVD, choose to emulate a Pixel 2, as shown in [Figure 1.18](#ch01s08.xhtml_fig_tf_create_new_avd_template "Figure 1.18  Choosing a virtual device"). Click <samp class="guilabel">Next</samp>.

**Figure 1.18  Choosing a virtual device**

![Choosing a virtual device](Images/tf_create_new_avd_device_type.png)

On the next screen, choose a system image for your emulator. For this emulator, select an x86 Pie emulator and select <samp class="guilabel">Next</samp> ([Figure 1.19](#ch01s08.xhtml_fig_tf_create_new_avd_image "Figure 1.19  Choosing a system image")). (You may need to follow the steps to download the emulator’s components before you can click <samp class="guilabel">Next</samp>.)

**Figure 1.19  Choosing a system image**

![Choosing a system image](Images/tf_create_new_avd_device_image.png)

Finally, you can review and tweak properties of the emulator. You can also edit the properties of an existing emulator later. For now, name your emulator something that will help you to identify it later and click <samp class="guilabel">Finish</samp> ([Figure 1.20](#ch01s08.xhtml_fig_tf_create_new_avd_properties "Figure 1.20  Updating emulator properties")).

**Figure 1.20  Updating emulator properties**

![Updating emulator properties](Images/tf_create_new_avd_device_properties.png)

Once you have an AVD, you can run GeoQuiz on it. From the Android Studio toolbar, click the run button (it looks like a green “play” symbol) or press Control-R (Ctrl-R). In the <samp class="guilabel">Select Deployment Target</samp> box that appears, choose the AVD you just configured and click <samp class="guibutton">OK</samp>. Android Studio will start your virtual device, install the application package on it, and run the app.

Starting up the emulator can take a while, but eventually your GeoQuiz app will launch on the AVD that you created. Press buttons and admire your toasts.

If GeoQuiz crashes when launching or when you press a button, useful information will appear in the Logcat tool window. (If Logcat did not open automatically when you ran GeoQuiz, you can open it by clicking the <samp class="guibutton">Logcat</samp> button at the bottom of the Android Studio window.) Type <samp class="guilabel">MainActivity</samp> into the search box at the top of the Logcat tool window to filter the log messages. Look for exceptions in the log; they will be an eye-catching red color ([Figure 1.21](#ch01s08.xhtml_fig_tf_possible_exception "Figure 1.21  An example NullPointerException")).

**Figure 1.21  An example `NullPointerException`**

![An example NullPointerException](Images/tf_possible_exception.png)

Compare your code with the code in the book to try to find the cause of the problem. Then try running again. (You will learn more about using Logcat in [Chapter 3](../Text/ch03.xhtml "3 The Activity Lifecycle") and about debugging in [Chapter 5](../Text/ch05.xhtml "5 Debugging Android Apps").)

Keep the emulator running – you do not want to wait for it to launch on every run.

You can stop the app by pressing the Back button on the emulator. The Back button is shaped like a left-pointing triangle (on older versions of Android, it looks like an arrow that is making a U-turn). Then rerun the app from Android Studio to test changes.

The emulator is useful, but testing on a real device gives more accurate results. In [Chapter 2](../Text/ch02.xhtml "2 Android and Model-View-Controller"), you will run GeoQuiz on a hardware device. You will also give GeoQuiz more geography questions with which to test the user.

## For the More Curious: The Android Build Process

By now, you probably have some burning questions about how the Android build process works. You have already seen that Android Studio builds your project automatically as you modify it, rather than on command. During the build process, the Android tools take your resources, code, and <samp class="filename">AndroidManifest.xml</samp> file (which contains metadata about the application) and turn them into an <samp class="filename">.apk</samp> file. This file is then signed with a debug key, which allows it to run on the emulator. (To distribute your <samp class="filename">.apk</samp> to the masses, you have to sign it with a release key. There is more information about this process in the Android developer documentation at [<samp class="uri">developer.android.com/​tools/​publishing/​preparing.html</samp>](https://developer.android.com/tools/publishing/preparing.html).)

How do the contents of <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp> turn into <samp class="classname">View</samp> objects in an application? As part of the build process, <samp class="application">aapt2</samp> (the Android Asset Packaging Tool) compiles layout file resources into a more compact format. These compiled resources are packaged into the <samp class="filename">.apk</samp> file. Then, when <samp class="methodname">setContentView(…)</samp> is called in <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>’s <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp> function, <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> uses the <samp class="classname">LayoutInflater</samp> class to instantiate each of the <samp class="classname">View</samp> objects as defined in the layout file ([Figure 1.22](#ch01s09.xhtml_fig_tf_voicerecorder_inflation "Figure 1.22  Inflating activity_main.xml")).

**Figure 1.22  Inflating `activity_main.xml`**

![Inflating activity_main.xml](Images/inflation.png)

(You can also create your view classes programmatically in the activity instead of defining them in XML. But there are benefits to separating your presentation from the logic of the application. The main one is taking advantage of configuration changes built into the SDK, which you will learn more about in [Chapter 3](../Text/ch03.xhtml "3 The Activity Lifecycle").)

You will learn more details of how the different XML attributes work and how views display themselves on the screen in [Chapter 10](../Text/ch10.xhtml "10 Creating User Interfaces with Layouts and Widgets").

### Android build tools

All of the builds you have seen so far have been executed from within Android Studio. This build is integrated into the IDE – it invokes standard Android build tools like `aapt2`, but the build process itself is managed by Android Studio.

You may, for your own reasons, want to perform builds from outside of Android Studio. The easiest way to do this is to use a command-line build tool. The Android build system uses a tool called Gradle.

(You will know if this section applies to you. If it does not, feel free to read along but do not be concerned if you are not sure why you might want to do this or if the commands below do not seem to work. Coverage of the ins and outs of using the command line is beyond the scope of this book.)

To use Gradle from the command line, navigate to your project’s directory and run the following command:

```
 $ ./gradlew tasks
```

On Windows, your command will look a little different:

```
 > gradlew.bat tasks
```

This will show you a list of available tasks you can execute. The one you want is called `installDebug`. Make it so with a command like this:

```
 $ ./gradlew installDebug
```

Or, on Windows:

```
 > gradlew.bat installDebug
```

This will install your app on whatever device is connected. However, it will not run the app. For that, you will need to pull up the launcher and launch the app by hand.

Copy the GeoQuiz folder and paste a new copy next to the original (on macOS, use the <samp class="guilabel">Duplicate</samp> feature). Rename the new folder GeoQuiz Challenge.
