# <samp class="chapter_number">2</samp>
<samp class="chapter_name">Android and Model-View-Controller</samp>

In this chapter, you are going to upgrade GeoQuiz to present more than one question, as shown in [Figure 2.1](#ch02.xhtml_fig_tf_second_chapter "Figure 2.1  Next!").

**Figure 2.1  Next!**

![Next!](Images/tf_second_chapter.png)

To make this happen, you are going to add a data class named <samp class="classname">Question</samp> to the GeoQuiz project. An instance of this class will encapsulate a single true/false question.

Then, you will create a collection of <samp class="classname">Question</samp> objects for <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> to manage.

## Creating a New Class

In the project tool window, right-click the com.bignerdranch.android.geoquiz package and select <samp class="guimenu">New</samp> → <samp class="guimenuitem">Kotlin File/Class</samp>. Enter <samp class="guilabel">Question</samp> for the name. Select <samp class="guilabel">Class</samp> from the <samp class="guilabel">Kind</samp> dropdown. Click <samp class="guilabel">OK</samp> ([Figure 2.2](#ch02s01.xhtml_fig_tf_create_new_class_1 "Figure 2.2  Creating the Question class")).

**Figure 2.2  Creating the `Question` class**

![Creating the Question class](Images/tf_create_new_class_1.png)

Android Studio will create and open a file called <samp class="filename">Question.kt</samp>. In this file, add two member variables and a constructor.

**Listing 2.1  Adding to `Question` class (`Question.kt`)**

```
class Question {
}
data class Question(@StringRes val textResId: Int, val answer: Boolean)
```

The <samp class="classname">Question</samp> class holds two pieces of data: the question text and the question answer (true or false).

The `@StringRes` annotation is not required, but we recommend you include it for two reasons. First, the annotation helps the code inspector built into Android Studio (named Lint) verify at compile time that usages of the constructor provide a valid string resource ID. This prevents runtime crashes where the constructor is used with an invalid resource ID (such as an ID that points to some resource other than a string). Second, the annotation makes your code more readable for other developers.

Why is <samp class="varname">textResId</samp> an <samp class="type">Int</samp> and not a <samp class="type">String</samp>? The <samp class="varname">textResId</samp> variable will hold the resource ID (always an <samp class="type">Int</samp>) of the string resource for a question.

We use the `data` keyword for all model classes in this book. Doing so clearly indicates that the class is meant to hold data. Also, the compiler does extra work for data classes that makes your life easier, such as automatically defining useful functions like <samp class="methodname">equals()</samp>, <samp class="methodname">hashCode()</samp>, and a nicely formatted <samp class="methodname">toString()</samp>.

Your <samp class="classname">Question</samp> class is now complete. In a moment, you will modify <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> to work with <samp class="classname">Question</samp>. First, let’s take a look at how the pieces of GeoQuiz will work together.

You are going to have <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> create a list of <samp class="classname">Question</samp> objects. It will then interact with the <samp class="classname">TextView</samp> and the three <samp class="classname">Button</samp>s to display questions and provide feedback. [Figure 2.3](#ch02s01.xhtml_fig_tf_object_diagram_mvc "Figure 2.3  Object diagram for GeoQuiz") diagrams these relationships.

**Figure 2.3  Object diagram for GeoQuiz**

![Object diagram for GeoQuiz](Images/tf_object_diagram_mvc.png)

## Model-View-Controller and Android

Notice that the objects in [Figure 2.3](#ch02s01.xhtml_fig_tf_object_diagram_mvc "Figure 2.3  Object diagram for GeoQuiz") are separated into three sections labeled Model, Controller, and View. The Android APIs were originally designed around an architecture called <samp class="firstterm">Model-View-Controller</samp>, or MVC. In MVC, all objects in your application must be a <samp class="firstterm">model object</samp>, a <samp class="firstterm">view object</samp>, or a <samp class="firstterm">controller object</samp>.

*   Model objects hold the application’s data and “business logic.” Model classes are typically designed to <samp class="emphasis">model</samp> the things your app is concerned with, such as a user, a product in a store, a photo on a server, a television show – or a true/false question. Model objects have no knowledge of the UI; their sole purpose is holding and managing data.

    In Android applications, model classes are generally custom classes you create. All of the model objects in your application compose its <samp class="firstterm">model layer</samp>.

    GeoQuiz’s model layer consists of the <samp class="classname">Question</samp> class.

*   View objects know how to draw themselves on the screen and how to respond to user input, like touches. A simple rule of thumb is that if you can see it onscreen, then it is a view.

    Android provides a wealth of configurable view classes. You can also create custom view classes. An application’s view objects make up its <samp class="firstterm">view layer</samp>.

    GeoQuiz’s view layer consists of the widgets that are inflated from <samp class="filename">res/layout/activity_main.xml</samp>.

*   Controller objects tie the view and model objects together. They contain “application logic.” Controllers are designed to respond to various events triggered by view objects and to manage the flow of data to and from model objects and the view layer.

    In Android, a controller is typically a subclass of <samp class="classname">Activity</samp> or <samp class="classname">Fragment</samp>. (You will learn about fragments in [Chapter 8](../Text/ch08.xhtml "8 UI Fragments and the Fragment Manager").)

    GeoQuiz’s controller layer, at present, consists solely of <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>.

[Figure 2.4](#ch02s02.xhtml_fig-AndroidMVC "Figure 2.4  MVC flow with user input") shows the flow of control between objects in response to a user event, like a press of a button. Notice that model and view objects do not talk to each other directly; controllers sit squarely in the middle of everything, receiving messages from some objects and dispatching instructions to others.

**Figure 2.4  MVC flow with user input**

![MVC flow with user input](Images/android_mvc.png)

### Deciding to use MVC

An application can accumulate features until it is too complicated to understand. Separating code into classes helps you design and understand the application as a whole; you can think in terms of classes instead of individual variables and functions.

Similarly, separating classes into model, view, and controller layers helps you design and understand an application; you can think in terms of layers instead of individual classes.

Although GeoQuiz is not a complicated app, you can still see the benefits of keeping layers separate. In a moment, you are going to update GeoQuiz’s view layer to include a <samp class="guibutton">NEXT</samp> button. When you do that, you will not need to remember a single thing about the <samp class="classname">Question</samp> class you just created.

MVC also makes classes easier to reuse. A class with restricted responsibilities is more reusable than one with its fingers in every pie.

For instance, your model class, <samp class="classname">Question</samp>, knows nothing about the widgets used to display a true/false question. This makes it easy to use <samp class="classname">Question</samp> throughout your app for different purposes. For example, if you wanted to display a list of all the questions at once, you could use the same object that you use here to display just one question at a time.

MVC works great for small, simple apps like GeoQuiz. In larger, more complicated apps, the controller layer can get very large and complex. In general, you want to keep your activities and other controllers <samp class="firstterm">thin</samp>. Thin activities contain as little business and setup logic as possible. Once MVC no longer lends itself to thin controllers in your app, you should consider alternative patterns, such as Model-View-View Model (which you will learn about in [Chapter 19](../Text/ch19.xhtml "19 Data Binding and MVVM")).

## Updating the View Layer

Now that you have been introduced to MVC, you are going to update GeoQuiz’s view layer to include a <samp class="guibutton">NEXT</samp> button.

In Android, objects in the view layer are typically inflated from XML within a layout file. The sole layout in GeoQuiz is defined in <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp>. This layout needs to be updated as shown in [Figure 2.5](#ch02s03.xhtml_fig_tf_second_layout "Figure 2.5  New button!"). (Note that to save space we are not showing the attributes of unchanged widgets.)

**Figure 2.5  New button!**

![New button!](Images/activity_main_layout_2.png)

So the changes you need to make to the view layer are:

*   Give the <samp class="classname">TextView</samp> an `android:id` attribute. This widget will need a resource ID so that you can set its text in <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>’s code. Position the <samp class="classname">TextView</samp>’s text in the center of the text view by setting `gravity` to `"center"`.

*   Remove the `android:text` attribute from the <samp class="classname">TextView</samp>. You no longer want a hardcoded question to be part of its definition. Instead, you will set the question text dynamically as the user clicks through the questions.

*   Specify a default string for the <samp class="guilabel">Design</samp> tab to display in the <samp class="classname">TextView</samp> when rendering a preview of your layout. To do this, add a `tools:text` attribute to the <samp class="classname">TextView</samp> and point it to a string resource representing a question using `@string/`.

    You will also need to add the `tools` namespace to the root tag of your layout so that Android Studio can make sense of the `tools:text` attribute. This namespace allows you to override any attribute on a widget for the purpose of displaying it in the Android Studio preview. The `tools` attributes are ignored when rendering the widgets on a device at runtime. You could use `android:text` and just overwrite the value at runtime, but using `tools:text` instead makes it clear that the value you provide is for preview purposes only.

*   Add the new <samp class="classname">Button</samp> widget as a child of the root <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp>.

Return to <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp> and make it happen.

**Listing 2.2  New button … and changes to the text view (`res/layout/activity_main.xml`)**

```
<LinearLayout xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
        xmlns:tools="http://schemas.android.com/tools"
        android:layout_width="match_parent"
        android:layout_height="match_parent"
        ... >

    <TextView
        android:id="@+id/question_text_view"
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:gravity="center"
        android:padding="24dp"
        android:text="@string/question_text"
        tools:text="@string/question_australia" />

    <LinearLayout ... >
        ...
    </LinearLayout>

    <Button
        android:id="@+id/next_button"
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:text="@string/next_button" />

</LinearLayout>
```

You will see familiar errors alerting you about missing string resources.

Return to <samp class="filename">res/values/strings.xml</samp>. Rename `question_text` and add a string for the new button.

**Listing 2.3  Updating strings (`res/values/strings.xml`)**

```
<string name="app_name">GeoQuiz</string>
<string name="question_text">Canberra is the capital of Australia.</string>
<string name="question_australia">Canberra is the capital of Australia.</string>
<string name="true_button">True</string>
<string name="false_button">False</string>
<string name="next_button">Next</string>
...
```

While you have <samp class="filename">strings.xml</samp> open, go ahead and add the strings for the rest of the geography questions that will be shown to the user.

**Listing 2.4  Adding question strings (`res/values/strings.xml`)**

```
<string name="question_australia">Canberra is the capital of Australia.</string>
<string name="question_oceans">The Pacific Ocean is larger than
  the Atlantic Ocean.</string>
<string name="question_mideast">The Suez Canal connects the Red Sea
  and the Indian Ocean.</string>
<string name="question_africa">The source of the Nile River is in Egypt.</string>
<string name="question_americas">The Amazon River is the longest river
  in the Americas.</string>
<string name="question_asia">Lake Baikal is the world\'s oldest and deepest
  freshwater lake.</string>
...
```

Notice that you use the escape sequence `\'` in the last value to get an apostrophe in your string. You can use all the usual escape sequences in your string resources, such as `\n` for a new line.

Return to <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp> and preview your layout changes in the graphical layout tool.

That is all for now for GeoQuiz’s view layer. Time to wire everything up in your controller class, <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>.

## Updating the Controller Layer

In the previous chapter, there was not much happening in GeoQuiz’s one controller, <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>. It displayed the layout defined in <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp>. It set listeners on two buttons and wired them to make toasts.

Now that you have multiple questions to retrieve and display, <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> will have to work harder to tie GeoQuiz’s model and view layers together.

Open <samp class="filename">MainActivity.kt</samp>. Create a list of <samp class="classname">Question</samp> objects and an index for the list.

**Listing 2.5  Adding a `Question` list (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {

    private lateinit var trueButton: Button
    private lateinit var falseButton: Button

    private val questionBank = listOf(
            Question(R.string.question_australia, true),
            Question(R.string.question_oceans, true),
            Question(R.string.question_mideast, false),
            Question(R.string.question_africa, false),
            Question(R.string.question_americas, true),
            Question(R.string.question_asia, true))

    private var currentIndex = 0
    ...
}
```

Here you call the <samp class="classname">Question</samp> constructor several times and create a list of <samp class="classname">Question</samp> objects.

(In a more complex project, this list would be created and stored elsewhere. In later apps, you will see better options for storing model data. For now, we are keeping it simple and just creating the list within your controller.)

You are going to use <samp class="varname">questionBank</samp>, <samp class="varname">currentIndex</samp>, and the properties in <samp class="classname">Question</samp> to get a parade of questions onscreen.

First add properties for the <samp class="classname">TextView</samp> and the new <samp class="classname">Button</samp>. Then get a reference for the <samp class="classname">TextView</samp> and set its text to the question at the current index. While you are at it, get a reference for the new <samp class="classname">Button</samp> as well (you will configure the click listener for the <samp class="guibutton">NEXT</samp> button later).

**Listing 2.6  Wiring up the `TextView` (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {

    private lateinit var trueButton: Button
    private lateinit var falseButton: Button
    private lateinit var nextButton: Button
    private lateinit var questionTextView: TextView
    ...
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        ...
        trueButton = findViewById(R.id.true_button)
        falseButton = findViewById(R.id.false_button)
        nextButton = findViewById(R.id.next_button)
        questionTextView = findViewById(R.id.question_text_view)

        trueButton.setOnClickListener { view: View ->
            ...
        }

        falseButton.setOnClickListener { view: View ->
            ...
        }

        val questionTextResId = questionBank[currentIndex].textResId
        questionTextView.setText(questionTextResId)
    }
}
```

Save your files and check for any errors. Then run GeoQuiz. You should see the first question in the array appear in the <samp class="classname">TextView</samp>.

Now let’s make the <samp class="guibutton">NEXT</samp> button functional. Set a <samp class="classname">View.OnClickListener</samp> on it. This listener will increment the index and update the <samp class="classname">TextView</samp>’s text.

**Listing 2.7  Wiring up the new button (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    ...
    falseButton.setOnClickListener { view: View ->
        ...
    }

    nextButton.setOnClickListener {
        currentIndex = (currentIndex + 1) % questionBank.size
        val questionTextResId = questionBank[currentIndex].textResId
        questionTextView.setText(questionTextResId)

    }

    val questionTextResId = questionBank[currentIndex].textResId
    questionTextView.setText(questionTextResId)
}
```

You now have the same code in two separate places that updates the text displayed in <samp class="varname">questionTextView</samp>. Take a moment to put this code into a function instead, as shown in [Listing 2.8](#ch02s04.xhtml_pl_tf_add_private_method "Listing 2.8  Encapsulating with a function (MainActivity.kt)"). Then invoke that function in the <samp class="varname">nextButton</samp>’s listener and at the end of <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp> to initially set the text in the activity’s view.

**Listing 2.8  Encapsulating with a function (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    ...
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        ...
        nextButton.setOnClickListener {
            currentIndex = (currentIndex + 1) % questionBank.size
            val questionTextResId = questionBank[currentIndex].textResId
            questionTextView.setText(questionTextResId)
            updateQuestion()
        }

        val questionTextResId = questionBank[currentIndex].textResId
        questionTextView.setText(questionTextResId)
        updateQuestion()
    }

    private fun updateQuestion() {
        val questionTextResId = questionBank[currentIndex].textResId
        questionTextView.setText(questionTextResId)
    }
}
```

Run GeoQuiz and test your new <samp class="guibutton">NEXT</samp> button.

Now that you have the questions behaving appropriately, it is time to turn to the answers. At the moment, GeoQuiz thinks that the answer to every question is “true.” Let’s rectify that. You will add a private named function to <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> to encapsulate code rather than writing similar code in two places:

```
 private fun checkAnswer(userAnswer: Boolean)
```

This function will accept a `Boolean` variable that identifies whether the user pressed <samp class="guibutton">TRUE</samp> or <samp class="guibutton">FALSE</samp>. Then, it will check the user’s answer against the answer in the current <samp class="classname">Question</samp> object. Finally, after determining whether the user answered correctly, it will make a <samp class="classname">Toast</samp> that displays the appropriate message to the user.

In <samp class="filename">MainActivity.kt</samp>, add the implementation of <samp class="methodname">checkAnswer(Boolean)</samp> shown in [Listing 2.9](#ch02s04.xhtml_pl_tf_add_check_answer "Listing 2.9  Adding checkAnswer(Boolean) (MainActivity.kt)").

**Listing 2.9  Adding `checkAnswer(Boolean)` (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    ...
    private fun updateQuestion() {
        ...
    }

    private fun checkAnswer(userAnswer: Boolean) {
        val correctAnswer = questionBank[currentIndex].answer

        val messageResId = if (userAnswer == correctAnswer) {
            R.string.correct_toast
        } else {
            R.string.incorrect_toast
        }

        Toast.makeText(this, messageResId, Toast.LENGTH_SHORT)
                .show()
    }
}
```

Within the buttons’ listeners, call <samp class="methodname">checkAnswer(Boolean)</samp>, as shown in [Listing 2.10](#ch02s04.xhtml_pl_tf_call_check_answer "Listing 2.10  Calling checkAnswer(Boolean) (MainActivity.kt)").

**Listing 2.10  Calling `checkAnswer(Boolean)` (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    ...
    trueButton.setOnClickListener { view: View ->
        Toast.makeText(
            this,
            R.string.correct_toast,
            Toast.LENGTH_SHORT
        )
            .show()
        checkAnswer(true)
    }

    falseButton.setOnClickListener { view: View ->
        Toast.makeText(
            this,
            R.string.correct_toast,
            Toast.LENGTH_SHORT
        )
            .show()
        checkAnswer(false)
    }
    ...
}
```

Run GeoQuiz. Verify that the toasts display the right message based on the answer to the current question and the button you press.

## Adding an Icon

GeoQuiz is up and running, but the UI would be spiffier if the <samp class="guibutton">NEXT</samp> button also displayed a right-pointing arrow icon.

You can find such an arrow in the solutions file for this book, which is a collection of Android Studio projects for each chapter of this book. The solutions are hosted at [<samp class="uri">www.bignerdranch.com/​solutions/​AndroidProgramming4e.zip</samp>](https://www.bignerdranch.com/solutions/AndroidProgramming4e.zip).

Download the solutions file and open the <samp class="filename">02_MVC/GeoQuiz/app/src/main/res</samp> directory. Within this directory, locate the <samp class="filename">drawable-hdpi</samp>, <samp class="filename">drawable-mdpi</samp>, <samp class="filename">drawable-xhdpi</samp>, <samp class="filename">drawable-xxhdpi</samp>, and <samp class="filename">drawable-xxxhdpi</samp> directories.

The suffixes on these directory names refer to the screen pixel density of a device:

| <samp class="filename">mdpi</samp> |
| <samp class="filename">hdpi</samp> |
| <samp class="filename">xhdpi</samp> |
| <samp class="filename">xxhdpi</samp> |
| <samp class="filename">xxxhdpi</samp> |

(There are a few other density categories that are omitted from the solutions, including ldpi and tvdpi.)

Within each directory, you will find two image files – <samp class="filename">arrow_right.png</samp> and <samp class="filename">arrow_left.png</samp>. These files have been customized for the screen pixel density specified in the directory’s name.

You are going to include all the image files from the solutions in GeoQuiz. When the app runs, the OS will choose the best image file for the specific device running the app. Note that by duplicating the images multiple times, you increase the size of your application. In this case, this is not a problem because GeoQuiz is a simple app.

If an app runs on a device that has a screen density not included in any of the application’s screen density qualifiers, Android will automatically scale the available image to the appropriate size for the device. Thanks to this feature, it is not necessary to provide images for all of the pixel density buckets. To reduce the size of your application, you can focus on one or a few of the higher-resolution buckets and selectively optimize for lower resolutions when Android’s automatic scaling provides an image with artifacts on those lower-resolution devices.

(You will see alternatives to duplicating images at different densities, along with an explanation of the <samp class="filename">mipmap</samp> directory, in [Chapter 22](../Text/ch22.xhtml "22 XML Drawables").)

### Adding resources to a project

The next step is to add the image files to GeoQuiz’s resources.

Make sure the project tool window is displaying the <samp class="guilabel">Project</samp> view. Expand the contents of <samp class="filename">GeoQuiz/app/src/main/res</samp>, as shown in [Figure 2.6](#ch02s05.xhtml_ss_tf_explore_folders_in_android_studio_project_view "Figure 2.6  Exploring resources in Project view"). You will see that some folders, such as <samp class="filename">mipmap-hdpi</samp> and <samp class="filename">mipmap-xhdpi</samp>, already exist.

**Figure 2.6  Exploring resources in Project view**

![Exploring resources in Project view](Images/tf_toggle_android_studio_project_view.png)

Back in the solutions files, select and copy the five directories that you located earlier: <samp class="filename">drawable-hdpi</samp>, <samp class="filename">drawable-mdpi</samp>, <samp class="filename">drawable-xhdpi</samp>, <samp class="filename">drawable-xxhdpi</samp>, and <samp class="filename">drawable-xxxhdpi</samp>. In Android Studio, click on the <samp class="filename">app/src/main/res</samp> directory in the project tool window and paste the copied directories. Click <samp class="guibutton">OK</samp> in the confirmation pop-up. You should now have five density-qualified drawable directories, each with an <samp class="filename">arrow_left.png</samp> and <samp class="filename">arrow_right.png</samp> file, as shown in [Figure 2.7](#ch02s05.xhtml_fig_tf_drawable_dirs "Figure 2.7  Arrow icons in GeoQuiz drawable directories").

**Figure 2.7  Arrow icons in GeoQuiz `drawable` directories**

![Arrow icons in GeoQuiz drawable directories](Images/tf_drawable_dirs.png)

If you switch the project tool window back to the <samp class="guilabel">Android</samp> view, you will see the newly added drawable files summarized (as shown in [Figure 2.8](#ch02s05.xhtml_fig_tf_drawable_dirs_summary "Figure 2.8  Summary of arrow icons in GeoQuiz drawable directories")).

**Figure 2.8  Summary of arrow icons in GeoQuiz `drawable` directories**

![Summary of arrow icons in GeoQuiz drawable directories](Images/tf_drawable_dirs_summary.png)

Including images in your app is as simple as that. Any <samp class="filename">.png</samp>, <samp class="filename">.jpg</samp>, or <samp class="filename">.gif</samp> file you add to a <samp class="filename">res/drawable</samp> folder will be automatically assigned a resource ID. (Note that filenames must be lowercase and have no spaces.)

These resource IDs are not qualified by screen density, so you do not need to determine the device’s screen density at runtime. All you have to do is use this resource ID in your code. When the app runs, the OS will determine the appropriate image to display on that particular device.

You will learn more about how the Android resource system works starting in [Chapter 3](../Text/ch03.xhtml "3 The Activity Lifecycle"). For now, let’s put that right arrow to work.

### Referencing resources in XML

You use resource IDs to reference resources in code. But you want to configure the <samp class="guibutton">NEXT</samp> button to display the arrow in the layout definition. How do you reference a resource from XML?

Answer: with a slightly different syntax. Open <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp> and add two attributes to the <samp class="classname">Button</samp> widget definition.

**Listing 2.11  Adding an icon to the NEXT button (`res/layout/activity_main.xml`)**

```
<LinearLayout ... >
    ...
    <LinearLayout ... >
        ...
    </LinearLayout>

    <Button
        android:id="@+id/next_button"
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:text="@string/next_button"
        android:drawableEnd="@drawable/arrow_right"
        android:drawablePadding="4dp" />

</LinearLayout>
```

In an XML resource, you refer to another resource by its resource type and name. A reference to a string resource begins with `@string/`. A reference to a drawable resource begins with `@drawable/`.

You will learn more about naming resources and working in the <samp class="filename">res</samp> directory structure starting in [Chapter 3](../Text/ch03.xhtml "3 The Activity Lifecycle").

Run GeoQuiz and admire your button’s new appearance. Then test it to make sure it still works as before.

## Screen Pixel Densities

In <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp>, you specified attribute values in terms of `dp` units. Now it is time to learn what they are.

Sometimes you need to specify values for view attributes in terms of specific sizes (usually in pixels, but sometimes points, millimeters, or inches). You see this most commonly with attributes for text size, margins, and padding. Text size is the pixel height of the text on the device’s screen. Margins specify the distances between views, and padding specifies the distance between a view’s outside edges and its content.

As you saw in [the section called *Adding an Icon*](../Text/ch02s05.xhtml "Adding an Icon"), Android automatically scales images to different screen pixel densities using density-qualified drawable folders (such as <samp class="filename">drawable-xhdpi</samp>). But what happens when your images scale, but your margins do not? Or when the user configures a larger-than-default text size?

To solve these problems, Android provides density-independent dimension units that you can use to get the same size on different screen densities. Android translates these units into pixels at runtime, so there is no tricky math for you to do ([Figure 2.9](#ch02s06.xhtml_pixel_scaling_examples "Figure 2.9  Dimension units in action on TextView")).

**Figure 2.9  Dimension units in action on `TextView`**

![Dimension units in action on TextView](Images/pixel_scaling.png)

| <samp class="literal">px</samp> |
| <samp class="literal">dp</samp> |
| <samp class="literal">sp</samp> |
| <samp class="literal">pt</samp>, <samp class="literal">mm</samp>, <samp class="literal">in</samp> |

In practice and in this book, you will use <samp class="literal">dp</samp> and <samp class="literal">sp</samp> almost exclusively. Android will translate these values into pixels at runtime.

## Running on a Device

It is fun to interact with your app on an emulator. It is even more fun to interact with your app on physical Android device. In this section, you will set up your system, device, and application to get GeoQuiz running on your hardware device.

First, plug the device into your computer. If you are developing on a Mac, your system should recognize the device right away. On Windows, you may need to install the <samp class="filename">adb</samp> (Android Debug Bridge) driver. If Windows cannot find the <samp class="filename">adb</samp> driver, then download one from the device manufacturer’s website.

Second, enable USB debugging on your Android device. To do this, you need to access the <samp class="guilabel">Developer options</samp> settings menu, which is not visible by default. To enable developer options, go to <samp class="guimenu">Settings</samp> → <samp class="guimenuitem">About Tablet/Phone</samp>. Scroll down and press <samp class="guilabel">Build Number</samp> seven times in quick succession. After several presses, you will see a message telling you how many steps (presses of the build number) you are from being a developer. When you see <samp class="guilabel">You are now a developer!</samp>, you can stop. Then you can return to <samp class="guilabel">Settings</samp>, see <samp class="guilabel">Developer options</samp> (you may need to expand the <samp class="guilabel">Advanced</samp> section), and enable <samp class="guilabel">USB debugging</samp>.

The options vary considerably across devices. If you are having problems enabling your device, visit [<samp class="uri">developer.android.com/​tools/​device.html</samp>](https://developer.android.com/tools/device.html) for more help.

Finally, confirm that your device is recognized by opening the Logcat tool window using its button at the bottom of Android Studio. At the top left of this window, you will see a drop-down list of connected devices ([Figure 2.10](#ch02s07.xhtml_fig_tf_view_connected_devices "Figure 2.10  Viewing connected devices")). You should see your AVD, also known as your emulator, and your hardware device listed.

**Figure 2.10  Viewing connected devices**

![Viewing connected devices](Images/tf_view_connected_devices.png)

If you are having trouble getting your device recognized, verify that your device is turned on and that the USB debugging option is enabled.

If you are still unable to see your device in the devices view, you can find more help on the Android developers’ site. Start at [<samp class="uri">developer.android.com/​tools/​device.html</samp>](https://developer.android.com/tools/device.html). You can also visit this book’s forum at [<samp class="uri">forums.bignerdranch.com</samp>](https://forums.bignerdranch.com) for more troubleshooting help.

Run GeoQuiz as before. Android Studio will offer a choice between running on the virtual device or the hardware device plugged into your system. Select the hardware device and continue. GeoQuiz will launch on your device.

If Android Studio defaults to your emulator without offering a choice of device to run the app on, recheck the steps above and make sure your device is plugged in. Next, ensure that your run configuration is correct. To modify the run configuration, select the <samp class="guilabel">app</samp> drop-down list near the top of the window, as shown in [Figure 2.11](#ch02s07.xhtml_fig_tf_view_run_configurations "Figure 2.11  Run configurations").

**Figure 2.11  Run configurations**

![Run configurations](Images/tf_view_run_configurations.png)

Choose <samp class="guilabel">Edit Configurations...</samp> and you will be presented with a new window with details about your run configuration ([Figure 2.12](#ch02s07.xhtml_fig_tf_run_configuration_properties "Figure 2.12  Run configuration properties")).

**Figure 2.12  Run configuration properties**

![Run configuration properties](Images/tf_run_configuration_properties.png)

Select <samp class="guilabel">app</samp> in the left pane and verify that <samp class="guilabel">Deployment Target Options</samp> is set to <samp class="guilabel">Open Select Deployment Target Dialog</samp> and that <samp class="guilabel">Use same device for future launches</samp> is unchecked. Select <samp class="guibutton">OK</samp> and rerun the app. You should now be presented with a choice of device to launch the app on.

## Challenge: From Button to ImageButton

Perhaps the UI would look even better if the next and previous buttons showed <samp class="emphasis">only</samp> icons, as in [Figure 2.14](#ch02s10.xhtml_fig_tf_challenge_3_interface "Figure 2.14  Icon-only buttons").

**Figure 2.14  Icon-only buttons**

![Icon-only buttons](Images/tf_challenge_3_interface.png)

To accomplish this challenge, these two widgets must become <samp class="classname">ImageButton</samp>s instead of regular <samp class="classname">Button</samp>s.

<samp class="classname">ImageButton</samp> is a widget that inherits from <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp>. <samp class="classname">Button</samp>, on the other hand, inherits from <samp class="classname">TextView</samp>. [Figure 2.15](#ch02s10.xhtml_fig_tf_view_hierarchy "Figure 2.15  Inheritance diagram for ImageButton and Button") shows their different inheritance hierarchies.

**Figure 2.15  Inheritance diagram for `ImageButton` and `Button`**

![Inheritance diagram for ImageButton and Button](Images/view_hierarchy.png)

You can replace the text and drawable attributes on the <samp class="guibutton">NEXT</samp> button with a single <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> attribute:

```
 <Button ImageButton
    android:id="@+id/next_button"
    android:layout_width="wrap_content"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="@string/next_button"
    android:drawableEnd="@drawable/arrow_right"
    android:drawablePadding="4dp"
    android:src="@drawable/arrow_right"
    />
```

Of course, you will need to modify <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> to work with <samp class="classname">ImageButton</samp>.

After you have changed the buttons to <samp class="classname">ImageButton</samp>s, Android Studio will warn you about a missing `android:contentDescription` attribute. This attribute supports accessibility for users with vision impairments. You set the value to a string, which is read aloud when users have the appropriate settings applied.

Add an `android:contentDescription` attribute to each <samp class="classname">ImageButton</samp> to complete the challenge.

# <samp class="chapter_number">3</samp>
<samp class="chapter_name">The Activity Lifecycle</samp>

In this chapter you will learn the cause of the dreaded – and very common – “rotation problem.” You will also learn how to leverage the mechanics underlying the rotation problem to display an alternate layout when the device is in landscape mode ([Figure 3.1](#ch03.xhtml_ss_tf_activity_lifecycle_final "Figure 3.1  GeoQuiz in landscape orientation")).

**Figure 3.1  GeoQuiz in landscape orientation**

![GeoQuiz in landscape orientation](Images/tf_landscape_interface.png)

## Rotating GeoQuiz

GeoQuiz works great … until you rotate the device. While the app is running, press the <samp class="guibutton">NEXT</samp> button to show another question. Then rotate the device. If you are running on the emulator, click the rotate left or rotate right button in the floating toolbar to rotate ([Figure 3.2](#ch03s01.xhtml_fig_tf_emulator_controls "Figure 3.2  Control the roll")).

**Figure 3.2  Control the roll**

![Control the roll](Images/tf_emulator_controls_rotate.png)

If the emulator does not rotate after you press one of the rotate buttons, turn auto-rotate on. Swipe down from the top of the screen to open Quick Settings. Press the auto-rotate icon, which is the third icon from the left ([Figure 3.3](#ch03s01.xhtml_fig_tf_emulator_auto_rotate "Figure 3.3  Quick Setting for auto-rotate")). The icon will change from grayed out to a teal color to indicate that auto-rotate is now on.

**Figure 3.3  Quick Setting for auto-rotate**

![Quick Setting for auto-rotate](Images/fig_tf_emulator_auto_rotate.png)

After you rotate, you will see the first question again. How and why did this happen? The answers to these questions have to do with the activity lifecycle.

You will learn how to fix this problem in [Chapter 4](../Text/ch04.xhtml "4 Persisting UI State"). But first, it is important to understand the root of the problem so you can avoid related bugs that might creep up.

## Activity States and Lifecycle Callbacks

Every instance of <samp class="classname">Activity</samp> has a lifecycle. During this lifecycle, an activity transitions between four states: resumed, paused, stopped, and nonexistent. For each transition, there is an <samp class="classname">Activity</samp> function that notifies the activity of the change in its state. [Figure 3.4](#ch03s02.xhtml_fig_tf_activity_lifecycle_simple "Figure 3.4  Activity state diagram") shows the activity lifecycle, states, and functions.

**Figure 3.4  Activity state diagram**

![Activity state diagram](Images/activity_lifecycle_simple.png)

[Figure 3.4](#ch03s02.xhtml_fig_tf_activity_lifecycle_simple "Figure 3.4  Activity state diagram") indicates for each state whether the activity has an instance in memory, is visible to the user, or is active in the foreground (accepting user input). [Table 3.1](#ch03s02.xhtml_table_tf_activity_state "Table 3.1  Activity states") summarizes this information.

**Table 3.1  Activity states**

| State | In memory? | Visible to user? | In foreground? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| nonexistent | no | no | no |
| stopped | yes | no | no |
| paused | yes | yes/partially* | no |
| resumed | yes | yes | yes |

(* Depending on the circumstances, a paused activity may be fully or partially visible.)

<samp class="firstterm">Nonexistent</samp> represents an activity that has not been launched yet or an activity that was just destroyed (by the user pressing the Back button, for example). For that reason, this state is sometimes referred to as the “destroyed” state. There is no instance in memory, and there is no associated view for the user to see or interact with.

<samp class="firstterm">Stopped</samp> represents an activity that has an instance in memory but whose view is not visible on the screen. This state occurs in passing when the activity is first spinning up and re-occurs any time the view is fully occluded (such as when the user launches another full-screen activity to the foreground, presses the Home button, or uses the overview screen to switch tasks).

<samp class="firstterm">Paused</samp> represents an activity that is not active in the foreground but whose view is visible or partially visible. An activity would be partially visible, for example, if the user launched a new dialog-themed or transparent activity on top of it. An activity could also be fully visible but not in the foreground if the user is viewing two activities in multi-window mode (also called “split-screen mode”).

<samp class="firstterm">Resumed</samp> represents an activity that is in memory, fully visible, and in the foreground. It is the activity the user is currently interacting with. Only one activity across the entire system can be in the resumed state at any given time. That means that if one activity is moving into the resumed state, another is likely moving out of the resumed state.

Subclasses of <samp class="classname">Activity</samp> can take advantage of the functions named in [Figure 3.4](#ch03s02.xhtml_fig_tf_activity_lifecycle_simple "Figure 3.4  Activity state diagram") to get work done at critical transitions in the activity’s lifecycle. These functions are often called <samp class="firstterm">lifecycle callbacks</samp>.

You are already acquainted with one of these lifecycle callback functions – <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp>. The OS calls this function after the activity instance is created but before it is put onscreen.

Typically, an activity overrides <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp> to prepare the specifics of its UI:

*   inflating widgets and putting them on screen (in the call to <samp class="methodname">setContentView(Int)</samp>)

*   getting references to inflated widgets

*   setting listeners on widgets to handle user interaction

*   connecting to external model data

It is important to understand that you never call <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp> or any of the other <samp class="classname">Activity</samp> lifecycle functions yourself. You simply override the callbacks in your activity subclass. Then Android calls the lifecycle callbacks at the appropriate time (in relation to what the user is doing and what is happening across the rest of the system) to notify the activity that its state is changing.

## Logging the Activity Lifecycle

In this section, you are going to override lifecycle functions to eavesdrop on <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>’s lifecycle. Each implementation will simply log a message informing you that the function has been called. This will help you see how <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>’s state changes at runtime in relation to what the user is doing.

### Making log messages

In Android, the <samp class="classname">android.util.Log</samp> class sends log messages to a shared system-level log. <samp class="classname">Log</samp> has several functions for logging messages. Here is the one that you will use most often in this book:

```
 public static Int d(String tag, String msg)
```

The <samp class="methodname">d</samp> stands for “debug” and refers to the level of the log message. (There is more about the <samp class="classname">Log</samp> levels in [the section called *For the More Curious: Log Levels*](../Text/ch03s07.xhtml "For the More Curious: Log Levels") near the end of this chapter.) The first parameter identifies the source of the message, and the second is the contents of the message.

The first string is typically a <samp class="varname">TAG</samp> constant with the class name as its value. This makes it easy to determine the source of a particular message.

Open <samp class="filename">MainActivity.kt</samp> and add a <samp class="varname">TAG</samp> constant to <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>:

**Listing 3.1  Adding a `TAG` constant (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
import ...

private const val TAG = "MainActivity"

class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    ...
}
```

Next, in <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp>, call <samp class="methodname">Log.d(…)</samp> to log a message.

**Listing 3.2  Adding a log statement to `onCreate(Bundle?)` (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    Log.d(TAG, "onCreate(Bundle?) called")
    setContentView(R.layout.activity_main)
    ...
}
```

Now override five more lifecycle functions in <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> by adding the following after <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp>:

**Listing 3.3  Overriding more lifecycle functions (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    ...
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        ...
    }

    override fun onStart() {
        super.onStart()
        Log.d(TAG, "onStart() called")
    }

    override fun onResume() {
        super.onResume()
        Log.d(TAG, "onResume() called")
    }

    override fun onPause() {
        super.onPause()
        Log.d(TAG, "onPause() called")
    }

    override fun onStop() {
        super.onStop()
        Log.d(TAG, "onStop() called")
    }

    override fun onDestroy() {
        super.onDestroy()
        Log.d(TAG, "onDestroy() called")
    }

    private fun updateQuestion() {
        ...
    }
    ...
}
```

Notice that you call the superclass implementations before you log your messages. These superclass calls are required. Calling the superclass implementation should be the first line of each callback function override implementation.

You may have been wondering about the `override` keyword. This asks the compiler to ensure that the class actually has the function that you want to override. For example, the compiler would be able to alert you to the following misspelled function name:

```
 override fun onCreat(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        ...
    }
```

The parent <samp class="classname">AppCompatActivity</samp> class does not have an <samp class="methodname">onCreat(Bundle?)</samp> function, so the compiler will complain. This way you can fix the typo now, rather than waiting until you run the app and see strange behavior to discover the error.

### Using Logcat

Run GeoQuiz and messages will start materializing in the Logcat tool window at the bottom of Android Studio, as shown in [Figure 3.5](#ch03s03.xhtml_fig_tf_workspace_with_logcat "Figure 3.5  Android Studio with Logcat"). If Logcat did not open automatically when you ran GeoQuiz, you can open it by clicking the <samp class="guibutton">Logcat</samp> button at the bottom of the Android Studio window.

**Figure 3.5  Android Studio with Logcat**

![Android Studio with Logcat](Images/tf_workbench_with_logcat.png)

You will see your own messages along with some system output. To make your messages easier to find, you can filter the output using the value you set for the <samp class="varname">TAG</samp> constant. In Logcat, click the dropdown in the top right that reads <samp class="guilabel">Show only selected application</samp>. This is the filter dropdown, which is currently set to show messages from only your app.

In the filter dropdown, select <samp class="guilabel">Edit Filter Configuration</samp> to create a new filter. Name the filter <samp class="guilabel">MainActivity</samp> and enter <samp class="guilabel">MainActivity</samp> in the <samp class="guilabel">Log Tag</samp> field ([Figure 3.6](#ch03s03.xhtml_fig_tf_new_logcat_filter "Figure 3.6  Creating a filter in Logcat")).

**Figure 3.6  Creating a filter in Logcat**

![Creating a filter in Logcat](Images/tf_new_logcat_filter.png)

Click <samp class="guilabel">OK</samp>. Now, only messages tagged “MainActivity” will be visible in Logcat ([Figure 3.7](#ch03s03.xhtml_fig_tf_logcat_on_launch "Figure 3.7  Launching GeoQuiz creates, starts, and resumes an activity")).

**Figure 3.7  Launching GeoQuiz creates, starts, and resumes an activity**

![Launching GeoQuiz creates, starts, and resumes an activity](Images/tf_launch_with_filter_cropped_text.png)

## Exploring How the Activity Lifecycle Responds to User Actions

Three lifecycle functions were called after GeoQuiz was launched and the initial instance of <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> was created: <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp>, <samp class="methodname">onStart()</samp>, and <samp class="methodname">onResume()</samp> ([Figure 3.7](#ch03s03.xhtml_fig_tf_logcat_on_launch "Figure 3.7  Launching GeoQuiz creates, starts, and resumes an activity")). Your <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> instance is now in the resumed state (in memory, visible, and active in the foreground).

As you continue through the book, you will override the different activity lifecycle functions to do real things for your application. When you do, you will learn more about the uses of each function. For now, have some fun familiarizing yourself with how the lifecycle behaves in common usage scenarios by interacting with your app and checking out the logs in Logcat.

### Temporarily leaving an activity

If GeoQuiz is not already running on your device, run the app from Android Studio. Now press the Home button. The home screen displays, and <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> moves completely out of view. What state is <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> in now? Check Logcat for a hint. Your activity received calls to <samp class="methodname">onPause()</samp> and <samp class="methodname">onStop()</samp>, but not <samp class="methodname">onDestroy()</samp> ([Figure 3.8](#ch03s04.xhtml_fig_tf_logcat_on_pressing_home "Figure 3.8  Pressing the Home button stops the activity")).

**Figure 3.8  Pressing the Home button stops the activity**

![Pressing the Home button stops the activity](Images/tf_press_home_logcat_cropped_text.png)

By pressing the Home button, the user is telling Android, “I’m going to go look at something else, but I might come back. I’m not really done with this screen yet.” Android pauses and ultimately stops the activity.

So after you press the Home button from GeoQuiz, your instance of <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> hangs out in the stopped state (in memory, not visible, and not active in the foreground). Android does this so it can quickly and easily restart <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> where you left off when you come back to GeoQuiz later.

(This is not the whole story about pressing the Home button. Stopped applications can be destroyed at the discretion of the OS. See [Chapter 4](../Text/ch04.xhtml "4 Persisting UI State") for the rest of the story.)

Go back to GeoQuiz by selecting the GeoQuiz task card from the <samp class="firstterm">overview screen</samp>. To do this, press the Recents button, which is next to the Home button ([Figure 3.9](#ch03s04.xhtml_ss_device_nav_buttons "Figure 3.9  Back, Home, and Recents buttons")).

**Figure 3.9  Back, Home, and Recents buttons**

![Back, Home, and Recents buttons](Images/tf_new_device_buttons.png)

If your device does not have a Recents button, and instead has a single Home button (as shown in [Figure 3.10](#ch03s04.xhtml_ss_new_home_button "Figure 3.10  Single Home button")), swipe up from the bottom of the screen to open the overview screen. If neither of these approaches works on your device, consult the device manufacturer’s user guide.

**Figure 3.10  Single Home button**

![Single Home button](Images/tf_new_home_button.png)

Each card in the overview screen represents an app the user has interacted with in the past ([Figure 3.11](#ch03s04.xhtml_ss_tf_overview_screen "Figure 3.11  Overview screen")). (By the way, the overview screen is often called the “Recents screen” or “task manager” by users. We defer to the developer documentation, which calls it the “overview screen.”)

**Figure 3.11  Overview screen**

![Overview screen](Images/tf_overview_screen.png)

Click on the GeoQuiz task card in the overview screen. <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> will fill the screen.

A quick look at Logcat shows that your activity got calls to <samp class="methodname">onStart()</samp> and <samp class="methodname">onResume()</samp>. Note that <samp class="methodname">onCreate(…)</samp> was not called. This is because <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> was in the stopped state after the user pressed the Home button. Because the activity instance was still in memory, it did not need to be created. Instead, the activity only had to be started (moved to the paused/visible state) and then resumed (moved to the resumed/foreground state).

Earlier, we said that it is possible for an activity to hang out in the paused state, either partially visible (such as when a new activity with either a transparent background or a smaller-than-screen size is launched on top) or fully visible (in multi-window mode). Let’s see multi-window mode in action.

Multi-window mode is only available on Android 7.0 Nougat and higher, so use an emulator to test it if your device is running an earlier version of Android. Open the overview screen again and long-press the icon at the top of the GeoQuiz card. Select <samp class="guilabel">Split screen</samp> (shown on the left in [Figure 3.12](#ch03s04.xhtml_ss_tf_multi_window_mode "Figure 3.12  Opening two apps in multi-window mode")), and a new window appears on the bottom portion of the screen displaying a list of app cards (shown in the center in [Figure 3.12](#ch03s04.xhtml_ss_tf_multi_window_mode "Figure 3.12  Opening two apps in multi-window mode")). Click on one of the cards to launch the corresponding app.

This launches multi-window mode with GeoQuiz in the top window and the second app you selected in the bottom window (shown on the right in [Figure 3.12](#ch03s04.xhtml_ss_tf_multi_window_mode "Figure 3.12  Opening two apps in multi-window mode")).

**Figure 3.12  Opening two apps in multi-window mode**

![Opening two apps in multi-window mode](Images/tf_multi_window_mode.png)

Now, click on the app in the bottom window and look at the logs in Logcat. <samp class="methodname">onPause()</samp> was called on <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>, so the activity is now in the paused state. Click on GeoQuiz in the top window. <samp class="methodname">onResume()</samp> was called on <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>, so the activity is now in the resumed state.

To exit multi-window mode, swipe the window separator in the middle of the screen down to the bottom of the screen to dismiss the bottom window. (Swiping the separator up dismisses the top window.)

### Finishing an activity

Press the Back button on the device and then check Logcat. Your activity received calls to <samp class="methodname">onPause()</samp>, <samp class="methodname">onStop()</samp>, and <samp class="methodname">onDestroy()</samp> ([Figure 3.13](#ch03s04.xhtml_fig_tf_logcat_on_pressing_back "Figure 3.13  Pressing the Back button destroys the activity")). Your <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> instance is now in the nonexistent state (not in memory and thus not visible – and certainly not active in the foreground).

**Figure 3.13  Pressing the Back button destroys the activity**

![Pressing the Back button destroys the activity](Images/tf_press_back_logcat_cropped_text.png)

When you pressed the Back button, you as the user of the app <samp class="firstterm">finished</samp> the activity. In other words, you told Android, “I’m done with this activity, and I won’t need it anymore.” Android then destroyed your activity’s view and removed all traces of the activity from memory. This is Android’s way of being frugal with your device’s limited resources.

Another way the user can finish an activity is to swipe the app’s card from the overview screen. As a developer, you can programmatically finish an activity by calling <samp class="methodname">Activity.finish()</samp>.

### Rotating an activity

Now it is time to get back to the bug you found at the beginning of this chapter. Run GeoQuiz, press the <samp class="guibutton">NEXT</samp> button to reveal the second question, and then rotate the device. (On the emulator, click the rotation icon in the toolbar.)

After rotating, GeoQuiz will display the first question again. Check Logcat to see what has happened. Your output should look like [Figure 3.14](#ch03s04.xhtml_fig_tf_logcat_on_rotation "Figure 3.14  MainActivity is dead. Long live MainActivity!").

**Figure 3.14  `MainActivity` is dead. Long live `MainActivity`!**

![MainActivity is dead. Long live MainActivity!](Images/tf_rotate_logcat_cropped_text.png)

When you rotated the device, the instance of <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> that you were looking at was destroyed, and a new one was created. Rotate the device again to witness another round of destruction and rebirth.

This is the source of your GeoQuiz bug. Each time you rotate the device, the current <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> instance is completely destroyed. The value that was stored in <samp class="varname">currentIndex</samp> in that instance is wiped from memory. This means that when you rotate, GeoQuiz forgets which question you were looking at. As rotation finishes, Android creates a new instance of <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> from scratch. <samp class="varname">currentIndex</samp> is initialized to `0` in <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp>, and the user starts over at the first question.

You will fix this bug in [Chapter 4](../Text/ch04.xhtml "4 Persisting UI State"). Before making the fix, take a closer look at why the OS destroys your activity when the user rotates the device.

## Device Configuration Changes and the Activity Lifecycle

Rotating the device changes the <samp class="firstterm">device configuration</samp>. The device configuration is a set of characteristics that describe the current state of an individual device. The characteristics that make up the configuration include screen orientation, screen density, screen size, keyboard type, dock mode, language, and more.

Typically, applications provide alternative resources to match device configurations. You saw an example of this when you added multiple arrow icons to your project for different screen densities.

When a <samp class="firstterm">runtime configuration change</samp> occurs, there may be resources that are a better match for the new configuration. So Android destroys the activity, looks for resources that are the best fit for the new configuration, and then rebuilds a new instance of the activity with those resources. To see this in action, create an alternative resource for Android to find and use when the device’s screen orientation changes to landscape.

### Creating a landscape layout

In the project tool window, right-click the <samp class="guilabel">res</samp> directory and select <samp class="guimenu">New</samp> → <samp class="guimenuitem">Android Resource File</samp>. You should see a window similar to [Figure 3.15](#ch03s05.xhtml_fig_tf_new_res_folder "Figure 3.15  Creating a new resource file") that lists the resource types and qualifiers for those types. Type <samp class="guilabel">activity_main</samp> in the <samp class="guilabel">File name</samp> field. Select <samp class="guilabel">Layout</samp> in the <samp class="guilabel">Resource type</samp> dropdown. Type <samp class="guilabel">FrameLayout</samp> in the <samp class="guilabel">Root element</samp> field. Leave the <samp class="guilabel">Source set</samp> option set to <samp class="guilabel">main</samp>.

**Figure 3.15  Creating a new resource file**

![Creating a new resource file](Images/tf_new_res_directory.png)

Next, you will choose how the new layout resource will be qualified. Select <samp class="guilabel">Orientation</samp> in the <samp class="guilabel">Available qualifiers</samp> list and click the <samp class="guibutton">>></samp> button to move <samp class="guilabel">Orientation</samp> to the <samp class="guilabel">Chosen qualifiers</samp> section.

Finally, ensure that <samp class="guilabel">Landscape</samp> is selected in the <samp class="guilabel">Screen orientation</samp> dropdown, as shown in [Figure 3.16](#ch03s05.xhtml_fig_tf_new_res_folder_land "Figure 3.16  Creating res/layout-land/activity_main.xml"). Verify that the <samp class="guilabel">Directory name</samp> now shows <samp class="guilabel">layout-land</samp>. While this window looks fancy, its purpose is just to determine the name of the directory where the new resource file will be placed. Click <samp class="guibutton">OK</samp>.

**Figure 3.16  Creating `res/layout-land/activity_main.xml`**

![Creating res/layout-land/activity_main.xml](Images/tf_new_res_directory_land.png)

Android Studio will create the <samp class="filename">res/layout-land/</samp> folder in your project and place a new layout file named <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp> in the new folder. Switch the project tool window to the <samp class="guilabel">Project</samp> view to see the files and folders in your project as they actually are. Switch back to the <samp class="guilabel">Android</samp> view to see the summary of the files.

As you have seen, configuration qualifiers on <samp class="filename">res</samp> subdirectories are how Android identifies which resources best match the current device configuration. The <samp class="filename">-land</samp> suffix is another example of a configuration qualifier. You can find the list of configuration qualifiers that Android recognizes and the aspects of the device configuration that they refer to at [<samp class="uri">developer.android.com/​guide/​topics/​resources/​providing-resources.html</samp>](https://developer.android.com/guide/topics/resources/providing-resources.html).

You now have a landscape layout and a default layout. When the device is in landscape orientation, Android will find and use layout resources in the <samp class="filename">res/layout-land</samp> directory. Otherwise, it will stick with the default in <samp class="filename">res/layout/</samp>. Note that the two layout files must have the same filename so that they can be referenced with the same resource ID.

At the moment, <samp class="filename">res/layout-land/activity_main.xml</samp> displays an empty screen. To fix this, copy all the contents except the root <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp> open and closing tags from <samp class="filename">res/layout/activity_main.xml</samp>. Paste the code into <samp class="filename">res/layout-land/activity_main.xml</samp>, between the open and closing <samp class="classname">FrameLayout</samp> tags.

Next, make the changes shown in [Listing 3.4](#ch03s05.xhtml_pl_tweak_landscape "Listing 3.4  Tweaking the landscape layout (res/layout-land/activity_main.xml)") to the landscape layout so that it is different from the default.

**Listing 3.4  Tweaking the landscape layout (`res/layout-land/activity_main.xml`)**

```
<FrameLayout xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    xmlns:tools="http://schemas.android.com/tools"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="match_parent" >

    <TextView
        android:id="@+id/question_text_view"
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:gravity="center"
        android:layout_gravity="center_horizontal"
        android:padding="24dp"
        tools:text="@string/question_australia"/>

    <LinearLayout
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:orientation="horizontal"
        android:layout_gravity="center_vertical|center_horizontal">

        <Button
            .../>

        <Button
            .../>

    </LinearLayout>

    <Button
        android:id="@+id/next_button"
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:layout_gravity="bottom|right"
        android:text="@string/next_button"
        android:drawableEnd="@drawable/arrow_right"
        android:drawablePadding="4dp"/>

</FrameLayout>
```

<samp class="classname">FrameLayout</samp> is the simplest <samp class="classname">ViewGroup</samp> and does not arrange its children in any particular manner. In this layout, child views will be arranged according to their `android:layout_gravity` attributes. This is why you added `android:layout_gravity` to <samp class="classname">TextView</samp>, <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp>, and <samp class="classname">Button</samp> – they are all children of the <samp class="classname">FrameLayout</samp>. The <samp class="classname">Button</samp> children of the nested <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp> can stay exactly the same since they are not direct children of the <samp class="classname">FrameLayout</samp>.

Run GeoQuiz again. Rotate the device to landscape to see the new layout ([Figure 3.17](#ch03s05.xhtml_ss_tf_landscape "Figure 3.17  MainActivity in landscape orientation")). Of course, this is not just a new layout – it is a new <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> instance as well.

**Figure 3.17  `MainActivity` in landscape orientation**

![MainActivity in landscape orientation](Images/tf_landscape_interface.png)

Rotate back to portrait to see the default layout and yet another new <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>.

What good is an app that resets itself when the user rotates the device, even if it has a lovely landscape-specific layout? In [Chapter 4](../Text/ch04.xhtml "4 Persisting UI State"), you will learn how to fix the GeoQuiz bug caused by the rotation problem.

## For the More Curious: UI Updates and Multi-Window Mode

Prior to Android 7.0 Nougat, most activities spent very little time in the paused state. Instead, activities passed through the paused state quickly on their way to either the resumed state or the stopped state. Because of this, many developers assumed they only needed to update their UI when their activity was in the resumed state. It was common practice to use <samp class="methodname">onResume()</samp> and <samp class="methodname">onPause()</samp> to start or stop any ongoing updates related to the UI (such as animations or data refreshes).

When multi-window mode was introduced in Nougat, it broke the assumption that resumed activities were the only fully visible activities. This, in turn, broke the intended behavior of many apps. Now, paused activities can be fully visible for extended periods of time when the user is in multi-window mode. And users will expect those paused activities to behave as if they were resumed.

Consider video, for example. Suppose you have a pre-Nougat app that provides simple video playback. You start (or resume) video playback in <samp class="methodname">onResume()</samp> and pause playback in <samp class="methodname">onPause()</samp>. Multi-window mode comes along, but your app stops playback when it is paused and users are interacting with another app in the second window. Users start complaining, because they want to watch their videos <samp class="emphasis">while</samp> they send a text message in a separate window.

Luckily, the fix is relatively simple: Move your playback resuming and pausing to <samp class="methodname">onStart()</samp> and <samp class="methodname">onStop()</samp>. This goes for any live-updating data, like a photo gallery app that refreshes to show new images as they are pushed to a Flickr stream (as you will see later in this book).

In short, in the post-Nougat world, your activities should update the UI during their entire visible lifecycle, from <samp class="methodname">onStart()</samp> to <samp class="methodname">onStop()</samp>.

Unfortunately, not everyone got the memo, and many apps still misbehave in multi-window mode. To fix this, the Android team introduced a spec to support <samp class="firstterm">multi-resume</samp> for multi-window mode in November 2018\. Multi-resume means that the fully visible activity in each of the windows will be in the resumed state when the device is in multi-window mode, regardless of which window the user last touched.

You can opt in to using multi-resume mode for your app when it is running on Android 9.0 Pie by adding metadata to your Android manifest: `<meta-data android:name="android.allow_multiple_resumed_activities" android:value="true" />`. You will learn more about the manifest in [Chapter 6](../Text/ch06.xhtml "6 Your Second Activity").

Even if you opt in, multi-resume will only work on devices whose manufacturer implemented the multi-resume spec. And, as of this writing, no devices on the market implement it. However, there are rumors that the spec will become mandatory in the next version of Android (the yet-to-be-named Android Q).

Until multi-resume becomes a readily available standard across most devices in the marketplace, use your knowledge of the activity lifecycle to reason about where to place UI update code. You will get a lot of practice doing so throughout the course of this book.

## For the More Curious: Log Levels

When you use the <samp class="classname">android.util.Log</samp> class to send log messages, you control not only the content of a message but also a <samp class="firstterm">level</samp> that specifies how important the message is. Android supports five log levels, shown in [Table 3.2](#ch03s07.xhtml_table_tf_log_levels "Table 3.2  Log levels and functions"). Each level has a corresponding function in the <samp class="classname">Log</samp> class. Sending output to the log is as simple as calling the corresponding <samp class="classname">Log</samp> function.

**Table 3.2  Log levels and functions**

| Log level | Function | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ERROR | <samp class="methodname">Log.e(…)</samp> | errors |
| WARNING | <samp class="methodname">Log.w(…)</samp> | warnings |
| INFO | <samp class="methodname">Log.i(…)</samp> | informational messages |
| DEBUG | <samp class="methodname">Log.d(…)</samp> | debug output (may be filtered out) |
| VERBOSE | <samp class="methodname">Log.v(…)</samp> | development only |

In addition, each of the logging functions has two signatures: one that takes a <samp class="varname">TAG</samp> string and a message string, and a second that takes those two arguments plus an instance of <samp class="classname">Throwable</samp>, which makes it easy to log information about a particular exception that your application might throw. [Listing 3.5](#ch03s07.xhtml_fig_os_android_log_methods "Listing 3.5  Different ways of logging in Android") shows some sample log function signatures.

**Listing 3.5  Different ways of logging in Android**

```
// Log a message at DEBUG log level
Log.d(TAG, "Current question index: $currentIndex")

try {
    val question = questionBank[currentIndex]
} catch (ex: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException) {
    // Log a message at ERROR log level, along with an exception stack trace
    Log.e(TAG, "Index was out of bounds", ex)
}
```

Once a user provides an answer for a particular question, disable the buttons for that question to prevent multiple answers being entered.

# <samp class="chapter_number">4</samp>
<samp class="chapter_name">Persisting UI State</samp>

Android does a great job of providing alternative resources at the right time. However, destroying and re-creating activities on rotation can cause headaches, such as GeoQuiz’s bug of reverting back to the first question when the device is rotated.

To fix this bug, the post-rotation <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> instance needs to know the old value of <samp class="varname">currentIndex</samp>. You need a way to save this data across a runtime configuration change, like rotation.

In this chapter you will fix GeoQuiz’s UI state loss on rotation bug by storing its UI data in a <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp>. You will also address a less easily discoverable, but equally problematic, bug – UI state loss on process death – using Android’s saved instance state mechanism.

## Including the ViewModel Dependency

In a moment, you are going to add a <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> class to your project. The <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> class comes from an Android Jetpack library called `lifecycle-extensions`, one of many libraries that you will use throughout this book. (You will learn more about Jetpack later in this chapter.) To use the class, you must first include the library in the list of <samp class="firstterm">dependencies</samp> for your project.

Your project’s dependencies live in a file called <samp class="filename">build.gradle</samp> (recall that Gradle is the Android build tool). In the project tool window, with the <samp class="guilabel">Android</samp> view enabled, expand the <samp class="guilabel">Gradle scripts</samp> section and take a look at the contents. Your project actually comes with two <samp class="filename">build.gradle</samp> files: one for the project as a whole and one for your app module. Open the <samp class="filename">build.gradle</samp> file located in your app module. You should see something similar to [Listing 4.1](#ch04s01.xhtml_tfUIState_gradle_dependencies "Listing 4.1  Gradle dependencies (app/build.gradle)").

**Listing 4.1  Gradle dependencies (`app/build.gradle`)**

```
apply plugin: 'com.android.application'

apply plugin: 'kotlin-android'

apply plugin: 'kotlin-android-extensions'

android {
    ...
}

dependencies {
    implementation fileTree(dir: 'libs', include: ['*.jar'])
    implementation"org.jetbrains.kotlin:kotlin-stdlib-jdk7:$kotlin_version"
    implementation 'androidx.appcompat:appcompat:1.0.0-beta01'
    ...
}
```

The first line in the `dependencies` section specifies that the project depends on all of the <samp class="filename">.jar</samp> files in its <samp class="filename">libs</samp> directory. The other lines list libraries that were automatically included in your project based on the settings you selected when you created it.

Gradle also allows for the specification of new dependencies. When your app is compiled, Gradle will find, download, and include the dependencies for you. All you have to do is specify an exact string incantation and Gradle will do the rest.

Add the `lifecycle-extensions` dependency to your <samp class="filename">app/build.gradle</samp> file, as shown in [Listing 4.2](#ch04s01.xhtml_tfUIState_add_viewmodel_dependency "Listing 4.2  Adding lifecycle-extensions dependency (app/build.gradle)"). Its exact placement in the `dependencies` section does not matter, but to keep things tidy it is good to put new dependencies under the last existing `implementation` dependency.

**Listing 4.2  Adding `lifecycle-extensions` dependency (`app/build.gradle`)**

```
dependencies {
    ...
    implementation 'androidx.constraintlayout:constraintlayout:1.1.2'
    implementation 'androidx.lifecycle:lifecycle-extensions:2.0.0'
    ...
}
```

When you make any change to <samp class="filename">build.gradle</samp>, Android Studio will prompt you to sync the file ([Figure 4.1](#ch04s01.xhtml_ss_tfUIState_gradle_sync_prompt "Figure 4.1  Gradle sync prompt")).

**Figure 4.1  Gradle sync prompt**

![Gradle sync prompt](Images/tf_gradle_sync_prompt.png)

This sync asks Gradle to update the build based on your changes by either downloading or removing dependencies. To sync, either click <samp class="guilabel">Sync Now</samp> in the prompt or select <samp class="guimenu">File</samp> → <samp class="guimenuitem">Sync Project with Gradle Files</samp>.

## Adding a ViewModel

Now, back to <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp>. A <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> is related to one particular screen and is a great place to put logic involved in formatting the data to display on that screen. A <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> holds on to a model object and “decorates” the model – adding functionality to display onscreen that you might not want in the model itself. Using a <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> aggregates all the data the screen needs in one place, formats the data, and makes it easy to access the end result.

<samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> is part of the androidx.lifecycle package, which contains lifecycle-related APIs including <samp class="firstterm">lifecycle-aware</samp> components. Lifecycle-aware components observe the lifecycle of some other component, such as an activity, and take the state of that lifecycle into account.

Google created the androidx.lifecycle package and its contents to make dealing with the activity lifecycle (and other lifecycles, which you will learn about later in this book) a little less painful. You will learn about <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp>, another lifecycle-aware component, in [Chapter 11](../Text/ch11.xhtml "11 Databases and the Room Library"). And you will learn how to create your own lifecycle-aware components in [Chapter 25](../Text/ch25.xhtml "25 Loopers, Handlers, and HandlerThread").

Now you are ready to create your <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> subclass, <samp class="classname">QuizViewModel</samp>. In the project tool window, right-click the <samp class="guilabel">com.bignerdranch.android.geoquiz</samp> package and select <samp class="guimenu">New</samp> → <samp class="guimenuitem">Kotlin File/Class</samp>. Enter <samp class="guilabel">QuizViewModel</samp> for the name and select <samp class="guilabel">Class</samp> from the <samp class="guilabel">Kind</samp> dropdown.

In <samp class="filename">QuizViewModel.kt</samp>, add an `init` block and override <samp class="methodname">onCleared()</samp>. Log the creation and destruction of the <samp class="classname">QuizViewModel</samp> instance, as shown in [Listing 4.3](#ch04s02.xhtml_tfUIState_add_empty_viewmodel "Listing 4.3  Creating a ViewModel class (QuizViewModel.kt)").

**Listing 4.3  Creating a `ViewModel` class (`QuizViewModel.kt`)**

```
private const val TAG = "QuizViewModel"

class QuizViewModel : ViewModel() {

    init {
        Log.d(TAG, "ViewModel instance created")
    }

    override fun onCleared() {
        super.onCleared()
        Log.d(TAG, "ViewModel instance about to be destroyed")
    }
}
```

The <samp class="methodname">onCleared()</samp> function is called just before a <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> is destroyed. This is a useful place to perform any cleanup, such as un-observing a data source.
