For now, you simply log the fact that the <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> is about to be destroyed so that you can explore its lifecycle (the same way you explored the lifecycle of <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> in [Chapter 3](../Text/ch03.xhtml "3 The Activity Lifecycle")).

Now, open <samp class="filename">MainActivity.kt</samp> and, in <samp class="methodname">onCreate(…)</samp>, associate the activity with an instance of <samp class="classname">QuizViewModel</samp>.

**Listing 4.4  Accessing the `ViewModel` (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    ...
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        ...
        setContentView(R.layout.activity_main)

        val provider: ViewModelProvider = ViewModelProviders.of(this)
        val quizViewModel = provider.get(QuizViewModel::class.java)
        Log.d(TAG, "Got a QuizViewModel: $quizViewModel")

        trueButton = findViewById(R.id.true_button)
        ...
    }
    ...
}
```

The <samp class="classname">ViewModelProviders</samp> class (note the plural “Providers”) provides instances of the <samp class="classname">ViewModelProvider</samp> class. Your call to <samp class="function">ViewModelProviders.of(this)</samp> creates and returns a <samp class="classname">ViewModelProvider</samp> associated with the activity.

<samp class="classname">ViewModelProvider</samp> (no plural), on the other hand, provides instances of <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> to the activity. Calling <samp class="methodname">provider.get(QuizViewModel::class.java)</samp> returns an instance of <samp class="classname">QuizViewModel</samp>. You will most often see these functions chained together, like so:

```
 ViewModelProviders.of(this).get(QuizViewModel::class.java)
```

The <samp class="classname">ViewModelProvider</samp> acts like a registry of <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp>s. When the activity queries for a <samp class="classname">QuizViewModel</samp> for the first time, <samp class="classname">ViewModelProvider</samp> creates and returns a new <samp class="classname">QuizViewModel</samp> instance. When the activity queries for the <samp class="classname">QuizViewModel</samp> after a configuration change, the instance that was first created is returned. When the activity is finished (such as when the user presses the Back button), the <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp>-<samp class="classname">Activity</samp> pair is removed from memory.

### ViewModel lifecycle and ViewModelProvider

You learned in [Chapter 3](../Text/ch03.xhtml "3 The Activity Lifecycle") that activities transition between four states: resumed, paused, stopped, and nonexistent. You also learned about different ways an activity can be destroyed: either by the user finishing the activity or by the system destroying it as a result of a configuration change.

When the user finishes an activity, they expect their UI state to be reset. When the user rotates an activity, they expect their UI state to be the same before and after rotation.

You can determine which of these two scenarios is happening by checking the activity’s `isFinishing` property. If `isFinishing` is `true`, the activity is being destroyed because the user finished the activity (such as by pressing the Back button or by clearing the app’s card from the overview screen). If `isFinishing` is `false`, the activity is being destroyed by the system because of a configuration change.

But you do not need to track `isFinishing` and preserve UI state manually when it is `false` just to meet your user’s expectations. Instead, you can use a <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> to keep an activity’s UI state data in memory across configuration changes. A <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp>’s lifecycle more closely mirrors the user’s expectations: It survives configuration changes and is destroyed only when its associated activity is finished.

You associate a <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> instance with an activity’s lifecycle, as you did in [Listing 4.4](#ch04s02.xhtml_tfUIState_access_viewmodel "Listing 4.4  Accessing the ViewModel (MainActivity.kt)"). The <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> is then said to be <samp class="firstterm">scoped</samp> to that activity’s lifecycle. This means the <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> will remain in memory, regardless of the activity’s state, until the activity is finished. Once the activity is finished (such as by the user pressing the Back button), the <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> instance is destroyed ([Figure 4.2](#ch04s02.xhtml_dig_activity_isfinishing_affect_on_viewmodel "Figure 4.2  QuizViewModel scoped to MainActivity")).

**Figure 4.2  `QuizViewModel` scoped to `MainActivity`**

![QuizViewModel scoped to MainActivity](Images/dig_activity_isfinishing_affect_on_viewmodel.png)

This means that the <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> stays in memory during a configuration change, such as rotation. During the configuration change, the activity instance is destroyed and re-created, but the <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp>s scoped to the activity stay in memory. This is depicted in [Figure 4.3](#ch04s02.xhtml_dig_rotation_with_ViewModel "Figure 4.3  MainActivity and QuizViewModel across rotation"), using <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> and <samp class="classname">QuizViewModel</samp>.

**Figure 4.3  `MainActivity` and `QuizViewModel` across rotation**

![MainActivity and QuizViewModel across rotation](Images/rotation_with_ViewModel.png)

To see this in action, run GeoQuiz. In Logcat, select <samp class="guilabel">Edit Filter Configuration</samp> in the dropdown to create a new filter. In the <samp class="guilabel">Log Tag</samp> box, enter <samp class="guilabel">QuizViewModel|MainActivity</samp> (that is, the two class names with the pipe character | between them) to show only logs tagged with either class name. Name the filter <samp class="guilabel">ViewModelAndActivity</samp> (or another name that makes sense to you) and click <samp class="guibutton">OK</samp> ([Figure 4.4](#ch04s02.xhtml_ss_tfUIState_log_filter "Figure 4.4  Filtering QuizViewModel and MainActivity logs")).

**Figure 4.4  Filtering `QuizViewModel` and `MainActivity` logs**

![Filtering QuizViewModel and MainActivity logs](Images/ss_tfUIState_log_filter.png)

Now look at the logs. When <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> first launches and queries for the <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> in <samp class="methodname">onCreate(…)</samp>, a new <samp class="classname">QuizViewModel</samp> instance is created. This is reflected in the logs ([Figure 4.5](#ch04s02.xhtml_ss_tfUIState_viewmodel_instance_created "Figure 4.5  QuizViewModel instance created")).

**Figure 4.5  `QuizViewModel` instance created**

![QuizViewModel instance created](Images/ss_tfUIState_viewmodel_instance_created.png)

Rotate the device. The logs show the activity is destroyed ([Figure 4.6](#ch04s02.xhtml_ss_tfUIState_viewmodel_cached_instance "Figure 4.6  MainActivity is destroyed and re-created; QuizViewModel persists")). The <samp class="classname">QuizViewModel</samp> is not. When the new instance of <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> is created after rotation, it requests a <samp class="classname">QuizViewModel</samp>. Since the original <samp class="classname">QuizViewModel</samp> is still in memory, the <samp class="classname">ViewModelProvider</samp> returns that instance rather than creating a new one.

**Figure 4.6  `MainActivity` is destroyed and re-created; `QuizViewModel` persists**

![MainActivity is destroyed and re-created; QuizViewModel persists](Images/ss_tfUIState_viewmodel_cached_instance.png)

Finally, press the Back button. <samp class="methodname">QuizViewModel.onCleared()</samp> is called, indicating that the <samp class="classname">QuizViewModel</samp> instance is about to be destroyed, as the logs show ([Figure 4.7](#ch04s02.xhtml_ss_tfUIState_viewmodel_cleared "Figure 4.7  MainActivity and QuizViewModel destroyed")). The <samp class="classname">QuizViewModel</samp> is destroyed, along with the <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> instance.

**Figure 4.7  `MainActivity` and `QuizViewModel` destroyed**

![MainActivity and QuizViewModel destroyed](Images/ss_tfUIState_viewmodel_cleared.png)

The relationship between <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> and <samp class="classname">QuizViewModel</samp> is unidirectional. The activity references the <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp>, but the <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> does not access the activity. Your <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> should never hold a reference to an activity or a view, otherwise you will introduce a <samp class="firstterm">memory leak</samp>.

A memory leak occurs when one object holds a strong reference to another object that should be destroyed. Holding the strong reference prevents the garbage collector from clearing the object from memory. Memory leaks due to a configuration change are common bugs. The details of strong reference and garbage collection are outside the scope of this book. If you are not sure about these concepts, we recommend reading up on them in a Kotlin or Java reference.

Your <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> instance stays in memory across rotation, while your original activity instance gets destroyed. If the <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> held a strong reference to the original activity instance, two problems would occur: First, the original activity instance would not be removed from memory, and thus the activity would be leaked. Second, the <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> would hold a reference to a stale activity. If the <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> tried to update the view of the stale activity, it would trigger an <samp class="classname">IllegalStateException</samp>.

### Add data to your ViewModel

Now it is finally time to fix GeoQuiz’s rotation bug. <samp class="classname">QuizViewModel</samp> is not destroyed on rotation the way <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> is, so you can stash the activity’s UI state data in the <samp class="classname">QuizViewModel</samp> instance and it, too, will survive rotation.

You are going to copy the question and current index data from your activity to your <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp>, along with all the logic related to them. Begin by cutting the `currentIndex` and `questionBank` properties from <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> ([Listing 4.5](#ch04s02.xhtml_tfUIState_remove_model_code_from_activity "Listing 4.5  Cutting model data from activity (MainActivity.kt)")).

**Listing 4.5  Cutting model data from activity (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    ...
    private val questionBank = listOf(
        Question(R.string.question_australia, true),
        Question(R.string.question_oceans, true),
        Question(R.string.question_mideast, false),
        Question(R.string.question_africa, false),
        Question(R.string.question_americas, true),
        Question(R.string.question_asia, true)
    )

    private var currentIndex = 0
    ...
}
```

Now, paste the `currentIndex` and `questionBank` properties into <samp class="classname">QuizViewModel</samp>, as shown in [Listing 4.6](#ch04s02.xhtml_tfUIState_add_data_to_viewmodel "Listing 4.6  Pasting model data into QuizViewModel (QuizViewModel.kt)").

Remove the `private` access modifier from `currentIndex` so the property value can be accessed by external classes, such as <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>. Leave the `private` access modifier on `questionBank` – <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> will not interact with the <samp class="varname">questionBank</samp> directly. Instead, it will call functions and computed properties you will add to <samp class="classname">QuizViewModel</samp>. While you are editing <samp class="classname">QuizViewModel</samp>, delete the <samp class="methodname">init</samp> and <samp class="methodname">onCleared()</samp> logging, as you will not use them again.

**Listing 4.6  Pasting model data into `QuizViewModel` (`QuizViewModel.kt`)**

```
class QuizViewModel : ViewModel() {

    init {
        Log.d(TAG, "ViewModel instance created")
    }

    override fun onCleared() {
        super.onCleared()
        Log.d(TAG, "ViewModel instance about to be destroyed")
    }

    private var currentIndex = 0

    private val questionBank = listOf(
       Question(R.string.question_australia, true),
       Question(R.string.question_oceans, true),
       Question(R.string.question_mideast, false),
       Question(R.string.question_africa, false),
       Question(R.string.question_americas, true),
       Question(R.string.question_asia, true)
   )
}
```

Next, add a function to <samp class="classname">QuizViewModel</samp> to advance to the next question. Also, add computed properties to return the text and answer for the current question.

**Listing 4.7  Adding business logic to `QuizViewModel` (`QuizViewModel.kt`)**

```
class QuizViewModel : ViewModel() {

    var currentIndex = 0

    private val questionBank = listOf(
       ...
    )

    val currentQuestionAnswer: Boolean
        get() = questionBank[currentIndex].answer

    val currentQuestionText: Int
        get() = questionBank[currentIndex].textResId

    fun moveToNext() {
        currentIndex = (currentIndex + 1) % questionBank.size
    }
}
```

Earlier, we said that a <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> stores all the data that its associated screen needs, formats it, and makes it easy to access. This allows you to remove presentation logic code from the activity, which in turn keeps your activity simpler. And keeping activities as simple as possible is a good thing: Any logic you put in your activity might be unintentionally affected by the activity’s lifecycle. Also, it allows the activity to be responsible for handling only what appears on the screen, not the logic behind determining the data to display.

However, you are going to leave the <samp class="methodname">updateQuestion()</samp> and <samp class="methodname">checkAnswer(Boolean)</samp> functions in <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>. You will update these functions shortly to call through to the new <samp class="classname">QuizViewModel</samp> computed properties you added. But you will keep them in <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> to help keep your activity code organized.

Next, add a lazily initialized property to stash the <samp class="classname">QuizViewModel</samp> instance associated with the activity.

**Listing 4.8  Lazily initializing `QuizViewModel` (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    ...
    private val quizViewModel: QuizViewModel by lazy {
        ViewModelProviders.of(this).get(QuizViewModel::class.java)
    }

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        ...
        val provider: ViewModelProvider = ViewModelProviders.of(this)
        val quizViewModel = provider.get(QuizViewModel::class.java)
        Log.d(TAG, "Got a QuizViewModel: $quizViewModel")
        ...
    }
    ...
}
```

Using `by lazy` allows you to make the <samp class="varname">quizViewModel</samp> property a `val` instead of a `var`. This is great, because you only need (and want) to grab and store the <samp class="classname">QuizViewModel</samp> when the activity instance is created – so <samp class="varname">quizViewModel</samp> should only be assigned a value one time.

More importantly, using `by lazy` means the <samp class="varname">quizViewModel</samp> calculation and assignment will not happen until the first time you access <samp class="varname">quizViewModel</samp>. This is good because you cannot safely access a <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> until <samp class="methodname">Activity.onCreate(…)</samp>. If you try to call <samp class="function">ViewModelProviders.of(this).get(QuizViewModel::class.java)</samp> before <samp class="methodname">Activity.onCreate(…)</samp>, your app will crash with an <samp class="classname">IllegalStateException</samp>.

Finally, update <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> to display content from and interact with your newly updated <samp class="classname">QuizViewModel</samp>.

**Listing 4.9  Updating question through `QuizViewModel` (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    ...
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        ...
        nextButton.setOnClickListener {
            currentIndex = (currentIndex + 1) % questionBank.size
            quizViewModel.moveToNext()
            updateQuestion()
        }
        ...
    }
    ...
    private fun updateQuestion() {
        val questionTextResId = questionBank[currentIndex].textResId
        val questionTextResId = quizViewModel.currentQuestionText
        questionTextView.setText(questionTextResId)
    }

    private fun checkAnswer(userAnswer: Boolean) {
        val correctAnswer = questionBank[currentIndex].answer
        val correctAnswer = quizViewModel.currentQuestionAnswer
        ...
    }
```

Run GeoQuiz, press <samp class="guibutton">NEXT</samp>, and rotate the device or emulator. No matter how many times you rotate, the newly minted <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> will “remember” what question you were on. Do a happy dance to celebrate solving the UI state loss on rotation bug.

But do not dance too long. There is another, less-easily-discoverable bug to squash.

## Saving Data Across Process Death

Configuration changes are not the only time the OS can destroy an activity even though the user does not intend it to. Each app gets its own <samp class="firstterm">process</samp> (more specifically, a Linux process) containing a single thread to execute UI-related work on and a piece of memory to store objects in.

An app’s process can be destroyed by the OS if the user navigates away for a while and Android needs to reclaim memory. When an app’s process is destroyed, all the objects stored in that process’s memory are destroyed. (You will learn more about Android application processes in [Chapter 23](../Text/ch23.xhtml "23 More About Intents and Tasks").)

Processes containing resumed or paused activities get higher priority than other processes. When the OS needs to free up resources, it will select lower-priority processes first. Practically speaking, a process containing a visible activity will not be reclaimed by the OS. If a foreground process does get reclaimed, that means something is horribly wrong with the device (and your app being killed is probably the least of the user’s concerns).

But stopped activities are fair game to be killed. So, for example, if the user presses the Home button and then goes and watches a video or plays a game, your app’s process might be destroyed.

(As of this writing, activities themselves are not individually destroyed in low-memory situations, even though the documentation reads like that is the case. Instead, Android clears an entire app process from memory, taking any of the app’s in-memory activities with it.)

When the OS destroys the app’s process, any of the app’s activities and <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp>s stored in memory will be wiped away. And the OS will not be nice about the destruction. It will not call any of the activity or <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> lifecycle callback functions.

So how can you save UI state data and use it to reconstruct the activity so that the user never even knows the activity was destroyed? One way to do this is to store data in <samp class="firstterm">saved instance state</samp>. Saved instance state is data the OS temporarily stores outside of the activity. You can add values to saved instance state by overriding <samp class="methodname">Activity.onSaveInstanceState(Bundle)</samp>.

The OS calls <samp class="methodname">Activity.onSaveInstanceState(Bundle)</samp> any time an activity that is not finished moves to the stopped state (such as when the user presses the Home button and then launches a different app). This timing is important, because stopped activities are marked as <samp class="firstterm">killable</samp>. If your app process is killed because it is a low-priority background app, then you can rest assured that <samp class="methodname">Activity.onSaveInstanceState(Bundle)</samp> was already called.

The default implementation of <samp class="methodname">onSaveInstanceState(Bundle)</samp> directs all of the activity’s views to save their state as data in the <samp class="classname">Bundle</samp> object. A <samp class="classname">Bundle</samp> is a structure that maps string keys to values of certain limited types.

You have seen this <samp class="classname">Bundle</samp> before. It is passed into <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp>:

```
 override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        ...
    }
```

When you override <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp>, you call <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp> on the activity’s superclass and pass in the bundle you just received. In the superclass implementation, the saved state of the views is retrieved and used to re-create the activity’s view hierarchy.

### Overriding onSaveInstanceState(Bundle)

You can override <samp class="methodname">onSaveInstanceState(Bundle)</samp> to save additional data to the bundle, which can then be read back in <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp>. This is how you are going to save the value of <samp class="varname">currentIndex</samp> across process death.

First, in <samp class="filename">MainActivity.kt</samp>, add a constant that will be the key for the key-value pair that will be stored in the bundle.

**Listing 4.10  Adding a key for the value (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
private const val TAG = "MainActivity"
private const val KEY_INDEX = "index"

class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    ...
}
```

Next, override <samp class="methodname">onSaveInstanceState(Bundle)</samp> to write the value of <samp class="varname">currentIndex</samp> to the bundle with the constant as its key.

**Listing 4.11  Overriding `onSaveInstanceState(…)` (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
override fun onPause() {
    ...
}

override fun onSaveInstanceState(savedInstanceState: Bundle) {
    super.onSaveInstanceState(savedInstanceState)
    Log.i(TAG, "onSaveInstanceState")
    savedInstanceState.putInt(KEY_INDEX,  quizViewModel.currentIndex)
}

override fun onStop() {
    ...
}
```

Finally, in <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp>, check for this value. If it exists, assign it to <samp class="varname">currentIndex</samp>. If a value with the key `"index"` does not exist in the bundle, or if the bundle object is null, set the value to 0.

**Listing 4.12  Checking bundle in `onCreate(Bundle?)` (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    Log.d(TAG, "onCreate(Bundle?) called")
    setContentView(R.layout.activity_main)

    val currentIndex = savedInstanceState?.getInt(KEY_INDEX, 0) ?: 0
    quizViewModel.currentIndex = currentIndex
    ...
}
```

<samp class="methodname">onCreate</samp> accepts a nullable bundle as input. This is because there is no state when a new instance of the activity is launched by the user the first time, so in this case the bundle would be null. When the activity is re-created after rotation or process death, the bundle object will be non-null. The non-null bundle will contain any key-value pairs you add in <samp class="methodname">onSaveInstanceState(Bundle)</samp>. The bundle may also contain additional information added by the framework, such as the contents of an <samp class="classname">EditText</samp> or other basic UI widget state.

Rotation is easy to test. And, luckily, so is the low-memory situation. Try it out now to see for yourself.

On your device or emulator, find and click on the Settings icon within the list of applications. You need to access the developer options, which are hidden by default. If you are using a hardware device, you may have enabled the developer options in [Chapter 2](../Text/ch02.xhtml "2 Android and Model-View-Controller"). If you are using an emulator (or you did not already enable developer options), go to <samp class="guimenu">System</samp> → <samp class="guimenuitem">About emulated device</samp> (or <samp class="guimenu">System</samp> → <samp class="guimenuitem">About Tablet/Phone</samp>). Scroll down and click (press) the <samp class="guilabel">Build number</samp> seven times in quick succession.

When you see <samp class="guilabel">You are now a developer!</samp>, use the Back button to return to the system settings. Scroll down to find <samp class="guilabel">Developer options</samp> (you may need to expand the <samp class="guilabel">Advanced</samp> section). On the <samp class="guilabel">Developer options</samp> screen you will see many possible settings. Scroll down to the <samp class="guilabel">Apps</samp> section and turn on the setting labeled <samp class="guilabel">Don’t keep activities</samp>, as shown in [Figure 4.8](#ch04s03.xhtml_ss_tf_apps_dev_tools_dont_keep_activities "Figure 4.8  Don’t keep activities").

**Figure 4.8  Don’t keep activities**

![Don’t keep activities](Images/ss_tf_apps_dev_tools_dont_keep_activities.png)

Now, run GeoQuiz, press <samp class="guibutton">NEXT</samp> to move to another question, and press the Home button. Pressing the Home button causes the activity to be paused and stopped, as you know. The logs tell you that the stopped activity has also been destroyed, just as if the Android OS had reclaimed it for its memory. However, as the logs also show, <samp class="methodname">onSaveInstanceState(Bundle)</samp> was also called – so there is hope.

Restore the app (using the list of apps on the device or emulator) to see whether your state was saved as you expected. Pat yourself on the back when GeoQuiz opens to the question you last saw.

Be sure to turn <samp class="guilabel">Don’t keep activities</samp> off when you are done testing, as it will cause a performance decrease. Remember that pressing the Back button instead of the Home button will always destroy the activity, regardless of whether you have this development setting on. Pressing the Back button tells the OS that the user is done with the activity.

### Saved instance state and activity records

How does the data you stash in <samp class="methodname">onSaveInstanceState(Bundle)</samp> survive the activity’s (and process’s) death? When <samp class="methodname">onSaveInstanceState(Bundle)</samp> is called, the data is saved to the <samp class="classname">Bundle</samp> object. That <samp class="classname">Bundle</samp> object is then stuffed into your activity’s <samp class="firstterm">activity record</samp> by the OS.

To understand the activity record, let’s add a <samp class="firstterm">stashed</samp> state to the activity lifecycle ([Figure 4.9](#ch04s03.xhtml_dig_criminalintent_activitylifecyclecomplete "Figure 4.9  The complete activity lifecycle")).

**Figure 4.9  The complete activity lifecycle**

![The complete activity lifecycle](Images/activity_lifecycle.png)

When your activity is stashed, an <samp class="classname">Activity</samp> object does not exist, but the activity record object lives on in the OS. The OS can reanimate the activity using the activity record when it needs to.

Note that your activity can pass into the stashed state without <samp class="methodname">onDestroy()</samp> being called. You can rely on <samp class="methodname">onStop()</samp> and <samp class="methodname">onSaveInstanceState(Bundle)</samp> being called (unless something has gone horribly wrong on the device). Typically, you override <samp class="methodname">onSaveInstanceState(Bundle)</samp> to stash small, transient-state data that belongs to the current activity in your <samp class="classname">Bundle</samp>. Override <samp class="methodname">onStop()</samp> to save any permanent data, such as things the user is editing, because your activity may be killed at any time after this function returns.

So when does the activity record get snuffed? When the activity finishes, it really gets destroyed, once and for all. At that point, your activity record is discarded. Activity records are also discarded on reboot. (For a reminder about what it means for an activity to finish, see [the section called *Finishing an activity*](#ch03s04.xhtml_sect-ci-user-initiated-dismissal "Finishing an activity") in [Chapter 3](../Text/ch03.xhtml "3 The Activity Lifecycle").)

## ViewModel vs Saved Instance State

While saved instance state stores an activity record across process death, it also stores an activity record across a configuration change. When you first launch the activity, the saved instance state bundle is null. When you rotate the device, the OS calls <samp class="methodname">onSaveInstanceState(Bundle)</samp> on your activity. The OS then passes the data you stashed in the bundle to <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp>.

If saved instance state protects from both configuration changes and process death, why bother with a <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> at all? To be fair, GeoQuiz is so simple that you could have gotten away with saved instance state only.

However, most apps do not rely on a small, hardcoded question bank data set like GeoQuiz does. Most apps these days pull dynamic data from a database, from the internet, or from a combination of both. These operations are asynchronous, can be slow, and use precious battery and networking resources. And tying these operations to the activity lifecycle can be very tedious and error prone.

<samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> really shines when you use it to orchestrate dynamic data for the activity, as you will see firsthand in [Chapter 11](../Text/ch11.xhtml "11 Databases and the Room Library") and [Chapter 24](../Text/ch24.xhtml "24 HTTP and Background Tasks"). For example, <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> makes continuing a download operation across a configuration change simple. It also offers an easy way to keep data that was expensive to load in memory across a configuration change. And, as you have seen, <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> gets cleaned up automatically once the user finishes the activity.

<samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> does not shine in the process death scenario since it gets wiped away from memory along with the process and everything in it. This is where saved instance state takes center stage. But saved instance state has its own limitations. Since saved instance state is serialized to disk, you should avoid stashing any large or complex objects.

As of this writing, the Android team is actively working to improve the developer experience using <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp>s. `lifecycle-viewmodel-savedstate` is a new library that was just released to allow <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp>s to save their state across process death. This should alleviate some of the difficulties of using <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp>s alongside saved instance state from your activities.

So it is not a matter of “which is better, <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> or saved instance state?” Savvy developers use saved instance state and <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> in harmony.

Use saved instance state to store the minimal amount of information necessary to re-create the UI state (for example, the current question index). Use <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> to cache the rich set of data needed to populate the UI in memory across configuration changes for quick and easy access. When the activity is re-created after process death, use the saved instance state information to set up the <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> as if the <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> and activity were never destroyed.

As of this writing, there is no easy way to determine whether an activity is being re-created after process death versus a configuration change. Why does this matter? A <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> stays in memory during a configuration change. So if you use the saved instance state data to update the <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> after the configuration change, you are making your app do unnecessary work. If the work causes the user to wait or uses their resources (like battery) unnecessarily, this redundant work is problematic.

One way to fix this problem is to make your <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> a little smarter. When setting a <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> value might result in more work, first check whether the data is fresh before doing the work to pull in and update the rest of the data:

```
 class SomeFancyViewModel : ViewModel() {
        ...
        fun setCurrentIndex(index: Int) {
            if (index != currentIndex) {
                currentIndex = index
                // Load current question from database
            }
        }
    }
```

Neither <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> nor saved instance state is a solution for long-term storage. If your app needs to store data that should live on as long as the app is installed on the device, regardless of your activity’s state, use a persistent storage alternative. You will learn about two local persistent storage options in this book: databases, in [Chapter 11](../Text/ch11.xhtml "11 Databases and the Room Library"), and shared preferences, in [Chapter 26](../Text/ch26.xhtml "26 SearchView and SharedPreferences"). Shared preferences is fine for very small, very simple data. A local database is a better option for larger, more complex data. In addition to local storage, you could store data on a remote server somewhere. You will learn how to access data from a web server in [Chapter 24](../Text/ch24.xhtml "24 HTTP and Background Tasks").

If GeoQuiz had many more questions, it could make sense to store the questions in a database or on a web server, rather than hardcoding them into the <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp>. Since the questions are constant, it makes sense to persist them independent of activity lifecycle state. But accessing databases is a relatively slow operation, compared to accessing values in memory. So it makes sense to load what you need to display your UI and retain that in memory while the UI is showing using a <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp>.

In this chapter, you squashed GeoQuiz’s state-loss bugs by correctly accounting for configuration changes and process death. In the next chapter, you will learn how to use Android Studio’s debugging tools to troubleshoot other, more app-specific bugs that might arise.

## For the More Curious: Jetpack, AndroidX, and Architecture Components

The `lifecycle-extensions` library containing <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> is part of Android Jetpack Components. Android Jetpack Components, called Jetpack for short, is a set of libraries created by Google to make various aspects of Android development easier. You can see a listing of all the Jetpack libraries at [<samp class="uri">developer.android.com/​jetpack</samp>](https://developer.android.com/jetpack). You can include any of these libraries in your project by adding the corresponding dependency to your <samp class="filename">build.gradle</samp> file, as you did in this chapter.

Each of the Jetpack libraries is located in a package that starts with `androidx`. For this reason, you will sometimes hear the terms “AndroidX” and “Jetpack” used interchangeably.

You may recall that the New Project wizard, as shown in [Figure 4.10](#ch04s05.xhtml_fig_tf_new_project_androidx "Figure 4.10  Adding Jetpack libraries"), has a checkbox for <samp class="guilabel">Use AndroidX artifacts</samp>. In almost every case, you should enable this option, as you did for GeoQuiz. This will add some initial Jetpack libraries to your project and set your app up to use them by default.

**Figure 4.10  Adding Jetpack libraries**

![Adding Jetpack libraries](Images/tf_new_project_1.png)

The Jetpack libraries are broken into four categories: foundation, architecture, behavior, and UI. Libraries in Jetpack’s architecture category are often referred to as <samp class="firstterm">architecture components</samp>. <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> is one such architecture component. You will learn about other major architecture components later in this book, including Room ([Chapter 11](../Text/ch11.xhtml "11 Databases and the Room Library")), Data Binding ([Chapter 19](../Text/ch19.xhtml "19 Data Binding and MVVM")), and WorkManager ([Chapter 27](../Text/ch27.xhtml "27 WorkManager")).

You will also learn about some foundation Jetpack libraries, including AppCompat ([Chapter 14](../Text/ch14.xhtml "14 The App Bar")), Test ([Chapter 20](../Text/ch20.xhtml "20 Unit Testing and Audio Playback")), and Android KTX ([Chapter 26](../Text/ch26.xhtml "26 SearchView and SharedPreferences")). You will use Notifications, a behavior Jetpack library, in [Chapter 27](../Text/ch27.xhtml "27 WorkManager"). And you will also use some UI Jetpack libraries, including Fragment ([Chapter 8](../Text/ch08.xhtml "8 UI Fragments and the Fragment Manager")) and Layouts ([Chapter 9](../Text/ch09.xhtml "9 Displaying Lists with RecyclerView") and [Chapter 10](../Text/ch10.xhtml "10 Creating User Interfaces with Layouts and Widgets")).

Some of the Jetpack components are entirely new. Others have been around for a while but were previously lumped into a handful of much larger libraries collectively called the Support Library. If you hear or see anything about the Support Library, know that you should now use the Jetpack (AndroidX) version of that library instead.

## For the More Curious: Avoiding a Half-Baked Solution

Some people try to address the UI state loss on configuration change bug in their app by disabling rotation. If the user cannot rotate the app, they never lose their UI state, right? That is true – but, sadly, this approach leaves your app prone to other bugs. While this smooths over the rough edge of rotation, it leaves other lifecycle bugs that users will surely encounter, but that will not necessarily present themselves during development and testing.

First, there are other configuration changes that can occur at runtime, such as window resizing and night mode changes. And yes, you could also capture and ignore or handle those changes. But this is just bad practice – it disables a feature of the system, which is to automatically select the right resources based on the runtime configuration changes.

Second, handling configuration changes or disabling rotation does not solve the process death issue.

If you want to lock your app into portrait or landscape mode <samp class="emphasis">because it makes sense for your app</samp>, you should still program defensively against configuration changes and process death. You are equipped to do so with your newfound knowledge of <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> and saved instance state.

In short, dealing with UI state loss by blocking configuration changes is bad form. We are only mentioning it so that you will recognize it as such if you see it out in the wild.

# <samp class="chapter_number">5</samp>
<samp class="chapter_name">Debugging Android Apps</samp>

In this chapter, you will find out what to do when apps get buggy. You will learn how to use Logcat, Android Lint, and the debugger that comes with Android Studio.

To practice debugging, the first step is to break something. In <samp class="filename">MainActivity.kt</samp>, comment out the code in <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp> where you find <samp class="varname">questionTextView</samp> by its ID.

**Listing 5.1  Commenting out a crucial line (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    ...
    trueButton = findViewById(R.id.true_button)
    falseButton = findViewById(R.id.false_button)
    nextButton = findViewById(R.id.next_button)
    // questionTextView = findViewById(R.id.question_text_view)
    ...
}
```

Run GeoQuiz and see what happens. The app will crash and burn almost immediately.

On versions before Android Pie (API 28), an error message appears telling you that the app crashed. On a device running Android Pie, if you watch the screen, you may see the app appear for a brief moment before vanishing without a word. In this case, launch the app again by pressing the GeoQuiz icon on the launcher screen. This time, when the app crashes you will see a message like the one shown in [Figure 5.1](#ch05.xhtml_ss_ci_debug_npe "Figure 5.1  GeoQuiz is about to E.X.P.L.O.D.E.").

**Figure 5.1  GeoQuiz is about to E.X.P.L.O.D.E.**

![GeoQuiz is about to E.X.P.L.O.D.E.](Images/exception_dialog.png)

Of course, you know exactly what is wrong with your app. But if you did not, it might help to look at your app from a new perspective.

## Exceptions and Stack Traces

Expand the Logcat tool window so that you can see what has happened. If you scroll up and down in Logcat, you should eventually find an expanse of red, as shown in [Figure 5.2](#ch05s01.xhtml_ss_ci_debug_logcat_view "Figure 5.2  Exception and stack trace in Logcat"). This is a standard `AndroidRuntime` exception report.

If you do not see much in Logcat and cannot find the exception, you may need to select the <samp class="guilabel">No Filters</samp> option in the filter dropdown. On the other hand, if you see too much in Logcat, you can adjust the <samp class="guilabel">Log Level</samp> to <samp class="guilabel">Error</samp>, which will show only the most severe log messages. You can also search for the text <samp class="guilabel">fatal exception</samp>, which will bring you straight to the exception that caused the app to crash.

**Figure 5.2  Exception and stack trace in Logcat**

![Exception and stack trace in Logcat](Images/logcat_exception.png)

The report tells you the top-level exception and its stack trace, then the exception that caused that exception and <samp class="emphasis">its</samp> stack trace, and so on until it finds an exception with no cause.

It may seem strange to see a java.lang exception in the stack trace, since you are writing Kotlin code. When building for Android, Kotlin code is compiled to the same kind of low-level bytecode to which Java code is compiled. During that process, many Kotlin exceptions are mapped to java.lang exception classes under the hood through type-aliasing. <samp class="classname">kotlin.RuntimeException</samp> is the superclass of <samp class="classname">kotlin.UninitializedPropertyAccessException</samp>, and it is aliased to <samp class="classname">java.lang.RuntimeException</samp> when running on Android.

In most of the code you will write, that last exception with no cause is the interesting one. Here, the exception without a cause is a <samp class="classname">kotlin.UninitializedPropertyAccessException</samp>. The line just below this exception is the first line in its stack trace. This line tells you the class and function where the exception occurred as well as what file and line number the exception occurred on. Click the blue link, and Android Studio will take you to that line in your source code.

The line to which you are taken is the first use of the <samp class="varname">questionTextView</samp> variable, inside <samp class="methodname">updateQuestion()</samp>. The name <samp class="classname">UninitializedPropertyAccessException</samp> gives you a hint to the problem: This variable was not initialized.

Uncomment the line initializing <samp class="varname">questionTextView</samp> to fix the bug.

**Listing 5.2  Uncommenting a crucial line (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    ...
    trueButton = findViewById(R.id.true_button)
    falseButton = findViewById(R.id.false_button)
    nextButton = findViewById(R.id.next_button)
    // questionTextView = findViewById(R.id.question_text_view)
    ...
}
```

When you encounter runtime exceptions, remember to look for the last exception in Logcat and the first line in its stack trace that refers to code that you have written. That is where the problem occurred, and it is the best place to start looking for answers.

If a crash occurs while a device is not plugged in, all is not lost. The device will store the latest lines written to the log. The length and expiration of the stored log depends on the device, but you can usually count on retrieving log results within 10 minutes. Just plug in the device and select it in the <samp class="guilabel">Devices</samp> view. Logcat will fill itself with the stored log.

### Diagnosing misbehaviors

Problems with your apps will not always be crashes. In some cases, they will be misbehaviors. For example, suppose that every time you pressed the <samp class="guibutton">NEXT</samp> button, nothing happened. That would be a noncrashing, misbehaving bug.

In <samp class="filename">MainActivity.kt</samp>, make a change to the <samp class="varname">nextButton</samp> listener to comment out the code that increments the question index.

**Listing 5.3  Forgetting a critical line of code (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    ...
    nextButton.setOnClickListener {
        // quizViewModel.moveToNext()
        updateQuestion()
    }
    ...
}
```

Run GeoQuiz and press the <samp class="guibutton">NEXT</samp> button. You should see no effect.

This bug is trickier than the last bug. It is not throwing an exception, so fixing the bug is not a simple matter of making the exception go away. On top of that, this misbehavior could be caused in two different ways: The index might not be changed, or <samp class="methodname">updateQuestion()</samp> might not be called.

You know what caused this bug, because you just introduced it intentionally. But if this type of bug popped up on its own and you had no idea what was causing the problem, you would need to track down the culprit. In the next few sections, you will see two ways to do this: diagnostic logging of a stack trace and using the debugger to set a breakpoint.

### Logging stack traces

In <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>, add a log statement to <samp class="methodname">updateQuestion()</samp>.

**Listing 5.4  `Exception` for fun and profit (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
private fun updateQuestion() {
    Log.d(TAG, "Updating question text", Exception())
    val questionTextResId = quizViewModel.currentQuestionText
    questionTextView.setText(questionTextResId)
}
```

The <samp class="methodname">Log.d(String, String, Throwable)</samp> version of <samp class="methodname">Log.d</samp> logs the entire stack trace, like the <samp class="classname">UninitializedPropertyAccessException</samp> you saw earlier. The stack trace will tell you where the call to <samp class="methodname">updateQuestion()</samp> was made.

The exception that you pass to <samp class="methodname">Log.d(String, String, Throwable)</samp> does not have to be a thrown exception that you caught. You can create a brand new <samp class="classname">Exception</samp> and pass it to the function without ever throwing it, and you will get a report of where the exception was created.

Run GeoQuiz, press the <samp class="guibutton">NEXT</samp> button, and then check the output in Logcat ([Figure 5.3](#ch05s01.xhtml_ss_ci_exception_logging "Figure 5.3  The results")).

**Figure 5.3  The results**

![The results](Images/ci_exception_logging_mac_cropped.png)

The top line in the stack trace is the line where you logged out the <samp class="classname">Exception</samp>. A few lines after that you can see where <samp class="methodname">updateQuestion()</samp> was called from within your <samp class="methodname">onClick(View)</samp> implementation. Click the link on this line, and you will be taken to where you commented out the line to increment your question index. But do not get rid of the bug; you are going to use the debugger to find it again in a moment.

Logging out stack traces is a powerful tool, but it is also a verbose one. Leave a bunch of these hanging around, and soon Logcat will be an unmanageable mess. Also, a competitor might steal your ideas by reading your stack traces to understand what your code is doing.

On the other hand, sometimes a stack trace showing what your code does is exactly what you need. If you are seeking help with a problem at [<samp class="uri">stackoverflow.com</samp>](https://stackoverflow.com) or [<samp class="uri">forums.bignerdranch.com</samp>](https://forums.bignerdranch.com), it often helps to include a stack trace. You can copy and paste lines directly from Logcat.

Before continuing, delete the log statement in <samp class="filename">MainActivity.kt</samp>.

**Listing 5.5  Farewell, old friend (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
private fun updateQuestion() {
    Log.d(TAG, "Updating question text", Exception())
    val questionTextResId = quizViewModel.currentQuestionText
    questionTextView.setText(questionTextResId)
}
```

### Setting breakpoints

Now you will use the debugger that comes with Android Studio to track down the same bug. You will set a <samp class="firstterm">breakpoint</samp> on <samp class="methodname">updateQuestion()</samp> to see whether it was called. A breakpoint pauses execution before the line executes and allows you to examine line by line what happens next.

In <samp class="filename">MainActivity.kt</samp>, return to the <samp class="methodname">updateQuestion()</samp> function. Next to the first line of this function, click the gray gutter area in the lefthand margin. You should now see a red circle in the left gutter like the one shown in [Figure 5.4](#ch05s01.xhtml_breakpoint "Figure 5.4  A breakpoint"). This is a breakpoint. You can also toggle a breakpoint on and off by placing the cursor on the desired line and pressing Command-F8 (Ctrl-F8).

**Figure 5.4  A breakpoint**

![A breakpoint](Images/ci_debug_set_breakpoint.png)

To engage the debugger and trigger your breakpoint, you need to debug your app instead of running it. To debug your app, click the <samp class="guilabel">Debug 'app'</samp> button ([Figure 5.5](#ch05s01.xhtml_debugg_app_buttons "Figure 5.5  Debug app buttons")). You can also navigate to <samp class="guimenu">Run</samp> → <samp class="guimenuitem">Debug 'app'</samp> in the menu bar. Your device will report that it is waiting for the debugger to attach, and then it will proceed normally.

**Figure 5.5  Debug app buttons**

![Debug app buttons](Images/run_and_attach_debugger_buttons.png)

In some circumstances, you may want to debug a running app without relaunching it. You can attach the debugger to a running application by clicking the <samp class="guilabel">Attach Debugger to Android Process</samp> button shown in [Figure 5.5](#ch05s01.xhtml_debugg_app_buttons "Figure 5.5  Debug app buttons") or by navigating to <samp class="guimenu">Run</samp> → <samp class="guimenuitem">Attach to process...</samp>. Choose your app’s process on the dialog that appears and click <samp class="guibutton">OK</samp>, and the debugger will attach. Note that breakpoints are only active when the debugger is attached, so any breakpoints that are hit before you attach the debugger will be ignored.

You want to debug GeoQuiz from the start of your code, which is why you used the <samp class="guilabel">Debug 'app'</samp> option. Shortly after your app is up and running with the debugger attached, it will pause. Firing up GeoQuiz called <samp class="methodname">MainActivity.onCreate(Bundle?)</samp>, which called <samp class="methodname">updateQuestion()</samp>, which hit your breakpoint. (If you had attached the debugger to the process after it had started, then the app likely would not pause, because <samp class="methodname">MainActivity.onCreate(Bundle?)</samp> would have executed before you could attach the debugger.)

In [Figure 5.6](#ch05s01.xhtml_debug_tool_window "Figure 5.6  Stop right there!"), you can see that <samp class="filename">MainActivity.kt</samp> is now open in the editor tool window and that the line with the breakpoint where execution has paused is highlighted. The debug tool window at the bottom of the screen is now visible. It contains the <samp class="guilabel">Frames</samp> and <samp class="guilabel">Variables</samp> views. (If the debug tool window did not open automatically, you can open it by clicking <samp class="guilabel">Debug</samp> at the bottom of the Android Studio window.)

**Figure 5.6  Stop right there!**

![Stop right there!](Images/ci_debug_tool_window.png)

You can use the arrow buttons at the top of the debug tool window ([Figure 5.7](#ch05s01.xhtml_debug_view "Figure 5.7  Debug tool window controls")) to step through your program. You can use the <samp class="guilabel">Evaluate Expression</samp> button to execute simple Kotlin statements on demand during debugging, which is a powerful tool.

**Figure 5.7  Debug tool window controls**

![Debug tool window controls](Images/debug_view_labeled.png)

You can see from the stack trace on the left that <samp class="methodname">updateQuestion()</samp> has been called from inside <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp>. But you are interested in investigating the <samp class="guibutton">NEXT</samp> button’s behavior, so click the <samp class="guilabel">Resume Program</samp> button to continue execution. Then press the <samp class="guibutton">NEXT</samp> button in GeoQuiz to see if your breakpoint is hit and execution is stopped. (It should be.)

Now that you are stopped at an interesting point of execution, you can take a look around. The <samp class="guilabel">Variables</samp> view allows you to examine the values of the objects in your program. At the top, you should see the value <samp class="varname">this</samp> (the <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> instance itself).

Expand the <samp class="varname">this</samp> variable to see all the variables declared in <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>, in <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>’s superclass (<samp class="classname">Activity</samp>), in <samp class="classname">Activity</samp>’s superclass, in its super-superclass, and so on. For now, focus on the variables that you created.

You are only interested in one value: <samp class="varname">quizViewModel.currentIndex</samp>. Scroll down in the variables view until you see <samp class="varname">quizViewModel</samp>. Expand <samp class="varname">quizViewModel</samp> and look for <samp class="varname">currentIndex</samp> ([Figure 5.8](#ch05s01.xhtml_variable_view "Figure 5.8  Inspecting variable values at runtime")).

**Figure 5.8  Inspecting variable values at runtime**

![Inspecting variable values at runtime](Images/debug_view_variable_pane.png)

You would expect <samp class="varname">currentIndex</samp> to have a value of `1`. You pressed the <samp class="guibutton">NEXT</samp> button, which should have resulted in <samp class="varname">currentIndex</samp> being incremented from `0` to `1`. However, as shown in [Figure 5.8](#ch05s01.xhtml_variable_view "Figure 5.8  Inspecting variable values at runtime"), <samp class="varname">currentIndex</samp> still has a value of <samp class="constant">0</samp>.

Check the code in the editor tool window. The code in <samp class="methodname">MainActivity.updateQuestion()</samp> simply updates the question text based the contents of <samp class="classname">QuizViewModel</samp>. There is no problem there. So where does the bug originate?

To continue your investigation, you need to step out of this function to determine what code was executed just before <samp class="methodname">MainActivity.updateQuestion()</samp>. To do this, click the <samp class="guilabel">Step Out</samp> button.

Check the editor tool window. It has now jumped you over to your <samp class="varname">nextButton</samp>’s <samp class="classname">OnClickListener</samp>, right after <samp class="methodname">updateQuestion()</samp> was called. Pretty nifty.

As you already knew, the problematic behavior is a result of <samp class="methodname">quizViewModel.moveToNext()</samp> never being called (because you commented it out). You will want to fix this implementation – but before you make any changes to code, you should stop debugging your app. If you edit your code while debugging, the code running with the debugger attached will be out of date compared to what is in the editor tool window, so the debugger can show misleading information compared to the updated code.

You can stop debugging in two ways: You can stop the program, or you can simply disconnect the debugger. To stop the program, click the <samp class="guibutton">Stop</samp> button shown in [Figure 5.7](#ch05s01.xhtml_debug_view "Figure 5.7  Debug tool window controls").

Now return your <samp class="classname">OnClickListener</samp> to its former glory.

**Listing 5.6  Returning to normalcy (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    ...
    nextButton.setOnClickListener {
        // quizViewModel.moveToNext()
        updateQuestion()
    }
    ...
}
```

You have tried out two ways of tracking down a misbehaving line of code: stack trace logging and setting a breakpoint in the debugger. Which is better? Each has its uses, and one or the other will probably end up being your favorite.

Logging out stack traces has the advantage that you can see stack traces from multiple places in one log. The downside is that to learn something new you have to add new log statements, rebuild, deploy, and navigate through your app to see what happened.

The debugger is more convenient. If you run your app with the debugger attached (or attach the debugger to the application’s process after it has started), then you can set a breakpoint while the application is running and poke around to get information about multiple issues.

## Android-Specific Debugging

Most Android debugging is just like Kotlin debugging. However, you will sometimes run into issues with Android-specific parts, such as resources, that the Kotlin compiler knows nothing about. In this section, you will learn about two kinds of Android-specific issues: Android Lint issues and issues with the <samp class="classname">R</samp> class.

### Using Android Lint

Android Lint (or just “Lint”) is a <samp class="firstterm">static analyzer</samp> for Android code. A static analyzer is a program that examines your code to find defects without running it. Lint uses its knowledge of the Android frameworks to look deeper into your code and find problems that the compiler cannot. In many cases, Lint’s advice is worth taking.

In [Chapter 7](../Text/ch07.xhtml "7 Android SDK Versions and Compatibility"), you will see Lint warn you about compatibility problems. Lint can also perform type-checking for objects that are defined in XML.

You can manually run Lint to see all of the potential issues in your project, including those that are less serious. Select <samp class="guimenu">Analyze</samp> → <samp class="guimenuitem">Inspect Code...</samp> from the menu bar. You will be asked which parts of your project you would like to inspect. Choose <samp class="guilabel">Whole project</samp> and click <samp class="guibutton">OK</samp>. Android Studio will run Android Lint as well as a few other static analyzers on your code, such as spelling and Kotlin checks.

Once the scan is complete, you will see categories of potential issues in the inspection tool window. Expand the <samp class="guilabel">Android</samp> and <samp class="guilabel">Lint</samp> categories to see Lint’s information about your project ([Figure 5.9](#ch05s02.xhtml_ss_ci_debug_lint_warnings "Figure 5.9  Lint warnings")).

**Figure 5.9  Lint warnings**

![Lint warnings](Images/ci_debug_lint_warnings_button.png)

(Do not be concerned if you see a different number of Lint warnings. The Android toolchain is constantly evolving, and new checks may have been added to Lint, new restrictions may have been added to the Android framework, and newer versions of tools and dependencies may have become available.)

Expand <samp class="guilabel">Internationalization</samp> and then, under it, expand <samp class="guilabel">Bidirectional Text</samp> to see more detailed information on this issue in your project. Click on <samp class="guilabel">Using left/right instead of start/end attributes</samp> to learn about this particular warning ([Figure 5.10](#ch05s02.xhtml_ss_ci_debug_lint_RTL_warnings "Figure 5.10  Lint warning description")).

**Figure 5.10  Lint warning description**

![Lint warning description](Images/ss_ci_debug_lint_RTL_warnings.png)

Lint is warning you that using `right` and `left` values for layout attributes could be problematic if your app is used on a device set to a language that reads from right to left instead of left to right. (You will learn about making your app ready for international use in [Chapter 17](../Text/ch17.xhtml "17 Localization").)

Dig further to see which file and line or lines of code caused the warning. Expand <samp class="guilabel">Using left/right instead of start/end attributes</samp>. Click on the offending file, <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp>, to see the snippet of code with the problem ([Figure 5.11](#ch05s02.xhtml_ss_ci_debug_lint_RTL_warnings_activity_main "Figure 5.11  Viewing the code that caused the warning")).

**Figure 5.11  Viewing the code that caused the warning**

![Viewing the code that caused the warning](Images/ss_ci_debug_lint_RTL_warnings_activity_main.png)

Double-click on the warning description that appears under the filename. This will open <samp class="filename">res/layout/land/activity_main.xml</samp> in the editor tool window and place the cursor on the line causing the warning:

```
 <Button
            android:id="@+id/next_button"
            android:layout_width="wrap_content"
            android:layout_height="wrap_content"
            android:layout_gravity="bottom|right"
            android:text="@string/next_button"
            android:drawableEnd="@drawable/arrow_right"
            android:drawablePadding="4dp"/>
```

The line Lint is concerned about sets the gravity of the <samp class="guibutton">NEXT</samp> button so that it appears in the bottom-right corner of the landscape layout. To fix the warning, change the value `bottom|right` to `bottom|end`. This way, the button will be positioned on the bottom left on a device set to a language that reads right to left instead of left to right.

**Listing 5.7  Addressing bidirectional text warning (`res/layout/land/activity_main.xml`)**

```
...
<Button
        android:id="@+id/next_button"
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:layout_gravity="bottom|right"
        android:layout_gravity="bottom|end"
        android:text="@string/next_button"
        android:drawableEnd="@drawable/arrow_right"
        android:drawablePadding="4dp"/>
...
```

Rerun Lint to confirm that the bidirectional text issue you just fixed is no longer listed in the Lint results. To preview how the layout will look on devices with right to left locales, open the <samp class="guibutton">Design</samp> tab in the editor tool window. Change the selection in the <samp class="guilabel">Locale for Preview</samp> dropdown from <samp class="guilabel">Default (en-us)</samp> to <samp class="guilabel">Preview Right to Left</samp> ([Figure 5.12](#ch05s02.xhtml_ss_tfDebugging_rtl_vs_ltr_preview "Figure 5.12  Previewing left to right and right to left")). If you do not see the <samp class="guilabel">Locale for Preview</samp> dropdown, click <samp class="guilabel">>></samp> at the top of the preview pane to expand preview options.

**Figure 5.12  Previewing left to right and right to left**

![Previewing left to right and right to left](Images/rtl_vs_ltr_preview.png)

For the most part, your app will execute just fine even if you do not address the things Lint warns you about. Often, though, addressing Lint warnings can help prevent problems in the future or make your users’ experience better. We recommend you take all Lint warnings seriously, even if you ultimately decide not to address them (as in this case). Otherwise you could get used to ignoring Lint and miss a serious problem.

The Lint tool provides detailed information about each issue it finds and provides suggestions for how to address it. We leave it to you as an exercise to review the issues Lint found in GeoQuiz. You can ignore the issues, fix them as Lint recommends, or use the <samp class="guibutton">Suppress</samp> button in the problem description pane to suppress the warnings in the future. For the remainder of the GeoQuiz chapters, we will assume you left the remaining Lint issues unaddressed.

### Issues with the R class

You are familiar with build errors that occur when you reference resources before adding them or delete resources that other files refer to. Usually, resaving the files once the resource is added or the references are removed will cause Android Studio to rebuild without any fuss.

Sometimes, however, these build errors will persist or appear seemingly out of nowhere. If this happens to you, here are some things you can try:

<samp class="emphasis">Recheck the validity of the XML in your resource files</samp>

If your <samp class="filename">R.java</samp> file was not generated for the last build, you will see errors in your project wherever you reference a resource. Often, this is caused by a typo in one of your XML files. Layout XML is not always validated, so typos in these files may not be pointedly brought to your attention. Finding the typo and resaving the file should cause <samp class="filename">R.java</samp> to regenerate.

<samp class="emphasis">Clean your project</samp>

Select <samp class="guimenu">Build</samp> → <samp class="guimenuitem">Clean Project</samp>. Android Studio will rebuild the project from scratch, which often results in an error-free build. We can all use a deep clean every now and then.

<samp class="emphasis">Sync your project with Gradle</samp>

If you make changes to your <samp class="filename">build.gradle</samp> file, you will need to sync those changes to update your project’s build settings. Select <samp class="guimenu">File</samp> → <samp class="guimenuitem">Sync Project with Gradle Files</samp>. Android Studio will rebuild the project from scratch with the correct project settings, which can help to resolve issues after changing your Gradle configuration.

<samp class="emphasis">Run Android Lint</samp>

Pay close attention to the warnings from Lint. With this tool, you will often discover unexpected issues.

If you are still having problems with resources (or having different problems), give the error messages and your layout files a fresh look. It is easy to overlook mistakes in the heat of the moment. Check out any Lint errors and warnings as well. A cool-headed reconsideration of the error messages may turn up a bug or typo.

Finally, if you are stuck or having other issues with Android Studio, check the archives at [<samp class="uri">stackoverflow.com</samp>](https://stackoverflow.com) or visit the forum for this book at [<samp class="uri">forums.bignerdranch.com</samp>](https://forums.bignerdranch.com).

## Challenge: Exploring the Layout Inspector

For support debugging layout file issues, the layout inspector can be used to interactively inspect how a layout file is rendered to the screen. To use the layout inspector, make sure GeoQuiz is running in the emulator and select <samp class="guimenu">Tools</samp> → <samp class="guimenuitem">Layout Inspector</samp> from the menu bar. Once the inspector is activated, you can explore the properties of your layout by clicking the elements within the layout inspector view.

## Challenge: Exploring the Profiler

The profiler tool window creates detailed reports for how your application is using an Android device’s resources, such as CPU and memory. It is useful when assessing and tuning the performance of your app.

To view the profiler tool window, run your app on a connected Android device or emulator and select <samp class="guimenu">View</samp> → <samp class="guisubmenu">Tool Windows</samp> → <samp class="guimenuitem">Profiler</samp> from the menu bar. Once the profiler is open, you can see a timeline with sections for CPU, memory, network, and energy.

Click into a section to see more details about your app’s usage of that resource. On the CPU view, make sure to hit the <samp class="guilabel">Record</samp> button to capture more information about CPU usage. Once you have performed any interactions with your app that you would like to record, hit the <samp class="guilabel">Stop</samp> button to stop the recording.

# <samp class="chapter_number">6</samp>
<samp class="chapter_name">Your Second Activity</samp>

In this chapter, you will add a second activity to GeoQuiz. An activity controls a screen of information, and this activity will add a second screen that offers users a chance to cheat on the current question by showing the answer. [Figure 6.1](#ch06.xhtml_fig_tf_cheat_answer_hidden "Figure 6.1  CheatActivity offers the chance to peek at the answer") shows the new activity.

**Figure 6.1  `CheatActivity` offers the chance to peek at the answer**

![CheatActivity offers the chance to peek at the answer](Images/tf_cheat_portrait.png)

If users choose to view the answer and then return to the <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> and answer the question, they will get a new message, shown in [Figure 6.2](#ch06.xhtml_fig_tf_cheating_is_wrong "Figure 6.2  MainActivity knows if you’ve been cheating").

**Figure 6.2  `MainActivity` knows if you’ve been cheating**

![MainActivity knows if you’ve been cheating](Images/tf_scold_quiz_portrait.png)

Why is this a good Android programming exercise? Because you will learn how to:

*   Create a new activity and a new layout for it.

*   Start an activity from another activity. <samp class="firstterm">Starting</samp> an activity means asking the OS to create an activity instance and call its <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp> function.

*   Pass data between the parent (starting) activity and the child (started) activity.

## Setting Up a Second Activity

There is a lot to do in this chapter. Fortunately, some of the grunt work can be done for you by Android Studio’s New Activity wizard.

Before you invoke the magic, open <samp class="filename">res/values/strings.xml</samp> and add all the strings you will need for this chapter.

**Listing 6.1  Adding strings (`res/values/strings.xml`)**

```
<resources>
    ...
    <string name="incorrect_toast">Incorrect!</string>
    <string name="warning_text">Are you sure you want to do this?</string>
    <string name="show_answer_button">Show Answer</string>
    <string name="cheat_button">Cheat!</string>
    <string name="judgment_toast">Cheating is wrong.</string>

</resources> 
```

### Creating a new activity

Creating an activity typically involves touching at least three files: the Kotlin class file, an XML layout file, and the application manifest. If you touch those files in the wrong ways, Android can get mad. To ensure that you do it right, you can use Android Studio’s New Activity wizard.

Launch the New Activity wizard by right-clicking on the <samp class="filename">app/java</samp> folder in the project tool window. Choose <samp class="guimenu">New</samp> → <samp class="guisubmenu">Activity</samp> → <samp class="guimenuitem">Empty Activity</samp>, as shown in [Figure 6.3](#ch06s01.xhtml_fig_tf_new_activity_blank_activity_menu "Figure 6.3  The New Activity menu").

**Figure 6.3  The New Activity menu**

![The New Activity menu](Images/tf_new_activity_blank_activity_menu.png)

You should then see a dialog like [Figure 6.4](#ch06s01.xhtml_fig_tf_new_activity_wizard "Figure 6.4  The New Empty Activity wizard"). Set <samp class="guilabel">Activity Name</samp> to <samp class="guilabel">CheatActivity</samp>. This is the name of your <samp class="classname">Activity</samp> subclass. <samp class="guilabel">Layout Name</samp> will be automatically set to <samp class="guilabel">activity_cheat</samp>. This will be the base name of the layout file the wizard creates.

**Figure 6.4  The New Empty Activity wizard**

![The New Empty Activity wizard](Images/tf_new_cheat_activity_wizard.png)

The defaults for the remaining fields are fine, but take care to ensure that the package name is what you expect. This determines where <samp class="filename">CheatActivity.kt</samp> will live on the filesystem. Click the <samp class="guibutton">Finish</samp> button to make the magic happen.

Now it is time to make the UI look good. The screenshot at the beginning of the chapter shows you what <samp class="classname">CheatActivity</samp>’s view should look like. [Figure 6.5](#ch06s01.xhtml_fig_tf_activity_cheat_layout "Figure 6.5  Diagram of layout for CheatActivity") shows the widget definitions.

**Figure 6.5  Diagram of layout for `CheatActivity`**

![Diagram of layout for CheatActivity](Images/activity_cheat_layout.png)

Open <samp class="filename">res/layout/activity_cheat.xml</samp> and switch to the <samp class="guilabel">Text</samp> view.

Try creating the XML for the layout using [Figure 6.5](#ch06s01.xhtml_fig_tf_activity_cheat_layout "Figure 6.5  Diagram of layout for CheatActivity") as a guide. Replace the sample layout with a new <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp> and so on down the tree. You can check your work against [Listing 6.2](#ch06s01.xhtml_pl_tf_activity_cheat_layout "Listing 6.2  Filling out the second activity’s layout (res/layout/activity_cheat.xml)").

**Listing 6.2  Filling out the second activity’s layout (`res/layout/activity_cheat.xml`)**

```
<LinearLayout xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
```

You will not be creating a landscape alternative for <samp class="filename">activity_cheat.xml</samp>, but there is a way to preview how the default layout will appear in landscape.

In the <samp class="guilabel">Design</samp> tab of the editor tool window, find the button in the toolbar above the preview pane that looks like a device with curved arrows. Click this button to change the orientation of the preview to landscape ([Figure 6.6](#ch06s01.xhtml_fig_tf_cheat_landscape_preview "Figure 6.6  Previewing activity_cheat.xml in landscape")).

![Previewing activity_cheat.xml in landscape](Images/tf_cheat_landscape_preview.png)

The default layout works well enough in both orientations, so let’s move on to fleshing out the activity subclass.

### A new activity subclass

<samp class="filename">CheatActivity.kt</samp> may have opened automatically in the editor tool window. If it did not, open it from the project tool window.

The <samp class="classname">CheatActivity</samp> class already includes a basic implementation of <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp> that passes the resource ID of the layout defined in <samp class="filename">activity_cheat.xml</samp> to <samp class="methodname">setContentView(…)</samp>.

<samp class="classname">CheatActivity</samp> will eventually do more in its <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp> function. For now, let’s take a look at another thing the New Activity wizard did for you: declaring <samp class="classname">CheatActivity</samp> in the application’s manifest.

### Declaring activities in the manifest

The <samp class="firstterm">manifest</samp> is an XML file containing metadata that describes your application to the Android OS. The file is always named <samp class="filename">AndroidManifest.xml</samp>, and it lives in the <samp class="filename">app/manifests</samp> directory of your project.

In the project tool window, find and open <samp class="filename">manifests/AndroidManifest.xml</samp>. You can also use Android Studio’s Find File dialog by pressing Command-Shift-O (Ctrl-Shift-N) and starting to type the filename. Once it has guessed the right file, press Return to open it.

Every activity in an application must be declared in the manifest so that the OS can access it.

When you used the New Project wizard to create <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>, the wizard declared the activity for you. Likewise, the New Activity wizard declared <samp class="classname">CheatActivity</samp> by adding the XML highlighted in [Listing 6.3](#ch06s01.xhtml_pl_tf_manifest_new_activity "Listing 6.3  Declaring CheatActivity in the manifest (manifests/AndroidManifest.xml)").

**Listing 6.3  Declaring `CheatActivity` in the manifest (`manifests/AndroidManifest.xml`)**

```
<manifest xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    package="com.bignerdranch.android.geoquiz">

    <application
        android:allowBackup="true"
        android:icon="@mipmap/ic_launcher"
        android:label="@string/app_name"
        android:roundIcon="@mipmap/ic_launcher_round"
        android:supportsRtl="true"
        android:theme="@style/AppTheme">
        <activity android:name=".CheatActivity">
        </activity>
        <activity android:name=".MainActivity">
            <intent-filter>
                <action android:name="android.intent.action.MAIN" />

                <category android:name="android.intent.category.LAUNCHER" />
            </intent-filter>
        </activity>
    </application>

</manifest>
```

The `android:name` attribute is required, and the dot at the start of this attribute’s value tells the OS that this activity’s class is in the package specified in the `package` attribute in the `manifest` element at the top of the file.

You will sometimes see a fully qualified `android:name` attribute, like `android:name="com.bignerdranch.android.geoquiz.CheatActivity"`. The long-form notation is identical to the version in [Listing 6.3](#ch06s01.xhtml_pl_tf_manifest_new_activity "Listing 6.3  Declaring CheatActivity in the manifest (manifests/AndroidManifest.xml)").

There are many interesting things in the manifest, but for now, let’s stay focused on getting <samp class="classname">CheatActivity</samp> up and running. You will learn about the different parts of the manifest in later chapters.

### Adding a cheat button to MainActivity

The plan is for the user to press a button in <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> to get an instance of <samp class="classname">CheatActivity</samp> onscreen. So you need new buttons in <samp class="filename">res/layout/activity_main.xml</samp> and <samp class="filename">res/layout-land/activity_main.xml</samp>.

You can see in [Figure 6.2](#ch06.xhtml_fig_tf_cheating_is_wrong "Figure 6.2  MainActivity knows if you’ve been cheating") that the new <samp class="guibutton">CHEAT!</samp> button is positioned above the <samp class="guibutton">NEXT</samp> button. In the default layout, define the new button as a direct child of the root <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp>, right before the definition of the <samp class="guibutton">NEXT</samp> button.

```
    <Button

        android:layout_marginTop="24dp"
        android:text="@string/cheat_button" />

    <Button
        android:id="@+id/next_button"
        .../>

</LinearLayout> 
```

In the landscape layout, have the new button appear at the bottom and center of the root <samp class="classname">FrameLayout</samp>.
