```
    ): View? {
        val view = inflater.inflate(R.layout.fragment_crime, container, false)

        titleField = view.findViewById(R.id.crime_title) as EditText

        return view
    }
}
```

Getting references in <samp class="methodname">Fragment.onCreateView(…)</samp> works nearly the same as in <samp class="methodname">Activity.onCreate(Bundle?)</samp>. The only difference is that you call <samp class="methodname">View.findViewById(Int)</samp> on the fragment’s view. The <samp class="methodname">Activity.findViewById(Int)</samp> function that you used before is a convenience function that calls <samp class="methodname">View.findViewById(Int)</samp> behind the scenes. The <samp class="classname">Fragment</samp> class does not have a corresponding convenience function, so you have to call the real thing.

Once the reference is set, add a listener in the <samp class="methodname">onStart()</samp> lifecycle callback.

**Listing 8.8  Adding a listener to the `EditText` widget (`CrimeFragment.kt`)**

```
class CrimeFragment : Fragment() {
    ...
    override fun onCreateView(
        inflater: LayoutInflater,
        container: ViewGroup?,
        savedInstanceState: Bundle?
    ): View? {
        ...
    }

    override fun onStart() {
        super.onStart()

        val titleWatcher = object : TextWatcher {

            override fun beforeTextChanged(
                sequence: CharSequence?,
                start: Int,
                count: Int,
                after: Int
            ) {
                // This space intentionally left blank
            }

            override fun onTextChanged(
                sequence: CharSequence?,
                start: Int,
                before: Int,
                count: Int
            ) {
                crime.title = sequence.toString()
            }

            override fun afterTextChanged(sequence: Editable?) {
                // This one too
            }
        }

        titleField.addTextChangedListener(titleWatcher)
    }
}
```

Setting listeners in a fragment works exactly the same as in an activity. Here, you create an anonymous class that implements the verbose <samp class="interfacename">TextWatcher</samp> interface. <samp class="interfacename">TextWatcher</samp> has three functions, but you only care about one: <samp class="methodname">onTextChanged(…)</samp>.

In <samp class="methodname">onTextChanged(…)</samp>, you call <samp class="methodname">toString()</samp> on the <samp class="type">CharSequence</samp> that is the user’s input. This function returns a string, which you then use to set the <samp class="classname">Crime</samp>’s title.

Notice that the <samp class="classname">TextWatcher</samp> listener is set up in <samp class="methodname">onStart()</samp>. Some listeners are triggered not only when the user interacts with them but also when data is set on them when the view state is restored, such as on rotation. Listeners that react to data input, such as the <samp class="classname">TextWatcher</samp> for an <samp class="classname">EditText</samp> or an <samp class="classname">OnCheckChangedListener</samp> for a <samp class="classname">CheckBox</samp>, are susceptible to this behavior.

Listeners that only react to user interaction, such as an <samp class="classname">OnClickListener</samp>, are not susceptible to this, because they are not impacted by setting data on a view. This is the reason you did not encounter this in GeoQuiz. That app only used click listeners, which are not triggered on rotation, so you could set everything up in <samp class="methodname">onCreate(…)</samp> – before any state restoration.

View state is restored after <samp class="methodname">onCreateView(…)</samp> and before <samp class="methodname">onStart()</samp>. When the state is restored, the contents of the <samp class="classname">EditText</samp> will get set to whatever value is currently in `crime.title`. At this point, if you have already set a listener on the <samp class="classname">EditText</samp> (such as in <samp class="methodname">onCreate(…)</samp> or <samp class="methodname">onCreateView(…)</samp>), <samp class="classname">TextWatcher</samp>’s <samp class="methodname">beforeTextChanged(…)</samp>, <samp class="methodname">onTextChanged(…)</samp>, and <samp class="methodname">afterTextChanged(…)</samp> functions will execute. Setting the listener in <samp class="methodname">onStart()</samp> avoids this behavior since the listener is hooked up after the view state is restored.

Next, connect the <samp class="classname">Button</samp> to display the date of the crime.

**Listing 8.9  Setting `Button` text (`CrimeFragment.kt`)**

```
class CrimeFragment : Fragment() {

    private lateinit var crime: Crime
    private lateinit var titleField: EditText
    private lateinit var dateButton: Button
    ...
    override fun onCreateView(
        inflater: LayoutInflater,
        container: ViewGroup?,
        savedInstanceState: Bundle?
    ): View? {
        val view = inflater.inflate(R.layout.fragment_crime, container, false)

        titleField = view.findViewById(R.id.crime_title) as EditText
        dateButton = view.findViewById(R.id.crime_date) as Button

        dateButton.apply {
            text = crime.date.toString()
            isEnabled = false
        }

        return view
    }
}
```

Disabling the button ensures that it will not respond in any way to the user pressing it. It also changes its appearance to advertise its disabled state. In [Chapter 13](../Text/ch13.xhtml "13 Dialogs"), you will enable the button and allow the user to choose the date of the crime.

Moving on to the <samp class="classname">CheckBox</samp>, get a reference to it in <samp class="methodname">onCreateView(…)</samp>. Then, set a listener in <samp class="methodname">onStart()</samp> that will update the <samp class="varname">solvedCheckBox</samp> field of the <samp class="classname">Crime</samp>, as shown in [Listing 8.10](#ch08s05.xhtml_pl_watson_scene_activity_checkbox "Listing 8.10  Listening for CheckBox changes (CrimeFragment.kt)"). Even though the <samp class="classname">OnClickListener</samp> is not triggered by the state restoration of the fragment, putting it in <samp class="methodname">onStart</samp> helps keep all of your listeners in one place and easy to find.

**Listing 8.10  Listening for `CheckBox` changes (`CrimeFragment.kt`)**

```
class CrimeFragment : Fragment() {

    private lateinit var crime: Crime
    private lateinit var titleField: EditText
    private lateinit var dateButton: Button
    private lateinit var solvedCheckBox: CheckBox
    ...
    override fun onCreateView(
        inflater: LayoutInflater,
        container: ViewGroup?,
        savedInstanceState: Bundle?
    ): View? {
        val view = inflater.inflate(R.layout.fragment_crime, container, false)

        titleField = view.findViewById(R.id.crime_title) as EditText
        dateButton = view.findViewById(R.id.crime_date) as Button
        solvedCheckBox = view.findViewById(R.id.crime_solved) as CheckBox
        ...
    }

    override fun onStart() {
        ...
        titleField.addTextChangedListener(titleWatcher)

        solvedCheckBox.apply {
            setOnCheckedChangeListener { _, isChecked ->
                crime.isSolved = isChecked
            }
        }
    }
}
```

Your code for <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> is now complete. It would be great if you could run CriminalIntent and play with the code you have written. But you cannot. Fragments cannot put their views onscreen on their own. To realize your efforts, you first have to add a <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> to <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>.

## Hosting a UI Fragment

To host a UI fragment, an activity must:

*   define a spot in its layout for the fragment’s view

*   manage the lifecycle of the fragment instance

You can attach fragments to your activities in code. You determine when the fragment is added to the activity and what happens to it after that. You can remove the fragment, replace it with another, and then add the first fragment back again.

The code details will come later in the chapter. First, you are going to define <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>’s layout.

### Defining a container view

You will be adding a UI fragment in the hosting activity’s code, but you still need to make a spot for the fragment’s view in the activity’s view hierarchy. Locate <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>’s layout at <samp class="filename">res/layout/activity_main.xml</samp>. Open this file and replace the default layout with a <samp class="classname">FrameLayout</samp>. Your XML should match [Listing 8.11](#ch08s06.xhtml_create_fragment_activity_xml "Listing 8.11  Creating the fragment container layout (res/layout/activity_main.xml)").

**Listing 8.11  Creating the fragment container layout (`res/layout/activity_main.xml`)**

```
<androidx.constraintlayout.widget.ConstraintLayout
        xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
        xmlns:tools="http://schemas.android.com/tools"
        xmlns:app="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res-auto"
        android:layout_width="match_parent"
        android:layout_height="match_parent"
        tools:context=".MainActivity">

    <TextView
            android:layout_width="wrap_content"
            android:layout_height="wrap_content"
            android:text="Hello World!"
            app:layout_constraintBottom_toBottomOf="parent"
            app:layout_constraintLeft_toLeftOf="parent"
            app:layout_constraintRight_toRightOf="parent"
            app:layout_constraintTop_toTopOf="parent"/>

</androidx.constraintlayout.widget.ConstraintLayout>
<FrameLayout
        xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
        android:id="@+id/fragment_container"
        android:layout_width="match_parent"
        android:layout_height="match_parent"/>
```

This <samp class="classname">FrameLayout</samp> will be the <samp class="firstterm">container view</samp> for a <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp>. Notice that the container view is completely generic; it does not name the <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> class. You can and will use this same layout to host other fragments.

Note that while <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp> consists solely of a container view for a single fragment, an activity’s layout can be more complex and define multiple container views as well as widgets of its own.

Run CriminalIntent to check your code. You will see an empty <samp class="classname">FrameLayout</samp> below a toolbar containing the app name ([Figure 8.12](#ch08s06.xhtml_fig_ci_empty_frame_layout "Figure 8.12  An empty FrameLayout")).

**Figure 8.12  An empty `FrameLayout`**

![An empty FrameLayout](Images/ci_empty_frame_layout.png)

The <samp class="classname">FrameLayout</samp> is empty because the <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> is not yet hosting a fragment. Later, you will write code that puts a fragment’s view inside this <samp class="classname">FrameLayout</samp>. But first, you need to create a fragment.

(The toolbar at the top of your app is included automatically because of the way you configured your activity. You will learn more about the toolbar in [Chapter 14](../Text/ch14.xhtml "14 The App Bar").)

### Adding a UI fragment to the FragmentManager

When the <samp class="classname">Fragment</samp> class was introduced in Honeycomb, the <samp class="classname">Activity</samp> class was changed to include a piece called the <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp>. The <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> handles two things: a list of fragments and a back stack of fragment transactions (which you will learn about shortly) ([Figure 8.13](#ch08s06.xhtml_fig_fragmentmanager "Figure 8.13  The FragmentManager")). It is responsible for adding the fragments’ views to the activity’s view hierarchy and driving the fragments’ lifecycles.

**Figure 8.13  The `FragmentManager`**

![The FragmentManager](Images/fragmentmanager.png)

For CriminalIntent, you will only be concerned with the <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp>’s list of fragments.

#### Fragment transactions

Now that you have the <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp>, add the following code to give it a fragment to manage. (We will step through this code afterward. Just get it in for now.)

**Listing 8.12  Adding a `CrimeFragment` (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContentView(R.layout.activity_main)

        val currentFragment =
            supportFragmentManager.findFragmentById(R.id.fragment_container)

        if (currentFragment == null) {
            val fragment = CrimeFragment()
            supportFragmentManager
                .beginTransaction()
                .add(R.id.fragment_container, fragment)
                .commit()
        }
    }
}
```

To add a fragment to an activity in code, you make explicit calls to the activity’s <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp>. You can access the activity’s fragment manager using the <samp class="varname">supportFragmentManager</samp> property. You use <samp class="varname">supportFragmentManager</samp> because you are using the Jetpack library and the <samp class="classname">AppCompatActivity</samp> class. The name is prefixed with “support” because the property originated in the v4 support library, but the support library has since been repackaged as an `androidx` library within Jetpack.

The best place to start understanding the rest of the code you just added is not at the beginning. Instead, find the <samp class="methodname">add(…)</samp> operation and the code around it. This code creates and commits a <samp class="firstterm">fragment transaction</samp>.

```
 if (currentFragment == null) {
        val fragment = CrimeFragment()
        supportFragmentManager
            .beginTransaction()
            .add(R.id.fragment_container, fragment)
            .commit()
    }
```

Fragment transactions are used to add, remove, attach, detach, or replace fragments in the fragment list. They allow you to group multiple operations together, such as adding multiple fragments to different containers at the same time. They are the heart of how you use fragments to compose and recompose screens at runtime.

The <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> maintains a back stack of fragment transactions that you can navigate. If your fragment transaction includes multiple operations, they are reversed when the transaction is removed from the back stack. This provides more control over your UI state when you group your fragment operations into a single transaction.

The <samp class="methodname">FragmentManager.beginTransaction()</samp> function creates and returns an instance of <samp class="classname">FragmentTransaction</samp>. The <samp class="classname">FragmentTransaction</samp> class uses a <samp class="firstterm">fluent interface</samp> – functions that configure <samp class="classname">FragmentTransaction</samp> return a <samp class="classname">FragmentTransaction</samp> instead of `Unit`, which allows you to chain them together. So the code highlighted above says, “Create a new fragment transaction, include one add operation in it, and then commit it.”

The <samp class="methodname">add(…)</samp> function is the meat of the transaction. It has two parameters: a container view ID and the newly created <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp>. The container view ID should look familiar. It is the resource ID of the <samp class="classname">FrameLayout</samp> that you defined in <samp class="filename">activity_main.xml</samp>.

A container view ID serves two purposes:

*   It tells the <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> where in the activity’s view the fragment’s view should appear.

*   It is used as a unique identifier for a fragment in the <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp>’s list.

When you need to retrieve the <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> from the <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp>, you ask for it by container view ID:

```
 val currentFragment =
        supportFragmentManager.findFragmentById(R.id.fragment_container)

    if (currentFragment == null) {
        val fragment = CrimeFragment()
        supportFragmentManager
            .beginTransaction()
            .add(R.id.fragment_container, fragment)
            .commit()
    }
```

It may seem odd that the <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> identifies the <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> using the resource ID of a <samp class="classname">FrameLayout</samp>. But identifying a UI fragment by the resource ID of its container view is built into how the <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> operates. If you are adding multiple fragments to an activity, you would typically create separate containers with separate IDs for each of those fragments.

Now we can summarize the code you added in [Listing 8.12](#ch08s06.xhtml_hook_up_fragment "Listing 8.12  Adding a CrimeFragment (MainActivity.kt)") from start to finish:

First, you ask the <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> for the fragment with a container view ID of `R.id.fragment_container`. If this fragment is already in the list, the <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> will return it.

Why would a fragment already be in the list? The call to <samp class="methodname">MainActivity.onCreate(Bundle?)</samp> could be in response to <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> being <samp class="emphasis">re-created</samp> after being destroyed on rotation or to reclaim memory. When an activity is destroyed, its <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> saves out its list of fragments. When the activity is re-created, the new <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> retrieves the list and re-creates the listed fragments to make everything as it was before.

On the other hand, if there is no fragment with the given container view ID, then <samp class="varname">fragment</samp> will be null. In this case, you create a new <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> and a new fragment transaction that adds the fragment to the list.

<samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> is now hosting a <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp>. Run CriminalIntent to prove it. You should see the view defined in <samp class="filename">fragment_crime.xml</samp>, as shown in [Figure 8.14](#ch08s06.xhtml_empty_episode_1 "Figure 8.14  CrimeFragment’s view hosted by MainActivity").

**Figure 8.14  `CrimeFragment`’s view hosted by `MainActivity`**

![CrimeFragment’s view hosted by MainActivity](Images/ci_end_of_first_chapter.png)

#### The FragmentManager and the fragment lifecycle

[Figure 8.15](#ch08s06.xhtml_fragment_lifecycle_1 "Figure 8.15  Fragment lifecycle diagram") shows the fragment lifecycle. The fragment lifecycle is similar to the activity lifecycle: It has stopped, paused, and resumed states, and it has functions you can override to get things done at critical points – many of which correspond to activity lifecycle functions.

**Figure 8.15  Fragment lifecycle diagram**

![Fragment lifecycle diagram](Images/fragment_lifecycle_typical.png)

The correspondence is important. Because a fragment works on behalf of an activity, its state should reflect the activity’s state. Thus, it needs corresponding lifecycle functions to handle the activity’s work.

One critical difference between the fragment lifecycle and the activity lifecycle is that fragment lifecycle functions are called by the <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> of the hosting activity, not the OS. The OS knows nothing about the fragments that an activity is using to manage things. Fragments are the activity’s internal business. The <samp class="methodname">onAttach(Context?)</samp>, <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp>, <samp class="methodname">onCreateView(…)</samp>, and <samp class="methodname">onViewCreated(…)</samp> functions are called when you add the fragment to the <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp>.

The <samp class="methodname">onActivityCreated(Bundle?)</samp> function is called after the hosting activity’s <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp> function has executed. You are adding the <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> in <samp class="methodname">MainActivity.onCreate(Bundle?)</samp>, so this function will be called after the fragment has been added.

What happens if you add a fragment while the activity is already resumed? In that case, the <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> immediately walks the fragment through whatever steps are necessary to get it caught up to the activity’s state. For example, as a fragment is added to an activity that is already resumed, that fragment gets calls to <samp class="methodname">onAttach(Context?)</samp>, <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp>, <samp class="methodname">onCreateView(…)</samp>, <samp class="methodname">onViewCreated(…)</samp>, <samp class="methodname">onActivityCreated(Bundle?)</samp>, <samp class="methodname">onStart()</samp>, and then <samp class="methodname">onResume()</samp>.

Once the fragment’s state is caught up to the activity’s state, the hosting activity’s <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> will call further lifecycle functions around the same time it receives the corresponding calls from the OS to keep the fragment’s state aligned with that of the activity.

## Application Architecture with Fragments

Designing your app with fragments the right way is supremely important. Many developers, after first learning about fragments, try to use them for each and every component in their application. This is the wrong way to use fragments.

Fragments are intended to encapsulate major components in a reusable way. A major component in this case would be on the level of an entire screen of your application. If you have a significant number of fragments onscreen at once, your code will be littered with fragment transactions and unclear responsibility. A better architectural solution for reuse with smaller components is to extract them into a custom view (a class that subclasses <samp class="classname">View</samp> or one of its subclasses).

Use fragments responsibly. A good rule of thumb is to have no more than two or three fragments on the screen at a time ([Figure 8.16](#ch08s07.xhtml_fragment_architecture "Figure 8.16  Less is more")).

**Figure 8.16  Less is more**

![Less is more](Images/ci_fragment_architecture.png)

### Deciding whether to use fragments

Fragments are the topic of a lot of discussion in the Android community. Some people are very opposed to the additional complexity involved with fragments and their lifecycles, so they never use them in their projects. An issue with this approach is that there are several APIs in Android that rely on fragments, such as <samp class="classname">ViewPager</samp> and the Jetpack Navigation library. If you need to use these options in your app, then you must use fragments to get their benefits.

If you do not need fragment-dependent APIs, fragments are more useful in larger applications that have more requirements. For simple, single-screen applications, the complexity introduced by fragments and their lifecycle is often unnecessary.

One thing to consider when starting a new app is that adding fragments later can be a minefield. Changing an activity to an activity hosting a UI fragment is not difficult, but there are swarms of annoying gotchas. Keeping some interfaces managed by activities and having others managed by fragments only makes things worse, because you have to keep track of this meaningless distinction. It is far easier to write your code using fragments from the beginning and not worry about the pain and annoyance of reworking it later, or having to remember which style of controller you are using in each part of your application.

Therefore, when it comes to fragments, we have a different principle: Almost always use fragments. If you know that the app you are building will remain very small, the extra effort of using fragments may not be worth it, so they can be left out. For larger apps, the complexity introduced is offset by the flexibility fragments provide, making it easier to justify having them in the project.

From here on, some of the apps in this book will use fragments and others will not. You will build some small applications during a single chapter, and you will make building these apps easier by <samp class="emphasis">not</samp> using fragments. However, the larger apps in this book do use fragments to give you extra experience using them and to make the apps easier to extend in the future.

# <samp class="chapter_number">9</samp>
<samp class="chapter_name">Displaying Lists with RecyclerView</samp>

CriminalIntent’s model layer currently consists of a single instance of <samp class="classname">Crime</samp>. In this chapter, you will update CriminalIntent to work with a list of crimes. The list will display each <samp class="classname">Crime</samp>’s title and date, as shown in [Figure 9.1](#ch09.xhtml_fig_crime_list "Figure 9.1  A list of crimes").

**Figure 9.1  A list of crimes**

![A list of crimes](Images/ci_with_custom_list_items.png)

[Figure 9.2](#ch09.xhtml_ci_object_diagram_4_abbrev "Figure 9.2  CriminalIntent with a list of crimes") shows the overall plan for CriminalIntent in this chapter.

**Figure 9.2  CriminalIntent with a list of crimes**

![CriminalIntent with a list of crimes](Images/ci_object_diagram_4_abbrev.png)

In the controller layer, you have a new <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> that will encapsulate the data for the new screen. <samp class="classname">CrimeListViewModel</samp> will store a list of <samp class="classname">Crime</samp> objects.

Displaying a list of crimes requires a new fragment in CriminalIntent’s controller layer: <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp>. <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> will host an instance of <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp>, which will in turn display the list of crimes on the screen.

(Where is <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> in [Figure 9.2](#ch09.xhtml_ci_object_diagram_4_abbrev "Figure 9.2  CriminalIntent with a list of crimes")? It is part of the detail view, so we are not showing it here. In [Chapter 12](../Text/ch12.xhtml "12 Fragment Navigation"), you will connect the list and detail parts of CriminalIntent.)

In [Figure 9.2](#ch09.xhtml_ci_object_diagram_4_abbrev "Figure 9.2  CriminalIntent with a list of crimes"), you can also see the view objects associated with <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> and <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp>. The activity’s view will consist of the same single fragment-containing <samp class="classname">FrameLayout</samp>. The fragment’s view will consist of a <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp>. You will learn more about the <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> class later in the chapter.

## Adding a New Fragment and ViewModel

The first step is to add a new <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> to store the <samp class="classname">List</samp> of <samp class="classname">Crime</samp> objects you will eventually display on the screen. As you learned in [Chapter 4](../Text/ch04.xhtml "4 Persisting UI State"), the <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> class is part of the `lifecycle-extensions` library. So begin by adding the `lifecycle-extensions` dependency to your <samp class="filename">app/build.gradle</samp> file.

**Listing 9.1  Adding `lifecycle-extensions` dependency (`app/build.gradle`)**

```
dependencies {
    ...
    implementation 'androidx.appcompat:appcompat:1.1.0-alpha02'
    implementation 'androidx.core:core-ktx:1.1.0-alpha04'
    implementation 'androidx.lifecycle:lifecycle-extensions:2.0.0'
    ...
}
```

Do not forget to sync your Gradle files after making this change.

Next, create a new Kotlin class called <samp class="classname">CrimeListViewModel</samp>. Update the new <samp class="classname">CrimeListViewModel</samp> class to extend from <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp>. Add a property to store a list of <samp class="classname">Crime</samp>s. In the `init` block, populate the list with dummy data.

**Listing 9.2  Generating crimes (`CrimeListViewModel.kt`)**

```
class CrimeListViewModel : ViewModel() {

    val crimes = mutableListOf<Crime>()

    init {
        for (i in 0 until 100) {
            val crime = Crime()
            crime.title = "Crime #$i"
            crime.isSolved = i % 2 == 0
            crimes += crime
        }
    }
}
```

Eventually, the <samp class="classname">List</samp> will contain user-created <samp class="classname">Crime</samp>s that can be saved and reloaded. For now, you populate the <samp class="classname">List</samp> with 100 boring <samp class="classname">Crime</samp> objects.

The <samp class="classname">CrimeListViewModel</samp> is not a solution for long-term storage of data, but it does encapsulate all the data necessary to populate <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp>’s view. In [Chapter 11](../Text/ch11.xhtml "11 Databases and the Room Library"), you will learn more about long-term data storage when you update CriminalIntent to store the crime list in a database.

The next step is to add a new <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> class and associate it with <samp class="classname">CrimeListViewModel</samp>. Create the <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> class and make it a subclass of <samp class="classname">androidx.fragment.app.Fragment</samp>.

**Listing 9.3  Implementing `CrimeListFragment` (`CrimeListFragment.kt`)**

```
private const val TAG = "CrimeListFragment"

class CrimeListFragment : Fragment() {

    private val crimeListViewModel: CrimeListViewModel by lazy {
        ViewModelProviders.of(this).get(CrimeListViewModel::class.java)
    }

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        Log.d(TAG, "Total crimes: ${crimeListViewModel.crimes.size}")
    }

    companion object {
        fun newInstance(): CrimeListFragment {
            return CrimeListFragment()
        }
    }
}
```

For now, <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> is an empty shell of a fragment. It logs the number of crimes found in <samp class="classname">CrimeListViewModel</samp>. You will flesh this fragment out later in the chapter.

One good practice to follow is to provide a <samp class="methodname">newInstance(…)</samp> function that your activities can call to get an instance of your fragment. This is similar to the <samp class="methodname">newIntent()</samp> function you used in GeoQuiz. You will see how to pass data to your fragments in [Chapter 12](../Text/ch12.xhtml "12 Fragment Navigation").

### ViewModel lifecycle with fragments

In [Chapter 4](../Text/ch04.xhtml "4 Persisting UI State") you learned about the <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> lifecycle when used with an activity. This lifecycle is slightly different when the <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> is used with a fragment. It still only has two states, created or destroyed/nonexistent, but it is now tied to the lifecycle of the fragment instead of the activity.

The <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> will remain active as long as the fragment’s view is onscreen. The <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> will persist across rotation (even though the fragment instance will not) and be accessible to the new fragment instance.

The <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> will be destroyed when the fragment is destroyed. This can happen when the user presses the Back button to dismiss the screen. It can also happen if the hosting activity replaces the fragment with a different one. Even though the same activity is on the screen, both the fragment and its associated <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> will be destroyed, since they are no longer needed.

One special case is when you add the fragment transaction to the back stack. When the activity replaces the current fragment with a different one, if the transaction is added to the back stack, the fragment instance and its <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> will not be destroyed. This maintains your state: If the user presses the Back button, the fragment transaction is reversed. The original fragment instance is put back on the screen, and all the data in the <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> is preserved.

Next, update <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> to host an instance of <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> instead of <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp>.

**Listing 9.4  Adding `CrimeListFragment` with a fragment transaction (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        ...
        if (currentFragment == null) {
            val fragment = CrimeFragment() CrimeListFragment.newInstance()
            supportFragmentManager
                .beginTransaction()
                .add(R.id.fragment_container, fragment)
                .commit()
        }
    }
}
```

For now, you have hardcoded <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> to always display a <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp>. In [Chapter 12](../Text/ch12.xhtml "12 Fragment Navigation") you will update <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> to swap out <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> and <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> on demand as the user navigates through the app.

Run CriminalIntent, and you will see <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>’s <samp class="classname">FrameLayout</samp> hosting an empty <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp>, as shown in [Figure 9.3](#ch09s01.xhtml_fig_blank_list_activity "Figure 9.3  Blank MainActivity screen").

**Figure 9.3  Blank `MainActivity` screen**

![Blank MainActivity screen](Images/ci_blank_list_activity.png)

Search the Logcat output for <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp>. You will see a log statement showing the total number of crimes available:

```
 2019-02-25 15:19:39.950 26140-26140/com.bignerdranch.android.criminalintent
        D/CrimeListFragment: Total crimes: 100
```

## Adding a RecyclerView

You want <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> to display a list of crimes to the user. To do this you will use a <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp>.

The <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> class lives in another Jetpack library. The first step to using a <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> is to add the RecyclerView library as a dependency.

**Listing 9.5  Adding RecyclerView dependency (`app/build.gradle`)**

```
dependencies {
    ...
    implementation 'androidx.lifecycle:lifecycle-extensions:2.0.0'
    implementation 'androidx.recyclerview:recyclerview:1.0.0'
    ...
}
```

Again, sync your Gradle files before moving on.

Your <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> will live in <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp>’s layout file. First, you must create the layout file. Create a new layout resource file named <samp class="guilabel">fragment_crime_list</samp>. For the <samp class="guilabel">Root element</samp>, specify <samp class="guilabel">androidx.recyclerview.widget.RecyclerView</samp> ([Figure 9.4](#ch09s02.xhtml_ss_ciRecyclerView_add_fragment_layout_file "Figure 9.4  Adding CrimeListFragment’s layout file")).

**Figure 9.4  Adding `CrimeListFragment`’s layout file**

![Adding CrimeListFragment’s layout file](Images/ciRecyclerView_add_fragment_layout_file.png)

In the new <samp class="filename">layout/fragment_crime_list.xml</samp> file, add an ID attribute to the <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp>. Collapse the close tag into the opening tag, since you will not add any children to the <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp>.

**Listing 9.6  Adding `RecyclerView` to a layout file (`layout/fragment_crime_list.xml`)**

```
<androidx.recyclerview.widget.RecyclerView
        xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
        android:id="@+id/crime_recycler_view"
        android:layout_width="match_parent"
        android:layout_height="match_parent">
        android:layout_height="match_parent"/>

</androidx.recyclerview.widget.RecyclerView>
```

Now that <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp>’s view is set up, hook up the view to the fragment. Modify <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> to use this layout file and to find the <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> in the layout file, as shown in [Listing 9.7](#ch09s02.xhtml_pl_crime_list_fragmnet_view_creation "Listing 9.7  Setting up the view for CrimeListFragment (CrimeListFragment.kt)").

**Listing 9.7  Setting up the view for `CrimeListFragment` (`CrimeListFragment.kt`)**

```
class CrimeListFragment : Fragment() {

    private lateinit var crimeRecyclerView: RecyclerView

    private val crimeListViewModel: CrimeListViewModel by lazy {
        ViewModelProviders.of(this).get(CrimeListViewModel::class.java)
    }

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        Log.d(TAG, "Total crimes: ${crimeListViewModel.crimes.size}")
    }

    override fun onCreateView(
        inflater: LayoutInflater,
        container: ViewGroup?,
        savedInstanceState: Bundle?
    ): View? {
        val view = inflater.inflate(R.layout.fragment_crime_list, container, false)

        crimeRecyclerView =
            view.findViewById(R.id.crime_recycler_view) as RecyclerView
        crimeRecyclerView.layoutManager = LinearLayoutManager(context)

        return view
    }
}
```

Note that as soon as you create your <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp>, you give it another object called a <samp class="classname">LayoutManager</samp>. <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> requires a <samp class="classname">LayoutManager</samp> to work. If you forget to give it one, it will crash.

<samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> does not position items on the screen itself. It delegates that job to the <samp class="classname">LayoutManager</samp>. The <samp class="classname">LayoutManager</samp> positions every item and also defines how scrolling works. So if <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> tries to do those things when the <samp class="classname">LayoutManager</samp> is not there, the <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> will immediately fall over and die.

There are a few built-in <samp class="classname">LayoutManager</samp>s to choose from, and you can find more as third-party libraries. You are using the <samp class="classname">LinearLayoutManager</samp>, which will position the items in the list vertically. Later on in this book, you will use <samp class="classname">GridLayoutManager</samp> to arrange items in a grid instead.

Run the app. You should again see a blank screen, but now you are looking at an empty <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp>.

## Creating an Item View Layout

<samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> is a subclass of <samp class="classname">ViewGroup</samp>. It displays a list of child <samp class="classname">View</samp> objects, called <samp class="firstterm">item views</samp>. Each item view represents a single object from the list of data backing the recycler view (in your case, a single crime from the crime list). Depending on the complexity of what you need to display, these child <samp class="classname">View</samp>s can be complex or very simple.

For your first implementation, each item in the list will display the title and date of a <samp class="classname">Crime</samp>, as shown in [Figure 9.5](#ch09s03.xhtml_fig_crime_list_showing_views "Figure 9.5  A RecyclerView with child Views").

**Figure 9.5  A `RecyclerView` with child `View`s**

![A RecyclerView with child Views](Images/ci_with_text_views.png)

Each item displayed on the <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> will have its own view hierarchy, exactly the way <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> has a view hierarchy for the entire screen. Specifically, the <samp class="classname">View</samp> object on each row will be a <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp> containing two <samp class="classname">TextView</samp>s.

You create a new layout for a list item view the same way you do for the view of an activity or a fragment. In the project tool window, right-click the <samp class="guilabel">res/layout</samp> directory and choose <samp class="guimenu">New</samp> → <samp class="guimenuitem">Layout resource file</samp>. Name the file <samp class="guilabel">list_item_crime</samp>, set the root element to <samp class="guilabel">LinearLayout</samp>, and click <samp class="guibutton">OK</samp>.

Update your layout file to add padding to the <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp> and to add the two <samp class="classname">TextView</samp>s, as shown in [Listing 9.8](#ch09s03.xhtml_fig_list_item_crime_linearlayout "Listing 9.8  Updating the list item layout file (layout/list_item_crime.xml)").

**Listing 9.8  Updating the list item layout file (`layout/list_item_crime.xml`)**

```
<LinearLayout xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
              android:orientation="vertical"
              android:layout_width="match_parent"
              android:layout_height="match_parent">
              android:layout_height="wrap_content"
              android:padding="8dp">

    <TextView
            android:id="@+id/crime_title"
            android:layout_width="match_parent"
            android:layout_height="wrap_content"
            android:text="Crime Title"/>

    <TextView
            android:id="@+id/crime_date"
            android:layout_width="match_parent"
            android:layout_height="wrap_content"
            android:text="Crime Date"/>

</LinearLayout>
```

Take a look at the design preview, and you will see that you have created exactly one row of the completed product. In a moment, you will see how <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> will create those rows for you.

## Implementing a ViewHolder

The <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> expects an item view to be wrapped in an instance of <samp class="classname">ViewHolder</samp>. A <samp class="classname">ViewHolder</samp> stores a reference to an item’s view (and sometimes references to specific widgets within that view).

Define a view holder by adding an inner class in <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> that extends from <samp class="classname">RecyclerView.ViewHolder</samp>.

**Listing 9.9  The beginnings of a `ViewHolder` (`CrimeListFragment.kt`)**

```
class CrimeListFragment : Fragment() {
    ...
    override fun onCreateView(
        inflater: LayoutInflater,
        container: ViewGroup?,
        savedInstanceState: Bundle?
    ): View? {
        ...
    }

    private inner class CrimeHolder(view: View)
        : RecyclerView.ViewHolder(view) {

    }
}
```

In <samp class="classname">CrimeHolder</samp>’s constructor, you take in the view to hold on to. Immediately, you pass it as the argument to the <samp class="classname">RecyclerView.ViewHolder</samp> constructor. The base <samp class="classname">ViewHolder</samp> class will then hold on to the view in a property named `itemView` ([Figure 9.6](#ch09s04.xhtml_fig_view_holder "Figure 9.6  The ViewHolder and its itemView")).

**Figure 9.6  The `ViewHolder` and its `itemView`**

![The ViewHolder and its itemView](Images/view_holder.png)

A <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> never creates <samp class="classname">View</samp>s by themselves. It always creates <samp class="classname">ViewHolder</samp>s, which bring their <samp class="varname">itemView</samp>s along for the ride ([Figure 9.7](#ch09s04.xhtml_fig_ci_recyclerview_with_viewholders "Figure 9.7  The ViewHolder visualized")).

**Figure 9.7  The `ViewHolder` visualized**

![The ViewHolder visualized](Images/ci_recyclerview_with_viewholders.png)

When the <samp class="classname">View</samp> for each item is simple, <samp class="classname">ViewHolder</samp> has few responsibilities. For more complicated <samp class="classname">View</samp>s, the <samp class="classname">ViewHolder</samp> makes wiring up the different parts of <samp class="varname">itemView</samp> to a <samp class="classname">Crime</samp> simpler and more efficient. (For example, you do not need to search through the item view hierarchy to get a handle to the title text view every time you need to set the title.)

Update <samp class="classname">CrimeHolder</samp> to find the title and date text views in `itemView`’s hierarchy when an instance is first created. Store references to the text views in properties.

**Listing 9.10  Pulling out views in the constructor (`CrimeListFragment.kt`)**

```
private inner class CrimeHolder(view: View)
    : RecyclerView.ViewHolder(view) {

    val titleTextView: TextView = itemView.findViewById(R.id.crime_title)
    val dateTextView: TextView = itemView.findViewById(R.id.crime_date)
}
```

The updated view holder now stashes references to the title and date text views so you can easily change the value displayed later without having to go back through the item’s view hierarchy ([Figure 9.8](#ch09s04.xhtml_fig_view_holder_revisualized "Figure 9.8  The ViewHolder re-visualized")).

**Figure 9.8  The `ViewHolder` re-visualized**

![The ViewHolder re-visualized](Images/ci_recyclerview_with_viewholders_revisualized.png)

Note that the <samp class="classname">CrimeHolder</samp> assumes that the view passed to its constructor has child text views with the IDs `R.id.crime_title` and `R.id.crime_date`. You may be wondering, “Who (or what) creates crime holder instances, and can I safely assume the view hierarchy passed to the constructor contains the child widgets I expect?” You will learn the answer to these questions in just a moment.

## Implementing an Adapter to Populate the RecyclerView

[Figure 9.7](#ch09s04.xhtml_fig_ci_recyclerview_with_viewholders "Figure 9.7  The ViewHolder visualized") is somewhat simplified. <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> does not create <samp class="classname">ViewHolder</samp>s itself. Instead, it asks an <samp class="firstterm">adapter</samp>. An adapter is a controller object that sits between the <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> and the data set that the <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> should display.

The adapter is responsible for:

*   creating the necessary <samp class="classname">ViewHolder</samp>s when asked

*   binding <samp class="classname">ViewHolder</samp>s to data from the model layer when asked

The recycler view is responsible for:

*   asking the adapter to create a new <samp class="classname">ViewHolder</samp>

*   asking the adapter to bind a <samp class="classname">ViewHolder</samp> to the item from the backing data at a given position

Time to create your adapter. Add a new inner class named <samp class="classname">CrimeAdapter</samp> to <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp>. Add a primary constructor that expects a list of crimes as input and stores the crime list passed in a property, as shown in [Listing 9.11](#ch09s05.xhtml_pl_crime_list_fragment_adapter_crimes "Listing 9.11  Creating CrimeAdapter (CrimeListFragment.kt)").

In your new <samp class="classname">CrimeAdapter</samp>, you are also going to override three functions: <samp class="methodname">onCreateViewHolder(…)</samp>, <samp class="methodname">onBindViewHolder(…)</samp>, and <samp class="methodname">getItemCount()</samp>. To save you typing (and typos), Android Studio can generate these overrides for you. Once you have typed the initial line of the new code, put your cursor on <samp class="classname">CrimeAdapter</samp> and press Option-Return (Alt-Enter). Select <samp class="guilabel">Implement members</samp> from the pop-up. In the <samp class="guilabel">Implement members</samp> dialog, select all three function names and click <samp class="guibutton">OK</samp>. Then you only need to fill in the bodies as shown.

**Listing 9.11  Creating `CrimeAdapter` (`CrimeListFragment.kt`)**

```
class CrimeListFragment : Fragment() {
    ...
    private inner class CrimeHolder(view: View)
        : RecyclerView.ViewHolder(view) {
        ...
    }

    private inner class CrimeAdapter(var crimes: List<Crime>)
        : RecyclerView.Adapter<CrimeHolder>() {

        override fun onCreateViewHolder(parent: ViewGroup, viewType: Int)
                : CrimeHolder {
            val view = layoutInflater.inflate(R.layout.list_item_crime, parent, false)
            return CrimeHolder(view)
        }

        override fun getItemCount() = crimes.size

        override fun onBindViewHolder(holder: CrimeHolder, position: Int) {
            val crime = crimes[position]
            holder.apply {
                titleTextView.text = crime.title
                dateTextView.text = crime.date.toString()
            }
        }
    }
}
```

<samp class="methodname">Adapter.onCreateViewHolder(…)</samp> is responsible for creating a view to display, wrapping the view in a view holder, and returning the result. In this case, you inflate <samp class="filename">list_item_view.xml</samp> and pass the resulting view to a new instance of <samp class="classname">CrimeHolder</samp>. (For now, you can ignore <samp class="methodname">onCreateViewHolder(…)</samp>’s parameters. You only need these values if you are doing something fancy, like displaying different types of views within the same recycler view. See [the section called *Challenge: RecyclerView ViewTypes*](../Text/ch09s10.xhtml "Challenge: RecyclerView ViewTypes") at the end of this chapter for more information.)

<samp class="methodname">Adapter.onBindViewHolder(holder: CrimeHolder, position: Int)</samp> is responsible for populating a given `holder` with the crime from a given `position`. In this case, you get the crime from the crime list at the requested position. You then use the title and data from that crime to set the text in the corresponding text views.

When the recycler view needs to know how many items are in the data set backing it (such as when the recycler view first spins up), it will ask its adapter by calling <samp class="methodname">Adapter.getItemCount()</samp>. Here, <samp class="methodname">getItemCount()</samp> returns the number of items in the list of crimes to answer the recycler view’s request.

The <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> itself does not know anything about the <samp class="classname">Crime</samp> object or the list of <samp class="classname">Crime</samp> objects to be displayed. Instead, the <samp class="classname">CrimeAdapter</samp> knows all of a <samp class="classname">Crime</samp>’s intimate and personal details. The adapter also knows about the list of crimes that backs the recycler view ([Figure 9.9](#ch09s05.xhtml_dig_ci_adapter_rv_relationship "Figure 9.9  Adapter sits between recycler view and data set")).

**Figure 9.9  `Adapter` sits between recycler view and data set**

![Adapter sits between recycler view and data set](Images/rv_adapter_dataset_simplified_schematic.png)

When the <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> needs a view object to display, it will have a conversation with its adapter. [Figure 9.10](#ch09s05.xhtml_dig_simplified_rv_adapter_interaction "Figure 9.10  A scintillating RecyclerView-Adapter conversation") shows an example of a conversation that a <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> might initiate.

**Figure 9.10  A scintillating `RecyclerView`-`Adapter` conversation**

![A scintillating RecyclerView-Adapter conversation](Images/recyclerview_adapter_interaction_abbreviated.png)

The <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> calls the adapter’s <samp class="methodname">onCreateViewHolder(ViewGroup, Int)</samp> function to create a new <samp class="classname">ViewHolder</samp>, along with its juicy payload: a <samp class="classname">View</samp> to display. The <samp class="classname">ViewHolder</samp> (and its <samp class="varname">itemView</samp>) that the adapter creates and hands back to the <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> has not yet been populated with data from a specific item in the data set.

Next, the <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> calls <samp class="methodname">onBindViewHolder(ViewHolder, Int)</samp>, passing a <samp class="classname">ViewHolder</samp> into this function along with the position. The adapter will look up the model data for that position and <samp class="firstterm">bind</samp> it to the <samp class="classname">ViewHolder</samp>’s <samp class="classname">View</samp>. To bind it, the adapter fills in the <samp class="classname">View</samp> to reflect the data in the model object.

After this process is complete, <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> will place a list item on the screen.

### Setting the RecyclerView’s adapter

Now that you have an <samp class="classname">Adapter</samp>, connect it to your <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp>. Implement a function called <samp class="methodname">updateUI</samp> that sets up <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp>’s UI. For now, it will create a <samp class="classname">CrimeAdapter</samp> and set it on the <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp>.

**Listing 9.12  Setting an `Adapter` (`CrimeListFragment.kt`)**

```
class CrimeListFragment : Fragment() {

    private lateinit var crimeRecyclerView: RecyclerView
    private var adapter: CrimeAdapter? = null
    ...
    override fun onCreateView(
        inflater: LayoutInflater,
        container: ViewGroup?,
        savedInstanceState: Bundle?
    ): View? {
        val view = inflater.inflate(R.layout.fragment_crime_list, container, false)

        crimeRecyclerView =
                view.findViewById(R.id.crime_recycler_view) as RecyclerView
        crimeRecyclerView.layoutManager = LinearLayoutManager(context)

        updateUI()

        return view
    }

    private fun updateUI() {
        val crimes = crimeListViewModel.crimes
        adapter = CrimeAdapter(crimes)
        crimeRecyclerView.adapter = adapter
    }
    ...
}
```

In later chapters, you will add more to <samp class="methodname">updateUI()</samp> as configuring your UI gets more involved.

Run CriminalIntent and scroll through your new <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp>, which should look like [Figure 9.11](#ch09s05.xhtml_fig_rv_populated_with_crimes "Figure 9.11  RecyclerView populated with Crimes").

**Figure 9.11  `RecyclerView` populated with `Crime`s**

![RecyclerView populated with Crimes](Images/ci_with_custom_list_items.png)

Swipe or drag down and you will see even more views scroll across your screen. Every visible <samp class="classname">CrimeHolder</samp> should display a distinct <samp class="classname">Crime</samp>. (If your rows are much taller than these, or if you only see one row on the screen, then double-check that the `layout_height` on your row’s <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp> is set to `wrap_content`.)

When you fling the view up, the scrolling animation should feel as smooth as warm butter. This effect is a direct result of keeping <samp class="methodname">onBindViewHolder(…)</samp> small and efficient, doing only the minimum amount of work necessary. Take heed: Always be efficient in your <samp class="methodname">onBindViewHolder(…)</samp>. Otherwise, your scroll animation could feel as chunky as cold Parmesan cheese.

## Recycling Views

[Figure 9.11](#ch09s05.xhtml_fig_rv_populated_with_crimes "Figure 9.11  RecyclerView populated with Crimes") shows 11 rows of <samp class="classname">View</samp>s. You can swipe to scroll through 100 <samp class="classname">View</samp>s to see all of your <samp class="classname">Crime</samp>s. Does that mean that you have 100 <samp class="classname">View</samp> objects in memory? Thanks to your <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp>, no.

Creating a <samp class="classname">View</samp> for every item in the list all at once could easily become unworkable. As you can imagine, a list can have far more than 100 items, and your list items can be much more involved than your simple implementation here. Also, a <samp class="classname">Crime</samp> only needs a <samp class="classname">View</samp> when it is onscreen, so there is no need to have 100 <samp class="classname">View</samp>s ready and waiting. It would make far more sense to create view objects only as you need them.

<samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> does just that. Instead of creating 100 <samp class="classname">View</samp>s, it creates just enough to fill the screen. When a view is scrolled off the screen, <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> reuses it rather than throwing it away. In short, it lives up to its name: It recycles views over and over.

Because of this, <samp class="methodname">onCreateViewHolder(ViewGroup, Int)</samp> will happen a lot less often than <samp class="methodname">onBindViewHolder(ViewHolder, Int)</samp>. Once enough <samp class="classname">ViewHolder</samp>s have been created, <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> stops calling <samp class="methodname">onCreateViewHolder(…)</samp>. Instead, it saves time and memory by recycling old <samp class="classname">ViewHolder</samp>s and passing those into <samp class="methodname">onBindViewHolder(ViewHolder, Int)</samp>.

## Cleaning Up Binding List Items

Right now, the <samp class="classname">Adapter</samp> binds crime data directly to a crime holder’s text views in <samp class="methodname">Adapter.onBindViewHolder(…)</samp>. This works fine, but it is better to more cleanly separate concerns between the view holder and the adapter. The adapter should know as little as possible about the inner workings and details of the view holder.

We recommend you place all the code that will do the real work of binding inside your <samp class="classname">CrimeHolder</samp>. First, add a property to stash the <samp class="classname">Crime</samp> being bound. While you are at it, make the existing text view properties private. Add a <samp class="methodname">bind(Crime)</samp> function to <samp class="classname">CrimeHolder</samp>. In this new function, cache the crime being bound into a property and set the text values on `titleTextView` and `dateTextView`.

**Listing 9.13  Writing a `bind(Crime)` function (`CrimeListFragment.kt`)**

```
private inner class CrimeHolder(view: View)
    : RecyclerView.ViewHolder(view) {

    private lateinit var crime: Crime

    private val titleTextView: TextView = itemView.findViewById(R.id.crime_title)
    private val dateTextView: TextView = itemView.findViewById(R.id.crime_date)

    fun bind(crime: Crime) {
        this.crime = crime
        titleTextView.text = this.crime.title
        dateTextView.text = this.crime.date.toString()
    }
}
```

When given a <samp class="classname">Crime</samp> to bind, <samp class="classname">CrimeHolder</samp> will now update the title <samp class="classname">TextView</samp> and date <samp class="classname">TextView</samp> to reflect the state of the <samp class="classname">Crime</samp>.

Next, call your newly minted <samp class="methodname">bind(Crime)</samp> function each time the <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> requests that a given <samp class="classname">CrimeHolder</samp> be bound to a particular crime.

**Listing 9.14  Calling the `bind(Crime)` function (`CrimeListFragment.kt`)**

```
private inner class CrimeAdapter(var crimes: List<Crime>)
    :  RecyclerView.Adapter<CrimeHolder>() {

    override fun onCreateViewHolder(parent: ViewGroup, viewType: Int): CrimeHolder {
        ...
    }

    override fun onBindViewHolder(holder: CrimeHolder, position: Int) {
        val crime = crimes[position]
        holder.apply {
            titleTextView.text = crime.title
            dateTextView.text = crime.date.toString()
        }
        holder.bind(crime)
    }

    override fun getItemCount() = crimes.size
}
```

Run CriminalIntent one more time. The result should look the same as it did in [Figure 9.11](#ch09s05.xhtml_fig_rv_populated_with_crimes "Figure 9.11  RecyclerView populated with Crimes").

## Responding to Presses

As icing on the <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> cake, CriminalIntent should also respond to a press on these list items. In [Chapter 12](../Text/ch12.xhtml "12 Fragment Navigation"), you will launch the detail view for a <samp class="classname">Crime</samp> when the user presses on that <samp class="classname">Crime</samp> in the list. For now, show a <samp class="classname">Toast</samp> when the user takes action on a <samp class="classname">Crime</samp>.

As you may have noticed, <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp>, while powerful and capable, has precious few real responsibilities. (May it be an example to us all.) The same goes here: Handling touch events is mostly up to you. If you need them, <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> can forward along raw touch events. But most of the time this is not necessary.

Instead, you can handle them like you normally do: by setting an <samp class="classname">OnClickListener</samp>. Since each <samp class="classname">View</samp> has an associated <samp class="classname">ViewHolder</samp>, you can make your <samp class="classname">ViewHolder</samp> the <samp class="classname">OnClickListener</samp> for its <samp class="classname">View</samp>.

Modify the <samp class="classname">CrimeHolder</samp> to handle presses for the entire row.

**Listing 9.15  Detecting presses in `CrimeHolder` (`CrimeListFragment.kt`)**

```
private inner class CrimeHolder(view: View)
    : RecyclerView.ViewHolder(view), View.OnClickListener {

    private lateinit var crime: Crime

    private val titleTextView: TextView = itemView.findViewById(R.id.crime_title)
    private val dateTextView: TextView = itemView.findViewById(R.id.crime_date)

    init {
        itemView.setOnClickListener(this)
    }

    fun bind(crime: Crime) {
        this.crime = crime
        titleTextView.text = this.crime.title
        dateTextView.text = this.crime.date.toString()
    }

    override fun onClick(v: View) {
        Toast.makeText(context, "${crime.title} pressed!", Toast.LENGTH_SHORT)
                .show()
    }
}
```

In [Listing 9.15](#ch09s08.xhtml_pl_crime_list_fragment_crimeholder_on_click "Listing 9.15  Detecting presses in CrimeHolder (CrimeListFragment.kt)"), the <samp class="classname">CrimeHolder</samp> itself is implementing the <samp class="interfacename">OnClickListener</samp> interface. On the <samp class="varname">itemView</samp>, which is the <samp class="classname">View</samp> for the entire row, the <samp class="classname">CrimeHolder</samp> is set as the receiver of click events.

Run CriminalIntent and press on an item in the list. You should see a <samp class="classname">Toast</samp> indicating that the item was pressed.

## For the More Curious: ListView and GridView

The core Android OS includes <samp class="classname">ListView</samp>, <samp class="classname">GridView</samp>, and <samp class="classname">Adapter</samp> classes. Until the release of Android 5.0, these were the preferred ways to create lists or grids of items.

The API for these components is very similar to that of a <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp>. The <samp class="classname">ListView</samp> or <samp class="classname">GridView</samp> class is responsible for scrolling a collection of items, but it does not know much about each of those items. The <samp class="classname">Adapter</samp> is responsible for creating each of the <samp class="classname">View</samp>s in the list. However, <samp class="classname">ListView</samp> and <samp class="classname">GridView</samp> do not enforce that you use the <samp class="classname">ViewHolder</samp> pattern (though you can – and should – use it).

These old implementations are replaced by the <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> implementation because of the complexity required to alter the behavior of a <samp class="classname">ListView</samp> or <samp class="classname">GridView</samp>.

Creating a horizontally scrolling <samp class="classname">ListView</samp>, for example, is not included in the <samp class="classname">ListView</samp> API and requires a lot of work. Creating custom layout and scrolling behavior with a <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> is still a lot of work, but <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> was built to be extended, so it is not quite so bad.

Another key feature of <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> is the animation of items in the list. Animating the addition or removal of items in a <samp class="classname">ListView</samp> or <samp class="classname">GridView</samp> is a complex and error-prone task. <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> makes this much easier, includes a few built-in animations, and allows for easy customization of these animations.

For example, if you found out that the crime at position 0 moved to position 5, you could animate that change like so:

```
 recyclerView.adapter.notifyItemMoved(0, 5)
```

## Challenge: RecyclerView ViewTypes

For this advanced challenge, you will create two types of rows in your <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp>: a normal row and a row for more serious crimes. To implement this, you will work with the <samp class="emphasis">view type</samp> feature available in <samp class="classname">RecyclerView.Adapter</samp>. Add a new property, <samp class="varname">requiresPolice</samp>, to the <samp class="classname">Crime</samp> object and use it to determine which view to load on the <samp class="classname">CrimeAdapter</samp> by implementing the <samp class="methodname">getItemViewType(Int)</samp> function ([<samp class="uri">developer.android.com/​reference/​android/​support/​v7/​widget/​RecyclerView.Adapter.html#getItemViewType</samp>](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/support/v7/widget/RecyclerView.Adapter.html#getItemViewType)).

In the <samp class="methodname">onCreateViewHolder(ViewGroup, Int)</samp> function, you will also need to add logic that returns a different <samp class="classname">ViewHolder</samp> based on the new <samp class="varname">viewType</samp> value returned by <samp class="methodname">getItemViewType(Int)</samp>. Use the original layout for crimes that do not require police intervention and a new layout with a streamlined interface containing a button that says “contact police” for crimes that do.

# <samp class="chapter_number">10</samp>
<samp class="chapter_name">Creating User Interfaces with Layouts and Widgets</samp>

In this chapter, you will learn more about layouts and widgets while adding some style to your list items in the <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp>. You will also learn how to use the graphical layout editor to arrange widgets within a <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp>. [Figure 10.1](#ch10.xhtml_fig_watson_by_chapter_end "Figure 10.1  CriminalIntent, now with beautiful pictures") shows what <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp>’s view will look like once you chisel down your existing app to build up your masterpiece.

**Figure 10.1  CriminalIntent, now with beautiful pictures**

![CriminalIntent, now with beautiful pictures](Images/ci_fresh_coat_of_paint.png)

In previous chapters you used nested layout hierarchies to arrange your widgets. For example, the <samp class="filename">layout/activity_main.xml</samp> file you created for GeoQuiz in [Chapter 1](../Text/ch01.xhtml "1 Your First Android Application") nested a <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp> within another <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp>. This nesting is hard for you as a developer to read and edit. Worse, nesting can degrade your app’s performance. Nested layouts can take a long time for the Android OS to measure and lay out, meaning your users might experience a delay before they see your views onscreen.

Flat, or non-nested, layouts are quicker for the OS to measure and lay out. And this is one of the areas where <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp> really shines. You can create beautifully intricate layouts without using nesting.

Before you dive in to <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp>, you must do a little legwork and learn a little background. You will need a copy of that fancy handcuff image from [Figure 10.1](#ch10.xhtml_fig_watson_by_chapter_end "Figure 10.1  CriminalIntent, now with beautiful pictures") in your project. Open the solutions file ([<samp class="uri">www.bignerdranch.com/​solutions/​AndroidProgramming4e.zip</samp>](https://www.bignerdranch.com/solutions/AndroidProgramming4e.zip)) and the <samp class="filename">09_LayoutsAndWidgets/CriminalIntent/app/src/main/res</samp> directory. Copy each density version of <samp class="filename">ic_solved.png</samp> into the appropriate drawable folder in your project.

## Introducing ConstraintLayout

With <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp>, instead of using nested layouts you add a series of <samp class="firstterm">constraints</samp> to your layout. A constraint is like a rubber band: It pulls two things toward each other. So, for example, if you have an <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp>, you can attach a constraint from its right edge to the right edge of its parent (the <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp> itself), as shown in [Figure 10.2](#ch10s01.xhtml_fig_ci_glt_constraint_right "Figure 10.2  ImageView with a constraint on the right edge"). The constraint will hold the <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> to the right.

**Figure 10.2  `ImageView` with a constraint on the right edge**

![ImageView with a constraint on the right edge](Images/ci_glt_constraint_rubber_band_one.png)

You can create a constraint from all four edges of your <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> (left, top, right, and bottom). If you have opposing constraints, they will equal out, and your <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> will be right in the center of the two constraints ([Figure 10.3](#ch10s01.xhtml_fig_ci_glt_constraint_right_and_left "Figure 10.3  ImageView with opposing constraints")).

**Figure 10.3  `ImageView` with opposing constraints**

![ImageView with opposing constraints](Images/ci_glt_constraint_rubber_band_two.png)

So that is the big picture: To place views where you want them to go in a <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp>, you give them constraints.

What about sizing widgets? For that, you have three options: Let the widget decide (your old friend `wrap_content`), decide for yourself, or let your widget expand to fit your constraints.

With those tools, you can achieve a great many layouts with a single <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp>, no nesting required. As you go through this chapter, you will see how to use constraints with your <samp class="filename">list_item_crime.xml</samp> layout file.

## Introducing the Graphical Layout Editor

So far, you have created layouts by typing XML. In this section, you will use Android Studio’s graphical layout tool.

Open <samp class="filename">layout/list_item_crime.xml</samp> and select the <samp class="guilabel">Design</samp> tab at the bottom of the file ([Figure 10.4](#ch10s02.xhtml_fig_ci_glt_first_look "Figure 10.4  Views in the graphical layout tool")).

**Figure 10.4  Views in the graphical layout tool**

![Views in the graphical layout tool](Images/ci_glt_first_look.png)

In the middle of the graphical layout editor is the preview you have seen before. To the right of the preview is the <samp class="guilabel">Blueprint</samp>, which, as you saw in [Chapter 1](../Text/ch01.xhtml "1 Your First Android Application"), is like the preview but shows an outline of each of your views. This can be useful when you need to see how big each view is, not just what it is displaying.

On the lefthand side of the screen is the palette, which contains all the widgets you could wish for, organized by category. The component tree is in the bottom left. The tree shows how the widgets are organized in the layout. If you do not see the palette or component tree, click on the tabs on the left side of the preview to open the windows.

On the right side of the screen is the <samp class="firstterm">attributes view</samp>. Here, you can view and edit the attributes of the widget selected in the component tree.

The first thing you need to do is convert <samp class="filename">list_item_crime.xml</samp> to use a <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp>. Right-click on your root <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp> in the component tree and select <samp class="guilabel">Convert LinearLayout to ConstraintLayout</samp> ([Figure 10.5](#ch10s02.xhtml_fig_ci_glt_convert_constraint_layout "Figure 10.5  Converting the root view to a ConstraintLayout")).

**Figure 10.5  Converting the root view to a `ConstraintLayout`**

![Converting the root view to a ConstraintLayout](Images/ci_glt_convert_constraint_layout.png)

Android Studio will ask you in a pop-up how aggressive you would like this conversion process to be ([Figure 10.6](#ch10s02.xhtml_fig_ci_glt_convert_constraint_layout_question "Figure 10.6  Converting with the default configuration")). Since <samp class="filename">list_item_crime.xml</samp> is a simple layout file, there is not much that Android Studio can optimize. Leave the default values checked and select <samp class="guilabel">OK</samp>.

**Figure 10.6  Converting with the default configuration**

![Converting with the default configuration](Images/ci_glt_convert_constraint_layout_question.png)

Be patient. The conversion process might take a little while. But when it is complete, you will have a fine, new <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp> to work with ([Figure 10.7](#ch10s02.xhtml_ss_ciLayoutsAndWidgets_conversion_done "Figure 10.7  Life as a ConstraintLayout")).

**Figure 10.7  Life as a `ConstraintLayout`**

![Life as a ConstraintLayout](Images/ss_ciLayoutsAndWidgets_conversion_done.png)

(Wondering why the component tree says you have a <samp class="guilabel">linearLayout</samp>? We will get to that in a moment.)

The toolbar above the preview has a few editing controls ([Figure 10.8](#ch10s02.xhtml_fig_ci_glt_constraint_options "Figure 10.8  Constraint controls")). You may need to click into the preview to see all the controls.

**Figure 10.8  Constraint controls**

![Constraint controls](Images/ci_glt_constraint_options.png)

| View Options |
| Toggle Autoconnect |
| Clear All Constraints |
| Infer Constraints |

## Using ConstraintLayout

When you converted <samp class="filename">list_item_crime.xml</samp> to use <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp>, Android Studio automatically added the constraints it thinks will replicate the behavior of your old layout. However, to learn how constraints work you are going to start from scratch.

Select the top-level view in the component tree, labeled <samp class="guilabel">linearLayout</samp>. Why does it say <samp class="guilabel">linearLayout</samp>, when you converted it to a <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp>? That is the ID the <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp> converter supplied. <samp class="guilabel">linearLayout</samp> is, in fact, your <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp>. You can check the XML version of your layout if you want to confirm this.

With <samp class="guilabel">linearLayout</samp> selected in the component tree, click the <samp class="guilabel">Clear All Constraints</samp> button (shown in [Figure 10.8](#ch10s02.xhtml_fig_ci_glt_constraint_options "Figure 10.8  Constraint controls")). You will immediately see red warning flags, including one at the top right of the screen. Click on it to see what that is all about ([Figure 10.9](#ch10s03.xhtml_ss_constraint_layout_warnings "Figure 10.9  ConstraintLayout warnings")).

**Figure 10.9  `ConstraintLayout` warnings**

![ConstraintLayout warnings](Images/constraint_layout_warnings.png)

When views do not have enough constraints, <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp> cannot know exactly where to put them. Your <samp class="classname">TextView</samp>s have no constraints at all, so they each have a warning that says they will not appear in the right place at runtime.

As you go through the chapter, you will add those constraints back to fix those warnings. In your own work, keep an eye on that warning indicator to avoid unexpected behavior at runtime.

### Making room

You need to make some room to work in the graphical layout editor. Your two <samp class="classname">TextView</samp>s are taking up the entire area, which will make it hard to wire up anything else. Time to shrink those two widgets.

Select <samp class="guilabel">crime_title</samp> in the component tree and look at the attributes view on the right ([Figure 10.10](#ch10s03.xhtml_fig_ci_glt_properties_view "Figure 10.10  Title TextView’s attributes")). If this pane is not open for you, click the <samp class="guilabel">Attributes</samp> tab on the right to open it.

**Figure 10.10  Title `TextView`’s attributes**

![Title TextView’s attributes](Images/ci_glt_constraint_layout_properties_size.png)

The vertical and horizontal sizes of your <samp class="classname">TextView</samp> are governed by the height setting and width setting, respectively. These can be set to one of three view size settings ([Figure 10.11](#ch10s03.xhtml_fig_ci_glt_properties_view_sizes "Figure 10.11  Three view size settings")), each of which corresponds to a value for `layout_width` or `layout_height`.

**Figure 10.11  Three view size settings**

![Three view size settings](Images/ci_glt_constraint_layout_view_type.png)

**Table 10.1  View size setting types**

| Setting type | Setting value | Usage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| fixed | `Xdp` | Specifies an explicit size (that will not change) for the view. The size is specified in `dp` units. (If you need a refresher on `dp` units, see [the section called *Screen Pixel Densities*](../Text/ch02s06.xhtml "Screen Pixel Densities") in [Chapter 2](../Text/ch02.xhtml "2 Android and Model-View-Controller").) |
| wrap content | `wrap_content` | Assigns the view its “desired” size. For a <samp class="classname">TextView</samp>, this means that the size will be just big enough to show its contents. |
| match constraint | `match_constraint` | Allows the view to stretch to meet the specified constraints. |

Both the title and date <samp class="classname">TextView</samp>s are set to a large fixed width, which is why they are taking up the whole screen. Adjust the width and height of both of these widgets. With <samp class="guilabel">crime_title</samp> still selected in the component tree, click the width setting until it cycles around to the wrap content setting. If necessary, adjust the height setting until the height is also set to wrap content ([Figure 10.12](#ch10s03.xhtml_fig_ci_glt_textview_width_height "Figure 10.12  Adjusting the title width and height")).

**Figure 10.12  Adjusting the title width and height**

![Adjusting the title width and height](Images/ci_glt_title_width_height.png)
