Repeat the process with the <samp class="guilabel">crime_date</samp> widget to set its width and height.

Now the two widgets are the correct size ([Figure 10.13](#ch10s03.xhtml_fig_ci_glt_overlap_textview "Figure 10.13  Correctly sized TextViews")), but they will still overlap when the app runs because they have no constraints. Note that the positioning you see in the preview differs from what you see when you run the app. The preview allows you to position the views to make it easier to add your constraints, but these positions are only valid in the preview, not at runtime.

**Figure 10.13  Correctly sized `TextView`s**

![Correctly sized TextViews](Images/ci_glt_overlap_constraint.png)

You will add constraints to correctly position your <samp class="classname">TextView</samp>s later. First, you will add the third view you need in your layout.

### Adding widgets

With your other widgets out of the way, you can add the handcuffs image to your layout. Add an <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> to your layout file. In the palette, find <samp class="guilabel">ImageView</samp> in the <samp class="guilabel">Common</samp> category ([Figure 10.14](#ch10s03.xhtml_fig_ci_glt_add_imageview "Figure 10.14  Finding the ImageView")). Drag it into your component tree as a child of the <samp class="guilabel">ConstraintLayout</samp>, just underneath <samp class="guilabel">crime_date</samp>.

**Figure 10.14  Finding the `ImageView`**

![Finding the ImageView](Images/ci_glt_add_imageview.png)

In the pop-up, expand the <samp class="guilabel">Project</samp> section and choose <samp class="guilabel">ic_solved</samp> as the resource for the <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> ([Figure 10.15](#ch10s03.xhtml_fig_ci_glt_add_imageview_resource "Figure 10.15  Choosing the ImageView’s resource")). This image will be used to indicate which crimes have been solved. Click <samp class="guibutton">OK</samp>.

**Figure 10.15  Choosing the `ImageView`’s resource**

![Choosing the ImageView’s resource](Images/ci_glt_add_imageview_resource.png)

The <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> is now a part of your layout, but it has no constraints. So while the graphical layout editor gives it a position, that position does not really mean anything.

Time to add some constraints. Click on your <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> in the preview pane. (You may want to zoom the preview in to get a better look. The zoom controls are in the toolbar above the constraint tools.) You will see dots on each side of the <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> ([Figure 10.16](#ch10s03.xhtml_fig_ci_glt_constraint_handle "Figure 10.16  ImageView’s constraint handles")). Each of these dots represents a <samp class="firstterm">constraint handle</samp>.

**Figure 10.16  `ImageView`’s constraint handles**

![ImageView’s constraint handles](Images/ci_glt_constraint_handle.png)

You want the <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> to be anchored in the right side of the view. To accomplish this, you need to create constraints from the top, right, and bottom edges of the <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp>.

Before adding constraints, drag the <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> to the right and down to move it away from the <samp class="classname">TextView</samp>s ([Figure 10.17](#ch10s03.xhtml_ss_ci_move_image_view_to_make_room "Figure 10.17  Moving a widget temporarily")). Do not worry about where you place the <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp>. This placement will be ignored once you get your constraints in place.

**Figure 10.17  Moving a widget temporarily**

![Moving a widget temporarily](Images/ci_move_image_view_to_make_room.png)

First, you are going to set a constraint between the top of the <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> and the top of the <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp>. In the preview, drag the top constraint handle from the <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> to the top of the <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp>. The handle will display an arrow and turn green ([Figure 10.18](#ch10s03.xhtml_ss_ci_create_top_constraint_midway "Figure 10.18  Part of the way through creating a top constraint")).

**Figure 10.18  Part of the way through creating a top constraint**

![Part of the way through creating a top constraint](Images/ci_create_top_constraint_midway.png)

Keep dragging. Watch for the constraint handle to turn blue, then release the mouse to create the constraint ([Figure 10.19](#ch10s03.xhtml_ss_ci_create_top_constraint "Figure 10.19  Creating a top constraint")).

**Figure 10.19  Creating a top constraint**

![Creating a top constraint](Images/ci_create_top_constraint.png)

Be careful to avoid clicking when the mouse cursor is a corner shape – this will resize your <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> instead. Also, make sure you do not inadvertently attach the constraint to one of your <samp class="classname">TextView</samp>s. If you do, click on the constraint handle to delete the bad constraint, then try again.

When you let go and set the constraint, the view will snap into position to account for the presence of the new constraint. This is how you move views around in a <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp> – by setting and removing constraints.

Verify that your <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> has a top constraint connected to the top of the <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp> by hovering over the <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> with your mouse. It should look like [Figure 10.20](#ch10s03.xhtml_ci_glt_imageview_top_constraint "Figure 10.20  ImageView with a top constraint").

**Figure 10.20  `ImageView` with a top constraint**

![ImageView with a top constraint](Images/ci_glt_imageview_top_constraint.png)

Do the same for the bottom constraint handle, dragging it from the <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> to the bottom of the root view ([Figure 10.21](#ch10s03.xhtml_fig_ci_glt_imageview_constraint_in_progress "Figure 10.21  ImageView with top and bottom constraints")), again taking care to avoid attaching it to the <samp class="classname">TextView</samp>s.

**Figure 10.21  `ImageView` with top and bottom constraints**

![ImageView with top and bottom constraints](Images/ci_glt_convert_constraint_bottom_imageview.png)

Finally, drag the right constraint handle from the <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> to the right side of the root view. That should set all of your constraints. Your constraints should look like [Figure 10.22](#ch10s03.xhtml_fig_ci_glt_imageview_with_constraints "Figure 10.22  ImageView’s three constraints").

**Figure 10.22  `ImageView`’s three constraints**

![ImageView’s three constraints](Images/ci_glt_convert_constraint_on_imageview.png)

### ConstraintLayout’s inner workings

Any edits that you make with the graphical layout editor are reflected in the XML behind the scenes. You can still edit the raw <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp> XML, but the graphical layout editor will often be easier for adding the initial constraints. <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp> is much more verbose than other <samp class="classname">ViewGroup</samp>s, so adding the initial constraints manually can be a lot of work. Working directly with the XML can be more useful when you need to make smaller changes to the layout.

(The graphical layout tools are useful, especially with <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp>. Not everyone is a fan, though. You do not have to choose sides – you can switch between the graphical layout editor and directly editing XML at any time. Use whichever tool you prefer to create the layouts in this book. You can decide for yourself how to create it – XML, graphical layout editor, or some of each.)

Switch to the text view to see what happened to the XML when you created the three constraints on your <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp>:

```
 <androidx.constraintlayout.widget.ConstraintLayout
            ... >
        ...
        <ImageView
            android:id="@+id/imageView"
            android:layout_width="wrap_content"
            android:layout_height="wrap_content"
            android:layout_marginTop="8dp"
            android:layout_marginEnd="8dp"
            android:layout_marginBottom="8dp"
            app:layout_constraintBottom_toBottomOf="parent"
            app:layout_constraintEnd_toEndOf="parent"
            app:layout_constraintTop_toTopOf="parent"
            app:srcCompat="@drawable/ic_solved" />

    </android.support.constraint.ConstraintLayout>
```

(You will still see errors related to the two <samp class="classname">TextView</samp>s. Leave them as is – you will fix them later.)

All of the widgets are direct children of the single <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp> – there are no nested layouts. If you had created the same layout using <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp>, you would have had to nest one inside another. As we said earlier, reducing nesting also reduces the time needed to render the layout, and that results in a quicker, more seamless user experience.

Take a closer look at the top constraint on the <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp>:

```
 app:layout_constraintTop_toTopOf="parent"
```

This attribute begins with `layout_`. All attributes that begin with `layout_` are known as <samp class="firstterm">layout parameters</samp>. Unlike other attributes, layout parameters are directions to that widget’s <samp class="emphasis">parent</samp>, not the widget itself. They tell the parent layout how to arrange the child element within itself. You have seen a few layout parameters so far, like `layout_width` and `layout_height`.

The name of the constraint is `constraintTop`. This means that this is the top constraint on your <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp>.

Finally, the attribute ends with `toTopOf="parent"`. This means that this constraint is connected to the top edge of the parent. The parent here is the <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp>.

Whew, what a mouthful. Time to leave the raw XML behind and return to the graphical layout editor.

### Making list items dynamic

Now that the layout includes the right constraints, update the <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> so that the handcuffs are only shown on crimes that have been solved.

First, update the ID of your <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp>. When you added the <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> to your <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp>, it was given a default name. That name is not very descriptive. Select your <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> and, in the attributes pane, update the <samp class="guilabel">ID</samp> attribute to <samp class="guilabel">crime_solved</samp> ([Figure 10.31](#ch10s03.xhtml_fig_ci_image_view_id "Figure 10.31  Updating the image ID")). You will be asked whether Android Studio should update all usages of the ID; select <samp class="guilabel">Yes</samp>.

**Figure 10.31  Updating the image ID**

![Updating the image ID](Images/ci_glt_imageview_id.png)

You may notice that you are using the same view IDs in different layouts. The `crime_solved` ID is used in both the <samp class="filename">list_item_crime.xml</samp> and <samp class="filename">fragment_crime.xml</samp> layouts. You may think reusing IDs would be an issue, but in this case it is not a problem. Layout IDs only need to be unique in the same layout. Since your IDs are defined in different layout files, there is no problem using the same ID in both.

With a proper ID in place, now you will update your code. Open <samp class="filename">CrimeListFragment.kt</samp>. In <samp class="classname">CrimeHolder</samp>, add an <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> instance variable and toggle its visibility based on the solved status of the crime.

**Listing 10.1  Updating handcuff visibility (`CrimeListFragment.kt`)**

```
private inner class CrimeHolder(view: View)
    : RecyclerView.ViewHolder(view), View.OnClickListener {
    ...
    private val dateTextView: TextView
    private val solvedImageView: ImageView = itemView.findViewById(R.id.crime_solved)

    init {
        ...
    }

    fun bind(crime: Crime) {
        this.crime = crime
        titleTextView.text = this.crime.title
        dateTextView.text = this.crime.date.toString()
        solvedImageView.visibility = if (crime.isSolved) {
            View.VISIBLE
        } else {
            View.GONE
        }
    }
    ...
}
```

Run CriminalIntent and verify that the handcuffs now appear on every other row. (Check <samp class="classname">CrimeListViewModel</samp> if you do not recall why this would be the case.)

### Styles, themes, and theme attributes

A <samp class="firstterm">style</samp> is an XML resource that contains attributes that describe how a widget should look and behave. For example, the following is a style resource that configures a widget with a larger-than-normal text size:

```
 <style name="BigTextStyle">
        <item name="android:textSize">20sp</item>
        <item name="android:padding">3dp</item>
      </style>
```

You can create your own styles (and you will in [Chapter 21](../Text/ch21.xhtml "21 Styles and Themes")). You add them to a styles file in <samp class="filename">res/values/</samp> and refer to them in layouts like this: `@style/my_own_style`.

Take another look at the <samp class="classname">TextView</samp> widgets in <samp class="filename">layout/fragment_crime.xml</samp> (not the <samp class="filename">list_item_crime.xml</samp> file you have been working in for this chapter). Each has a `style` attribute that refers to a style created by Android. This particular style makes the <samp class="classname">TextView</samp>s look like list separators and comes from the app’s <samp class="firstterm">theme</samp>. A theme is a collection of styles. Structurally, a theme is itself a style resource whose attributes point to other style resources.

Android provides platform themes that your apps can use. When you created CriminalIntent, the wizard set up a theme for the app that is referenced on the `application` tag in the manifest.

You can apply a style from the app’s theme to a widget using a <samp class="firstterm">theme attribute reference</samp>. This is what you are doing in <samp class="filename">fragment_crime.xml</samp> when you use the value `?android:listSeparatorTextViewStyle`.

In a theme attribute reference, you tell Android’s runtime resource manager, “Go to the app’s theme and find the attribute named `listSeparatorTextViewStyle`. This attribute points to another style resource. Put the value of that resource here.”

Every Android theme will include an attribute named `listSeparatorTextViewStyle`, but its definition will be different depending on the overall look and feel of the particular theme. Using a theme attribute reference ensures that the <samp class="classname">TextView</samp>s will have the correct look and feel for your app.

You will learn more about how styles and themes work in [Chapter 21](../Text/ch21.xhtml "21 Styles and Themes").

## For the More Curious: Margins vs Padding

In both GeoQuiz and CriminalIntent, you have given widgets margin and padding attributes. Beginning developers sometimes get confused about these two. Now that you understand what a layout parameter is, the difference is easier to explain.

Margin attributes are layout parameters. They determine the distance between widgets. Given that a widget can only know about itself, margins must be the responsibility of the widget’s parent.

Padding, on the other hand, is not a layout parameter. The `android:padding` attribute tells the widget how much bigger than its contents it should draw itself. For example, say you wanted the date button to be spectacularly large without changing its text size ([Figure 10.34](#ch10s05.xhtml_fig_ci_big_button "Figure 10.34  I like big buttons and I cannot lie...")).

**Figure 10.34  I like big buttons and I cannot lie...**

![I like big buttons and I cannot lie...](Images/ci_big_button.png)

You could add the following attribute to the <samp class="classname">Button</samp>:

```
 <Button
        android:id="@+id/crime_date"
        android:layout_width="match_parent"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:padding="80dp"
        tools:text="Wed Nov 14 11:56 EST 2018"/>
```

Alas, you should probably remove this attribute before continuing.

## For the More Curious: New Developments in ConstraintLayout

<samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp> has additional capabilities to help arrange its child views. In this chapter you positioned views by constraining them to the parent as well as to other, sibling views. <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp> also includes helper views, such as <samp class="classname">Guideline</samp>s, that simplify arranging views on the screen.

Guidelines do not display on the app screen; they are just a tool to help you position views the way you need. There are both horizontal and vertical guidelines, and they can be placed at a specific location on the screen using dp values or by setting them to be a percentage of the screen. Other views can be constrained to the guideline to ensure that they appear at the same location, even if the screen size is different.

[Figure 10.35](#ch10s06.xhtml_fig_ci_guideline "Figure 10.35  Using a Guideline") shows an example of using a vertical <samp class="classname">Guideline</samp>. It is positioned at 20 percent of the width of the parent. Both the crime title and date have a left constraint to the <samp class="classname">Guideline</samp> instead of to the parent.

**Figure 10.35  Using a `Guideline`**

![Using a Guideline](Images/ci_guideline.png)

<samp class="classname">MotionLayout</samp> is an extension of <samp class="classname">ConstraintLayout</samp> that simplifies adding animations to your views. To use <samp class="classname">MotionLayout</samp>, you create a MotionScene file that describes how the animations should be performed and which views map to each other in the starting and ending layouts. You can also set <samp class="classname">Keyframe</samp>s that provide intermediary views in the animation. <samp class="classname">MotionLayout</samp> can animate from the starting view through the various keyframes you provide, then ensure that the view animates to the ending layout appropriately.

## Challenge: Formatting the Date

The <samp class="classname">Date</samp> object is more of a timestamp than a conventional date. A timestamp is what you see when you call <samp class="methodname">toString()</samp> on a <samp class="classname">Date</samp>, so that is what you have in each of your <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> rows. While timestamps make for good documentation, it might be nicer if the rows just displayed the date as humans think of it – like “Jul 22, 2019.” You can do this with an instance of the <samp class="classname">android.text.format.DateFormat</samp> class. The place to start is the reference page for this class in the Android documentation.

You can use functions in the <samp class="classname">DateFormat</samp> class to get a common format. Or you can prepare your own format string. For a more advanced challenge, create a format string that will display the day of the week as well – for example, “Monday, Jul 22, 2019.”

# <samp class="chapter_number">11</samp>
<samp class="chapter_name">Databases and the Room Library</samp>

Almost every application needs a place to save data for the long term. In this chapter you will implement a database for CriminalIntent and seed it with dummy data. Then you will update the app to pull crime data from the database and display it in the crime list ([Figure 11.1](#ch11.xhtml_ss_database_crimes_end_goal "Figure 11.1  Displaying crimes from the database")).

**Figure 11.1  Displaying crimes from the database**

![Displaying crimes from the database](Images/database_crimes.png)

In [Chapter 4](../Text/ch04.xhtml "4 Persisting UI State") you learned how to persist transient UI state data across rotation and process death using <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> and saved instance state. These two approaches are great for small amounts of data tied to the UI. However, these approaches should not be used for storing non-UI data or data that is not tied to an activity or fragment instance and needs to persist regardless of UI state.

Instead, store your non-UI app data either locally (on the filesystem or in a database, as you will do for CriminalIntent) or on a web server.

## Room Architecture Component Library

Room is a Jetpack architecture component library that simplifies database setup and access. It allows you to define your database structure and queries using annotated Kotlin classes.

Room is composed of an API, annotations, and a compiler. The API contains classes you extend to define your database and build an instance of it. You use the annotations to indicate things like which classes need to be stored in the database, which class represents your database, and which class specifies the accessor functions to your database tables. The compiler processes the annotated classes and generates the implementation of your database.

To use Room, you first need to add the dependencies it requires. Add the `room-runtime` and `room-compiler` dependencies to your <samp class="filename">app/build.gradle</samp> file.

**Listing 11.1  Adding dependencies (`app/build.gradle`)**

```
apply plugin: 'kotlin-android-extensions'

apply plugin: 'kotlin-kapt'

android {
    ...
}
...
dependencies {
    ...
    implementation 'androidx.core:core-ktx:1.1.0-alpha04'
    implementation 'androidx.room:room-runtime:2.1.0-alpha04'
    kapt 'androidx.room:room-compiler:2.1.0-alpha04'
    ...
}
```

Near the top of the file, you added a new Android Studio <samp class="firstterm">plug-in</samp>. Plug-ins are a way to add functionality to the IDE. Check out [<samp class="uri">plugins.jetbrains.com/​androidstudio</samp>](https://plugins.jetbrains.com/androidstudio) for more plug-ins you can add.

`kotlin-kapt` stands for “Kotlin annotation processor tool.” When libraries generate code for you, you will often want to use those generated classes directly in your code. But by default, those generated classes are not visible to Android Studio, so you will see an error if you try to import them. Adding the `kotlin-kapt` plug-in makes library-generated files visible to Android Studio so that you can import them in your own classes.

The first dependency you added, `room-runtime`, is for the Room API containing all the classes and annotations you will need to define your database. The second dependency, `room-compiler`, is for the Room compiler, which will generate your database implementation based on the annotations you specify. The compiler uses the `kapt` keyword, instead of `implementation`, so that the generated classes from the compiler are visible to Android Studio, thanks to the `kotlin-kapt` plug-in.

Do not forget to sync your Gradle files. With your dependencies in place, you can move on to preparing your model layer for storage in the database.

## Creating a Database

There are three steps to creating a database with Room:

*   annotating your model class to make it a database entity

*   creating the class that will represent the database itself

*   creating a type converter so that your database can handle your model data

Room makes each of these steps straightforward, as you are about to see.

### Defining entities

Room structures the database tables for your application based on the <samp class="firstterm">entities</samp> you define. Entities are model classes you create, annotated with the `@Entity` annotation. Room will create a database table for any class with that annotation.

Since you want to store crime objects in your database, update <samp class="classname">Crime</samp> to be a Room entity. Open <samp class="filename">Crime.kt</samp> and add two annotations:

**Listing 11.2  Making `Crime` an entity (`Crime.kt`)**

```
@Entity
data class Crime(@PrimaryKey val id: UUID = UUID.randomUUID(),
                 var title: String = "",
                 var date: Date = Date(),
                 var isSolved: Boolean = false)
```

The first annotation, `@Entity`, is applied at the class level. This entity annotation indicates that the class defines the structure of a table, or set of tables, in the database. In this case, each row in the table will represent an individual <samp class="classname">Crime</samp>. Each property defined on the class will be a column in the table, with the name of the property as the name of the column. The table that stores your crimes will have four columns: `id`, `title`, `date`, and `isSolved`.

The other annotation you added is `@PrimaryKey`, which you added to the `id` property. This annotation specifies which column in your database is the <samp class="firstterm">primary key</samp>. The primary key in a database is a column that holds data that is unique for each entry, or row, so that it can be used to look up individual entries. The `id` property is unique for every <samp class="classname">Crime</samp>, so by adding `@PrimaryKey` to this property you will be able to query a single crime from the database using its `id`.

Now that your <samp class="classname">Crime</samp> class is annotated, you can move on to creating your database class.

### Creating a database class

Entity classes define the structure of database tables. A single entity class could be used across multiple databases, should your app have more than one database. That case is not common, but it is possible. For this reason, an entity class is not used by Room to create a table unless you explicitly associate it with a database, which you will do shortly.

First, create a new package called `database` for your database-specific code. In the project tool window, right-click the `com.bignerdranch.android.criminalintent` folder and choose <samp class="guimenu">New</samp> → <samp class="guimenuitem">Package</samp>. Name your new package <samp class="guilabel">database</samp>.

Now, create a new class called <samp class="classname">CrimeDatabase</samp> in the `database` package and define the class as shown below.

**Listing 11.3  Initial `CrimeDatabase` class (`database/CrimeDatabase.kt`)**

```
@Database(entities = [ Crime::class ], version=1)
abstract class CrimeDatabase : RoomDatabase() {
}
```

The `@Database` annotation tells Room that this class represents a database in your app. The annotation itself requires two parameters. The first parameter is a list of entity classes, which tells Room which entity classes to use when creating and managing tables for this database. In this case, you only pass the <samp class="classname">Crime</samp> class, since it is the only entity in the app.

The second parameter is the version of the database. When you first create a database, the version should be 1\. As you develop your app in the future, you may add new entities and new properties to existing entities. When this happens, you will need to modify your entities list and increment your database version to tell Room something has changed. (You will do this in [Chapter 15](../Text/ch15.xhtml "15 Implicit Intents").)

The database class itself is empty at this point. <samp class="classname">CrimeDatabase</samp> extends from <samp class="classname">RoomDatabase</samp> and is marked as `abstract`, so you cannot make an instance of it directly. You will learn how to use Room to get a database instance you can use later in this chapter.

#### Creating a type converter

Room uses SQLite under the hood. SQLite is an open source relational database, like MySQL or PostgreSQL. (SQL, short for Structured Query Language, is a standard language used for interacting with databases. People pronounce “SQL” as either “sequel” or as an initialism, “S-Q-L.”) Unlike other databases, SQLite stores its data in simple files you can read and write using the SQLite library. Android includes this SQLite library in its standard library, along with some additional helper classes.

Room makes using SQLite even easier and cleaner, serving as an object-relational mapping (or ORM) layer between your Kotlin objects and database implementation. For the most part, you do not need to know or care about SQLite when using Room, but if you want to learn more you can visit [<samp class="uri">www.sqlite.org</samp>](https://www.sqlite.org), which has complete SQLite documentation.

Room is able to store primitive types with ease in the underlying SQLite database tables, but other types will cause issues. Your <samp class="classname">Crime</samp> class relies on the <samp class="classname">Date</samp> and <samp class="classname">UUID</samp> objects, which Room does not know how to store by default. You need to give the database a hand so it knows how to store these types and how to pull them out of the database table correctly.

To tell Room how to convert your data types, you specify a <samp class="firstterm">type converter</samp>. A type converter tells Room how to convert a specific type to the format it needs to store in the database. You will need two functions, which you will annotate with `@TypeConverter`, for each type: One tells Room how to convert the type to store it in the database, and the other tells Room how to convert from the database representation back to the original type.

Create a class called <samp class="classname">CrimeTypeConverters</samp> in the `database` package and add two functions each for the <samp class="classname">Date</samp> and <samp class="classname">UUID</samp> types.

**Listing 11.4  Adding `TypeConverter` functions (`database/CrimeTypeConverters.kt`)**

```
class CrimeTypeConverters {

    @TypeConverter
    fun fromDate(date: Date?): Long? {
        return date?.time
    }

    @TypeConverter
    fun toDate(millisSinceEpoch: Long?): Date? {
        return millisSinceEpoch?.let {
            Date(it)
        }
    }

    @TypeConverter
    fun toUUID(uuid: String?): UUID? {
        return UUID.fromString(uuid)
    }

    @TypeConverter
    fun fromUUID(uuid: UUID?): String? {
        return uuid?.toString()
    }
}
```

The first two functions handle the <samp class="classname">Date</samp> object, and the second two handle the <samp class="classname">UUID</samp>s. Make sure you import the `java.util.Date` version of the <samp class="classname">Date</samp> class.

Declaring the converter functions does not enable your database to use them. You must explicitly add the converters to your database class.

**Listing 11.5  Enabling `TypeConverter`s (`database/CrimeDatabase.kt`)**

```
@Database(entities = [ Crime::class ], version=1)
@TypeConverters(CrimeTypeConverters::class)
abstract class CrimeDatabase : RoomDatabase() {
}
```

By adding the `@TypeConverters` annotation and passing in your <samp class="classname">CrimeTypeConverters</samp> class, you tell your database to use the functions in that class when converting your types.

With that, your database and table definitions are complete.

## Defining a Data Access Object

A database table does not do much good if you cannot edit or access its contents. The first step to interacting with your database tables is to create a <samp class="firstterm">data access object</samp>, or DAO. A DAO is an interface that contains functions for each database operation you want to perform. In this chapter, CriminalIntent’s DAO needs two query functions: one to return a list of all crimes in the database and another to return a single crime matching a given <samp class="classname">UUID</samp>.

Add a file named <samp class="filename">CrimeDao.kt</samp> to the <samp class="filename">database</samp> package. In it, define an empty interface named <samp class="classname">CrimeDao</samp> annotated with Room’s `@Dao` annotation.

**Listing 11.6  Creating an empty DAO (`database/CrimeDao.kt`)**

```
@Dao
interface CrimeDao {
}
```

The `@Dao` annotation lets Room know that <samp class="classname">CrimeDao</samp> is one of your data access objects. When you hook <samp class="classname">CrimeDao</samp> up to your database class, Room will generate implementations of the functions you add to this interface.

Speaking of adding functions, now is the time. Add two query functions to <samp class="classname">CrimeDao</samp>.

**Listing 11.7  Adding database query functions (`database/CrimeDao.kt`)**

```
@Dao
interface CrimeDao {

    @Query("SELECT * FROM crime")
    fun getCrimes(): List<Crime>

    @Query("SELECT * FROM crime WHERE id=(:id)")
    fun getCrime(id: UUID): Crime?
}
```

The `@Query` annotation indicates that <samp class="methodname">getCrimes()</samp> and <samp class="methodname">getCrime(UUID)</samp> are meant to pull information out of the database, rather than inserting, updating, or deleting items from the database. The return type of each query function in the DAO interface reflects the type of result the query will return.

The `@Query` annotation expects a string containing a SQL command as input. In most cases you only need to know minimal SQL to use Room, but if you are interested in learning more check out the SQL Syntax section at [<samp class="uri">www.sqlite.org</samp>](https://www.sqlite.org).

`SELECT * FROM crime` asks Room to pull all columns for all rows in the `crime` database table. `SELECT * FROM crime WHERE id=(:id)` asks Room to pull all columns from only the row whose `id` matches the ID value provided.

With that, the <samp class="classname">CrimeDao</samp> is complete, at least for now. In [Chapter 12](../Text/ch12.xhtml "12 Fragment Navigation") you will add a function to update an existing crime. In [Chapter 14](../Text/ch14.xhtml "14 The App Bar") you will add a function to insert a new crime.

Next, you need to register your DAO class with your database class. Since the <samp class="classname">CrimeDao</samp> is an interface, Room will handle generating the concrete version of the class for you. But for that to work, you need to tell your database class to generate an instance of the DAO.

To hook up your DAO, open <samp class="filename">CrimeDatabase.kt</samp> and add an abstract function that has <samp class="classname">CrimeDao</samp> as the return type.

**Listing 11.8  Registering the DAO in the database (`database/CrimeDatabase.kt`)**

```
@Database(entities = [ Crime::class ], version=1)
@TypeConverters(CrimeTypeConverters::class)
abstract class CrimeDatabase : RoomDatabase() {

    abstract fun crimeDao(): CrimeDao
}
```

Now, when the database is created, Room will generate a concrete implementation of the DAO that you can access. Once you have a reference to the DAO, you can call any of the functions defined on it to interact with your database.

## Accessing the Database Using the Repository Pattern

To access your database, you will use the <samp class="firstterm">repository pattern</samp> recommended by Google in its Guide to App Architecture ([<samp class="uri">developer.android.com/​jetpack/​docs/​guide</samp>](https://developer.android.com/jetpack/docs/guide)).

A <samp class="firstterm">repository</samp> class encapsulates the logic for accessing data from a single source or a set of sources. It determines how to fetch and store a particular set of data, whether locally in a database or from a remote server. Your UI code will request all the data from the repository, because the UI does not care how the data is actually stored or fetched. Those are implementation details of the repository itself.

Since CriminalIntent is a simpler app, the repository will only handle fetching data from the database.

Create a class called <samp class="classname">CrimeRepository</samp> in the `com.bignerdranch.android.criminalintent` package and define a companion object in the class.

**Listing 11.9  Implementing a repository (`CrimeRepository.kt`)**

```
class CrimeRepository private constructor(context: Context) {

     companion object {
        private var INSTANCE: CrimeRepository? = null

         fun initialize(context: Context) {
             if (INSTANCE == null) {
                 INSTANCE = CrimeRepository(context)
             }
        }

         fun get(): CrimeRepository {
            return INSTANCE ?:
            throw IllegalStateException("CrimeRepository must be initialized")
        }
    }
} 
```

<samp class="classname">CrimeRepository</samp> is a <samp class="firstterm">singleton</samp>. This means there will only ever be one instance of it in your app process.

A singleton exists as long as the application stays in memory, so storing any properties on the singleton will keep them available throughout any lifecycle changes in your activities and fragments. Be careful with singleton classes, as they are destroyed when Android removes your application from memory. The <samp class="classname">CrimeRepository</samp> singleton is not a solution for long-term storage of data. Instead, it gives the app an owner for the crime data and provides a way to easily pass that data between controller classes.

To make <samp class="classname">CrimeRepository</samp> a singleton, you add two functions to its companion object. One initializes a new instance of the repository, and the other accesses the repository. You also mark the constructor as private to ensure no components can go rogue and create their own instance.

The getter function is not very nice if you have not called <samp class="methodname">initialize()</samp> before it. It will throw an <samp class="classname">IllegalStateException</samp>, so you need to make sure that you initialize your repository when your application is starting.

To do work as soon as your application is ready, you can create an <samp class="classname">Application</samp> subclass. This allows you to access lifecycle information about the application itself. Create a class called <samp class="classname">CriminalIntentApplication</samp> that extends <samp class="classname">Application</samp> and override <samp class="methodname">Application.onCreate()</samp> to set up the repository initialization.

**Listing 11.10  Creating an application subclass (`CriminalIntentApplication.kt`)**

```
class CriminalIntentApplication : Application() {

    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        CrimeRepository.initialize(this)
    }
} 
```

Similar to <samp class="methodname">Activity.onCreate(…)</samp>, <samp class="methodname">Application.onCreate()</samp> is called by the system when your application is first loaded in to memory. That makes it a good place to do any kind of one-time initialization operations.

The application instance does not get constantly destroyed and re-created, like your activity or fragment classes. It is created when the app launches and destroyed when your app process is destroyed. The only lifecycle function you will override in CriminalIntent is <samp class="methodname">onCreate()</samp>.

In a moment, you are going to pass the application instance to your repository as a <samp class="classname">Context</samp> object. This object is valid as long as your application process is in memory, so it is safe to hold a reference to it in the repository class.

But in order for your application class to be used by the system, you need to register it in your manifest. Open <samp class="filename">AndroidManifest.xml</samp> and specify the `android:name` property to set up your application.

**Listing 11.11  Hooking up the application subclass (`manifests/AndroidManifest.xml`)**

```
<manifest xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
          package="com.bignerdranch.android.criminalintent">

    <application
            android:name=".CriminalIntentApplication"
            android:allowBackup="true"
            ... >
        ...
    </application>

</manifest>
```

With the application class registered in the manifest, the OS will create an instance of <samp class="classname">CriminalIntentApplication</samp> when launching your app. The OS will then call <samp class="methodname">onCreate()</samp> on the <samp class="classname">CriminalIntentApplication</samp> instance. Your <samp class="classname">CrimeRepository</samp> will be initialized, and you can access it from your other components.

Next, add two properties on your <samp class="classname">CrimeRepository</samp> to store references to your database and DAO objects.

**Listing 11.12  Setting up repository properties (`CrimeRepository.kt`)**

```
private const val DATABASE_NAME = "crime-database"

class CrimeRepository private constructor(context: Context) {

    private val database : CrimeDatabase = Room.databaseBuilder(
        context.applicationContext,
        CrimeDatabase::class.java,
        DATABASE_NAME
    ).build()

    private val crimeDao = database.crimeDao()

    companion object {
        ...
    }
}
```

<samp class="methodname">Room.databaseBuilder()</samp> creates a concrete implementation of your abstract <samp class="classname">CrimeDatabase</samp> using three parameters. It first needs a <samp class="classname">Context</samp> object, since the database is accessing the filesystem. You pass in the application context because, as discussed above, the singleton will most likely live longer than any of your activity classes.

The second parameter is the database class that you want Room to create. The third is the name of the database file you want Room to create for you. You are using a private string constant defined in the same file, since no other components need to access it.

Next, fill out your <samp class="classname">CrimeRepository</samp> so your other components can perform any operations they need to on your database. Add a function to your repository for each function in your DAO.

**Listing 11.13  Adding repository functions (`CrimeRepository.kt`)**

```
class CrimeRepository private constructor(context: Context) {

    ...
    private val crimeDao = database.crimeDao()

    fun getCrimes(): List<Crime> = crimeDao.getCrimes()

    fun getCrime(id: UUID): Crime? = crimeDao.getCrime(id)

    companion object {
        ...
    }
}
```

Since Room provides the query implementations in the DAO, you call through to those implementations from your repository. This helps keep your repository code short and easy to understand.

This may seem like a lot of work for little gain, since the repository is just calling through to functions on your <samp class="classname">CrimeDao</samp>. But fear not; you will be adding functionality soon to encapsulate additional work the repository needs to handle.

## Testing Queries

With your repository in place, there is one last step before you can test your query functions. Currently, your database is empty, because you have not added any crimes to it. To speed things up, you will upload existing database files to your emulator to populate your database. The database files have been provided for you in the solutions file for this chapter ([<samp class="uri">www.bignerdranch.com/​solutions/​AndroidProgramming4e.zip</samp>](https://www.bignerdranch.com/solutions/AndroidProgramming4e.zip)).

You could programmatically generate and insert dummy data into the database, like the 100 dummy crimes you have been using. However, you have not yet implemented a DAO function to insert new database entries (you will do so in [Chapter 14](../Text/ch14.xhtml "14 The App Bar")). Uploading a preexisting database file allows you to easily seed the database without altering your app’s code unnecessarily. Plus, it gives you practice using the <samp class="guilabel">Device File Explorer</samp> to view the contents of your emulator’s local storage system.

Having said that, there is one drawback to this method of testing. You can only access your app’s private files (where the database files are located) when you are on an emulator (or a “rooted” device). You cannot upload the database files to a typical physical device.

### Uploading test data

Each application on an Android device has a directory in the device’s <samp class="firstterm">sandbox</samp>. Keeping files in the sandbox protects them from being accessed by other applications or even the prying eyes of users (unless the device has been rooted, in which case the user can get to whatever they like).

An application’s sandbox directory is a child of the device’s <samp class="filename">data/data</samp> directory named after the application package. For CriminalIntent, the full path to the sandbox directory is <samp class="filename">data/data/com.bignerdranch.android.criminalintent</samp>.

To upload the files, make sure the emulator is running and open the <samp class="guilabel">Device File Explorer</samp> toolbar window in Android Studio by clicking its tab in the bottom right of the window. The file explorer pane will show all of the files currently on the emulator ([Figure 11.2](#ch11s05.xhtml_fig_device_file_explorer "Figure 11.2  Device File Explorer window")).

**Figure 11.2  Device File Explorer window**

![Device File Explorer window](Images/fig_device_file_explorer.png)

To find the folder for CriminalIntent, open the `data/data/` folder and find the subfolder with the name matching the package ID of the project ([Figure 11.3](#ch11s05.xhtml_fig_app_sandbox_folder "Figure 11.3  App sandbox folder")). Files in this folder are private to your app by default, so no other apps can read them. This is where you will upload the database files.

**Figure 11.3  App sandbox folder**

![App sandbox folder](Images/fig_app_sandbox_folder.png)

To upload the <samp class="filename">databases</samp> folder, right-click on the package-name folder and select <samp class="guilabel">Upload...</samp> ([Figure 11.4](#ch11s05.xhtml_fig_upload_files "Figure 11.4  Uploading database files")).

**Figure 11.4  Uploading database files**

![Uploading database files](Images/fig_upload_files.png)

This will show you a file navigator where you can select the files to upload. Navigate to the solutions folder for this chapter. Make sure you upload the entire <samp class="filename">databases</samp> folder. Room needs the files to be in a folder called <samp class="filename">databases</samp>, or it will not work. When you finish the upload, your app sandbox folder should look like [Figure 11.5](#ch11s05.xhtml_fig_uploaded_database_files "Figure 11.5  Uploaded database files").

**Figure 11.5  Uploaded database files**

![Uploaded database files](Images/fig_uploaded_database_files.png)

With your database files uploaded, you now have data you can query using your repository. Currently, your <samp class="classname">CrimeListViewModel</samp> creates 100 fake crimes to display in the list. Remove the code that generates the fake crimes and replace it with a call to the <samp class="methodname">getCrimes()</samp> function on your <samp class="classname">CrimeRepository</samp>.

**Listing 11.14  Accessing the repository in `ViewModel` (`CrimeListViewModel.kt`)**

```
class CrimeListViewModel : ViewModel() {

    val crimes = mutableListOf<Crime>()

    init {
        for (i in 0 until 100) {
            val crime = Crime()
            crime.title = "Crime #$i"
            crime.isSolved = i % 2 == 0
            crimes += crime
        }
    }

    private val crimeRepository = CrimeRepository.get()
    val crimes = crimeRepository.getCrimes()
}
```

Now, run your app to see the outcome. You may be surprised to find … your app crashes.

Do not worry, this is the expected behavior. (At least, it is what <samp class="emphasis">we</samp> expected. Sorry.) Take a look at the exception in Logcat to see what happened.

```
 java.lang.IllegalStateException: Cannot access database on the main thread since
    it may potentially lock the UI for a long period of time.
```

This error originates from the Room library. Room is unhappy with your attempt to access the database on the main thread. Throughout the remainder of this chapter, you will learn about the threading model Android uses, as well as the purpose of the main thread and considerations for the type of work you run on the main thread. Additionally, you will move your database interactions to a background thread. That will make Room happy and get rid of the exception, which will in turn fix the crash.

## Application Threads

Reading from the database does not happen immediately. Because access can take so long, Room disallows all database operations on the main thread. If you try to violate this rule, Room will throw the <samp class="classname">IllegalStateException</samp> you have just seen.

Why? To understand that, you need to understand what a thread is, what the main thread is, and what the main thread does.

A thread is a single sequence of execution. Code running within a single thread will execute one step after another. Every Android app starts life with a <samp class="firstterm">main thread</samp>. The main thread, however, is not a preordained list of steps. Instead, it sits in an infinite loop and waits for events initiated by the user or the system. Then it executes code in response to those events as they occur ([Figure 11.6](#ch11s06.xhtml_event_loop_simple "Figure 11.6  Regular threads vs the main thread")).

**Figure 11.6  Regular threads vs the main thread**

![Regular threads vs the main thread](Images/event_loop_simple.png)

Imagine that your app is an enormous shoe store and that you only have one employee – The Flash. (Who hasn’t dreamed of that?) There are a lot of things to do in a store to keep the customers happy: arranging the merchandise, fetching shoes for customers, wielding the Brannock device. The Flash is so fast that everyone is taken care of in a timely fashion, even though there is only one guy doing all the work.

For this situation to work, The Flash cannot spend too much time doing any one thing. What if a shipment of shoes goes missing? Someone will have to spend a lot of time on the phone straightening it out. Your customers will get mighty impatient waiting for shoes while The Flash is on hold.

The Flash is like the main thread in your application. It runs all the code that updates the UI. This includes the code executed in response to different UI-related events – activity startup, button presses, and so on. (Because the events are all related to the UI in some way, the main thread is sometimes called the <samp class="firstterm">UI thread</samp>.)

The event loop keeps the UI code in sequence. It makes sure that none of these operations step on each other, while still ensuring that the code is executed in a timely fashion. So far, all of the code you have written has been executed on the main thread.

### Background threads

Database access is a lot like a phone call to your shoe distributor: It takes a long time compared to other tasks. During that time, the UI will be completely unresponsive, which might result in an <samp class="firstterm">application not responding</samp>, or ANR.

An ANR occurs when Android’s watchdog determines that the main thread has failed to respond to an important event, like pressing the Back button. To the user, it looks like [Figure 11.7](#ch11s06.xhtml_criminalintent_anr "Figure 11.7  Application not responding").

**Figure 11.7  Application not responding**

![Application not responding](Images/criminalintent_anr.png)

In your store, you would solve the problem by (naturally) hiring a second Flash to call the shoe distributor. In Android, you do something similar – you create a <samp class="firstterm">background thread</samp> and access the database from there.

There are two important rules to consider when you start adding background threads to your apps:

*   <samp class="emphasis">All long-running tasks should be done on a background thread.</samp> This ensures that your main thread is free to handle UI-related tasks to keep the UI responsive for your users.

*   <samp class="emphasis">The UI can only be updated from the main thread.</samp> You will get an error if you try to modify the UI from a background thread, so you need to make sure any data generated from a background thread is sent to the main thread to update the UI.

There are many ways to execute work on a background thread on Android. You will learn how to make asynchronous network requests in [Chapter 24](../Text/ch24.xhtml "24 HTTP and Background Tasks"), use <samp class="classname">Handler</samp>s to perform many small background operations in [Chapter 25](../Text/ch25.xhtml "25 Loopers, Handlers, and HandlerThread"), and perform periodic background work with WorkManager in [Chapter 27](../Text/ch27.xhtml "27 WorkManager").

For CriminalIntent, you will use two options to execute your database calls in the background. In this chapter you will use <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> to wrap your query data. In [Chapter 12](../Text/ch12.xhtml "12 Fragment Navigation") and [Chapter 14](../Text/ch14.xhtml "14 The App Bar") you will use <samp class="classname">Executor</samp> to insert and update data.

## Using LiveData

<samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> is a data holder class found in the Jetpack `lifecycle-extensions` library. Room is built to work with <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp>. Since you already included the `lifecycle-extensions` library in your <samp class="filename">app/build.gradle</samp> file in [Chapter 4](../Text/ch04.xhtml "4 Persisting UI State"), you have access to the <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> class in your project.

<samp class="classname">LiveData</samp>’s goal is to simplify passing data between different parts of your application, such as from your <samp class="classname">CrimeRepository</samp> to the fragment that needs to display the crime data. <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> also enables passing data between threads. This makes it a perfect fit for respecting the threading rules we laid out above.

When you configure queries in your Room DAO to return <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp>, Room will automatically execute those query operations on a background thread and then publish the results to the <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> object when the query is done. You can set your activity or fragment up to observe the <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> object, in which case your activity or fragment will be notified on the main thread of results when they are ready.

In this chapter, you will focus on using the cross-thread communication functionality of <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> to perform your database queries. To begin, open <samp class="filename">CrimeDao.kt</samp> and update the return type of your query functions to return a <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> object that wraps the original return type.

**Listing 11.15  Returning `LiveData` in the DAO (`database/CrimeDao.kt`)**

```
@Dao
interface CrimeDao {

  @Query("SELECT * FROM crime")
  fun getCrimes(): List<Crime>
  fun getCrimes(): LiveData<List<Crime>>

  @Query("SELECT * FROM crime WHERE id=(:id)")
  fun getCrime(id: UUID): Crime?
  fun getCrime(id: UUID): LiveData<Crime?>
}
```

By returning an instance of <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> from your DAO class, you signal Room to run your query on a background thread. When the query completes, the <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> object will handle sending the crime data over to the main thread and notify any observers.

Next, update <samp class="classname">CrimeRepository</samp> to return <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> from its query functions.

**Listing 11.16  Returning `LiveData` from the repository (`CrimeRepository.kt`)**

```
class CrimeRepository private constructor(context: Context) {
  ...
  private val crimeDao = database.crimeDao()

  fun getCrimes(): List<Crime> = crimeDao.getCrimes()
  fun getCrimes(): LiveData<List<Crime>> = crimeDao.getCrimes()

  fun getCrime(id: UUID): Crime? = crimeDao.getCrime(id)
  fun getCrime(id: UUID): LiveData<Crime?> = crimeDao.getCrime(id)
  ...
}
```

### Observing LiveData

To display the crimes from the database in the crime list screen, update <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> to observe the <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> returned from <samp class="methodname">CrimeRepository.getCrimes()</samp>.

First, open <samp class="filename">CrimeListViewModel.kt</samp> and rename the `crimes` property so it is more clear what data the property holds.

**Listing 11.17  Accessing the repository in the `ViewModel` (`CrimeListViewModel.kt`)**

```
class CrimeListViewModel : ViewModel() {

    private val crimeRepository = CrimeRepository.get()
    val crimes crimeListLiveData = crimeRepository.getCrimes()
}
```

Next, clean up <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> to reflect the fact that <samp class="classname">CrimeListViewModel</samp> now exposes the <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> returned from your repository ([Listing 11.18](#ch11s07.xhtml_ci_database_remove_ref_to_old_viewmodel "Listing 11.18  Removing references to the old version of ViewModel (CrimeListFragment.kt)")). Remove the <samp class="methodname">onCreate(…)</samp> implementation, since it references `crimeListViewModel.crimes`, which no longer exists (and since you no longer need the logging you put in place there). In <samp class="methodname">updateUI()</samp>, remove the reference to `crimeListViewModel.crimes` and add a parameter to accept a list of crimes as input.

Finally, remove the call to <samp class="methodname">updateUI()</samp> from <samp class="methodname">onCreateView(…)</samp>. You will implement a call to <samp class="methodname">updateUI()</samp> from another place shortly.

**Listing 11.18  Removing references to the old version of `ViewModel` (`CrimeListFragment.kt`)**

```
private const val TAG = "CrimeListFragment"

class CrimeListFragment : Fragment() {
    ...
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        Log.d(TAG, "Total crimes: ${crimeListViewModel.crimes.size}")
    }
    ...
    override fun onCreateView(
        ...
    ): View? {
        ...
        crimeRecyclerView.layoutManager = LinearLayoutManager(context)

        updateUI()

        return view
    }

    private fun updateUI() {
    private fun updateUI(crimes: List<Crime>) {
        val crimes = crimeListViewModel.crimes
        adapter = CrimeAdapter(crimes)
        crimeRecyclerView.adapter = adapter
    }
    ...
}
```

Now, update <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> to observe the <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> that wraps the list of crimes returned from the database. Since the fragment will have to wait for results from the database before it can populate the recycler view with crimes, initialize the recycler view adapter with an empty crime list to start. Then set up the recycler view adapter with the new list of crimes when new data is published to the <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp>.

**Listing 11.19  Hooking up the `RecyclerView` (`CrimeListFragment.kt`)**

```
private const val TAG = "CrimeListFragment"

class CrimeListFragment : Fragment() {

    private lateinit var crimeRecyclerView: RecyclerView
    private var adapter: CrimeAdapter? = null
    private var adapter: CrimeAdapter? = CrimeAdapter(emptyList())
    ...
    override fun onCreateView(
        ...
    ): View? {
        ...
        crimeRecyclerView.layoutManager = LinearLayoutManager(context)
        crimeRecyclerView.adapter = adapter
        return view
    }

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onViewCreated(view, savedInstanceState)
        crimeListViewModel.crimeListLiveData.observe(
            viewLifecycleOwner,
            Observer { crimes ->
                crimes?.let {
                    Log.i(TAG, "Got crimes ${crimes.size}")
                    updateUI(crimes)
                }
        })
    }
    ...
}
```

The <samp class="methodname">LiveData.observe(LifecycleOwner, Observer)</samp> function is used to register an observer on the <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> instance and tie the life of the observation to the life of another component, such as an activity or fragment.

The second parameter to the <samp class="methodname">observe(…)</samp> function is an <samp class="classname">Observer</samp> implementation. This object is responsible for reacting to new data from the <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp>. In this case, the observer’s code block is executed whenever the <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp>’s list of crimes gets updated. The observer receives a list of crimes from the <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> and prints a log statement if the property is not null.

If you never unsubscribe or cancel your <samp class="classname">Observer</samp> from listening to the <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp>’s changes, your <samp class="classname">Observer</samp> implementation might try to update your fragment’s view when the view is in an invalid state (such as when the view is being torn down). And if you attempt to update an invalid view, your app can crash.

This is where the <samp class="classname">LifecycleOwner</samp> parameter to <samp class="methodname">LiveData.observe(…)</samp> comes in. The lifetime of the <samp class="classname">Observer</samp> you provide is scoped to the lifetime of the Android component represented by the <samp class="classname">LifecycleOwner</samp> you provide. In the code above, you scope the observer to the life of the fragment’s view.

As long as the <samp class="firstterm">lifecycle owner</samp> you scope your observer to is in a valid lifecycle state, the <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> object will notify the observer of any new data coming in. The <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> object will automatically unregister the <samp class="classname">Observer</samp> when the associated lifecycle is no longer in a valid state. Because <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> reacts to changes in a lifecycle, it is called a <samp class="firstterm">lifecycle-aware component</samp>. You will learn more about lifecycle-aware components in [Chapter 25](../Text/ch25.xhtml "25 Loopers, Handlers, and HandlerThread").

A lifecycle owner is a component that implements the <samp class="classname">LifecycleOwner</samp> interface and contains a <samp class="classname">Lifecycle</samp> object. A <samp class="classname">Lifecycle</samp> is an object that keeps track of an Android lifecycle’s current state. (Recall that activities, fragments, views, and even the application process itself all have their own lifecycle.) The lifecycle states, such as created and resumed, are enumerated in <samp class="classname">Lifecycle.State</samp>. You can query a <samp class="classname">Lifecycle</samp>’s state using <samp class="methodname">Lifecycle.getCurrentState()</samp> or register to be notified of changes in state.

The AndroidX <samp class="classname">Fragment</samp> is a lifecycle owner directly – <samp class="classname">Fragment</samp> implements <samp class="classname">LifecycleOwner</samp> and has a <samp class="classname">Lifecycle</samp> object representing the state of the fragment instance’s lifecycle.

A fragment’s view lifecycle is owned and tracked separately by <samp class="classname">FragmentViewLifecycleOwner</samp>. Each <samp class="classname">Fragment</samp> has an instance of <samp class="classname">FragmentViewLifecycleOwner</samp> that keeps track of the lifecycle of that fragment’s view.

In the code above, you scope the observation to the fragment’s view lifecycle, rather than the lifecycle of the fragment itself, by passing the `viewLifecycleOwner` to the <samp class="methodname">observe(…)</samp> function. The fragment’s view lifecycle, though separate from the lifecycle of the <samp class="classname">Fragment</samp> instance itself, mirrors the lifecycle of the fragment. It is possible to change this default behavior by <samp class="firstterm">retaining</samp> the fragment (which you will not do in CriminalIntent). You will learn more about the view lifecycle and retaining fragments in [Chapter 25](../Text/ch25.xhtml "25 Loopers, Handlers, and HandlerThread").

<samp class="methodname">Fragment.onViewCreated(…)</samp> is called after <samp class="methodname">Fragment.onCreateView(…)</samp> returns, signaling that the fragment’s view hierarchy is in place. You observe the <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> from <samp class="methodname">onViewCreated(…)</samp> to ensure that your view is ready to display the crime data. This is also the reason you pass the `viewLifecycleOwner` to the <samp class="methodname">observe()</samp> function, rather than the fragment itself. You only want to receive the list of crimes while your view is in a good state, so using the view’s lifecycle owner ensures that you will not receive updates when your view is not on the screen.

When the list of crimes is ready, the observer you defined prints a log message and sends the list to the <samp class="methodname">updateUI()</samp> function to prepare the adapter.

With everything in place, run CriminalIntent. You should no longer see the crash you saw earlier. Instead, you should see the fake crimes from the database file you uploaded to your emulator ([Figure 11.8](#ch11s07.xhtml_ss_database_crimes "Figure 11.8  Database crimes")).

**Figure 11.8  Database crimes**

![Database crimes](Images/database_crimes.png)

In the next chapter you will connect the crime list and crime detail screens and populate the crime detail screen with data for the crime you clicked on from the database.

## Challenge: Addressing the Schema Warning

If you look through your build logs, you will find a warning about your app not providing a schema export directory:

```
 warning: Schema export directory is not provided to the annotation processor
    so we cannot export the schema. You can either provide `room.schemaLocation`
    annotation processor argument OR set exportSchema to false.
```

A database <samp class="firstterm">schema</samp> represents the structure of the database, including what tables are in the database, what columns are in those tables, and any constraints on and relationships between those tables. Room supports exporting your database schema into a file so you can store it in a source control. Exporting your schema is often useful so that you have a versioned history of your database.

The warning you see means that you are not providing a file location where Room can save your database schema. You can either provide a schema location to the `@Database` annotation, or you can disable the export to remove the warning. For this challenge, resolve the schema warning by choosing one of these options.

To provide a location for the export, you provide a path for the annotation processor’s `room.schemaLocation` property. To do this, add the following `kapt{}` block to your <samp class="filename">app/build.gradle</samp> file:

```
 ...
    android {
        ...
        buildTypes {
            ...
        }
        kapt {
            arguments {
                arg("room.schemaLocation", "some/path/goes/here/")
            }
        }
    }
    ...
```

To disable the export, set `exportSchema` to `false`:

```
 @Database(entities = [ Crime::class ], version=1, exportSchema = false)
    @TypeConverters(CrimeTypeConverters::class)
    abstract class CrimeDatabase : RoomDatabase() {

        abstract fun crimeDao(): CrimeDao
    }
```

## For the More Curious: Singletons

The singleton pattern, as used in the <samp class="classname">CrimeRepository</samp>, is very common in Android. Singletons get a bad rap because they can be misused in a way that makes an app hard to maintain.

Singletons are often used in Android because they outlive a single fragment or activity. A singleton will still exist across rotation and will exist as you move between activities and fragments in your application.

Singletons also make a convenient owner of your model objects. Imagine a more complex CriminalIntent application with many activities and fragments modifying crimes. When one controller modifies a crime, how would you make sure that updated crime was sent over to the other controllers?

If the <samp class="classname">CrimeRepository</samp> is the owner of crimes and all modifications to crimes pass through it, propagating changes is much easier. As you transition between controllers, you can pass the crime ID as an identifier for a particular crime and have each controller pull the full crime object from the <samp class="classname">CrimeRepository</samp> using that ID.

However, singletons do have a few downsides. For example, while they allow for an easy place to stash data with a longer lifetime than a controller, singletons do have a lifetime. Singletons will be destroyed, along with all of their instance variables, as Android reclaims memory at some point after you switch out of an application. Singletons are not a long-term storage solution. (Writing the files to disk or sending them to a web server is.)

Singletons can also make your code hard to unit test (you will learn more about unit testing in [Chapter 20](../Text/ch20.xhtml "20 Unit Testing and Audio Playback")). There is not a great way to replace the <samp class="classname">CrimeRepository</samp> instance in this chapter with a mock version of itself. In practice, Android developers usually solve this problem using a tool called a <samp class="firstterm">dependency injector</samp>. This tool allows for objects to be shared as singletons, while still making it possible to replace them when needed. To learn more about dependency injection, read [the section called *For the More Curious: Managing Dependencies*](../Text/ch24s08.xhtml "For the More Curious: Managing Dependencies") in [Chapter 24](../Text/ch24.xhtml "24 HTTP and Background Tasks").

And, as we said, singletons have the potential to be misused. It can be tempting to use singletons for everything, because they are convenient – you can get to them wherever you are, and you can store in them whatever information you need to get at later. But when you do that, you are avoiding answering important questions: Where is this data used? Where is this function important?

A singleton does not answer those questions. So whoever comes after you will open up your singleton and find something that looks like somebody’s disorganized junk drawer. Batteries, zip ties, old photographs? What is all this here for? Make sure that anything in your singleton is truly global and has a strong reason for being there.

On balance, singletons are a key component of a well-architected Android app – when used correctly.

# <samp class="chapter_number">12</samp>
<samp class="chapter_name">Fragment Navigation</samp>

In this chapter, you will get the list and the detail parts of CriminalIntent working together. When a user presses an item in the list of crimes, <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> will swap out <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> with a new instance of <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp>. <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> will display the details for the crime that was pressed ([Figure 12.1](#ch12.xhtml_ci_fragment_activity_startup "Figure 12.1  Swapping CrimeListFragment for CrimeFragment")).

**Figure 12.1  Swapping `CrimeListFragment` for `CrimeFragment`**

![Swapping CrimeListFragment for CrimeFragment](Images/ci_fragment_swap.png)

To get this working you will learn how to implement navigation by having the hosting activity change out fragments in response to user actions. You will also learn how to pass data to a fragment instance using <samp class="firstterm">fragment arguments</samp>. Finally, you will learn how to use <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> <samp class="firstterm">transformations</samp> to load immutable data in response to UI changes.

## Single Activity: Fragment Boss

In GeoQuiz, you had one activity (<samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>) start another activity (<samp class="classname">CheatActivity</samp>). In CriminalIntent, you are instead going to use a <samp class="firstterm">single activity architecture</samp>. An app that uses single activity architecture has one activity and multiple fragments. The activity’s job is to swap fragments in and out in response to user events.

To implement the navigation from <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> to <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> in response to the user pressing on a crime in the list, you might think to initiate a fragment transaction on the hosting activity’s fragment manager in <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp>’s <samp class="methodname">CrimeHolder.onClick(View)</samp>. This <samp class="methodname">onClick(View)</samp> would get <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>’s <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> and commit a fragment transaction that replaces <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> with <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp>.

The code in your <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment.CrimeHolder</samp> would look like this:

```
 fun onClick(view: View) {
        val fragment = CrimeFragment.newInstance(crime.id)
        val fm = activity.supportFragmentManager
        fm.beginTransaction()
          .replace(R.id.fragment_container, fragment)
          .commit()
    }
```

This works, but it is not how stylish Android programmers do things. Fragments are intended to be standalone, composable units. If you write a fragment that adds fragments to the activity’s <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp>, then that fragment is making assumptions about how the hosting activity works, and your fragment is no longer a standalone, composable unit.

For example, in the code above, <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> adds a <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> to <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> and assumes that <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> has a `fragment_container` in its layout. This is business that should be handled by <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp>’s hosting activity instead of <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp>.

To maintain the independence of your fragments, you will delegate work back to the hosting activity by defining callback interfaces in your fragments. The hosting activities will implement these interfaces to perform fragment-bossing duties and layout-dependent behavior.

### Fragment callback interfaces

To delegate functionality back to the hosting activity, a fragment typically defines a custom callback interface named <samp class="interfacename">Callbacks</samp>. This interface defines work that the fragment needs done by its boss, the hosting activity. Any activity that will host the fragment must implement this interface.

With a callback interface, a fragment is able to call functions on its hosting activity without having to know anything about which activity is hosting it.

Use a callback interface to delegate on-click events from <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> back to its hosting activity. First, open <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> and define a <samp class="classname">Callbacks</samp> interface with a single callback function. Add a <samp class="varname">callbacks</samp> property to hold an object that implements <samp class="classname">Callbacks</samp>. Override <samp class="methodname">onAttach(Context)</samp> and <samp class="methodname">onDetach()</samp> to set and unset the <samp class="varname">callbacks</samp> property.

**Listing 12.1  Adding a callback interface (`CrimeListFragment.kt`)**

```
class CrimeListFragment : Fragment() {

    /**
     * Required interface for hosting activities
     */
    interface Callbacks {
        fun onCrimeSelected(crimeId: UUID)
    }

    private var callbacks: Callbacks? = null

    private lateinit var crimeRecyclerView: RecyclerView
    private var adapter: CrimeAdapter = CrimeAdapter(emptyList())
    private val crimeListViewModel: CrimeListViewModel by lazy {
        ViewModelProviders.of(this).get(CrimeListViewModel::class.java)
    }

    override fun onAttach(context: Context) {
        super.onAttach(context)
        callbacks = context as Callbacks?
    }

    override fun onCreateView(
        ...
    ): View? {
        ...
    }

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        ...
    }

    override fun onDetach() {
        super.onDetach()
        callbacks = null
    }
    ...
}
```

The <samp class="methodname">Fragment.onAttach(Context)</samp> lifecycle function is called when a fragment is attached to an activity. Here you stash the <samp class="classname">Context</samp> argument passed to <samp class="methodname">onAttach(…)</samp> in your <samp class="varname">callbacks</samp> property. Since <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> is hosted in an activity, the <samp class="classname">Context</samp> object passed to <samp class="classname">onAttach(…)</samp> is the activity instance hosting the fragment.

Remember, <samp class="classname">Activity</samp> is a subclass of <samp class="classname">Context</samp>, so <samp class="methodname">onAttach(…)</samp> passes a <samp class="classname">Context</samp> as a parameter, which is more flexible. Ensure that you use the <samp class="methodname">onAttach(Context)</samp> signature for <samp class="methodname">onAttach(…)</samp> and not the deprecated <samp class="methodname">onAttach(Activity)</samp> function, which may be removed in future versions of the API.

Similarly, you set the variable to <samp class="constant">null</samp> in the corresponding waning lifecycle function, <samp class="classname">Fragment.onDetach()</samp>. You set the variable to <samp class="constant">null</samp> here because afterward you cannot access the activity or count on the activity continuing to exist.

Note that <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> performs an unchecked cast of its activity to <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment.Callbacks</samp>. This means that the hosting activity <samp class="emphasis">must</samp> implement <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment.Callbacks</samp>. That is not a bad dependency to have, but it is important to document it.

Now <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> has a way to call functions on its hosting activity. It does not matter which activity is doing the hosting. As long as the activity implements <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment.Callbacks</samp>, everything in <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> can work the same.

Next, update the click listener for individual items in the crime list so that pressing a crime notifies the hosting activity via the <samp class="classname">Callbacks</samp> interface. Call <samp class="methodname">onCrimeSelected(Crime)</samp> in <samp class="methodname">CrimeHolder.onClick(View)</samp>.

**Listing 12.2  Calling all callbacks! (`CrimeListFragment.kt`)**

```
class CrimeListFragment : Fragment() {
    ...
    private inner class CrimeHolder(view: View)
        : RecyclerView.ViewHolder(view), View.OnClickListener {
        ...
        fun bind(crime: Crime) {
            ...
        }

        override fun onClick(v: View?) {
            Toast.makeText(context, "${crime.title} clicked!", Toast.LENGTH_SHORT)
                .show()
            callbacks?.onCrimeSelected(crime.id)
        }
    }
    ...
}
```
