Finally, update <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> to implement <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment.Callbacks</samp>. Log a debug statement in <samp class="methodname">onCrimeSelected(UUID)</samp> for now.

**Listing 12.3  Implementing callbacks (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
private const val TAG = "MainActivity"
class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity(),
    CrimeListFragment.Callbacks {

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        ...
    }

    override fun onCrimeSelected(crimeId: UUID) {
        Log.d(TAG, "MainActivity.onCrimeSelected: $crimeId")
    }
}
```

Run CriminalIntent. Search or filter Logcat to view <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>’s log statements. Each time you press a crime in the list you should see a log statement indicating the click event was propagated from <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> to <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> through <samp class="methodname">Callbacks.onCrimeSelected(UUID)</samp>.

### Replacing a fragment

Now that your callback interface is wired up correctly, update <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>’s <samp class="methodname">onCrimeSelected(UUID)</samp> to swap out the <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> with an instance of <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> when the user presses a crime in <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp>’s list. For now, ignore the crime ID passed to the callback.

**Listing 12.4  Replacing `CrimeListFragment` with `CrimeFragment` (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity(),
    CrimeListFragment.Callbacks {

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        ...
    }

    override fun onCrimeSelected(crimeId: UUID) {
        Log.d(TAG, "MainActivity.onCrimeSelected: $crimeId")
        val fragment = CrimeFragment()
        supportFragmentManager
            .beginTransaction()
            .replace(R.id.fragment_container, fragment)
            .commit()
    }
}
```

<samp class="methodname">FragmentTransaction.replace(Int, Fragment)</samp> replaces the fragment hosted in the activity (in the container with the integer resource ID specified) with the new fragment provided. If a fragment is not already hosted in the container specified, the new fragment is added, just as if you had called <samp class="methodname">FragmentTransaction.add(Int, fragment)</samp>.

Run CriminalIntent. Press a crime in the list. You should see the crime detail screen appear ([Figure 12.2](#ch12s01.xhtml_fig_crime_empty "Figure 12.2  A blank CrimeFragment")).

**Figure 12.2  A blank `CrimeFragment`**

![A blank CrimeFragment](Images/ci_end_of_chapter_2.png)

For now, the crime detail screen is empty, because you have not told <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> which <samp class="classname">Crime</samp> to display. You will populate the detail screen shortly. But first, you need to file down a remaining sharp edge in your navigation implementation.

Press the Back button. This dismisses <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>. This is because the only item in your app’s back stack is the <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> instance that was launched when you launched the app.

Users will expect that pressing the Back button from the crime detail screen will bring them back to the crime list. To implement this behavior, add the replace transaction to the back stack.

**Listing 12.5  Adding fragment transaction to the back stack (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity(),
    CrimeListFragment.Callbacks {
    ...
    override fun onCrimeSelected(crimeId: UUID) {
        val fragment = CrimeFragment()
        supportFragmentManager
            .beginTransaction()
            .replace(R.id.fragment_container, fragment)
            .addToBackStack(null)
            .commit()
    }
}
```

When you add a transaction to the back stack, this means that when the user presses the Back button the transaction will be reversed. So, in this case, <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> will be replaced with <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp>.

You can name the back stack state you are adding by passing a <samp class="type">String</samp> to <samp class="methodname">FragmentTransaction.addToBackStack(String)</samp>. Doing so is optional and, since you do not care about the name in this implementation, you pass `null`.

Run your app. Select a crime from the list to launch <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp>. Press the Back button to go back to <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp>. Enjoy the simple pleasure of your app’s navigation matching what users will expect.

## Fragment Arguments

<samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> now notifies its hosting activity (<samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>) when a crime is selected and passes along the ID of the selected crime.

That is all fine and dandy. But what you really need is a way to pass the selected crime ID from <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> to <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp>. This way, <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> can pull data for that crime from the database and populate the UI with that data.

Fragment arguments offer a solution to this problem – they allow you to stash pieces of data someplace that belongs to the fragment. The “someplace” that belongs to a fragment is known as its <samp class="firstterm">arguments bundle</samp>. The fragment can retrieve data from the arguments bundle without relying on its parent activity or some other outside source.

Fragment arguments help you keep your fragment encapsulated. A well-encapsulated fragment is a reusable building block that can easily be hosted in any activity.

To create fragment arguments, you first create a <samp class="classname">Bundle</samp> object. This bundle contains key-value pairs that work just like the intent extras of an <samp class="classname">Activity</samp>. Each pair is known as an argument. Next, you use type-specific “put” functions of <samp class="classname">Bundle</samp> (similar to those of <samp class="classname">Intent</samp>) to add arguments to the bundle:

```
 val args = Bundle().apply {
      putSerializable(ARG_MY_OBJECT, myObject)
      putInt(ARG_MY_INT, myInt)
      putCharSequence(ARG_MY_STRING, myString)
    }
```

Every fragment instance can have a fragment arguments <samp class="classname">Bundle</samp> object attached to it.

### Attaching arguments to a fragment

To attach the arguments bundle to a fragment, you call <samp class="methodname">Fragment.setArguments(Bundle)</samp>. Attaching arguments to a fragment must be done after the fragment is created but before it is added to an activity.

To accomplish this, Android programmers follow a convention of adding a companion object that contains the <samp class="methodname">newInstance(…)</samp> function to the <samp class="classname">Fragment</samp> class. This function creates the fragment instance and bundles up and sets its arguments.

When the hosting activity needs an instance of that fragment, you have it call the <samp class="methodname">newInstance(…)</samp> function rather than calling the constructor directly. The activity can pass in any required parameters to <samp class="methodname">newInstance(…)</samp> that the fragment needs to create its arguments.

In <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp>, write a <samp class="methodname">newInstance(UUID)</samp> function that accepts a <samp class="classname">UUID</samp>, creates an arguments bundle, creates a fragment instance, and then attaches the arguments to the fragment.

**Listing 12.6  Writing a `newInstance(UUID)` function (`CrimeFragment.kt`)**

```
private const val ARG_CRIME_ID = "crime_id"

class CrimeFragment : Fragment() {
    ...
    override fun onStart() {
        ...
    }

    companion object {

        fun newInstance(crimeId: UUID): CrimeFragment {
            val args = Bundle().apply {
                putSerializable(ARG_CRIME_ID, crimeId)
            }
            return CrimeFragment().apply {
                arguments = args
            }
        }
    }
}
```

Update <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> to call <samp class="methodname">CrimeFragment.newInstance(UUID)</samp> when it needs to create a <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp>. Pass along the <samp class="classname">UUID</samp> that was received in <samp class="methodname">MainActivity.onCrimeSelected(UUID)</samp>.

**Listing 12.7  Using `CrimeFragment.newInstance(UUID)` (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity(),
    CrimeListFragment.Callbacks {
    ...
    override fun onCrimeSelected(crimeId: UUID) {
        val fragment = CrimeFragment()
        val fragment = CrimeFragment.newInstance(crimeId)
        supportFragmentManager
            .beginTransaction()
            .replace(R.id.fragment_container, fragment)
            .addToBackStack(null)
            .commit()
    }
}
```

Notice that the need for independence does not go both ways. <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> has to know plenty about <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp>, including that it has a <samp class="methodname">newInstance(UUID)</samp> function. This is fine. Hosting activities should know the specifics of how to host their fragments, but fragments should not have to know specifics about their activities. At least, not if you want to maintain the flexibility of independent fragments.

### Retrieving arguments

To access a fragment’s arguments, reference the <samp class="classname">Fragment</samp> property named <samp class="varname">arguments</samp>. Then use one of the type-specific “get” functions of <samp class="classname">Bundle</samp> to pull individual values out of the arguments bundle.

Back in <samp class="methodname">CrimeFragment.onCreate(…)</samp>, retrieve the <samp class="classname">UUID</samp> from the fragment arguments. For now, log the ID so you can verify that the argument was attached as expected.

**Listing 12.8  Getting crime ID from the arguments (`CrimeFragment.kt`)**

```
private const val TAG = "CrimeFragment"
private const val ARG_CRIME_ID = "crime_id"

class CrimeFragment : Fragment() {
    ...
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        crime = Crime()
        val crimeId: UUID = arguments?.getSerializable(ARG_CRIME_ID) as UUID
        Log.d(TAG, "args bundle crime ID: $crimeId")
        // Eventually, load crime from database
    }
    ...
}
```

Run CriminalIntent. The app will behave the same, but you should feel all warm and fuzzy inside for passing the crime ID along to <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> while still maintaining <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp>’s independence.

## Using LiveData Transformations

Now that <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> has the crime ID, it needs to pull the crime object from the database so it can display the crime’s data. Since this requires a database lookup that you do not want to repeat unnecessarily on rotation, add a <samp class="classname">CrimeDetailViewModel</samp> to manage the database query.

When <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> requests to load a crime with a given ID, its <samp class="classname">CrimeDetailViewModel</samp> should kick off a <samp class="methodname">getCrime(UUID)</samp> database request. When the request completes, <samp class="classname">CrimeDetailViewModel</samp> should notify <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> and pass along the crime object that resulted from the query.

Create a new class named <samp class="classname">CrimeDetailViewModel</samp> and expose a <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> property to store and publish the <samp class="classname">Crime</samp> pulled from the database. Use <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> to implement a relationship where changing the crime ID triggers a new database query.

**Listing 12.9  Adding `ViewModel` for `CrimeFragment` (`CrimeDetailViewModel.kt`)**

```
class CrimeDetailViewModel() : ViewModel() {

    private val crimeRepository = CrimeRepository.get()
    private val crimeIdLiveData = MutableLiveData<UUID>()

    var crimeLiveData: LiveData<Crime?> =
        Transformations.switchMap(crimeIdLiveData) { crimeId ->
            crimeRepository.getCrime(crimeId)
        }

    fun loadCrime(crimeId: UUID) {
        crimeIdLiveData.value = crimeId
    }
}
```

The `crimeRepository` property stores a handle to the <samp class="classname">CrimeRepository</samp>. This is not necessary, but later on <samp class="classname">CrimeDetailViewModel</samp> will communicate with the repository in more than one place, so the property will prove useful at that point.

`crimeIdLiveData` stores the ID of the crime currently displayed (or about to be displayed) by <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp>. When <samp class="classname">CrimeDetailViewModel</samp> is first created, the crime ID is not set. Eventually, <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> will call <samp class="methodname">CrimeDetailViewModel.loadCrime(UUID)</samp> to let the <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> know which crime it needs to load.

Note that you explicitly defined `crimeLiveData`’s type as <samp class="classname">LiveData<Crime?></samp>. Since `crimeLiveData` is publicly exposed, you should ensure it is not exposed as a <samp class="classname">MutableLiveData</samp>. In general, <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp>s should never expose <samp class="classname">MutableLiveData</samp>.

It may seem strange to wrap the crime ID in <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp>, since it is private to <samp class="classname">CrimeDetailViewModel</samp>. What within this <samp class="classname">CrimeDetailViewModel</samp>, you may wonder, needs to listen for changes to the private ID value?

The answer lies in the live data <samp class="classname">Transformation</samp> statement. A <samp class="firstterm">live data transformation</samp> is a way to set up a trigger-response relationship between two <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> objects. A transformation function takes two inputs: a <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> object used as a <samp class="firstterm">trigger</samp> and a <samp class="firstterm">mapping function</samp> that must return a <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> object. The transformation function returns a new <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> object, which we call the <samp class="firstterm">transformation result</samp>, whose value gets updated every time a new value gets set on the trigger <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> instance.

The transformation result’s value is calculated by executing the mapping function. The `value` property on the <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> returned from the mapping function is used to set the `value` property on the live data transformation result.

Using a transformation this way means the <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> only has to observe the exposed `CrimeDetailViewModel.crimeLiveData` one time. When the fragment changes the ID it wants to display, the <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> just publishes the new crime data to the existing live data stream.

Open <samp class="filename">CrimeFragment.kt</samp>. Associate <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> with <samp class="classname">CrimeDetailViewModel</samp>. Request that the <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> load the <samp class="classname">Crime</samp> in <samp class="methodname">onCreate(…)</samp>.

**Listing 12.10  Hooking `CrimeFragment` up to `CrimeDetailViewModel` (`CrimeFragment.kt`)**

```
class CrimeFragment : Fragment() {

    private lateinit var crime: Crime
    ...
    private lateinit var solvedCheckBox: CheckBox
    private val crimeDetailViewModel: CrimeDetailViewModel by lazy {
        ViewModelProviders.of(this).get(CrimeDetailViewModel::class.java)
    }

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        crime = Crime()
        val crimeId: UUID = arguments?.getSerializable(ARG_CRIME_ID) as UUID
        Log.d(TAG, "args bundle crime ID: $crimeId")
        // Eventually, load crime from database
        crimeDetailViewModel.loadCrime(crimeId)
    }
    ...
}
```

Next, observe <samp class="classname">CrimeDetailViewModel</samp>’s <samp class="varname">crimeLiveData</samp> and update the UI any time new data is published.

**Listing 12.11  Observing changes (`CrimeFragment.kt`)**

```
class CrimeFragment : Fragment() {

    private lateinit var crime: Crime
    ...

    override fun onCreateView(
        ...
    ): View? {
        ...
    }

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onViewCreated(view, savedInstanceState)
        crimeDetailViewModel.crimeLiveData.observe(
            viewLifecycleOwner,
            Observer { crime ->
                crime?.let {
                    this.crime = crime
                    updateUI()
                }
            })
    }

    override fun onStart() {
        ...
    }

    private fun updateUI() {
        titleField.setText(crime.title)
        dateButton.text = crime.date.toString()
        solvedCheckBox.isChecked = crime.isSolved
    }
    ...
}
```

(Be sure to import <samp class="classname">androidx.lifecycle.Observer</samp>.)

You may have noticed that <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> has its own <samp class="classname">Crime</samp> state stored in its `crime` property. The values in this `crime` property represent the edits the user is currently making. The crime in <samp class="varname">CrimeDetailViewModel.crimeLiveData</samp> represents the data as it is currently saved in the database. <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> “publishes” the user’s edits when the fragment moves to the stopped state by writing the updated data to the database.

Run your app. Press a crime in the list. If all goes as planned, you should see the crime detail screen appear, populated with data from the crime you pressed in the list ([Figure 12.3](#ch12s03.xhtml_activity_stack_ci "Figure 12.3  CriminalIntent’s back stack")).

**Figure 12.3  CriminalIntent’s back stack**

![CriminalIntent’s back stack](Images/activity_stack_ci_new.png)

When <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> displays, you may see the checkbox animating to the checked state if you are viewing a crime marked as solved. This is expected, since the checkbox state gets set as the result of an asynchronous operation. The database query for the crime kicks off when the user first launches <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp>. When the database query completes, the fragment’s `crimeDetailViewModel.crimeLiveData` observer is notified and in turn updates the data displayed in the widgets.

Clean this up by skipping over the animation when you programmatically set the checkbox checked state. You do this by calling <samp class="methodname">View.jumpDrawablesToCurrentState()</samp>. Note that if the lag as the crime detail screen loads is unacceptable based on your app’s requirements, you could pre-load the crime data into memory ahead of time (as the app launches, for example) and stash it in a shared place. For CriminalIntent, the lag is very slight, so the simple solution of skipping the animation is enough.

**Listing 12.12  Skipping checkbox animation (`CrimeFragment.kt`)**

```
class CrimeFragment : Fragment() {
    ...
    private fun updateUI() {
        titleField.setText(crime.title)
        dateButton.text = crime.date.toString()
        solvedCheckBox.isChecked = crime.isSolved
        solvedCheckBox.apply {
            isChecked = crime.isSolved
            jumpDrawablesToCurrentState()
        }
    }
    ...
}
```

Run your app again. Press a solved crime in the list. Notice the checkbox no longer animates as the screen spins up. If you press the checkbox, the animation does happen, as desired.

Now, edit the crime’s title. Press the Back button to go back to the crime list screen. Sadly, the changes you made were not saved. Luckily, this is easy to fix.

## Updating the Database

The database serves as the single source of truth for crime data. In CriminalIntent, when the user leaves the detail screen, any edits they made should be saved to the database. (Other apps might have other requirements, like having a “save” button or saving updates as the user types.)

First, add a function to your <samp class="classname">CrimeDao</samp> to update an existing crime. While you are at it, also add a function to insert a new crime. You will mostly ignore the insert function for now, but you will use it in [Chapter 14](../Text/ch14.xhtml "14 The App Bar") when you add a menu option to the UI to create new crimes.

**Listing 12.13  Adding update and insert database functions (`database/CrimeDao.kt`)**

```
@Dao
interface CrimeDao {

  @Query("SELECT * FROM crime")
  fun getCrimes(): LiveData<List<Crime>>

  @Query("SELECT * FROM crime WHERE id=(:id)")
  fun getCrime(id: UUID): LiveData<Crime?>

  @Update
  fun updateCrime(crime: Crime)

  @Insert
  fun addCrime(crime: Crime)
}
```

The annotations for these functions do not require any parameters. Room can generate the appropriate SQL command for these operations.

The <samp class="methodname">updateCrime()</samp> function uses the `@Update` annotation. This function takes in a crime object, uses the ID stored in that crime to find the associated row, and then updates the data in that row based on the new data in the crime object.

The <samp class="methodname">addCrime()</samp> function uses the `@Insert` annotation. The parameter is the crime you want to add to the database table.

Next, update the repository to call through to the new insert and update DAO functions. Recall that Room automatically executes the database queries for <samp class="methodname">CrimeDao.getCrimes()</samp> and <samp class="methodname">CrimeDao.getCrime(UUID)</samp> on a background thread because those DAO functions return <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp>. In those cases, <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> handles ferrying the data over to your main thread so you can update your UI.

You cannot, however, rely on Room to automatically run your insert and update database interactions on a background thread for you. Instead, you must execute those DAO calls on a background thread explicitly. A common way to do this is to use an <samp class="firstterm">executor</samp>.

### Using an executor

An <samp class="classname">Executor</samp> is an object that references a thread. An executor instance has a function called <samp class="methodname">execute</samp> that accepts a block of code to run. The code you provide in the block will run on whatever thread the executor points to.

You are going to create an executor that uses a new thread (which will always be a background thread). Any code in the block will run on that thread, so you can perform your database operations there safely.

You cannot implement an executor in the <samp class="classname">CrimeDao</samp> directly, because Room generates the function implementations for you based on the interface you define. Instead, implement the executor in <samp class="classname">CrimeRepository</samp>. Add a property to the executor to hold a reference, then execute your insert and update functions using the executor.

**Listing 12.14  Inserting and updating with an executor (`CrimeRepository.kt`)**

```
class CrimeRepository private constructor(context: Context) {
  ...
  private val crimeDao = database.crimeDao()
  private val executor = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor()

  fun getCrimes(): LiveData<List<Crime>> = crimeDao.getCrimes()

  fun getCrime(id: UUID): LiveData<Crime?> = crimeDao.getCrime(id)

  fun updateCrime(crime: Crime) {
      executor.execute {
          crimeDao.updateCrime(crime)
      }
  }

  fun addCrime(crime: Crime) {
      executor.execute {
          crimeDao.addCrime(crime)
      }
  }
  ...
}
```

The <samp class="methodname">newSingleThreadExecutor()</samp> function returns an executor instance that points to a new thread. Any work you execute with the executor will therefore happen off the main thread.

Both <samp class="methodname">updateCrime()</samp> and <samp class="methodname">addCrime()</samp> wrap their calls to the DAO inside the <samp class="methodname">execute {}</samp> block. This pushes these operations off the main thread so you do not block your UI.

### Tying database writes to the fragment lifecycle

Last but not least, update your app to write the values the user enters in the crime detail screen to the database when the user navigates away from the screen.

Open <samp class="filename">CrimeDetailViewModel.kt</samp> and add a function to save a crime object to the database.

**Listing 12.15  Adding save capability (`CrimeDetailViewModel.kt`)**

```
class CrimeDetailViewModel() : ViewModel() {
    ...
    fun loadCrime(crimeId: UUID) {
        crimeIdLiveData.value = crimeId
    }

    fun saveCrime(crime: Crime) {
        crimeRepository.updateCrime(crime)
    }
}
```

<samp class="methodname">saveCrime(Crime)</samp> accepts a <samp class="classname">Crime</samp> and writes it to the database. Since <samp class="classname">CrimeRepository</samp> handles running the update request on a background thread, the database integration here is very simple.

Now, update <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> to save the user’s edited crime data to the database.

**Listing 12.16  Saving in `onStop()` (`CrimeFragment.kt`)**

```
class CrimeFragment : Fragment() {
    ...
    override fun onStart() {
        ...
    }

    override fun onStop() {
        super.onStop()
        crimeDetailViewModel.saveCrime(crime)
    }

    private fun updateUI() {
        ...
    }
    ...
}
```

<samp class="methodname">Fragment.onStop()</samp> is called any time your fragment moves to the stopped state (that is, any time the fragment moves entirely out of view). This means the data will get saved when the user finishes the detail screen (such as by pressing the Back button). The data will also be saved when the user switches tasks (such as by pressing the Home button or using the overview screen). Thus, saving in <samp class="methodname">onStop()</samp> meets the requirement of saving the data whenever the user leaves the detail screen and also ensures that, if the process is killed due to memory pressure, the edited data is not lost.

Run CriminalIntent and select a crime from the list. Change data in that crime. Press the Back button and pat yourself on the back for your most recent success: The changes you made on the detail screen are now reflected in the list screen. In the next chapter, you will hook up the date button on the detail screen to allow the user to select the date when the crime occurred.

## For the More Curious: Why Use Fragment Arguments?

In this chapter you added a <samp class="methodname">newInstance(…)</samp> function to your fragment to pass along arguments when creating a new instance of fragment. While this pattern is helpful from a code organization standpoint, it is also necessary in the case of fragment arguments. You cannot use a constructor to pass arguments to a fragment instance.

For instance, you might consider adding a one-argument constructor to <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> that expects a <samp class="classname">UUID</samp> crime ID as input, rather than adding a <samp class="methodname">newInstance(UUID)</samp> function. However, this approach is flawed. When a configuration change occurs, the current activity’s fragment manager automatically re-creates the fragment that was hosted before the configuration change occurred. The fragment manager then adds that new fragment instance to the new activity.

When the fragment manager re-creates the fragment after a configuration change, it calls the fragment’s default, parameterless constructor. This means that after rotation, the new fragment instance would not receive the crime ID data.

So how are fragment arguments any different? Fragment arguments are stored across fragment death. The fragment manager reattaches the arguments to the new fragment it re-creates after rotation. That new fragment can then use the arguments bundle to re-create its state.

This all seems so complicated. Why not just set an instance variable on the <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> when it is created?

Because it would not always work. When the OS re-creates your fragment – either across a configuration change or when the user has switched out of your app and the OS reclaims memory – all of your instance variables will be lost. Also, remember that there is no way to cheat low-memory death, no matter how hard you try.

If you want something that works in all cases, you have to persist your arguments.

One option is to use the saved instance state mechanism. You can store the crime ID as a normal instance variable, save the crime ID in <samp class="methodname">onSaveInstanceState(Bundle)</samp>, and snag it from the <samp class="classname">Bundle</samp> in <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp>. This will work in all situations.

However, that solution is hard to maintain. If you revisit this fragment in a few years and add another argument, you may not remember to save the argument in <samp class="methodname">onSaveInstanceState(Bundle)</samp>. Going this route is less explicit.

Android developers prefer the fragment arguments solution because it is very explicit and clear in its intentions. In a few years, you will come back and know that the crime ID is an argument and is safely shuttled along to new instances of this fragment. If you add another argument, you will know to stash it in the arguments bundle.

## For the More Curious: Navigation Architecture Component Library

As you have seen, there are several ways of navigating users through your app. You can have multiple activities, one for each screen, and start them as the user interacts with your UI. You can also go with a single activity that hosts several fragments that make up your UI instead.

In an effort to simplify app navigation, the Android team introduced the Navigation architecture component library as part of Jetpack. This library simplifies the implementation of your navigation by providing a GUI-based editor where you can configure your navigation flow ([Figure 12.4](#ch12s06.xhtml_navigation_editor_screenshot "Figure 12.4  Navigation editor")).

**Figure 12.4  Navigation editor**

![Navigation editor](Images/navigation_editor.png)

The Navigation library is opinionated about how you should implement navigation in your project. It prefers navigation using fragments with a single activity over using an activity for each screen. You can provide the arguments your fragments need directly in the navigation editor tool.

For a big challenge, create a copy of CriminalIntent and implement the app’s navigation using the Navigation architecture component ([<samp class="uri">developer.android.com/​topic/​libraries/​architecture/​navigation</samp>](https://developer.android.com/topic/libraries/architecture/navigation)). The documentation will be very useful on your journey. There are many parts involved, but once your setup is complete it is simple to add new screens to your app and hook up the actions between them.

As of this writing, the stable version of the Navigation architecture component was just officially released. The timing did not allow us to incorporate it into this edition, but this tool has major promise, and we believe it will be the way of the future for many Android developers. We recommend you try it out and see what you think. We are in the process of doing that as well.

## Challenge: Efficient RecyclerView Reloading

Right now, when the user returns to the list screen after editing a single crime, <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> redraws all of the visible crimes in the recycler view. The is wildly inefficient, because at most one <samp class="classname">Crime</samp> will have changed.

Update <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp>’s <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> implementation to redraw only the row associated with the changed crime. To do this, update <samp class="classname">CrimeAdapter</samp> to extend from <samp class="classname">androidx.recyclerview.widget.ListAdapter<Crime, CrimeHolder></samp> instead of <samp class="classname">RecyclerView.Adapter<CrimeHolder></samp>.

<samp class="classname">ListAdapter</samp> is a <samp class="classname">RecyclerView.Adapter</samp> that figures out the difference between the current data set backing the recycler view and a new data set you apply to back the recycler view. The comparison happens on a background thread, so it does not slow down the UI. <samp class="classname">ListAdapter</samp> in turn tells the recycler view to only redraw rows for data that has changed.

<samp class="classname">ListAdapter</samp> uses <samp class="classname">androidx.recyclerview.widget.DiffUtil</samp> to determine which parts of the data set have changed. To finish this challenge, you will need to provide a <samp class="classname">DiffUtil.ItemCallback<Crime></samp> implementation to your <samp class="classname">ListAdapter</samp>.

You will also need to update <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> to submit an updated crime list to the recycler view’s adapter, rather than reassigning the recycler view’s adapter to a new adapter object every time you want to update the UI. You can submit a new list by calling <samp class="methodname">ListAdapter.submitList(MutableList<T>?)</samp>. Or you can set up <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> and observe the changes.

See the API reference pages for <samp class="classname">androidx.recyclerview.widget.DiffUtil</samp> and <samp class="classname">androidx.recyclerview.widget.ListAdapter</samp> on [<samp class="uri">developer.android.com/​reference/​kotlin</samp>](https://developer.android.com/reference/kotlin) for more details on how to use these tools.

# <samp class="chapter_number">13</samp>
<samp class="chapter_name">Dialogs</samp>

Dialogs demand attention and input from the user. They are useful for presenting a choice or important information. In this chapter, you will add a dialog in which users can change the date of a crime. Pressing the date button in <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> will present this dialog ([Figure 13.1](#ch13.xhtml_ss_ci_dialog_complete "Figure 13.1  A dialog for picking the date of a crime")).

**Figure 13.1  A dialog for picking the date of a crime**

![A dialog for picking the date of a crime](Images/ci_date_picker.png)

The dialog in [Figure 13.1](#ch13.xhtml_ss_ci_dialog_complete "Figure 13.1  A dialog for picking the date of a crime") is an instance of <samp class="classname">DatePickerDialog</samp>, a subclass of <samp class="classname">AlertDialog</samp>. <samp class="classname">DatePickerDialog</samp> displays a date selection prompt to the user and provides a listener interface you can implement to capture the selection. For creating more custom dialogs, <samp class="classname">AlertDialog</samp> is the all-purpose <samp class="classname">Dialog</samp> subclass that you will use most often.

## Creating a DialogFragment

When displaying a <samp class="classname">DatePickerDialog</samp>, it is a good idea to wrap it in an instance of <samp class="classname">DialogFragment</samp>, a subclass of <samp class="classname">Fragment</samp>. It is possible to display a <samp class="classname">DatePickerDialog</samp> without a <samp class="classname">DialogFragment</samp>, but it is not recommended. Having the <samp class="classname">DatePickerDialog</samp> managed by the <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> gives you more options for presenting the dialog.

In addition, a bare <samp class="classname">DatePickerDialog</samp> will vanish if the device is rotated. If the <samp class="classname">DatePickerDialog</samp> is wrapped in a fragment, then the dialog will be re-created and put back onscreen after rotation.

For CriminalIntent, you are going to create a <samp class="classname">DialogFragment</samp> subclass named <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp>. Within <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp>, you will create and configure an instance of <samp class="classname">DatePickerDialog</samp>. <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp> will be hosted by <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>.

[Figure 13.2](#ch13s01.xhtml_fig_ci_object_diagram_dialog "Figure 13.2  Object diagram for two fragments hosted by MainActivity") shows you an overview of these relationships.

**Figure 13.2  Object diagram for two fragments hosted by `MainActivity`**

![Object diagram for two fragments hosted by MainActivity](Images/ci_object_diagram_dialog.png)

Your first tasks are:

*   creating the <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp> class

*   building a <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp>

*   getting the dialog onscreen via the <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp>

Later in this chapter, you will pass the necessary data between <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> and <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp>.

Create a new class named <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp> and make its superclass <samp class="classname">DialogFragment</samp>. Be sure to choose the Jetpack version of <samp class="classname">DialogFragment</samp>: <samp class="classname">androidx.fragment.app.DialogFragment</samp>.

<samp class="classname">DialogFragment</samp> includes the following function:

```
 onCreateDialog(savedInstanceState: Bundle?): Dialog
```

The <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> of the hosting activity calls this function as part of putting the <samp class="classname">DialogFragment</samp> onscreen.

In <samp class="filename">DatePickerFragment.kt</samp>, add an implementation of <samp class="methodname">onCreateDialog(Bundle?)</samp> that builds a <samp class="classname">DatePickerDialog</samp> initialized with the current date ([Listing 13.1](#ch13s01.xhtml_pl_ci_dialogs_initial_date_dialog "Listing 13.1  Creating a DialogFragment (DatePickerFragment.kt)")).

**Listing 13.1  Creating a `DialogFragment` (`DatePickerFragment.kt`)**

```
class DatePickerFragment : DialogFragment() {

    override fun onCreateDialog(savedInstanceState: Bundle?): Dialog {
        val calendar = Calendar.getInstance()
        val initialYear = calendar.get(Calendar.YEAR)
        val initialMonth = calendar.get(Calendar.MONTH)
        val initialDay = calendar.get(Calendar.DAY_OF_MONTH)

        return DatePickerDialog(
            requireContext(),
            null,
            initialYear,
            initialMonth,
            initialDay
        )
    }
}
```

The <samp class="classname">DatePickerDialog</samp> constructor takes in several parameters. The first is a context object, which is required to access the necessary resources for the view. The second parameter is for the date listener, which you will add later in this chapter. The last three parameters are the year, month, and day that the date picker should be initialized to. Until you know the date of the crime, you can just initialize it to the current date.

### Showing a DialogFragment

Like all fragments, instances of <samp class="classname">DialogFragment</samp> are managed by the <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> of the hosting activity.

To get a <samp class="classname">DialogFragment</samp> added to the <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> and put onscreen, you can call either of the following functions on the fragment instance:

```
 show(manager: FragmentManager, tag: String)
    show(transaction: FragmentTransaction, tag: String)
```

The string parameter uniquely identifies the <samp class="classname">DialogFragment</samp> in the <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp>’s list. Whether you use the <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> or <samp class="classname">FragmentTransaction</samp> version is up to you. If you pass in a <samp class="classname">FragmentTransaction</samp>, you are responsible for creating and committing that transaction. If you pass in a <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp>, a transaction will automatically be created and committed for you.

Here, you will pass in a <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp>.

In <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp>, add a constant for the <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp>’s tag.

Then, in <samp class="methodname">onCreateView(…)</samp>, remove the code that disables the date button. Set a <samp class="interfacename">View.OnClickListener</samp> that shows a <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp> when the date button is pressed in <samp class="methodname">onStart()</samp>.

**Listing 13.2  Showing your `DialogFragment` (`CrimeFragment.kt`)**

```
private const val TAG = "CrimeFragment"
private const val ARG_CRIME_ID = "crime_id"
private const val DIALOG_DATE = "DialogDate"

class CrimeFragment : Fragment() {
    ...
    override fun onCreateView(inflater: LayoutInflater,
                              container: ViewGroup?,
                              savedInstanceState: Bundle?): View? {
        ...
        solvedCheckBox = view.findViewById(R.id.crime_solved) as CheckBox

        dateButton.apply {
            text = crime.date.toString()
            isEnabled = false
        }

        return view
    }
    ...
    override fun onStart() {
        ...
        solvedCheckBox.apply {
            ...
        }

        dateButton.setOnClickListener {
            DatePickerFragment().apply {
                show(this@CrimeFragment.requireFragmentManager(), DIALOG_DATE)
            }
        }
    }
    ...
}
```

`this@CrimeFragment` is needed to call <samp class="methodname">requireFragmentManager()</samp> from the <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> instead of the <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp>. `this` references the <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp> inside the `apply` block, so you need to specify the `this` from the outer scope.

<samp class="classname">DialogFragment</samp>’s <samp class="methodname">show(FragmentManager, String)</samp> requires a non-null value for the fragment manager argument. The <samp class="varname">Fragment.fragmentManager</samp> property is nullable, so you cannot pass it directly to <samp class="methodname">show(…)</samp>. Instead, you use <samp class="classname">Fragment</samp>’s <samp class="methodname">requireFragmentManager()</samp> function, whose return type is a non-null <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp>. If the fragment’s <samp class="varname">fragmentManager</samp> property is null when <samp class="methodname">Fragment.requireFragmentManager()</samp> is called, the function will throw an <samp class="classname">IllegalStateException</samp> stating that the fragment is not currently associated with a fragment manager.

Run CriminalIntent and press the date button to see the dialog ([Figure 13.3](#ch13s01.xhtml_ss_ci_dialogs_simpledialog "Figure 13.3  A configured dialog")).

**Figure 13.3  A configured dialog**

![A configured dialog](Images/ci_date_picker.png)

Your dialog is onscreen and looks good. In the next section, you will wire it up to present the <samp class="classname">Crime</samp>’s date and allow the user to change it.

## Passing Data Between Two Fragments

You have passed data between two activities using intent extras, passed data between a fragment and an activity using a callbacks interface, and passed data from an activity to a fragment using fragment arguments. Now you need to pass data between two fragments that are hosted by the same activity – <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> and <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp> ([Figure 13.4](#ch13s02.xhtml_fig_ci_dialog_data_flow "Figure 13.4  Conversation between CrimeFragment and DatePickerFragment")).

**Figure 13.4  Conversation between `CrimeFragment` and `DatePickerFragment`**

![Conversation between CrimeFragment and DatePickerFragment](Images/ci_dialog_data_flow.png)

To get the <samp class="classname">Crime</samp>’s date to <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp>, you are going to write a <samp class="methodname">newInstance(Date)</samp> function and make the <samp class="classname">Date</samp> an argument on the fragment.

To get the new date back to the <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> so that it can update the model layer and its own view, you will declare a callbacks interface function in <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp> that accepts the new date parameter, as shown in [Figure 13.5](#ch13s02.xhtml_fig_ci_sequence_dialog "Figure 13.5  Sequence of events between CrimeFragment and DatePickerFragment").

**Figure 13.5  Sequence of events between `CrimeFragment` and `DatePickerFragment`**

![Sequence of events between CrimeFragment and DatePickerFragment](Images/ci_sequence_dialog.png)

### Passing data to DatePickerFragment

To get data into your <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp>, you are going to stash the date in <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp>’s arguments bundle, where the <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp> can access it.

Creating and setting fragment arguments is typically done in a <samp class="methodname">newInstance(…)</samp> function, as you saw in [Chapter 12](../Text/ch12.xhtml "12 Fragment Navigation"). In <samp class="filename">DatePickerFragment.kt</samp>, add a <samp class="methodname">newInstance(Date)</samp> function in a companion object.

**Listing 13.3  Adding a `newInstance(Date)` function (`DatePickerFragment.kt`)**

```
private const val ARG_DATE = "date"

class DatePickerFragment : DialogFragment() {

    override fun onCreateDialog(savedInstanceState: Bundle?): Dialog {
        ...
    }

    companion object {
        fun newInstance(date: Date): DatePickerFragment {
            val args = Bundle().apply {
                putSerializable(ARG_DATE, date)
            }

            return DatePickerFragment().apply {
                arguments = args
            }
        }
    }
}
```

In <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp>, remove the call to the <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp> constructor and replace it with a call to <samp class="methodname">DatePickerFragment.newInstance(Date)</samp>.

**Listing 13.4  Adding a call to `newInstance(…)` (`CrimeFragment.kt`)**

```
override fun onStart() {
    ...
    dateButton.setOnClickListener {
        DatePickerFragment().apply {
        DatePickerFragment.newInstance(crime.date).apply {
            show(this@CrimeFragment.requireFragmentManager(), DIALOG_DATE)
        }
    }
}
```

<samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp> needs to initialize the <samp class="classname">DatePickerDialog</samp> using the information held in the <samp class="classname">Date</samp>. However, initializing the <samp class="classname">DatePickerDialog</samp> requires <samp class="type">Int</samp>s for the month, day, and year. <samp class="classname">Date</samp> is more of a timestamp and cannot provide <samp class="type">Int</samp>s like this directly.

To get the <samp class="type">Int</samp>s you need, you provide the <samp class="classname">Date</samp> to the <samp class="classname">Calendar</samp> object. Then you can retrieve the required information from the <samp class="classname">Calendar</samp>.

In <samp class="methodname">onCreateDialog(Bundle?)</samp>, get the <samp class="classname">Date</samp> from the arguments and use it and the <samp class="classname">Calendar</samp> to initialize the <samp class="classname">DatePickerDialog</samp>.

**Listing 13.5  Extracting the date and initializing `DatePickerDialog` (`DatePickerFragment.kt`)**

```
class DatePickerFragment : DialogFragment() {

    override fun onCreateDialog(savedInstanceState: Bundle?): Dialog {
        val date = arguments?.getSerializable(ARG_DATE) as Date
        val calendar = Calendar.getInstance()
        calendar.time = date
        val initialYear = calendar.get(Calendar.YEAR)
        val initialMonth = calendar.get(Calendar.MONTH)
        val initialDate = calendar.get(Calendar.DAY_OF_MONTH)

        return DatePickerDialog(
            requireContext(),
            null,
            initialYear,
            initialMonth,
            initialDate
        )
    }
    ...
}
```

Now <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> is successfully telling <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp> what date to show. You can run CriminalIntent and make sure that everything works as before.

### Returning data to CrimeFragment

To have <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> receive the date back from <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp>, you need a way to keep track of the relationship between the two fragments.

With activities, you call <samp class="methodname">startActivityForResult(…)</samp>, and the <samp class="classname">ActivityManager</samp> keeps track of the parent-child activity relationship. When the child activity dies, the <samp class="classname">ActivityManager</samp> knows which activity should receive the result.

#### Setting a target fragment

You can create a similar connection by making <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> the <samp class="firstterm">target fragment</samp> of <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp>. This connection is automatically re-established after both <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> and <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp> are destroyed and re-created by the OS. To create this relationship, you call the following <samp class="classname">Fragment</samp> function:

```
 setTargetFragment(fragment: Fragment, requestCode: Int)
```

This function accepts the fragment that will be the target and a request code just like the one you send in <samp class="methodname">startActivityForResult(…)</samp>.

The <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> keeps track of the target fragment and request code. You can retrieve them by accessing the <samp class="varname">targetFragment</samp> and <samp class="varname">targetRequestCode</samp> properties on the fragment that has set the target.

In <samp class="filename">CrimeFragment.kt</samp>, create a constant for the request code and then make <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> the target fragment of the <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp> instance.

**Listing 13.6  Setting a target fragment (`CrimeFragment.kt`)**

```
private const val DIALOG_DATE = "DialogDate"
private const val REQUEST_DATE = 0

class CrimeFragment : Fragment() {
    ...
    override fun onStart() {
        ...
        dateButton.setOnClickListener {
            DatePickerFragment.newInstance(crime.date).apply {
                setTargetFragment(this@CrimeFragment, REQUEST_DATE)
                show(this@CrimeFragment.requireFragmentManager(), DIALOG_DATE)
            }
        }
    }
    ...
}
```

#### Sending data to the target fragment

Now that you have a connection between <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> and <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp>, you need to send the date back to <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp>. You are going to create a callbacks interface in <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp> that <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> will implement.

In <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp>, create a callbacks interface with a single function called <samp class="classname">onDateSelected()</samp>.

**Listing 13.7  Creating a callbacks interface (`DatePickerFragment.kt`)**

```
class DatePickerFragment : DialogFragment() {

    interface Callbacks {
        fun onDateSelected(date: Date)
    }

    override fun onCreateDialog(savedInstanceState: Bundle?): Dialog {
        ...
    }
    ...
}
```

Next, implement the <samp class="classname">Callbacks</samp> interface in <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp>. In <samp class="methodname">onDateSelected()</samp>, set the date on the crime property and update the UI.

**Listing 13.8  Implementing the callbacks interface (`CrimeFragment.kt`)**

```
class CrimeFragment : Fragment(), DatePickerFragment.Callbacks {
    ...
    override fun onStop() {
        ...
    }

    override fun onDateSelected(date: Date) {
        crime.date = date
        updateUI()
    }
    ...
}
```

Now that <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> can respond to new dates, <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp> needs to send the new date when the user selects one. In <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp>, add a listener to the <samp class="classname">DatePickerDialog</samp> that sends the date back to <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> ([Listing 13.9](#ch13s02.xhtml_sending_back_the_date "Listing 13.9  Sending back the date (DatePickerFragment.kt)")).

**Listing 13.9  Sending back the date (`DatePickerFragment.kt`)**

```
class DatePickerFragment : DialogFragment() {
    ...
    override fun onCreateDialog(savedInstanceState: Bundle?): Dialog {
        val dateListener = DatePickerDialog.OnDateSetListener {
                _: DatePicker, year: Int, month: Int, day: Int ->

            val resultDate : Date = GregorianCalendar(year, month, day).time

            targetFragment?.let { fragment ->
                (fragment as Callbacks).onDateSelected(resultDate)
            }
        }

        val date = arguments?.getSerializable(ARG_DATE) as Date
        ...
        return DatePickerDialog(
            requireContext(),
            null,
            dateListener,
            initialYear,
            initialMonth,
            initialDate
        )
    }
    ...
}
```

The <samp class="classname">OnDateSetListener</samp> is used to receive the date the user selects. The first parameter is for the <samp class="classname">DatePicker</samp> the result is coming from. Since you are not using that parameter in this case, you name it `_`. This is a Kotlin convention to denote parameters that are unused.

The selected date is provided in year, month, and day format, but you need a <samp class="classname">Date</samp> to send back to <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp>. You pass these values to the <samp class="classname">GregorianCalendar</samp> and access the <samp class="varname">time</samp> property to get a <samp class="classname">Date</samp> object.

Once you have the date, it needs to be sent back to <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp>. The <samp class="varname">targetFragment</samp> property stores the fragment instance that started your <samp class="classname">DatePickerFragment</samp>. Since it is nullable, you wrap it in a safe-call `let` block. You then cast the fragment instance to your <samp class="classname">Callbacks</samp> interface and call the <samp class="methodname">onDateSelected()</samp> function, passing in your new date.

Now the circle is complete. The dates must flow. He who controls the dates controls time itself. Run CriminalIntent to ensure that you can, in fact, control the dates. Change the date of a <samp class="classname">Crime</samp> and confirm that the new date appears in <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp>’s view. Then return to the list of crimes and check the <samp class="classname">Crime</samp>’s date to ensure that the model layer was updated.

## Challenge: More Dialogs

Write another dialog fragment named <samp class="classname">TimePickerFragment</samp> that allows the user to select what time of day the crime occurred using a <samp class="classname">TimePicker</samp> widget. Add another button to <samp class="classname">CrimeFragment</samp> to display a <samp class="classname">TimePickerFragment</samp>.

# <samp class="chapter_number">14</samp>
<samp class="chapter_name">The App Bar</samp>

A key component of any well-designed Android app is the <samp class="firstterm">app bar</samp>. The app bar includes actions that the user can take, provides an additional mechanism for navigation, and also provides design consistency and branding.

In this chapter, you will add a menu option to the app bar that lets users add a new crime ([Figure 14.1](#ch14.xhtml_fig_ci_action_bar_adds "Figure 14.1  CriminalIntent’s app bar")).

**Figure 14.1  CriminalIntent’s app bar**

![CriminalIntent’s app bar](Images/ci_options_menu_complete_annotated.png)

The app bar is often referred to as either the <samp class="firstterm">action bar</samp> or <samp class="firstterm">toolbar</samp>, depending on who you ask. You will learn more about these overlapping terms in [the section called *For the More Curious: App Bar vs Action Bar vs Toolbar*](../Text/ch14s04.xhtml "For the More Curious: App Bar vs Action Bar vs Toolbar") near the end of this chapter.

## AppCompat Default App Bar

CriminalIntent already has a simple app bar in place ([Figure 14.2](#ch14s01.xhtml_fig_ci_appcompat_toolbar "Figure 14.2  The app bar")).

**Figure 14.2  The app bar**

![The app bar](Images/ci_initial_appcompat_toolbar.png)

This is because Android Studio sets all new projects up to include an app bar by default for all activities that extend from <samp class="classname">AppCompatActivity</samp>. It does this by:

*   adding the Jetpack AppCompat foundation library dependency

*   applying one of the AppCompat themes that includes an app bar

Open your <samp class="filename">app/build.gradle</samp> file to see the AppCompat dependency:

```
 dependencies {
        ...
        implementation 'androidx.appcompat:appcompat:1.0.0-beta01'
        ...
```

“AppCompat” is short for “application compatibility.” The Jetpack AppCompat foundation library contains classes and resources that are core to providing a consistent-looking UI across different versions of Android. You can explore what is contained in each of the AppCompat subpackages on the official API listings at [<samp class="uri">developer.android.com/​reference/​kotlin/​androidx/​packages</samp>](https://developer.android.com/reference/kotlin/androidx/packages).

Android Studio automatically sets your app’s <samp class="firstterm">theme</samp> to `Theme.AppCompat.Light.DarkActionBar` when it creates your project. The theme, which specifies default styling for your entire app, is set in <samp class="filename">res/values/styles.xml</samp>:

```
 <resources>

        <!-- Base application theme. -->
        <style name="AppTheme" parent="Theme.AppCompat.Light.DarkActionBar">
          <!-- Customize your theme here. -->
          <item name="colorPrimary">@color/colorPrimary</item>
          <item name="colorPrimaryDark">@color/colorPrimaryDark</item>
          <item name="colorAccent">@color/colorAccent</item>
        </style>

    </resources>
```

The theme for your application is specified at the application level and optionally per activity in your manifest. Open <samp class="filename">manifests/AndroidManifest.xml</samp> and look at the `<application>` tag. Notice the `android:theme` attribute. You should see something similar to this:

```
 <manifest ... >
        <application
            ...
            android:theme="@style/AppTheme" >
            ...
        </application>
    </manifest>
```

You will learn much more about styles and themes in [Chapter 21](../Text/ch21.xhtml "21 Styles and Themes"). Now it is time to add actions to the app bar.

## Menus

The top-right area of the app bar is reserved for the app bar’s menu. The menu consists of <samp class="firstterm">action items</samp> (sometimes also referred to as <samp class="firstterm">menu items</samp>), which can perform an action on the current screen or on the app as a whole. You will add an action item to allow the user to create a new crime.

Your new action item will require a string resource for its label. Open <samp class="filename">res/values/strings.xml</samp> and add a string label describing your new action.

**Listing 14.1  Adding a string for menu (`res/values/strings.xml`)**

```
<resources>
    ...
    <string name="crime_solved_label">Solved</string>
    <string name="new_crime">New Crime</string>

</resources>
```

### Defining a menu in XML

Menus are a type of resource, similar to layouts. You create an XML description of a menu and place the file in the <samp class="filename">res/menu</samp> directory of your project. Android generates a resource ID for the menu file that you then use to inflate the menu in code.

In the project tool window, right-click the <samp class="guilabel">res</samp> directory and select <samp class="guimenu">New</samp> → <samp class="guimenuitem">Android resource file</samp>. Name the menu resource <samp class="guilabel">fragment_crime_list</samp>, change the <samp class="guilabel">Resource type</samp> to <samp class="guilabel">Menu</samp>, and click <samp class="guibutton">OK</samp> ([Figure 14.3](#ch14s02.xhtml_fig_ci_create_options_menu_file "Figure 14.3  Creating a menu file")).

**Figure 14.3  Creating a menu file**

![Creating a menu file](Images/ci_create_options_menu_file.png)

Here, you use the same naming convention for menu files as you do for layout files. Android Studio will generate <samp class="filename">res/menu/fragment_crime_list.xml</samp>, which has the same name as your <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp>’s layout file but lives in the <samp class="filename">menu</samp> folder. In the new file, switch to the text view and add an `item` element, as shown in [Listing 14.2](#ch14s02.xhtml_pl_watson_scene_list_options "Listing 14.2  Creating a menu resource for CrimeListFragment (res/menu/fragment_crime_list.xml)").

**Listing 14.2  Creating a menu resource for `CrimeListFragment` (`res/menu/fragment_crime_list.xml`)**

```
<menu xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
      xmlns:app="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res-auto">
    <item
        android:id="@+id/new_crime"
        android:icon="@android:drawable/ic_menu_add"
        android:title="@string/new_crime"
        app:showAsAction="ifRoom|withText"/>
</menu>
```

The `showAsAction` attribute refers to whether the item will appear in the app bar itself or in the <samp class="firstterm">overflow menu</samp>. You have piped together two values, `ifRoom` and `withText`, so the item’s icon and text will appear in the app bar if there is room. If there is room for the icon but not the text, then only the icon will be visible. If there is no room for either, then the item will be relegated to the overflow menu.

If you have items in the overflow menu, those items will be represented by the three dots on the far-right side of the app bar, as shown in [Figure 14.4](#ch14s02.xhtml_ss_overflow_menu "Figure 14.4  Overflow menu in the app bar").

**Figure 14.4  Overflow menu in the app bar**

![Overflow menu in the app bar](Images/overflow_menu.png)

Other options for `showAsAction` include `always` and `never`. Using `always` is not recommended; it is better to use `ifRoom` and let the OS decide. Using `never` is a good choice for less-common actions. In general, you should only put action items that users will access frequently in the app bar to avoid cluttering the screen.

#### The app namespace

Notice that <samp class="filename">fragment_crime_list.xml</samp> uses the `xmlns` tag to define a new namespace, `app`, which is separate from the usual `android` namespace declaration. This `app` namespace is then used to specify the `showAsAction` attribute.

This unusual namespace declaration exists for legacy reasons with the AppCompat library. The app bar APIs (called “action bar” at the time) were first added in Android 3.0\. Originally, the AppCompat library was created to bundle a compatibility version of the action bar into apps supporting earlier versions of Android, so that the action bar would exist on any device, even those that did not support the native action bar. On devices running Android 2.3 or older, menus and their corresponding XML did exist, but the `android:showAsAction` attribute was only added with the release of the action bar.

The AppCompat library defines its own custom `showAsAction` attribute and does not look for the native `showAsAction` attribute.

### Creating the menu

In code, menus are managed by callbacks from the <samp class="classname">Activity</samp> class. When the menu is needed, Android calls the <samp class="classname">Activity</samp> function <samp class="methodname">onCreateOptionsMenu(Menu)</samp>.

However, your design calls for code to be implemented in a fragment, not an activity. <samp class="classname">Fragment</samp> comes with its own set of menu callbacks, which you will implement in <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp>. The functions for creating the menu and responding to the selection of an action item are:

```
 onCreateOptionsMenu(menu: Menu, inflater: MenuInflater)
    onOptionsItemSelected(item: MenuItem): Boolean
```

In <samp class="filename">CrimeListFragment.kt</samp>, override <samp class="methodname">onCreateOptionsMenu(Menu, MenuInflater)</samp> to inflate the menu defined in <samp class="filename">fragment_crime_list.xml</samp>.

**Listing 14.3  Inflating a menu resource (`CrimeListFragment.kt`)**

```
class CrimeListFragment : Fragment() {
    ...
    override fun onDetach() {
        super.onDetach()
        callbacks = null
    }

    override fun onCreateOptionsMenu(menu: Menu, inflater: MenuInflater) {
        super.onCreateOptionsMenu(menu, inflater)
        inflater.inflate(R.menu.fragment_crime_list, menu)
    }
    ...
}
```

Within this function, you call <samp class="methodname">MenuInflater.inflate(Int, Menu)</samp> and pass in the resource ID of your menu file. This populates the <samp class="classname">Menu</samp> instance with the items defined in your file.

Notice that you call through to the superclass implementation of <samp class="methodname">onCreateOptionsMenu(…)</samp>. This is not required, but we recommend calling through as a matter of convention. That way, any menu functionality defined by the superclass will still work. However, it is only a convention – the base <samp class="classname">Fragment</samp> implementation of this function does nothing.

The <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> is responsible for calling <samp class="methodname">Fragment.onCreateOptionsMenu(Menu, MenuInflater)</samp> when the activity receives its <samp class="methodname">onCreateOptionsMenu(…)</samp> callback from the OS. You must explicitly tell the <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> that your fragment should receive a call to <samp class="methodname">onCreateOptionsMenu(…)</samp>. You do this by calling the following <samp class="classname">Fragment</samp> function:

```
 setHasOptionsMenu(hasMenu: Boolean)
```

Define <samp class="methodname">CrimeListFragment.onCreate(Bundle?)</samp> and let the <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> know that <samp class="classname">CrimeListFragment</samp> needs to receive menu callbacks.

**Listing 14.4  Receiving menu callbacks (`CrimeListFragment.kt`)**

```
class CrimeListFragment : Fragment() {
    ...
    override fun onAttach(context: Context) {
        ...
    }

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setHasOptionsMenu(true)
    }
    ...
}
```

You can run CriminalIntent now to see your menu ([Figure 14.5](#ch14s02.xhtml_fig_ci_new_crime_jellybean_list "Figure 14.5  Icon for the New Crime action item in the app bar")).

**Figure 14.5  Icon for the New Crime action item in the app bar**
