Create an assets folder inside your project by right-clicking on your <samp class="filename">app</samp> module and selecting <samp class="guisubmenu">New</samp> → <samp class="guisubmenu">Folder</samp> → <samp class="guimenuitem">Assets Folder</samp>. In the dialog that pops up, leave the <samp class="guilabel">Change Folder Location</samp> checkbox unchecked and leave the <samp class="guilabel">Target Source Set</samp> set to <samp class="guilabel">main</samp> ([Figure 19.3](#ch19s05.xhtml_ss_creating_assets_folder "Figure 19.3  Creating the assets folder")).

**Figure 19.3  Creating the assets folder**

![Creating the assets folder](Images/creating_assets_folder.png)

Click <samp class="guilabel">Finish</samp> to create your assets folder.

Next, right-click on <samp class="filename">assets</samp> to create a subfolder for your sounds by selecting <samp class="guisubmenu">New</samp> → <samp class="guimenuitem">Directory</samp>. Enter <samp class="guilabel">sample_sounds</samp> for the directory name ([Figure 19.4](#ch19s05.xhtml_ss_create_assets_folders "Figure 19.4  Creating the sample_sounds folder")).

**Figure 19.4  Creating the sample_sounds folder**

![Creating the sample_sounds folder](Images/creating_sample_sounds_folder.png)

Everything inside the <samp class="filename">assets</samp> folder will be deployed with your app. For the sake of convenience and organization, you created a subfolder called <samp class="filename">sample_sounds</samp>. Unlike with resources, a subfolder is not required for assets. You include it to organize your sounds.

So where can you find the sounds? You will be using a Creative Commons-licensed sound set we initially found provided by the user plagasul at [<samp class="uri">freesound.org/​people/​plagasul/​packs/​3/</samp>](https://www.freesound.org/people/plagasul/packs/3/). We have put them in a zip file for you at [<samp class="uri">bignerdranch.com/​solutions/​sample_sounds.zip</samp>](https://www.bignerdranch.com/solutions/sample_sounds.zip).

Download the zip file and unzip its contents. Copy or move the unzipped sound files into <samp class="filename">assets/sample_sounds</samp> ([Figure 19.5](ch19s05.html_ss_imported_assets.png "Figure 19.5  Imported assets")).

**Figure 19.5  Imported assets**

![Imported assets](Images/imported_assets.png)

(Make sure only <samp class="filename">.wav</samp> files are in there, by the way – not the <samp class="filename">.zip</samp> file you got them from.)

Build your app to make sure everything is hunky-dory. The next step will be to list those assets and show them to the user.

## Accessing Assets

BeatBox will end up doing a lot of work related to asset management: finding assets, keeping track of them, and eventually playing them as sounds. To manage all this, create a new class called <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp> in `com.bignerdranch.android.beatbox`. Go ahead and add a couple of constants: one for logging and one to remember which folder you saved your boxing grunts in.

**Listing 19.10  New `BeatBox` class (`BeatBox.kt`)**

```
private const val TAG = "BeatBox"
private const val SOUNDS_FOLDER = "sample_sounds"

class BeatBox {

}
```

Assets are accessed using the <samp class="classname">AssetManager</samp> class. You can get an <samp class="classname">AssetManager</samp> from any <samp class="classname">Context</samp>. Since <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp> will need one, give it a constructor that takes in an <samp class="classname">AssetManager</samp> and stashes it for later.

**Listing 19.11  Stashing an `AssetManager` for safekeeping (`BeatBox.kt`)**

```
private const val TAG = "BeatBox"
private const val SOUNDS_FOLDER = "sample_sounds"

class BeatBox(private val assets: AssetManager) {

}
```

When accessing assets, in general you do not need to worry about which <samp class="classname">Context</samp> you are using. In every situation you are likely to encounter in practice, every <samp class="classname">Context</samp>’s <samp class="classname">AssetManager</samp> will be wired up to the same set of assets.

To get a listing of what you have in your assets, you can use the <samp class="methodname">list(String)</samp> function. Write a function called <samp class="methodname">loadSounds()</samp> that looks in your assets with <samp class="methodname">list(String)</samp>.

**Listing 19.12  Looking at assets (`BeatBox.kt`)**

```
class BeatBox(private val assets: AssetManager) {

    fun loadSounds(): List<String> {
        try {
            val soundNames = assets.list(SOUNDS_FOLDER)!!
            Log.d(TAG, "Found ${soundNames.size} sounds")
            return soundNames.asList()
        } catch (e: Exception) {
            Log.e(TAG, "Could not list assets", e)
            return emptyList()
        }
    }
}
```

<samp class="methodname">AssetManager.list(String)</samp> lists filenames contained in the folder path you pass in. By passing in your sounds folder, you should see every <samp class="filename">.wav</samp> file you put in there.

To verify that this is working correctly, create an instance of <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp> in <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> and invoke the <samp class="methodname">loadSounds()</samp> function.

**Listing 19.13  Creating a `BeatBox` instance (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {

    private lateinit var beatBox: BeatBox

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)

        beatBox = BeatBox(assets)
        beatBox.loadSounds()

        val binding: ActivityMainBinding =
            DataBindingUtil.setContentView(this, R.layout.activity_main)

        binding.recyclerView.apply {
            layoutManager = GridLayoutManager(context, 3)
            adapter = SoundAdapter()
        }
    }
    ...
}
```

Run your app, and you should see some log output telling you how many sound files were found. We provided 22 <samp class="filename">.wav</samp> files, so you should see:

```
 …1823-1823/com.bignerdranch.android.beatbox D/BeatBox: Found 22 sounds
```

## Wiring Up Assets for Use

Now that you have your asset filenames, you should present them to the user. Eventually, you will want the files to be played, so it makes sense to have an object responsible for keeping track of the filename, the name the user should see, and any other information related to that sound.

Create a <samp class="classname">Sound</samp> class to hold all of this.

**Listing 19.14  Creating `Sound` object (`Sound.kt`)**

```
private const val WAV = ".wav"

class Sound(val assetPath: String) {

    val name = assetPath.split("/").last().removeSuffix(WAV)
}
```

In the constructor, you do a little work to make a presentable name for your sound. First, you split off the filename using <samp class="methodname">String.split(String).last()</samp>. Once you have done that, you use <samp class="methodname">String.removeSuffix(String)</samp> to strip off the file extension, too.

Next, build up a list of <samp class="classname">Sound</samp>s in <samp class="methodname">BeatBox.loadSounds()</samp>.

**Listing 19.15  Creating `Sound`s (`BeatBox.kt`)**

```
class BeatBox(private val assets: AssetManager) {

    val sounds: List<Sound>

    init {
      sounds = loadSounds()
    }

    fun loadSounds(): List<String>List<Sound> {

        val soundNames: Array<String>

        try {
            val soundNames = assets.list(SOUNDS_FOLDER)!!
            Log.d(TAG, "Found ${soundNames.size} sounds")
            return soundNames.asList()
        } catch (e: Exception) {
            Log.e(TAG, "Could not list assets", e)
            return emptyList()
        }
        val sounds = mutableListOf<Sound>()
        soundNames.forEach { filename ->
            val assetPath = "$SOUNDS_FOLDER/$filename"
            val sound = Sound(assetPath)
            sounds.add(sound)
        }
        return sounds
    }
}
```

Now, wire up <samp class="classname">SoundAdapter</samp> to the <samp class="classname">List</samp> of <samp class="classname">Sound</samp>s.

**Listing 19.16  Hooking up to the `Sound` list (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
private inner class SoundAdapter(private val sounds: List<Sound>) :
        RecyclerView.Adapter<SoundHolder>() {
    ...

    override fun onBindViewHolder(holder: SoundHolder, position: Int) {
    }

    override fun getItemCount() = 0sounds.size
}
```

And now pass in <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp>’s sounds in <samp class="methodname">onCreate(Bundle?)</samp>.

**Listing 19.17  Passing in `Sound`s to the adapter (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    ...

    binding.recyclerView.apply {
        layoutManager = GridLayoutManager(context, 3)
        adapter = SoundAdapter(beatBox.sounds)
    }
}
```

Finally, remove the <samp class="methodname">BeatBox.loadSounds()</samp> function call in <samp class="methodname">onCreate</samp>.

**Listing 19.18  Removing `BeatBox.loadSounds()` from `onCreate(…)` (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    ...
    beatBox = BeatBox(assets)
    beatBox.loadSounds()
    ...
}
```

Since <samp class="methodname">BeatBox.loadSounds()</samp> is no longer being called from outside of <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp>’s initializer block, there is no need to keep this function `public`. To be a good citizen and avoid inadvertently calling <samp class="methodname">loadSounds()</samp> from other parts of the code, update its visibility modifier to `private`.

**Listing 19.19  Updating `BeatBox.loadSounds()`’s visibility modifier to `private` (`BeatBox.kt`)**

```
class BeatBox(private val assets: AssetManager) {
    ...
    private fun loadSounds(): List<Sound> {
        ...
    }
}
```

With that, you should see a grid of buttons when you run BeatBox ([Figure 19.6](#ch19s07.xhtml_ss_beatbox_empty_buttons "Figure 19.6  Empty buttons")).

**Figure 19.6  Empty buttons**

![Empty buttons](Images/beatbox_empty_buttons.png)

To populate the buttons with titles, you will use some additional tools from your new data binding utility belt.

## Binding to Data

With data binding, you can declare data objects within your layout file:

```
 <layout xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
            xmlns:tools="http://schemas.android.com/tools">
        <data>
            <variable
                name="crime"
                type="com.bignerdranch.android.criminalintent.Crime"/>
        </data>
        ...
    </layout> 
```

And then use values from those objects directly in your layout file by using the <samp class="firstterm">binding mustache</samp> operator, `@{}`:

```
 <CheckBox
        android:id="@+id/list_item_crime_solved_check_box"
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:layout_alignParentRight="true"
        android:checked="@{crime.isSolved()}"
        android:padding="4dp"/> 
```

In an object diagram, that would look like [Figure 19.7](#ch19s08.xhtml_dig_architecture_1 "Figure 19.7  The ties that bind"):

**Figure 19.7  The ties that bind**

![The ties that bind](Images/architecture_1.png)

Your goal right now is to put the sound names on their buttons. The most direct way to do that using data binding is to bind directly to a <samp class="classname">Sound</samp> object in <samp class="filename">list_item_sound.xml</samp> ([Figure 19.8](#ch19s08.xhtml_dig_architecture_2 "Figure 19.8  Direct hookup")):

**Figure 19.8  Direct hookup**

![Direct hookup](Images/architecture_2.png)

However, this causes some architectural issues. To see why, look at it from an MVC perspective ([Figure 19.9](#ch19s08.xhtml_dig_architecture_3 "Figure 19.9  Broken MVC")).

**Figure 19.9  Broken MVC**

![Broken MVC](Images/architecture_3.png)

The guiding principle behind any architecture is the <samp class="firstterm">Single Responsibility Principle</samp>. It says that each class you make should have exactly one responsibility. MVC gave you an idea of what those responsibilities should be: The model represents how your app works, the controller decides how to display your app, and the view displays it on the screen the way you want it to look.

Using data binding as shown in [Figure 19.8](#ch19s08.xhtml_dig_architecture_2 "Figure 19.8  Direct hookup") would break this division of responsibilities, because the <samp class="classname">Sound</samp> model object would likely end up with code that prepares the data for the view to display. This would quickly make your app a mess, as <samp class="filename">Sound.kt</samp> would become littered with two kinds of code: code that represents how your app works and code that prepares data for the view to display.

Instead of muddying up the responsibility of <samp class="classname">Sound</samp>, you will introduce a new object called a view model to use with data binding. This view model will take on the responsibility of preparing the data for the view to display ([Figure 19.10](#ch19s08.xhtml_dig_mvvm "Figure 19.10  Model-View-View Model")).

**Figure 19.10  Model-View-View Model**

![Model-View-View Model](Images/architecture_4.png)

This architecture, as we have said, is called MVVM, short for Model-View-View Model. Most of the work your controller classes once did at runtime to format data for display will go in the view model. Wiring widgets up with that data will be handled directly in the layout file using data binding to that view model. Your activity or fragment will be in charge of things like initializing the binding and the view model and creating the link between the two.

There is no controller with MVVM; rather, activities and fragments are considered part of the view.

### Creating a view model

Let’s create your view model. Create a new class called <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp> and give it two properties: a <samp class="classname">Sound</samp> for it to use and a <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp> to (eventually) play that sound with.

**Listing 19.20  Creating `SoundViewModel` (`SoundViewModel.kt`)**

```
class SoundViewModel {

    var sound: Sound? = null
        set(sound) {
            field = sound
        }
}
```

These properties are the interface your adapter will use. For the layout file, you will want an additional function to get the title that the button should display. Add it now to <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp>.

**Listing 19.21  Adding binding functions (`SoundViewModel.kt`)**

```
class SoundViewModel {

    var sound: Sound? = null
        set(sound) {
            field = sound
        }

    val title: String?
        get() = sound?.name
  }
```

### Binding to a view model

Now to integrate the view model into your layout file. The first step is to declare a property on your layout file, like so:

**Listing 19.22  Declaring the view model property (`res/layout/list_item_sound.xml`)**

```
<layout xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
        xmlns:tools="http://schemas.android.com/tools">
    <data>
        <variable
            name="viewModel"
            type="com.bignerdranch.android.beatbox.SoundViewModel"/>
    </data>
    ...
</layout>
```

This defines a property named `viewModel` on your binding class, including a getter and setter. Within your binding class, you can use `viewModel` in binding expressions.

**Listing 19.23  Binding your button title (`res/layout/list_item_sound.xml`)**

```
<layout xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
        xmlns:tools="http://schemas.android.com/tools">
    <data>
        <variable
            name="viewModel"
            type="com.bignerdranch.android.beatbox.SoundViewModel"/>
    </data>
    <Button
        android:layout_width="match_parent"
        android:layout_height="120dp"
        android:text="@{viewModel.title}"
        tools:text="Sound name"/>
</layout>
```

Within the binding mustache, you can write simple Java expressions, including chained function calls, math, and most anything else you want to include.

The last step is to hook up your view model. Create a <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp> and attach it to your binding class. Then add a binding function to your <samp class="classname">SoundHolder</samp>.

**Listing 19.24  Hooking up the view model (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
private inner class SoundHolder(private val binding: ListItemSoundBinding) :
        RecyclerView.ViewHolder(binding.root) {

    init {
        binding.viewModel = SoundViewModel()
    }

    fun bind(sound: Sound) {
        binding.apply {
            viewModel?.sound = sound
            executePendingBindings()
        }
    }
}
```

Inside your constructor, you construct and attach your view model. Then, in your <samp class="methodname">bind</samp> function, you update the data that view model is working with.

Calling <samp class="methodname">executePendingBindings()</samp> is not normally necessary. Here, though, you are updating binding data inside a <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp>, which updates views at a very high speed. By calling this function, you force the layout to immediately update itself, rather than waiting a millisecond or two. This keeps your <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> in sync with its <samp class="classname">RecyclerView.Adapter</samp>.

Finally, finish hooking up your view model by implementing <samp class="methodname">onBindViewHolder(…)</samp>.

**Listing 19.25  Calling `bind(Sound)` (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
private inner class SoundAdapter(private val sounds: List<Sound>) :
        RecyclerView.Adapter<SoundHolder>() {
    ...
    override fun onBindViewHolder(holder: SoundHolder, position: Int) {
        val sound = sounds[position]
        holder.bind(sound)
    }

    override fun getItemCount() = sounds.size
}
```

Run your app, and you will see titles on all the buttons on your screen ([Figure 19.11](#ch19s08.xhtml_ss_beatbox_finished_1 "Figure 19.11  Button titles filled in")).

**Figure 19.11  Button titles filled in**

![Button titles filled in](Images/beatbox_finished.png)

### Observable data

All may appear to be well, but darkness lies hidden in your code. You can see it if you scroll down ([Figure 19.12](#ch19s08.xhtml_ss_beatbox_not_quite_finished "Figure 19.12  Déjà vu")).

**Figure 19.12  Déjà vu**

![Déjà vu](Images/beatbox_not_quite_finished.png)

Did you see an item <samp class="guilabel">67_INDIOS2</samp> at the top, and then one that looks just like it at the bottom? Scroll up and down repeatedly, and you will see other file titles repeatedly appearing in unexpected, seemingly random places. If you do not see this, rotate the device into landscape mode and try again to see how deep the rabbit hole goes. Remember: We only offered you the truth – nothing more…

Worry not! This is not a glitch in the Matrix. This is happening because your layout has no way of knowing that you updated <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp>’s <samp class="classname">Sound</samp> inside <samp class="methodname">SoundHolder.bind(Sound)</samp>. In other words, the view model is not properly pushing data to your layout file as shown in [Figure 19.10](#ch19s08.xhtml_dig_mvvm "Figure 19.10  Model-View-View Model"). In addition to having a clear division of responsibilities, this step is the secret sauce that separates MVVM from other architectures like MVC, as discussed in [the section called *Different Architectures: Why Bother?*](../Text/ch19s01.xhtml "Different Architectures: Why Bother?") earlier in this chapter.

Your next job will be to make the view model communicate with the layout file when a change occurs. To do this, your view model needs to implement data binding’s <samp class="classname">Observable</samp> interface. This interface lets your binding class set listeners on your view model so that it can automatically receive callbacks when its fields are modified.

Implementing the whole interface is possible, but it requires extra work. We do not shy away from extra work here at Big Nerd Ranch, but we prefer to avoid it when we can. So we will instead show you how to do it the easy way, with data binding’s <samp class="classname">BaseObservable</samp> class.

Three steps are required:

1.  Subclass <samp class="classname">BaseObservable</samp> in your view model.

2.  Annotate your view model’s bindable properties with `@Bindable`.

3.  Call <samp class="methodname">notifyChange()</samp> or <samp class="methodname">notifyPropertyChanged(Int)</samp> each time a bindable property’s value changes.

In <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp>, this is only a few lines of code. Update <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp> to be observable.

**Listing 19.26  Making view model observable (`SoundViewModel.kt`)**

```
class SoundViewModel : BaseObservable() {

    var sound: Sound? = null
        set(sound) {
            field = sound
            notifyChange()
        }

    @get:Bindable
    val title: String?
        get() = sound?.name
}
```

When you call <samp class="methodname">notifyChange()</samp> here, it notifies your binding class that all of the <samp class="classname">Bindable</samp> properties on your objects have been updated. The binding class then runs the code inside the binding mustaches again to repopulate the view. So now, when the value of `sound` is set, <samp class="classname">ListItemSoundBinding</samp> will be notified and call <samp class="methodname">Button.setText(String)</samp> as you specified in <samp class="filename">list_item_sound.xml</samp>.

Above, we mentioned another function: <samp class="methodname">notifyPropertyChanged(Int)</samp>. The <samp class="methodname">notifyPropertyChanged(Int)</samp> function does the same thing as <samp class="methodname">notifyChange()</samp>, except it is more particular. By writing <samp class="methodname">notifyChange()</samp>, you say, “All of my bindable properties have changed; please update everything.” By writing <samp class="methodname">notifyPropertyChanged(BR.title)</samp>, you can instead say, “Only `title`’s value has changed.”

<samp class="methodname">BR.title</samp> is a constant that is generated by the data binding library. The <samp class="classname">BR</samp> class name is short for “binding resource.” Each property you annotate with <samp class="classname">@Bindable</samp> results in a generated BR constant with the same name.

Here are a few other examples:

```
 @get:Bindable val title: String // yields BR.title
    @get:Bindable val volume: Int // yields BR.volume
    @get:Bindable val etcetera: String // yields BR.etcetera
```

You may be thinking that using <samp class="classname">Observable</samp> seems similar to using <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp>, as you learned about in [Chapter 11](../Text/ch11.xhtml "11 Databases and the Room Library") – and you would be right. In fact, you can use <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> with data binding instead of the <samp class="classname">Observable</samp> interface. You will find out more about this in [the section called *For the More Curious: LiveData and Data Binding*](../Text/ch19s10.xhtml "For the More Curious: LiveData and Data Binding") at the end of this chapter.

Run BeatBox one more time. This time, you should see the right thing when you scroll around ([Figure 19.13](#ch19s08.xhtml_ss_beatbox_totally_finished "Figure 19.13  All done")).

**Figure 19.13  All done**

![All done](Images/beatbox_totally_finished.png)

## For the More Curious: More About Data Binding

Complete coverage of data binding is outside the scope of this book. And yet, reader, we must nevertheless try.

### Lambda expressions

You can write short callbacks directly in your layout file by using <samp class="firstterm">lambda expressions</samp>. These are simplified versions of Java’s lambda expressions:

```
 <Button
        android:layout_width="match_parent"
        android:layout_height="120dp"
        android:text="@{viewModel.title}"
        android:onClick="@{(view) -> viewModel.onButtonClick()}"
        tools:text="Sound name"/>
```

Like Java 8 lambda expressions, these are turned into implementations for the interface you use them for. (In this case, <samp class="classname">View.OnClickListener</samp>.) Unlike Java 8 lambda expressions, these expressions must use this exact syntax: The parameter must be in parentheses, and you must have exactly one expression on the right-hand side.

Also, unlike in Java lambdas, you can omit the lambda parameters if you are not using them. So this works fine, too:

```
 android:onClick="@{() -> viewModel.onButtonClick()}"
```

### Syntactic sugar

You also get a few additional bits of handy syntax for data binding. Particularly handy is the ability to use backticks for double quotes:

```
 android:text="@{`File name: ` + viewModel.title}"
```

Here, `` `File name` `` means the same thing as `"File name"`.

Binding expressions also have a null coalescing operator:

```
 android:text="@{`File name: ` + viewModel.title ?? `No file`}"
```

In the event that `title` is null, the `??` operator will yield the value `"No file"` instead.

In addition, automatic null handling is provided for you in data binding expressions. Even if `viewModel` is null in the code above, data binding will provide appropriate null checks so that it does not crash the app. Instead of crashing, the subexpression `viewModel.title` will yield `"null"`.

### BindingAdapters

By default, data binding interprets a binding expression as a property invocation. So this:

```
 android:text="@{`File name: ` + viewModel.title ?? `No file`}"
```

Is translated into an invocation of the <samp class="methodname">setText(String)</samp> function.

Sometimes that is not enough, and you want some custom behavior to be applied for a particular attribute. In those cases, you can write a <samp class="classname">BindingAdapter</samp>:

```
 @BindingAdapter("app:soundName")
    fun bindAssetSound(button: Button, assetFileName: String ) {
        ...
    }
```

Simply create a file-level function anywhere in your project and annotate it with `@BindingAdapter`, passing in the name of the attribute you want to bind as a parameter to the annotation and the <samp class="classname">View</samp> to which the annotation applies as the first parameter to the function. (Yes, this really works.)

In the example above, whenever data binding encounters a <samp class="classname">Button</samp> with an <samp class="varname">app:soundName</samp> attribute containing a <samp class="emphasis">binding expression</samp>, it will call your function, passing the <samp class="classname">Button</samp> and the result of the binding expression.

You can even create <samp class="classname">BindingAdapter</samp>s for more generalized views, such as <samp class="classname">View</samp> or <samp class="classname">ViewGroup</samp>. In this case the <samp class="classname">BindingAdapter</samp> will apply to that <samp class="classname">View</samp> and all of its subclasses.

For example, if you wanted to define an attribute <samp class="varname">app:isGone</samp> that would set the visibility of any <samp class="classname">View</samp> based on a Boolean value, you could do that like so:

```
 @BindingAdapter("app:isGone")
    fun bindIsGone(view: View, isGone: Boolean ) {
        view.visibility = if (isGone) View.GONE else View.VISIBLE
    }
```

Because <samp class="classname">View</samp> is the first argument to <samp class="methodname">bindIsGone</samp>, this attribute is available to <samp class="classname">View</samp> and all subclasses of <samp class="classname">View</samp> in your app module. This means you can use it with <samp class="classname">Button</samp>s, <samp class="classname">TextView</samp>s, <samp class="classname">LinearLayout</samp>s, and so on.

You will probably think of one or two operations you would like to use data binding with on the standard library widgets. Many common operations already have binding adapters defined – for example, <samp class="classname">TextViewBindingAdapter</samp> provides additional attributes for <samp class="classname">TextView</samp>. You can read these binding adapters yourself by viewing the source in Android Studio. So, before you write your own solution, type Command-Shift-O (Ctrl-Shift-O) to search for a class, open up the associated binding adapters file, and check to see whether it already exists.

## For the More Curious: LiveData and Data Binding

<samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> and data binding are similar in that they both provide a way to observe data and react when that data changes. In fact, it is possible to work with both <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> and data binding together, in tandem. The example below shows the changes that you would make to <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp> to bind the title property as <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> instead of an <samp class="classname">Observable</samp> property.

```
 class SoundViewModel : BaseObservable() {

        val title: MutableLiveData<String?> = MutableLiveData()

        var sound: Sound? = null
            set(sound) {
                field = sound
                notifyChange()
                title.postValue(sound?.name)
            }

        @get:Bindable
        val title: String?
            get() = sound?.name
    }
```

In this example, it is no longer necessary to subclass <samp class="classname">BaseObservable</samp> or provide `@Bindable` annotations, because <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> has its own mechanisms for notifying observers. However, as you learned in [Chapter 11](../Text/ch11.xhtml "11 Databases and the Room Library"), <samp class="classname">LiveData</samp> does require a <samp class="classname">LifecycleOwner</samp>. To tell the data binding framework which lifecycle owner to use when observing the title property, you would update <samp class="classname">SoundAdapter</samp>, setting the <samp class="varname">lifecycleOwner</samp> property after creating the binding:

```
 private inner class SoundAdapter(private val sounds: List<Sound>) :
            RecyclerView.Adapter<SoundHolder>() {
        ...
        override fun onCreateViewHolder(parent: ViewGroup, viewType: Int):
                SoundHolder {
            val binding = DataBindingUtil.inflate<ListItemSoundBinding>(
                layoutInflater,
                R.layout.list_item_sound,
                parent,
                false
            )

            binding.lifecycleOwner = this@MainActivity

            return SoundHolder(binding)
        }
    }
```

This would set <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> as the lifecycle owner. No changes to the view would be required as long as the property name, title, remained the same.

# <samp class="chapter_number">20</samp>
<samp class="chapter_name">Unit Testing and Audio Playback</samp>

One reason MVVM architecture is so appealing is that it makes a critical programming practice easier: <samp class="firstterm">unit testing</samp>. Unit testing is the practice of writing small programs that verify the standalone behavior of each unit of your main app. Because BeatBox’s units are each classes, classes are what your unit tests will test.

In this chapter, you will finally play all of the <samp class="filename">.wav</samp> files you loaded in the previous chapter. As you build and integrate sound playback, you will write unit tests for your <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp>’s integration with <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp>.

Android’s audio APIs are low level, for the most part, but there is a tool practically tailor-made for the app you are writing: <samp class="classname">SoundPool</samp>. <samp class="classname">SoundPool</samp> can load a large set of sounds into memory and control the maximum number of sounds that are playing back at any one time. So, if your app’s user gets a bit too excited and mashes all the buttons at the same time, it will not break your app or overtax the user’s phone.

Ready? Time to get started.

## Creating a SoundPool

Your first job is to build out sound playback inside <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp>. To do that, first create a <samp class="classname">SoundPool</samp> object ([Listing 20.1](#ch20s01.xhtml_create_sound_pool "Listing 20.1  Creating a SoundPool (BeatBox.kt)")).

**Listing 20.1  Creating a `SoundPool` (`BeatBox.kt`)**

```
private const val TAG = "BeatBox"
private const val SOUNDS_FOLDER = "sample_sounds"
private const val MAX_SOUNDS = 5

class BeatBox(private val assets: AssetManager) {

    val sounds: List<Sound>
    private val soundPool = SoundPool.Builder()
        .setMaxStreams(MAX_SOUNDS)
        .build()

    init {
        sounds = loadSounds()
    }
    ...
}
```

A <samp class="classname">Builder</samp> is used to create a <samp class="classname">SoundPool</samp> instance. The <samp class="methodname">setMaxStreams(Int)</samp> option on the builder specifies how many sounds can play at any given time. Here, you pass in `5`. If five sounds are playing and you try to play a sixth one, the <samp class="classname">SoundPool</samp> will stop playing the oldest one.

In addition to the max streams option, the <samp class="classname">SoundPool</samp> builder allows you to specify different attributes of the audio stream with the <samp class="methodname">setAudioAttributes(AudioAttributes)</samp> option. Check the documentation for more information on what this does. The default audio attributes work well enough in this example, so you can leave this option out for now.

## Accessing Assets

Recall that your sound files are stored in your app’s assets. Before you access those files to play the audio, let’s discuss a bit more about how assets work.

Your <samp class="classname">Sound</samp> object has an asset file path defined on it. Asset file paths will not work if you try to open them with a <samp class="classname">File</samp>; you must use them with an <samp class="classname">AssetManager</samp>:

```
 val assetPath = sound.assetPath

    val assetManager = context.assets

    val soundData = assetManager.open(assetPath)
```

This gives you a standard <samp class="classname">InputStream</samp> for the data, which you can use like any other <samp class="classname">InputStream</samp> in Kotlin.

Some APIs require <samp class="classname">FileDescriptor</samp>s instead. This is what you will use with <samp class="classname">SoundPool</samp>. If you need that, you can call <samp class="methodname">AssetManager.openFd(String)</samp> instead:

```
 val assetPath = sound.assetPath

    val assetManager = context.assets

    // AssetFileDescriptors are different from FileDescriptors...
    val assetFileDescriptor = assetManager.openFd(assetPath)

    // ... but you can get a regular FileDescriptor easily if you need to
    val fileDescriptor = assetFileDescriptor.fileDescriptor
```

## Loading Sounds

The next thing to do with your <samp class="classname">SoundPool</samp> is to load it up with sounds. The main benefit of using a <samp class="classname">SoundPool</samp> over some other methods of playing audio is that <samp class="classname">SoundPool</samp> responds quickly: When you tell it to play a sound, it will play the sound immediately, with no lag.

The trade-off for that is that you must load sounds into your <samp class="classname">SoundPool</samp> before you play them. Each sound you load will get its own integer ID. To track this ID, add a <samp class="varname">soundId</samp> property to <samp class="classname">Sound</samp>.

**Listing 20.2  Adding a sound ID property (`Sound.kt`)**

```
class Sound(val assetPath: String, var soundId: Int? = null) {
    val name = assetPath.split("/").last().removeSuffix(WAV)
}
```

By making <samp class="varname">soundId</samp> a nullable type (`Int?`), you make it possible to say that a <samp class="classname">Sound</samp> has no value set for <samp class="varname">soundId</samp> by assigning it a null value.

Now to load your sounds. Add a <samp class="methodname">load(Sound)</samp> function to <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp> to load a <samp class="classname">Sound</samp> into your <samp class="classname">SoundPool</samp>.

**Listing 20.3  Loading sounds into `SoundPool` (`BeatBox.kt`)**

```
class BeatBox(private val assets: AssetManager) {
    ...
    private fun loadSounds(): List<Sound> {
        ...
    }

    private fun load(sound: Sound) {
        val afd: AssetFileDescriptor = assets.openFd(sound.assetPath)
        val soundId = soundPool.load(afd, 1)
        sound.soundId = soundId
    }
}
```

Calling <samp class="methodname">soundPool.load(AssetFileDescriptor, Int)</samp> loads a file into your <samp class="methodname">SoundPool</samp> for later playback. To keep track of the sound and play it back again (or unload it), <samp class="methodname">soundPool.load(…)</samp> returns an `Int` ID, which you stash in the <samp class="varname">soundId</samp> field you just defined.

Be aware that since calling <samp class="methodname">openFd(String)</samp> can throw <samp class="classname">IOException</samp>, <samp class="methodname">load(Sound)</samp> can throw <samp class="classname">IOException</samp>, too. This means you will need to handle that exception any time <samp class="methodname">load(Sound)</samp> is called.

Now load up all your sounds by calling <samp class="methodname">load(Sound)</samp> inside <samp class="methodname">BeatBox.loadSounds()</samp>.

**Listing 20.4  Loading up all your sounds (`BeatBox.kt`)**

```
private fun loadSounds(): List<Sound> {
    ...
    val sounds = mutableListOf<Sound>()
    soundNames.forEach { filename ->
        val assetPath = "$SOUNDS_FOLDER/$filename"
        val sound = Sound(assetPath)
        sounds.add(sound)
        try {
            load(sound)
            sounds.add(sound)
        } catch (ioe: IOException) {
            Log.e(TAG, "Cound not load sound $filename", ioe)
        }
    }
    return sounds
}
```

Run BeatBox to make sure that all the sounds loaded correctly. If they did not, you will see red exception logs in Logcat.

## Playing Sounds

<samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp> also needs to be able to play sounds. Add the <samp class="methodname">play(Sound)</samp> function to <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp>.

**Listing 20.5  Playing sounds back (`BeatBox.kt`)**

```
class BeatBox(private val assets: AssetManager) {
    ...
    init {
        sounds = loadSounds()
    }

    fun play(sound: Sound) {
        sound.soundId?.let {
            soundPool.play(it, 1.0f, 1.0f, 1, 0, 1.0f)
        }
    }
    ...
}
```

Before playing your <samp class="varname">soundId</samp>, you check to make sure it is not null. This might happen if the <samp class="classname">Sound</samp> failed to load.

Once you are sure you have a non-null value, you play the sound by calling <samp class="methodname">SoundPool.play(Int, Float, Float, Int, Int, Float)</samp>. Those parameters are, respectively: the sound ID, volume on the left, volume on the right, priority, whether the audio should loop, and playback rate. For full volume and normal playback rate, you pass in `1.0`. Passing in `0` for the looping value says “do not loop.” (You can pass in `-1` if you want it to loop forever. We speculate that this would be incredibly annoying.)

With that function written, you are now ready to integrate sound playback into <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp>. You will perform this integration in a test-first manner – that is, you will first write a failing unit test and then implement the integration to make the test pass.

## Test Dependencies

Before you write your test, you will need to add a couple of tools to your testing environment: Mockito and Hamcrest. Mockito is a Java framework that makes it easy to create simple <samp class="firstterm">mock objects</samp>. These mock objects will help you isolate your tests of <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp> so that you do not accidentally test other objects at the same time.

Hamcrest is a library of <samp class="firstterm">matchers</samp>. Matchers are tools that make it easy to “match” conditions in your code and fail if your code does not match what you expect. You will use them to verify that your code works as you expect it to.

A version of Hamcrest is automatically included with the JUnit library, and JUnit is automatically included as a dependency when you create a new Android Studio project. This means that you only need to add the dependencies for Mockito to your test build. Open your app module’s <samp class="filename">build.gradle</samp> file and add the Mockito dependencies ([Listing 20.6](#ch20s05.xhtml_pl_add_mockito_import "Listing 20.6  Adding Mockito dependencies (app/build.gradle)")). Sync your files when you are done.

**Listing 20.6  Adding Mockito dependencies (`app/build.gradle`)**

```
dependencies {
    ...
    implementation 'androidx.recyclerview:recyclerview:1.0.0'
    testImplementation 'org.mockito:mockito-core:2.25.0'
    testImplementation 'org.mockito:mockito-inline:2.25.0'
}
```

The `testImplementation` scope means that this dependency will only be included in test builds of your app. That way, you do not bloat your APK with additional unused code.

`mockito-core` includes all of the functions you will use to create and configure your mock objects. `mockito-inline` is a special dependency that will make Mockito easier to use with Kotlin.

By default, all Kotlin classes are final. This means that you cannot inherit from these classes unless you explicitly mark them as `open`. Unfortunately, Mockito makes heavy use of inheritance when mocking classes. This means that Mockito cannot mock your Kotlin classes out of the box. The `mockito-inline` dependency includes functionality that allows Mockito to mock final classes and functions, working around this inheritance problem. This allows you to mock your Kotlin classes without needing to change your source files.

## Creating a Test Class

The most convenient way to write unit tests is within a <samp class="firstterm">testing framework</samp>. The framework makes it easier to write and run a suite of tests together and see their output in Android Studio.

JUnit is almost universally used as a testing framework on Android and has convenient integrations into Android Studio. Your first job is to create a class for your JUnit tests to live in. To do this, open up <samp class="filename">SoundViewModel.kt</samp> and key in Command-Shift-T (Ctrl-Shift-T). Android Studio attempts to navigate to a test class associated with the class you are looking at. If there is no test class (as is the case here), you are given the option to create a new test class ([Figure 20.1](#ch20s06.xhtml_ss_create_new_test_class "Figure 20.1  Trying to open a test class")).

**Figure 20.1  Trying to open a test class**

![Trying to open a test class](Images/create_new_test_class.png)

Choose <samp class="guilabel">Create New Test...</samp> to create the new test class. Select <samp class="guilabel">JUnit4</samp> for your testing library and check the box marked <samp class="guilabel">setUp/@Before</samp>. Leave all the other fields as they are ([Figure 20.2](#ch20s06.xhtml_ss_create_new_test_class_dialog "Figure 20.2  Creating a new test class")).

**Figure 20.2  Creating a new test class**

![Creating a new test class](Images/create_new_test_class_dialog.png)

Click <samp class="guilabel">OK</samp> to continue to the next dialog.

The last step is to choose what kind of test class you will create. Tests in the <samp class="filename">androidTest</samp> folder are called <samp class="firstterm">instrumentation tests</samp>. Instrumentation tests run on an Android device or emulator. The advantage of this is that you can test your app against the same system frameworks and APIs that your APK will be running against once the app is released. The downside is that instrumentation tests take longer to set up and run, because they are running against a full version of the Android OS.

Tests in the <samp class="filename">test</samp> folder are often referred to as unit tests. These tests run on a Java Virtual Machine, or JVM, without any of the Android runtime. Leaving out that baggage makes them quick.

The term “unit test” on Android is overloaded. It is sometimes used to describe a type of test that verifies a single class or unit of functionality in isolation. At other times, it is used to describe any test residing in the <samp class="filename">test</samp> directory. Unfortunately, a test in that directory might verify a single class or unit – but it might be an <samp class="firstterm">integration test</samp>, which tests a section of an app with many pieces working together. You will learn more about integration tests in [the section called *For the More Curious: Integration Testing*](../Text/ch20s11.xhtml "For the More Curious: Integration Testing") near the end of this chapter.

For the remainder of this chapter, we will use the term <samp class="firstterm">JVM test</samp> for a test of either type that lives in the <samp class="filename">test</samp> folder and runs on the JVM. We will reserve <samp class="emphasis">unit test</samp> for only those tests that verify a single class or unit.

Unit tests are the smallest kind of test you can write: a test of one component by itself. They should not need your entire app or a device to run, and they should run quickly enough for you to run them repeatedly as you work. Because of this, they are rarely run as instrumentation tests. With this in mind, choose the <samp class="filename">test</samp> folder for your test class ([Figure 20.3](#ch20s06.xhtml_ss_create_new_test_class_select_directory "Figure 20.3  Selecting a destination directory")) and click <samp class="guilabel">OK</samp>.

**Figure 20.3  Selecting a destination directory**

![Selecting a destination directory](Images/create_new_test_class_select_directory.png)

## Setting Up Your Test

Now to build out your <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp> test. Android Studio has created a class file for you, called <samp class="filename">SoundViewModelTest.kt</samp>. (You can find this class under the source set labeled <samp class="guilabel">test</samp> inside your <samp class="guilabel">app</samp> module.) The template starts out with a single function called <samp class="methodname">setUp()</samp>:

```
 class SoundViewModelTest {

        @Before
        fun setUp() {
        }
    }
```

A test needs to do the same work for most objects: build an instance of the object to test and create any other objects that object depends on. Instead of writing this same code for every test, JUnit provides an annotation called `@Before`. Code written inside a function marked `@Before` will be run once before each test executes. By convention, most JUnit test classes have one function marked `@Before` named <samp class="methodname">setUp()</samp>.

### Setting up the test subject

Inside your <samp class="methodname">setUp()</samp> function, you will construct an instance of <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp> to test. To do that, you need an instance of <samp class="classname">Sound</samp>, because <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp> needs a sound object to know how to display a title.

Create your <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp> and a <samp class="classname">Sound</samp> for it to use ([Listing 20.7](#ch20s07.xhtml_pl_create_soundviewmodel_in_test "Listing 20.7  Creating a SoundViewModel test subject (SoundViewModelTest.java)")). Since <samp class="classname">Sound</samp> is a simple data object with no behavior to break, it is safe not to mock it.

**Listing 20.7  Creating a `SoundViewModel` test subject (`SoundViewModelTest.java`)**

```
class SoundViewModelTest {

    private lateinit var sound: Sound
    private lateinit var subject: SoundViewModel

    @Before
    fun setUp() {
        sound = Sound("assetPath")
        subject = SoundViewModel()
        subject.sound = sound
    }
}
```

Anywhere else in this book, you would have named your <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp> <samp class="varname">soundViewModel</samp>. Here, though, you have named it <samp class="varname">subject</samp>. This is a convention we like to use in our tests at Big Nerd Ranch, for two reasons:

*   It makes it clear that <samp class="varname">subject</samp> is the object under test (and the other objects are not).

*   If any functions on <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp> are ever moved to a different class (say, <samp class="classname">BeatBoxSoundViewModel</samp>), the test functions can be cut and pasted over without renaming <samp class="varname">soundViewModel</samp> to <samp class="varname">beatBoxSoundViewModel</samp>.

## Writing Tests

Now that your initial <samp class="methodname">setUp()</samp> function is written, you are ready to write your tests. A test is a function in your test class annotated with `@Test`.

Start by writing a test that asserts existing behavior in <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp>: The `title` property is connected to the <samp class="classname">Sound</samp>’s `name` property. Write a function that tests this ([Listing 20.8](#ch20s08.xhtml_pl_write_assert_test "Listing 20.8  Testing the title property (SoundViewModelTest.kt)")).

**Listing 20.8  Testing the title property (`SoundViewModelTest.kt`)**

```
class SoundViewModelTest {
    ...
    @Before
    fun setUp() {
        ...
    }

    @Test
    fun exposesSoundNameAsTitle() {
        assertThat(subject.title, `is`(sound.name))
    }
}
```

Two functions will show up red: the <samp class="methodname">assertThat(…)</samp> function and the <samp class="methodname">is(…)</samp> function. Key in Option-Return (Alt-Enter) on <samp class="methodname">assertThat(…)</samp> and select <samp class="methodname">Assert.assertThat(…)</samp> from `org.junit`. Do the same for the <samp class="methodname">is(…)</samp> function, selecting <samp class="classname">Is.is</samp> from `org.hamcrest`.

This test uses the <samp class="methodname">is(…)</samp> Hamcrest matcher with JUnit’s <samp class="methodname">assertThat(…)</samp> function. The code reads almost like a sentence: “Assert that subject’s title property is the same value as sound’s name property.” If those two functions return different values, the test fails.

To run your unit tests, right-click on the <samp class="classname">SoundViewModelTest</samp> class name and select <samp class="guilabel">Run 'SoundViewModelTest'</samp>. Android Studio’s bottom pane shows the results ([Figure 20.4](#ch20s08.xhtml_ss_test_run_output_passed_first_time "Figure 20.4  Passing tests")).

**Figure 20.4  Passing tests**

![Passing tests](Images/test_run_output_passed_first_time.png)

By default, the test display only shows details for failing tests, since those are the only tests that are interesting. So this output means that everything is A-OK – your tests ran, and they passed.

### Testing object interactions

Now for the real work: building out the interactions between <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp> and your new <samp class="methodname">BeatBox.play(Sound)</samp> function. A common way to go about this is to write a test that shows what you expect a new function to do <samp class="emphasis">before</samp> you have written the function. You are going to write a new function on <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp> called <samp class="methodname">onButtonClicked()</samp> that calls <samp class="methodname">BeatBox.play(Sound)</samp>. Write a test function that calls <samp class="methodname">onButtonClicked()</samp> ([Listing 20.9](#ch20s08.xhtml_pl_write_onbuttonclicked_test "Listing 20.9  Writing a test for onButtonClicked() (SoundViewModelTest.kt)")).

**Listing 20.9  Writing a test for `onButtonClicked()` (`SoundViewModelTest.kt`)**

```
class SoundViewModelTest {
    ...
    @Test
    fun exposesSoundNameAsTitle() {
        assertThat(subject.title, `is`(sound.name))
    }

    @Test
    fun callsBeatBoxPlayOnButtonClicked() {
        subject.onButtonClicked()
    }
}
```

That function does not exist yet, so it shows up in red. Put your cursor over it and key in Option-Return (Alt-Enter). Then select <samp class="guilabel">Create member function 'SoundViewModel.onButtonClicked'</samp>, and the function will be created for you.

**Listing 20.10  Creating `onButtonClicked()` (`SoundViewModel.kt`)**

```
class SoundViewModel : BaseObservable() {
    fun onButtonClicked() {
        TODO("not implemented") //To change ...
    }
    ...
}
```

For now, leave it empty (or delete the `TODO`, if Android Studio adds one) and key in Command-Shift-T (Ctrl-Shift-T) to return to <samp class="classname">SoundViewModelTest</samp>.

Your test calls the function, but it should also verify that the function does what you say it does: calls <samp class="methodname">BeatBox.play(Sound)</samp>. The first step to implementing this is to provide <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp> with a <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp> object.

You could create an instance of <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp> in your test and pass it to the view model constructor. But if you do that in a unit test, you create a problem: If <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp> is broken, then tests you write in <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp> that use <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp> might break, too. That is not what you want. <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp>’s unit tests should only fail when <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp> is broken.

In other words, you want to test the behavior of <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp> and its interactions with other classes in isolation. This is a key tenet of unit testing.

The solution is to use a <samp class="firstterm">mocked</samp> <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp>. This mock object will be a subclass of <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp> that has all the same functions as <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp> – but none of those functions will do anything. That way, your test of <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp> can verify that <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp> itself is using <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp> correctly, without depending at all on how <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp> works.

To create a mock object with Mockito, you call the <samp class="methodname">mock(Class)</samp> static function, passing in the class you want to mock. Create a mock of <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp> and a field to store it in <samp class="classname">SoundViewModelTest</samp> ([Listing 20.11](#ch20s08.xhtml_pl_create_mock_beatbox "Listing 20.11  Creating a mock BeatBox (SoundViewModelTest.kt)")).

**Listing 20.11  Creating a mock `BeatBox` (`SoundViewModelTest.kt`)**

```
class SoundViewModelTest {

    private lateinit var beatBox: BeatBox
    private lateinit var sound: Sound
    private lateinit var subject: SoundViewModel

    @Before
    fun setUp() {
        beatBox = mock(BeatBox::class.java)
        sound = Sound("assetPath")
        subject = SoundViewModel()
        subject.sound = sound
    }
    ...
}
```

The <samp class="methodname">mock(Class)</samp> function will need to be imported, just like a class reference. This function will automatically create a mocked-out version of <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp> for you. Pretty slick.

With the mock <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp> ready, you can finish writing your test to verify that the play function is called. Mockito can help you do this odd-sounding job. All Mockito mock objects keep track of which of their functions have been called, as well as what parameters were passed in for each call. Mockito’s <samp class="methodname">verify(Object)</samp> function can then check to see whether those functions were called the way you expected them to be called.

Call <samp class="methodname">verify(Object)</samp> to ensure that <samp class="methodname">onButtonClicked()</samp> calls <samp class="methodname">BeatBox.play(Sound)</samp> with the <samp class="classname">Sound</samp> object you hooked up to your <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp> ([Listing 20.12](#ch20s08.xhtml_pl_verify_mock_interaction "Listing 20.12  Verifying that BeatBox.play(Sound) is called (SoundViewModelTest.kt)")).

**Listing 20.12  Verifying that `BeatBox.play(Sound)` is called (`SoundViewModelTest.kt`)**

```
class SoundViewModelTest {
    ...
    @Test
    fun callsBeatBoxPlayOnButtonClicked() {
        subject.onButtonClicked()

        verify(beatBox).play(sound)
    }
}
```

<samp class="methodname">verify(Object)</samp> uses a fluent interface. It is an abbreviation for the following code:

```
 verify(beatBox)
    beatBox.play(sound)
```

Calling <samp class="methodname">verify(beatBox)</samp> says, “I am about to verify that a function was called on <samp class="varname">beatBox</samp>.” The next function call is then interpreted as, “Verify that this function was called like this.” So your call to <samp class="methodname">verify(…)</samp> here means, “Verify that the <samp class="methodname">play(…)</samp> function was called on <samp class="varname">beatBox</samp> with this specific <samp class="varname">sound</samp> as a parameter.”

No such thing has happened, of course. <samp class="methodname">SoundViewModel.onButtonClicked()</samp> is empty, so <samp class="methodname">beatBox.play(Sound)</samp> has not been called. Also, <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp> does not even hold a reference to <samp class="varname">beatBox</samp>, so it cannot call any functions on it. This means that your test <samp class="emphasis">should</samp> fail. Because you are writing the test first, that is a good thing – if your test does not fail at first, it must not be testing anything.

Run your test to see it fail. You can follow the same steps from earlier, or key in Control-R (Shift-F10) to repeat the last run command you performed. The result is shown in [Figure 20.5](#ch20s08.xhtml_ss_test_run_output_error "Figure 20.5  Failing test output").

**Figure 20.5  Failing test output**

![Failing test output](Images/test_run_output_error.png)

The output says that your test expected a call to <samp class="methodname">beatBox.play(Sound)</samp> but did not receive it:

```
 Wanted but not invoked:
    beatBox.play(
        com.bignerdranch.android.beatbox.Sound@3571b748
    );
    -> at ….callsBeatBoxPlayOnButtonClicked(SoundViewModelTest.java:28)
    Actually, there were zero interactions with this mock.
```

Under the hood, <samp class="methodname">verify(Object)</samp> made an assertion, just like <samp class="methodname">assertThat(…)</samp> did. When that assertion failed, it caused the test to fail and logged this output describing what went wrong.

Now to fix your test. First, create a constructor property for <samp class="classname">SoundViewModel</samp> that accepts a <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp> instance.

**Listing 20.13  Providing a `BeatBox` to `SoundViewModel` (`SoundViewModel.kt`)**

```
class SoundViewModel(private val beatBox: BeatBox) : BaseObservable() {
    ...
}
```

This change will cause two errors in your code: one in your tests and one in your production code. Fix the production error first. Open <samp class="filename">MainActivity.kt</samp> and provide the <samp class="varname">beatBox</samp> object to your view models when they are created in <samp class="classname">SoundHolder</samp> ([Listing 20.14](#ch20s08.xhtml_fix_error_in_sound_holder "Listing 20.14  Fixing the error in SoundHolder (MainActivity.kt)")).

**Listing 20.14  Fixing the error in `SoundHolder` (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
private inner class SoundHolder(private val binding: ListItemSoundBinding) :
    RecyclerView.ViewHolder(binding.root) {

    init {
        binding.viewModel = SoundViewModel(beatBox)
    }

    fun bind(sound: Sound) {
        ...
    }
}
```

Next, provide the mock version of <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp> to your view model in your test class ([Listing 20.15](#ch20s08.xhtml_provide_mock_beat_box_in_test "Listing 20.15  Providing the mock BeatBox in test (SoundViewModelTest.kt)")).

**Listing 20.15  Providing the mock `BeatBox` in test (`SoundViewModelTest.kt`)**

```
class SoundViewModelTest {
    ...
    @Before
    fun setUp() {
        beatBox = mock(BeatBox::class.java)
        sound = Sound("assetPath")
        subject = SoundViewModel(beatBox)
        subject.sound = sound
    }
    ...
}
```

This gets you halfway to a passing test. Next, implement <samp class="methodname">onButtonClicked()</samp> to do what the test expects ([Listing 20.16](#ch20s08.xhtml_pl_implement_onbuttonclicked "Listing 20.16  Implementing onButtonClicked() (SoundViewModel.kt)")).

**Listing 20.16  Implementing `onButtonClicked()` (`SoundViewModel.kt`)**

```
class SoundViewModel(private val beatBox: BeatBox) : BaseObservable() {
    ...
    fun onButtonClicked() {
        sound?.let {
            beatBox.play(it)
        }
    }
}
```

Rerun your test. This time you should see green, indicating that all your tests passed ([Figure 20.6](#ch20s08.xhtml_ss_test_run_output_passed "Figure 20.6  All green, all good")).

**Figure 20.6  All green, all good**

![All green, all good](Images/test_run_output_passed_second_time.png)

## Data Binding Callbacks

One last step remains to get your buttons working: You need to hook <samp class="methodname">onButtonClicked()</samp> up to your buttons.

Remember how you used data binding to put data into your UI? You can also use it to hook up click listeners and the like by using lambda expressions. (To refresh your memory on lambda expressions, see [the section called *Lambda expressions*](#ch19s09.xhtml_sect-bb-mvvm-lambda-expressions "Lambda expressions") in [Chapter 19](../Text/ch19.xhtml "19 Data Binding and MVVM").)

Add a data binding callback expression to hook your buttons up to <samp class="methodname">SoundViewModel.onButtonClicked()</samp>.

**Listing 20.17  Hooking up your buttons (`list_item_sound.xml`)**

```
<Button
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="120dp"
    android:onClick="@{() -> viewModel.onButtonClicked()}"
    android:text="@{viewModel.title}"
    tools:text="Sound name"/>
```

The next time you run BeatBox, your buttons should play sounds for you. However, if you try to run BeatBox with the green run button now, your tests will run again. This is because running the tests changed your <samp class="firstterm">run configuration</samp> – the setting that determines what Android Studio will do when you click the run button.

To run your BeatBox app, click the run configuration selector next to the run button and switch back over to the <samp class="guilabel">app</samp> run configuration ([Figure 20.7](#ch20s09.xhtml_ss_switch_run_configuration "Figure 20.7  Changing your run configuration")).

**Figure 20.7  Changing your run configuration**

![Changing your run configuration](Images/switch_run_configuration.png)

Now run BeatBox and click on your buttons. You should hear your app make aggressive yelling sounds. Do not be afraid – this is what BeatBox was meant to do.

## Unloading Sounds

The app works, but to be a good citizen you should clean up your <samp class="classname">SoundPool</samp> by calling <samp class="methodname">SoundPool.release()</samp> when you are done with it ([Listing 20.18](#ch20s10.xhtml_release_sound_pool_in_beat_box "Listing 20.18  Releasing your SoundPool (BeatBox.kt)")).

**Listing 20.18  Releasing your `SoundPool` (`BeatBox.kt`)**

```
class BeatBox(private val assets: AssetManager) {
    ...
    fun play(sound: Sound) {
        ...
    }

    fun release() {
        soundPool.release()
    }

    private fun loadSounds(): List<Sound> {
        ...
    }
    ...
}
```

Then, add a matching <samp class="methodname">BeatBox.release()</samp> function in <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> ([Listing 20.19](#ch20s10.xhtml_call_release_in_main_activity "Listing 20.19  Releasing your BeatBox (MainActivity.kt)")).

**Listing 20.19  Releasing your `BeatBox` (`MainActivity.kt`)**

```
class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {

    private lateinit var beatBox: BeatBox

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        ...
    }

    override fun onDestroy() {
        super.onDestroy()
        beatBox.release()
    }
    ...
}
```

Run your app again to make sure it works correctly with your new <samp class="methodname">release()</samp> function. If you play a long sound and rotate the screen or hit the Back button, you should now hear the sound stop.

## For the More Curious: Integration Testing

We said earlier that <samp class="classname">SoundViewModelTest</samp> is a unit test and that your other option was to create an integration test. So: What is an integration test?

In a unit test, the item under test is an individual class. In an integration test, the item under test is a section of your app, with many pieces working together. Both of these tests are important and serve different purposes. Unit tests ensure correct behavior of each class unit and your expectations of how these units will interact with each other. Integration tests verify that the individually tested pieces actually do integrate together properly and function as expected.

Integration tests can be written for non-UI parts of your app, such as database interactions, but on Android they are most commonly written to test the app at the UI level by interacting with its UI and verifying expectations. They are usually written screen by screen. For example, you might test that when the <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> screen is fired up, the first button displays the name of the first file from <samp class="filename">sample_sounds</samp>: <samp class="filename">65_cjipie</samp>.

Integration testing against the UI requires framework classes such as activities and fragments. It may also require system services, file systems, and other pieces not available to a JVM test. For this reason, integration tests are most often implemented as instrumentation tests on Android.

Integration tests should pass when the app <samp class="emphasis">does</samp> what you expect, not when the app is <samp class="emphasis">implemented</samp> how you expect. Changing the name of a button ID does not affect what the application does, but if you write an integration test that says, “Call <samp class="methodname">findViewById(R.id.button)</samp> and make sure the button it finds is displaying the right text,” that test will break. So instead of using standard Android framework tools like <samp class="methodname">findViewById(Int)</samp>, UI integration tests are most often written with a UI testing framework that makes it easier to say things like, “Make sure there is a button with the text I expect on the screen somewhere.”

Espresso is a UI testing framework from Google for testing Android apps. You can include it by adding `com.android.support.test.espresso:espresso-core` as an `androidTestImplementation` artifact in your <samp class="filename">app/build.gradle</samp> file. Android Studio includes this dependency by default on new projects.

Once you have Espresso included as a dependency, you can use it to make assertions about an activity you have fired up to test. Here is an example test showing how to assert that a view exists on the screen, using the first <samp class="filename">sample_sounds</samp> test filename:

```
 @RunWith(AndroidJUnit4::class)
    class MainActivityTest {

        @get:Rule
        val activityRule = ActivityTestRule(MainActivity::class.java)

        @Test
        fun showsFirstFileName() {
            onView(withText("65_cjipie"))
                    .check(matches(isDisplayed()))
        }
    }
```

A couple of annotations get this code up and running. The `@RunWith(AndroidJUnit4.class)` annotation up top specifies that this is an Android instrumentation test that might want to work with activities and other Android runtime toys. After that, the `@get:Rule` annotation on <samp class="varname">activityRule</samp> signals to JUnit that it should fire up an instance of <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> before running each test.

With that setup done, you can make assertions about <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> in your test. In <samp class="methodname">showsFirstFileName()</samp>, the line `onView(withText("65_cjipie"))` finds a view with the text `65_cjipie` on it to perform a test operation on. The call to <samp class="methodname">check(matches(isDisplayed()))</samp> after that asserts that the view is visible on the screen – if there is no view with that text, the check will fail. The <samp class="methodname">check(…)</samp> function is Espresso’s way to make <samp class="methodname">assertThat(…)</samp>-type assertions about views.

Often you will want to click on a view, then make an assertion to verify the result of your click. You can also use Espresso to click on views or otherwise interact with them:

```
 onView(withText("65_cjipie"))
            .perform(click())
```

When you interact with a view, Espresso will wait until your application is <samp class="emphasis">idle</samp> before continuing your test. Espresso has built-in ways of detecting when your UI is done updating, but if you need Espresso to wait longer, you can use a subclass of <samp class="classname">IdlingResource</samp> to signal to Espresso that your app has not settled down quite yet.

For more information about how to use Espresso to manipulate and test the UI, see the Espresso documentation at [<samp class="uri">developer.android.com/​training/​testing/​espresso</samp>](https://developer.android.com/training/testing/espresso).

Remember, integration tests and unit tests each serve different purposes. Most people prefer to start with unit tests because they help you define and verify the behavior of the individual parts of your app. Integration tests depend on those individually tested parts and verify that the parts work well together as a whole. Each gives you a distinct, important view of the health of your app, so the best shops do both kinds of testing.

## For the More Curious: Mocks and Testing

Mocking has a much different role in integration testing than it does in unit testing. Mock objects exist to isolate the component under test by pretending to be other, unrelated components. Unit testing tests an individual class; each class will have its own distinct dependencies, so each test class has a different set of mock objects. Since the mock objects are different in each test class, and the behavior rarely matters, mock frameworks that make it easy to create simple mock objects (like Mockito) are a great fit for unit tests.

Integration tests, on the other hand, are meant to test a larger piece of the app as a whole. Instead of isolating pieces of the app from each other, you use mocks to isolate the app from anything external it might interact with – for example, by providing a web service with fake data and responses. In BeatBox, you would provide a fake <samp class="classname">SoundPool</samp> that could tell you when a particular sound file was played. Because the mocks are larger and shared among many tests, and because it is more common to implement mock behavior, it is better to avoid automatic mocking frameworks for integration tests and instead manually write mock objects.

In either case, the same rule applies: Mock out the entities at the boundary of the component under test. This focuses the scope of your test and keeps it from breaking except when the component itself is broken.

## Challenge: Playback Speed Control

In this challenge, you will add playback speed control to BeatBox to greatly expand the user’s repertoire of possible sounds ([Figure 20.8](#ch20s13.xhtml_fig_beatbox_playbackspeed "Figure 20.8  BeatBox with playback speed control")). Within <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp>, wire up a <samp class="classname">SeekBar</samp> to control the <samp class="varname">rate</samp> value <samp class="classname">SoundPool</samp>’s <samp class="methodname">play(Int, Float, Float, Int, Int, Float)</samp> function accepts.

**Figure 20.8  BeatBox with playback speed control**

![BeatBox with playback speed control](Images/beatbox-playbackspeed.png)

To make this happen, check out the docs at [<samp class="uri">developer.android.com/​reference/​android/​widget/​SeekBar.html</samp>](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/widget/SeekBar.html).

## Challenge: Play Sound Across Rotation

Currently, BeatBox will stop playing the sound if you rotate the device. This challenge will fix that.

The main issue in the current app is where you save your <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp> object. Your <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> holds a reference to your <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp>, but it is destroyed and re-created across rotation. This means that your initial <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp> releases the <samp class="classname">SoundPool</samp> and re-creates it every time you rotate.

You have already seen how to persist information across rotation in GeoQuiz and CriminalIntent. Add a Jetpack <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> to BeatBox to keep your <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp> object alive across rotation.

You can expose the <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp> object as a public property from your <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp>. This way, <samp class="classname">MainActivity</samp> can access the <samp class="classname">BeatBox</samp> instance from the Jetpack <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> to hand it to the data binding view model.

# <samp class="chapter_number">21</samp>
<samp class="chapter_name">Styles and Themes</samp>

Now that BeatBox sounds intimidating, it is time to make it look intimidating, too.

So far, BeatBox sticks with the default UI styles. The buttons are stock. The colors are stock. The app does not stand out. It does not have its own brand.

We can restyle it. We have the technology.

[Figure 21.1](#ch21.xhtml_final "Figure 21.1  A themed BeatBox") shows the better, stronger, faster – or at least more stylish – BeatBox.

**Figure 21.1  A themed BeatBox**

![A themed BeatBox](Images/beatbox_finished.png)

## Color Resources

Begin by defining a few colors that you will use throughout this chapter. Edit your <samp class="filename">res/values/colors.xml</samp> file to match [Listing 21.1](#ch21s01.xhtml_pl_bb_colors "Listing 21.1  Defining a few colors (res/values/colors.xml)").

**Listing 21.1  Defining a few colors (`res/values/colors.xml`)**

```
<resources>
    <color name="colorPrimary">#008577</color>
    <color name="colorPrimaryDark">#00574B</color>
    <color name="colorAccent">#D81B60</color>

    <color name="red">#F44336</color>
    <color name="dark_red">#C3352B</color>
    <color name="gray">#607D8B</color>
    <color name="soothing_blue">#0083BF</color>
    <color name="dark_blue">#005A8A</color>
</resources>
```

Color resources are a convenient way to specify color values in one place that you reference throughout your application.

## Styles

Now, update the buttons in BeatBox with a <samp class="firstterm">style</samp>. A style is a set of attributes that you can apply to a widget.

Navigate to <samp class="filename">res/values/styles.xml</samp> and add a style named <samp class="classname">BeatBoxButton</samp> ([Listing 21.2](#ch21s02.xhtml_add_button_style "Listing 21.2  Adding a style (res/values/styles.xml)")). (When you created BeatBox, your new project should have come with a built-in <samp class="filename">styles.xml</samp> file. If your project did not, create the file.)

**Listing 21.2  Adding a style (`res/values/styles.xml`)**

```
<resources>

    <style name="AppTheme" parent="Theme.AppCompat.Light.DarkActionBar">
        <!-- Customize your theme here. -->
        <item name="colorPrimary">@color/colorPrimary</item>
        <item name="colorPrimaryDark">@color/colorPrimaryDark</item>
        <item name="colorAccent">@color/colorAccent</item>
    </style>

    <style name="BeatBoxButton">
        <item name="android:background">@color/dark_blue</item>
    </style>

</resources>
```

Here, you create a style called <samp class="classname">BeatBoxButton</samp>. This style defines a single attribute, <samp class="varname">android:background</samp>, and sets it to a dark blue color. You can apply this style to as many widgets as you like and then update the attributes of all of those widgets in this one place.

Now that the style is defined, apply <samp class="classname">BeatBoxButton</samp> to your buttons.

**Listing 21.3  Using a style (`res/layout/list_item_sound.xml`)**

```
<Button
        style="@style/BeatBoxButton"
        android:layout_width="match_parent"
        android:layout_height="120dp"
        android:onClick="@{() -> viewModel.onButtonClicked()}"
        android:text="@{viewModel.title}"
        tools:text="Sound name"/>
```

Run BeatBox, and you will see that all of your buttons now have a dark blue background color ([Figure 21.2](#ch21s02.xhtml_background "Figure 21.2  BeatBox with button styles")).

**Figure 21.2  BeatBox with button styles**

![BeatBox with button styles](Images/beatbox_style_only.png)

You can create a style for any set of attributes that you want to reuse in your application. Pretty handy.

### Style inheritance

Styles also support inheritance: A style can inherit and override attributes from another style.

Create a new style called <samp class="classname">BeatBoxButton.Strong</samp> that inherits from <samp class="classname">BeatBoxButton</samp> and also bolds the text.

**Listing 21.4  Inheriting from `BeatBoxButton` (`res/values/styles.xml`)**

```
<style name="BeatBoxButton">
    <item name="android:background">@color/dark_blue</item>
</style>

<style name="BeatBoxButton.Strong">
    <item name="android:textStyle">bold</item>
</style> 
```

(While you could have added the <samp class="varname">android:textStyle</samp> attribute to the <samp class="classname">BeatBoxButton</samp> style directly, you created <samp class="classname">BeatBoxButton.Strong</samp> to demonstrate style inheritance.)

The naming convention here is a little strange. When you name your style <samp class="classname">BeatBoxButton.Strong</samp>, you are saying that your theme inherits attributes from <samp class="classname">BeatBoxButton</samp>.

There is also an alternative inheritance naming style. You can specify a <samp class="varname">parent</samp> when declaring the style:

```
 <style name="BeatBoxButton">
        <item name="android:background">@color/dark_blue</item>
    </style>

    <style name="StrongBeatBoxButton" parent="@style/BeatBoxButton">
        <item name="android:textStyle">bold</item>
    </style>
```

Stick with the <samp class="classname">BeatBoxButton.Strong</samp> style in BeatBox.

Update <samp class="filename">res/layout/list_item_sound.xml</samp> to use your newer, stronger style.

**Listing 21.5  Using a bolder style (`res/layout/list_item_sound.xml`)**

```
<Button
    style="@style/BeatBoxButton.Strong"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="120dp"
    android:onClick="@{() -> viewModel.onButtonClicked()}"
    android:text="@{viewModel.title}"
    tools:text="Sound name"/>
```
