Instead, <samp class="classname">FlickrFetchr</samp> relies on <samp class="classname">FlickrApi</samp> to know the endpoint URL, to connect to that endpoint, and to perform the actual work of downloading the JSON data. <samp class="classname">FlickrFetchr</samp> is said to have a <samp class="firstterm">dependency</samp> on <samp class="classname">FlickrApi</samp>.

You are initializing <samp class="classname">FlickrApi</samp> inside the <samp class="classname">FlickrFetchr</samp> `init` block:

```
 class FlickrFetchr {
        ...
        private val flickrApi: FlickrApi

        init {
            val retrofit: Retrofit = Retrofit.Builder()
                    .baseUrl("https://www.flickr.com/")
                    .addConverterFactory(ScalarsConverterFactory.create())
                    .build()

            flickrApi = retrofit.create(FlickrApi::class.java)
        }

        fun fetchContents(): LiveData<String> {
            ...
        }
    }
```

This works well for a simple application, but there are a few potential issues to consider.

First, it is difficult to unit test <samp class="classname">FlickrFetchr</samp>. Recall from [Chapter 20](../Text/ch20.xhtml "20 Unit Testing and Audio Playback") that the goal of a unit test is to verify the behavior of a class and its interactions with other classes. To properly unit test <samp class="classname">FlickrFetchr</samp>, you need to isolate it from the real <samp class="classname">FlickrApi</samp>. But this is a difficult – if not impossible – task, because <samp class="classname">FlickrApi</samp> is initialized inside of the <samp class="classname">FlickrFetchr</samp> `init` block.

Hence, there is no way to provide a mock instance of <samp class="classname">FlickrApi</samp> to <samp class="classname">FlickrFetchr</samp> for testing purposes. This is problematic, because any test you run against <samp class="methodname">fetchContents()</samp> will result in a network request. The success of your tests would be dependent on network state and the availability of the Flickr back-end API at the time of running the test.

Another issue is that <samp class="classname">FlickrApi</samp> is tedious to instantiate. You must build and configure an instance of <samp class="classname">Retrofit</samp> before you can build an instance of <samp class="classname">FlickrApi</samp>. This implementation requires you to duplicate five lines of Retrofit configuration code anywhere you want to create a <samp class="classname">FlickrApi</samp> instance.

Finally, creating a new instance of <samp class="classname">FlickrApi</samp> everywhere you want to use it results in unnecessary object creation. Object creation is expensive relative to the scarce resources available on a mobile device. Whenever practical, you should share instances of a class across your app and avoid needless object allocation. <samp class="classname">FlickrApi</samp> is a perfect candidate for sharing, since there is no variable instance state.

<samp class="firstterm">Dependency injection</samp> (or DI) is a design pattern that addresses these issues by centralizing the logic for creating dependencies, such as <samp class="classname">FlickrApi</samp>, and supplying the dependencies to the classes that need them. By applying DI to PhotoGallery, you could easily pass an instance of <samp class="classname">FlickrApi</samp> into <samp class="classname">FlickrFetchr</samp> each time a new instance of <samp class="classname">FlickrFetchr</samp> was constructed. Using DI would allow you to:

*   encapsulate the initialization logic of <samp class="classname">FlickrApi</samp> into a common place outside of <samp class="classname">FlickrFetchr</samp>

*   use a singleton instance of <samp class="classname">FlickrApi</samp> throughout the app

*   substitute a mock version of <samp class="classname">FlickrApi</samp> when unit testing

Applying the DI pattern to <samp class="classname">FlickrFetchr</samp> might look something like this:

```
 class FlickrFetchr(flickrApi: FlickrApi) {
        fun fetchContents(): LiveData<String> {
            ...
        }
    }
```

Note that DI does not enforce the singleton pattern for all dependencies. <samp class="classname">FlickrFetchr</samp> is passed an instance of <samp class="classname">FlickrApi</samp> on construction. This mechanism for constructing <samp class="classname">FlickrFetchr</samp> gives you the flexibility to provide a new instance or a shared instance of <samp class="classname">FlickrApi</samp> based on your use case.

DI is a broad topic with many facets that extend well beyond Android. This section just scratches the surface. There are entire books dedicated to the concept of DI and many libraries to make DI easier to implement. If you want to use DI in your app, you should consider using one of these libraries. It will help guide you through the process of DI and reduce the amount of code you need to write to implement the pattern.

At the time of this writing, Dagger 2 is the official Google-recommended library for implementing DI on Android. You can find detailed documentation, code samples, and tutorials about DI with Dagger 2 at [<samp class="uri">google.github.io/​dagger</samp>](https://google.github.io/dagger).

## Challenge: Adding a Custom Gson Deserializer

The JSON response from Flickr contains multiple layers of nested data ([Figure 24.6](#ch24s03.xhtml_dig_pg_json_object_diagram "Figure 24.6  JSON text, JSON hierarchy, and corresponding model objects")). In [the section called *Deserializing JSON text into model objects*](#ch24s03.xhtml_sect-deserialize-json "Deserializing JSON text into model objects"), you created model objects to map directly to the JSON hierarchy. But what if you did not care about the data in the outer layers? Wouldn’t it be nice to avoid cluttering your codebase with unnecessary model objects?

By default, Gson maps all of the JSON data directly to your model objects by matching Kotlin property names (or `@SerializedName` annotations) to JSON field names. You can customize this behavior by defining a custom <samp class="classname">com.google.gson.JsonDeserializer</samp>.

For this challenge, implement a custom deserializer to strip out the outermost layer of JSON data (the layer that maps to <samp class="classname">FlickrResponse</samp>). The deserializer should return a <samp class="classname">PhotoResponse</samp> object populated based on the JSON data. To do this, create a new class that extends from <samp class="classname">com.google.gson.JsonDeserializer</samp> and override the <samp class="methodname">deserialize(…)</samp> function:

```
 class PhotoDeserializer : JsonDeserializer<PhotoResponse> {

        override fun deserialize(
            json: JsonElement,
            typeOfT: Type?,
            context: JsonDeserializationContext?
        ): PhotoResponse {
            // Pull photos object out of JsonElement
            // and convert to PhotoResponse object
        }
    }
```

Check out the Gson API documentation to learn how to parse through the <samp class="classname">JsonElement</samp> and convert it to a model object. (Hint: Look closely at the docs for <samp class="classname">JsonElement</samp>, <samp class="classname">JsonObject</samp>, and <samp class="classname">Gson</samp>.)

Once you create the deserializer, update the <samp class="classname">FlickrFetchr</samp> initialization code:

*   Use <samp class="classname">GsonBuilder</samp> to create a <samp class="classname">Gson</samp> instance and register your custom deserializer as a type adapter.

*   Create a <samp class="classname">retrofit2.converter.gson.GsonConverterFactory</samp> instance that uses the <samp class="classname">Gson</samp> instance as its converter.

*   Update the Retrofit instance configuration to use this custom Gson converter factory instance.

Finally, remove <samp class="classname">FlickrResponse</samp> from your project and update any dependent code accordingly.

## Challenge: Paging

By default, `getList` returns one page of 100 results. There is an additional parameter you can use called `page` that will let you return page two, page three, and so on.

For this challenge, research the Jetpack Paging Library ([<samp class="uri">developer.android.com/​topic/​libraries/​architecture/​paging</samp>](https://developer.android.com/topic/libraries/architecture/paging)) and use it to implement paging for PhotoGallery. This library provides a framework for loading your app’s data when it is needed. While you could implement this functionality manually, the paging library will be less work and less prone to error.

## Challenge: Dynamically Adjusting the Number of Columns

Currently, the number of columns displayed in the grid is fixed at three. Update your code to provide a dynamic number of columns so more columns appear in landscape and on larger devices.

A simple approach could involve providing an integer resource qualified for different orientations and/or screen sizes. This is similar to the way you provided different strings for different screen sizes in [Chapter 17](../Text/ch17.xhtml "17 Localization"). Integer resources should be placed in the <samp class="filename">res/values</samp> folder(s). Check out the Android developer documentation for more details.

But providing qualified resources does not offer much in the way of granularity. For a more difficult challenge (and a more flexible implementation), calculate and set the number of columns each time the fragment’s view is created. Calculate the number of columns based on the current width of the <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> and some predetermined constant column width.

There is only one catch: You cannot calculate the number of columns in <samp class="methodname">onCreateView(…)</samp>, because the <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> will not be sized yet. Instead, implement a <samp class="classname">ViewTreeObserver.OnGlobalLayoutListener</samp> and put your column calculation code in <samp class="methodname">onGlobalLayout()</samp>. Add the listener to your <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> using <samp class="methodname">addOnGlobalLayoutListener()</samp>.

# <samp class="chapter_number">25</samp>
<samp class="chapter_name">Loopers, Handlers, and HandlerThread</samp>

Now that you have downloaded and parsed JSON data from Flickr, your next task is to download and display images. In this chapter, you will learn how to use <samp class="classname">Looper</samp>, <samp class="classname">Handler</samp>, and <samp class="classname">HandlerThread</samp> to dynamically download and display photos in PhotoGallery. Along the way you will gain a deeper understanding of your app’s main thread and further explore restrictions around what work can be done on the main thread versus what work can be done on a background thread. Finally, you will learn how to communicate between the main thread and a background thread.

## Preparing RecyclerView to Display Images

The current <samp class="classname">PhotoHolder</samp> in <samp class="classname">PhotoGalleryFragment</samp> simply provides <samp class="classname">TextView</samp>s for the <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp>’s <samp class="classname">GridLayoutManager</samp> to display. Each <samp class="classname">TextView</samp> displays the caption of a <samp class="classname">GalleryItem</samp>.

To display photos, you are going to update <samp class="classname">PhotoHolder</samp> to provide <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp>s instead. Eventually, each <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> will display a photo downloaded from the <samp class="varname">url</samp> of a <samp class="classname">GalleryItem</samp>.

Start by creating a new layout file for your gallery items called <samp class="filename">list_item_gallery.xml</samp>. This layout will consist of a single <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> ([Listing 25.1](#ch25s01.xhtml_pl_pg_imageview_layout "Listing 25.1  Gallery item layout (res/layout/list_item_gallery.xml)")).

**Listing 25.1  Gallery item layout (`res/layout/list_item_gallery.xml`)**

```
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<ImageView xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
           android:layout_width="match_parent"
           android:layout_height="120dp"
           android:layout_gravity="center"
           android:scaleType="centerCrop"/>
```

These <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp>s will be managed by <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp>’s <samp class="classname">GridLayoutManager</samp>, which means that their width will vary. Their height, on the other hand, will remain fixed. To make the most of the <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp>’s space, you have set its `scaleType` to `centerCrop`. This setting centers the image and then scales it up so that the smaller dimension is equal to the view and the larger one is cropped on both sides.

Next, update <samp class="classname">PhotoHolder</samp> to hold an <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> instead of a <samp class="classname">TextView</samp>. Replace <samp class="varname">bindTitle</samp> with a function reference to set the <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp>’s <samp class="classname">Drawable</samp>.

**Listing 25.2  Updating `PhotoHolder` (`PhotoGalleryFragment.kt`)**

```
class PhotoGalleryFragment : Fragment() {
    ...
    private class PhotoHolder(private val itemTextView: TextView)
        : RecyclerView.ViewHolder(itemTextView) {
    private class PhotoHolder(private val itemImageView: ImageView)
        : RecyclerView.ViewHolder(itemImageView) {

        val bindTitle: (CharSequence) -> Unit = itemTextView::setText
        val bindDrawable: (Drawable) -> Unit  = itemImageView::setImageDrawable
  }
  ...
}
```

Previously, the <samp class="classname">PhotoHolder</samp> constructor assumed it would be passed a <samp class="classname">TextView</samp>. The new version instead expects an <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp>.

Update <samp class="classname">PhotoAdapter</samp>’s <samp class="methodname">onCreateViewHolder(…)</samp> to inflate the <samp class="filename">list_item_gallery.xml</samp> file you created and pass it to <samp class="classname">PhotoHolder</samp>’s constructor. Add the `inner` keyword so <samp class="classname">PhotoAdapter</samp> can access the parent activity’s `layoutInflater` property directly. (You could get the inflater from `parent.context`, but you will need access to other properties and functions in the parent activity later, and using `inner` makes that easier.)

**Listing 25.3  Updating `PhotoAdapter`’s `onCreateViewHolder(…)` (`PhotoGalleryFragment.kt`)**

```
class PhotoGalleryFragment : Fragment() {
    ...
    private inner class PhotoAdapter(private val galleryItems: List<GalleryItem>)
        : RecyclerView.Adapter<PhotoHolder>() {

        override fun onCreateViewHolder(
            parent: ViewGroup,
            viewType: Int
        ): PhotoHolder {
            val textView = TextView(activity)
            return PhotoHolder(textView)
            val view = layoutInflater.inflate(
                R.layout.list_item_gallery,
                parent,
                false
            ) as ImageView
            return PhotoHolder(view)
        }
        ...
    }
    ...
}
```

Next, you will need a placeholder image for each <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> to display until you download an image to replace it. Find <samp class="filename">bill_up_close.png</samp> in the solutions file ([<samp class="uri">www.bignerdranch.com/​solutions/​AndroidProgramming4e.zip</samp>](https://www.bignerdranch.com/solutions/AndroidProgramming4e.zip)) and put it in <samp class="filename">res/drawable</samp>.

Update <samp class="classname">PhotoAdapter</samp>’s <samp class="classname">onBindViewHolder(…)</samp> to set the placeholder image as the <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp>’s <samp class="classname">Drawable</samp>.

**Listing 25.4  Binding the default image (`PhotoGalleryFragment.kt`)**

```
class PhotoGalleryFragment : Fragment() {
    ...
    private inner class PhotoAdapter(private val galleryItems: List<GalleryItem>)
        : RecyclerView.Adapter<PhotoHolder>() {
        ...
        override fun onBindViewHolder(holder: PhotoHolder, position: Int) {
            val galleryItem = galleryItems[position]
            holder.bindTitle(galleryItem.title)
            val placeholder: Drawable = ContextCompat.getDrawable(
                requireContext(),
                R.drawable.bill_up_close
            ) ?: ColorDrawable()
            holder.bindDrawable(placeholder)
        }
    }
    ...
}
```

Notice that you are providing a blank <samp class="classname">ColorDrawable</samp> object if <samp class="methodname">ContextCompat.getDrawable(…)</samp> returns null.

Run PhotoGallery, and you should see an array of close-up Bills, as in [Figure 25.1](#ch25s01.xhtml_ss_pg_uncomfortably_close_bills "Figure 25.1  A Billsplosion").

**Figure 25.1  A Billsplosion**

![A Billsplosion](Images/photogallery_all_placeholders.png)

## Preparing to Download Bytes from a URL

Your Retrofit API interface does not support downloading an image yet. Patch that hole now. Add a new function that accepts a URL string as input and returns an executable call object (<samp class="classname">retrofit2.Call</samp>) whose result will be an <samp class="classname">okhttp3.ResponseBody</samp>.

**Listing 25.5  Updating `FlickrApi` (`api/FlickrApi.kt`)**

```
interface FlickrApi {
    ...
    @GET
    fun fetchUrlBytes(@Url url: String): Call<ResponseBody>
}
```

This new API function looks a little different. It accepts a URL as input and uses that parameter value directly when determining where to download the data from. Using a parameterless `@GET` annotation combined with annotating the first parameter in <samp class="methodname">fetchUrlBytes(…)</samp> with `@Url` causes Retrofit to override the base URL completely. Instead, Retrofit will use the URL passed to the <samp class="methodname">fetchUrlBytes(…)</samp> function.

Add a function to <samp class="classname">FlickrFetchr</samp> to fetch the bytes from a given URL and decode them into a <samp class="classname">Bitmap</samp> ([Listing 25.6](#ch25s02.xhtml_pl_pg_add_fetchPhoto_to_FlickrFetchr "Listing 25.6  Adding image downloading to FlickrFetchr (FlickrFetchr.kt)") ).

**Listing 25.6  Adding image downloading to `FlickrFetchr` (`FlickrFetchr.kt`)**

```
class FlickrFetchr {
    ...
    @WorkerThread
    fun fetchPhoto(url: String): Bitmap? {
        val response: Response<ResponseBody> = flickrApi.fetchUrlBytes(url).execute()
        val bitmap = response.body()?.byteStream()?.use(BitmapFactory::decodeStream)
        Log.i(TAG, "Decoded bitmap=$bitmap from Response=$response")
        return bitmap
    }
}
```

Here, you use <samp class="methodname">Call.execute()</samp>, which executes the web request synchronously. As you have learned, networking on the main thread is not allowed. The `@WorkerThread` annotation indicates that this function should only be called on a background thread.

However, the annotation itself does not take care of making a thread or putting the work on a background thread. That is your job. (The `@WorkerThread` annotation will show a Lint error if the function you call it from is annotated with `@MainThread` or `@UiThread`. However, as of this writing, Android lifecycle functions are not annotated with `@MainThread` or `@UiThread`, even though all lifecycle functions execute on the main thread.) Eventually, you will call <samp class="methodname">fetchPhoto(String)</samp> from a background thread you create.

You pull a <samp class="classname">java.io.InputStream</samp> from the response body using the <samp class="methodname">ResponseBody.byteStream()</samp> function. Once you have the byte stream, you pass it to <samp class="methodname">BitmapFactory.decodeStream(InputStream)</samp>, which will create a <samp class="classname">Bitmap</samp> from the bytes in the stream.

The response and byte stream must be closed. Since <samp class="classname">InputStream</samp> implements <samp class="classname">Closeable</samp>, the Kotlin standard library function <samp class="methodname">use(…)</samp> will clean things up when <samp class="methodname">BitmapFactory.decodeStream(…)</samp> returns.

Finally, you return the bitmap that <samp class="classname">BitmapFactory</samp> constructed. With that, your API interface and repository are ready to download images.

But there is still (a lot) more work to do.

## Downloading Lots of Small Things

Currently, PhotoGallery’s networking works like this: <samp class="classname">PhotoGalleryViewModel</samp> calls <samp class="methodname">FlickrFetchr().fetchPhotos()</samp> to download JSON data from Flickr. <samp class="classname">FlickrFetchr</samp> immediately returns an empty <samp class="classname">LiveData<List<GalleryItem>></samp> object and enqueues an asynchronous Retrofit request to retrieve the data from Flickr. That network request executes on a background thread.

When the data download is complete, <samp class="classname">FlickrFetchr</samp> parses the JSON data into a list of <samp class="classname">GalleryItem</samp>s and publishes the list to the live data object it returned. Each <samp class="classname">GalleryItem</samp> now has a URL where a thumbnail-size photo lives.

The next step is to go and get those thumbnails. How will you go about this? <samp class="classname">FlickrFetchr</samp> requests only 100 URLs by default, so your <samp class="classname">GalleryItem</samp> list holds at most 100 URLs. So one option would be to download the images one after another until you have all 100, notify the <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp>, and ultimately display the images en masse in the <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp>.

However, downloading the thumbnails all at once would cause two problems. The first is that it could take a while, and the UI would not be updated until the downloading was complete. On a slow connection, users would be staring at a wall of Bills for a long time.

The second problem is the cost of having to store the entire set of images. One hundred thumbnails will fit into memory easily. But what if it were 1,000? What if you wanted to implement infinite scrolling? Eventually, you would run out of space.

Given these problems, real-world apps often download images only when they need to be displayed onscreen. Downloading on demand puts the responsibility on the <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> and its adapter. The adapter triggers the image downloading as part of its <samp class="methodname">onBindViewHolder(…)</samp> implementation.

OK, so how will you go about <samp class="emphasis">that</samp>? You could enqueue a separate asynchronous Retrofit request for each image download. However, you would need to keep track of all the <samp class="classname">Call</samp> objects and manage their lives in relation to each view holder and to the fragment itself.

Instead you are going to create a dedicated background thread. This thread will receive and process download requests one at a time, and it will provide the resulting image for each individual request as the corresponding download completes. Since all the requests are managed by the background thread, you can easily clean up all the requests or stop the thread altogether, rather than having to manage a whole bunch of separate requests.

## Assembling a Background Thread

Create a new class called <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> that extends <samp class="classname">HandlerThread</samp>. Then give it a constructor, a stub implementation of a function called <samp class="methodname">queueThumbnail()</samp>, and an override of the <samp class="methodname">quit()</samp> function that signals when your thread has quit. (Toward the end of the chapter, you will need this bit of information.)

**Listing 25.7  Initial thread code (`ThumbnailDownloader.kt`)**

```
private const val TAG = "ThumbnailDownloader"

class ThumbnailDownloader<in T>
    : HandlerThread(TAG) {

    private var hasQuit = false

    override fun quit(): Boolean {
        hasQuit = true
        return super.quit()
    }

    fun queueThumbnail(target: T, url: String) {
        Log.i(TAG, "Got a URL: $url")
    }
}
```

Notice that you gave the class a single generic argument, <samp class="varname"><T></samp>. Your <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp>’s user, <samp class="classname">PhotoGalleryFragment</samp> in this case, will need to use some object to identify each download and to determine which UI element to update with the image once it is downloaded. Rather than locking the user into a specific type of object as the identifier, using a generic makes the implementation more flexible.

The <samp class="methodname">queueThumbnail()</samp> function expects an object of type <samp class="type">T</samp> to use as the identifier for the download and a <samp class="type">String</samp> containing the URL to download. This is the function you will have <samp class="classname">PhotoAdapter</samp> call in its <samp class="methodname">onBindViewHolder(…)</samp> implementation.

### Making your thread lifecycle aware

Since the sole purpose of <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> is to download and serve images to <samp class="classname">PhotoGalleryFragment</samp>, tie the life of the thread to the user’s <samp class="firstterm">perceived lifetime</samp> of the fragment. In other words, spin the thread up when the user first launches the screen. Spin the thread down when the user finishes with the screen (e.g., by pressing the Back button or dismissing the task). Do not destroy and then re-create the thread when the user rotates the device – retain the thread instance across configuration changes.

The life of a <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> matches the user’s perceived life of the fragment. However, managing the thread in <samp class="classname">PhotoGalleryViewModel</samp> would make the implementation more complex than necessary and also cause some challenges with leaking views down the line. It would make more sense to push the thread management to some other component, such as the repository (<samp class="classname">FlickrFetchr</samp>). In a real-world app, you would likely do just that. But in this case, doing so would detract from the goal of understanding <samp class="classname">HandlerThread</samp>.

Instead, for the purposes of this chapter, directly tie a <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> instance to your <samp class="classname">PhotoGalleryFragment</samp>. First, retain <samp class="classname">PhotoGalleryFragment</samp> so that the life of the fragment instance matches the user’s perceived life of the fragment.

**Listing 25.8  Retaining `PhotoGalleryFragment` (`PhotoGalleryFragment.kt`)**

```
class PhotoGalleryFragment : Fragment() {
    ...
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)

        retainInstance = true
        ...
    }
    ...
}
```

(In general, you should avoid retaining fragments. You are only doing it here because retaining the fragment simplifies the implementation so you can focus on learning how <samp class="classname">HandlerThread</samp> works. You will learn more about the implications of retaining a fragment in [the section called *Retained Fragments*](../Text/ch25s07.xhtml "Retained Fragments") later in this chapter.)

Now that the fragment is retained, start the thread when <samp class="classname">PhotoGalleryFragment.onCreate(…)</samp> is called and quit the thread when <samp class="methodname">PhotoGalleryFragment.onDestroy()</samp> is called. You could achieve this by adding code to <samp class="classname">PhotoGalleryFragment</samp>’s lifecycle functions directly, but this would add unnecessary complexity to your fragment class. Instead, abstract the code into <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> by making <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> <samp class="firstterm">lifecycle aware</samp>.

A lifecycle-aware component, known as a <samp class="firstterm">lifecycle observer</samp>, observes the lifecycle of a <samp class="firstterm">lifecycle owner</samp>. <samp class="classname">Activity</samp> and <samp class="classname">Fragment</samp> are examples of lifecycle owners – they have a lifecycle and implement the <samp class="classname">LifecycleOwner</samp> interface.

Update <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> to implement the <samp class="classname">LifecycleObserver</samp> interface and observe the <samp class="methodname">onCreate(…)</samp> and <samp class="methodname">onDestroy</samp> functions of its lifecycle owner. Have <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> start itself when <samp class="methodname">onCreate(…)</samp> is called and stop itself when <samp class="methodname">onDestroy()</samp> is called.

**Listing 25.9  Making `ThumbnailDownloader` lifecycle aware (`ThumbnailDownloader.kt`)**

```
private const val TAG = "ThumbnailDownloader"

class ThumbnailDownloader<in T>
    : HandlerThread(TAG), LifecycleObserver {

    private var hasQuit = false

    override fun quit(): Boolean {
        hasQuit = true
        return super.quit()
    }

    @OnLifecycleEvent(Lifecycle.Event.ON_CREATE)
    fun setup() {
        Log.i(TAG, "Starting background thread")
    }

    @OnLifecycleEvent(Lifecycle.Event.ON_DESTROY)
    fun tearDown() {
        Log.i(TAG, "Destroying background thread")
    }

    fun queueThumbnail(target: T, url: String) {
        Log.i(TAG, "Got a URL: $url")
    }
}
```

Implementing <samp class="classname">LifecycleObserver</samp> means you can register <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> to receive lifecycle callbacks from any <samp class="classname">LifecycleOwner</samp>. You use the `@OnLifecycleEvent(Lifecycle.Event)` annotation to associate a function in your class with a lifecycle callback. `Lifecycle.Event.ON_CREATE` registers <samp class="methodname">ThumbnailDownloader.setup()</samp> to be called when <samp class="methodname">LifecycleOwner.onCreate(…)</samp> is called. `Lifecycle.Event.ON_DESTROY` registers <samp class="methodname">ThumbnailDownloader.tearDown()</samp> to be called when <samp class="methodname">LifecycleOwner.onDestroy()</samp> is called.

You can view a list of available <samp class="classname">Lifecycle.Event</samp> constants by visiting the API reference page ([<samp class="uri">developer.android.com/​reference/​android/​arch/​lifecycle/​Lifecycle.Event</samp>](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/arch/lifecycle/Lifecycle.Event)).

(By the way, <samp class="classname">LifecycleObserver</samp>, <samp class="classname">Lifecycle.Event</samp>, and <samp class="classname">OnLifecycleEvent</samp> are part of Jetpack, in the <samp class="filename">android.arch.lifecycle</samp> package. You already have access to these classes because you added the `lifecycle-extensions` dependency to your Gradle file in [Chapter 24](../Text/ch24.xhtml "24 HTTP and Background Tasks").)

Next, you need to create an instance of <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> and register it to receive lifecycle callbacks from <samp class="classname">PhotoGalleryFragment</samp>. Do that in <samp class="filename">PhotoGalleryFragment.kt</samp>.

**Listing 25.10  Creating a `ThumbnailDownloader` (`PhotoGalleryFragment.kt`)**

```
class PhotoGalleryFragment : Fragment() {

    private lateinit var photoGalleryViewModel: PhotoGalleryViewModel
    private lateinit var photoRecyclerView: RecyclerView
    private lateinit var thumbnailDownloader: ThumbnailDownloader<PhotoHolder>

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)

        retainInstance = true

        photoGalleryViewModel =
                ViewModelProviders.of(this).get(PhotoGalleryViewModel::class.java)

        thumbnailDownloader = ThumbnailDownloader()
        lifecycle.addObserver(thumbnailDownloader)
    }
    ...
    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        ...
    }

    override fun onDestroy() {
        super.onDestroy()
        lifecycle.removeObserver(
            thumbnailDownloader
        )
    }
    ...
}
```

You can specify any type for <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp>’s generic argument. However, recall that this argument specifies the type of the object that will be used as the identifier for your download. In this case, the <samp class="classname">PhotoHolder</samp> makes for a convenient identifier, since it is also the target where the downloaded images will eventually go.

Since <samp class="classname">Fragment</samp> implements <samp class="classname">LifecycleOwner</samp>, it has a `lifecycle` property. You use this property to add an observer to the fragment’s <samp class="classname">Lifecycle</samp>. Calling <samp class="function">lifecycle.addObserver(thumbnailDownloader)</samp> registers the thumbnail downloader instance to receive the fragment’s lifecycle callbacks. Now, when <samp class="methodname">PhotoGalleryFragment.onCreate(…)</samp> is called, <samp class="methodname">ThumbnailDownloader.setup()</samp> gets called. When <samp class="methodname">PhotoGalleryFragment.onDestroy()</samp> is called, <samp class="methodname">ThumbnailDownloader.tearDown()</samp> gets called.

You call <samp class="methodname">lifecycle.removeObserver(thumbnailDownloader)</samp> in <samp class="methodname">Fragment.onDestroy()</samp> to remove <samp class="varname">thumbnailDownloader</samp> as a lifecycle observer when the fragment instance is destroyed. You could rely on garbage collection to get rid of the fragment’s lifecycle and lifecycle observers when the garbage collector frees the fragment’s (and possibly activity’s) object graph. However, we prefer deterministic resource deallocation over waiting for the next time scavenging happens. This helps keep bugs close to the event that triggered them.

Run your app. You should still see a wall of close-up Bills. Check your log statements for the message `ThumbnailDownloader: Starting background thread` to verify that <samp class="methodname">ThumbnailDownloader.setup()</samp> got executed one time. Press the Back button to exit the application and finish (and destroy) <samp class="classname">PhotoGalleryActivity</samp> (and the <samp class="classname">PhotoGalleryFragment</samp> it hosts). Check your log statements again; the message `ThumbnailDownloader: Destroying background thread` verifies that <samp class="methodname">ThumbnailDownloader.tearDown()</samp> got executed one time.

### Starting and stopping a HandlerThread

Now that <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> is observing <samp class="classname">PhotoGalleryFragment</samp>’s lifecycle, update <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> to start itself when <samp class="methodname">PhotoGalleryFragment.onCreate(…)</samp> is called and stop itself when <samp class="methodname">PhotoGalleryFragment.onDestroy()</samp> is called.

**Listing 25.11  Starting and stopping the `ThumbnailDownloader` thread (`ThumbnailDownloader.kt`)**

```
class ThumbnailDownloader<in T>
    : HandlerThread(TAG), LifecycleObserver {
    ...
    @OnLifecycleEvent(Lifecycle.Event.ON_CREATE)
    fun setup() {
        Log.i(TAG, "Starting background thread")
        start()
        looper
    }

    @OnLifecycleEvent(Lifecycle.Event.ON_DESTROY)
    fun tearDown() {
        Log.i(TAG, "Destroying background thread")
        quit()
    }

    fun queueThumbnail(target: T, url: String) {
        Log.i(TAG, "Got a URL: $url")
    }
}
```

A couple of safety notes. One: Notice that you access <samp class="varname">looper</samp> after calling <samp class="methodname">start()</samp> on your <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> (you will learn more about the <samp class="classname">Looper</samp> in a moment). This is a way to ensure that the thread’s guts are ready before proceeding, to obviate a potential (though rarely occurring) race condition. Until you first access <samp class="varname">looper</samp>, there is no guarantee that <samp class="methodname">onLooperPrepared()</samp> has been called, so there is a possibility that calls to <samp class="methodname">queueThumbnail(…)</samp> will fail due to a null <samp class="classname">Handler</samp>.

Safety note number two: You call <samp class="methodname">quit()</samp> to terminate the thread. This is critical. If you do not quit your <samp class="classname">HandlerThread</samp>s, they will never die. Like zombies. Or rock and roll.

Finally, within <samp class="methodname">PhotoAdapter.onBindViewHolder(…)</samp>, call the thread’s <samp class="methodname">queueThumbnail()</samp> function and pass in the target <samp class="classname">PhotoHolder</samp> where the image will ultimately be placed and the <samp class="classname">GalleryItem</samp>’s URL to download from.

**Listing 25.12  Hooking up `ThumbnailDownloader` (`PhotoGalleryFragment.kt`)**

```
class PhotoGalleryFragment : Fragment() {
    ...
    private inner class PhotoAdapter(private val galleryItems: List<GalleryItem>)
        : RecyclerView.Adapter<PhotoHolder>() {
        ...
        override fun onBindViewHolder(holder: PhotoHolder, position: Int) {
            val galleryItem = galleryItems[position]
            ...
            thumbnailDownloader.queueThumbnail(holder, galleryItem.url)
        }
    }
}
```

Run PhotoGallery again and check out Logcat. When you scroll around the <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp>, you should see lines in Logcat signaling that <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> is getting each one of your download requests. You will still see a wall of Bills in the app (do not fear, you will fix this soon enough).

Now that you have a <samp class="classname">HandlerThread</samp> up and running, the next step is to communicate between your app’s main thread and your new background thread.

## Messages and Message Handlers

Your dedicated thread will download photos, but how will it work with the <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp>’s adapter to display them when it cannot directly access the main thread? (Recall that background threads are not allowed to execute code that modifies the view – only the main thread is permitted do that. The main thread cannot execute long-running tasks – only a background thread is permitted to do that.)

Think back to the shoe store with two Flashes. Background Flash has wrapped up his phone call to the distributor. He needs to tell Main Flash that the shoes are back in stock. If Main Flash is busy, Background Flash cannot do this right away. He would have to wait by the register to catch Main Flash at a spare moment. This would work, but it would not be very efficient.

The better solution is to give each Flash an inbox. Background Flash writes a message about the shoes being in stock and puts it on top of Main Flash’s inbox. Main Flash does the same thing when he wants to tell Background Flash that the stock of shoes has run out.

The inbox idea turns out to be really handy. The Flash (either Flash, that is) may have something that needs to be done soon, but not right at the moment. In that case, he can put a message in his own inbox and then handle it when he has time.

In Android, the inbox that threads use is called a <samp class="firstterm">message queue</samp>. A thread that works by using a message queue is called a <samp class="firstterm">message loop</samp>; it loops again and again looking for new messages on its queue ([Figure 25.2](#ch25s05.xhtml_fig_flashdance "Figure 25.2  Flash dance")).

**Figure 25.2  Flash dance**

![Flash dance](Images/flash_dance.png)

A message loop consists of a thread and a <samp class="firstterm">looper</samp>. The <samp class="classname">Looper</samp> is the object that manages a thread’s message queue.

The main thread is a message loop and has a looper. Everything your main thread does is performed by its looper, which grabs messages off of its message queue and performs the task they specify ([Figure 25.3](#ch25s05.xhtml_fig_UIThreadParts "Figure 25.3  Main thread is a HandlerThread")).

**Figure 25.3  Main thread is a `HandlerThread`**

![Main thread is a HandlerThread](Images/UIThreadParts.png)

You are going to create a background thread that is also a message loop. You will use a class called <samp class="classname">HandlerThread</samp> that prepares a <samp class="classname">Looper</samp> for you.

The main thread and your background thread will communicate with each other by placing messages in each other’s queue using <samp class="classname">Handler</samp>s ([Figure 25.4](#ch25s05.xhtml_fig_PhotoGalleryThreadCommunicationOverview "Figure 25.4  Communicating with Handlers")).

**Figure 25.4  Communicating with `Handler`s**

![Communicating with Handlers](Images/PhotoGalleryThreadCommunicationOverview.png)

Before you create a message, you need to understand what a <samp class="classname">Message</samp> is and the relationship it has with its <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> (often called its <samp class="firstterm">message handler</samp>).

### Message anatomy

Let’s start by looking closely at messages. The messages that a Flash might put in an inbox (its own inbox or that of another Flash) are not supportive notes, like, “You run very fast, Flash.” They are tasks that need to be handled.

A message is an instance of <samp class="classname">Message</samp> and contains several fields. Three are relevant to your implementation:

| <samp class="varname">what</samp> |
| <samp class="varname">obj</samp> |
| <samp class="varname">target</samp> |

The target of a <samp class="classname">Message</samp> is an instance of <samp class="classname">Handler</samp>. You can think of the name <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> as being short for “message handler.” When you create a <samp class="classname">Message</samp>, it will automatically be attached to a <samp class="classname">Handler</samp>. And when your <samp class="classname">Message</samp> is ready to be processed, <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> will be the object in charge of making it happen.

### Handler anatomy

To do any real work with messages, you first need an instance of <samp class="classname">Handler</samp>. A <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> is not just a target for processing your <samp class="classname">Message</samp>s. A <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> is your interface for creating and posting <samp class="classname">Message</samp>s, too. Take a look at [Figure 25.5](#ch25s05.xhtml_fig_looper_and_handler "Figure 25.5  Looper, Handler, HandlerThread, and Messages").

**Figure 25.5  `Looper`, `Handler`, `HandlerThread`, and `Message`s**

![Looper, Handler, HandlerThread, and Messages](Images/looper_and_handler.png)

<samp class="classname">Message</samp>s must be posted and consumed on a <samp class="classname">Looper</samp>, because the <samp class="classname">Looper</samp> owns the inbox of <samp class="classname">Message</samp> objects. So the <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> always has a reference to its coworker, the <samp class="classname">Looper</samp>.

A <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> is attached to exactly one <samp class="classname">Looper</samp>, and a <samp class="classname">Message</samp> is attached to exactly one target <samp class="classname">Handler</samp>, called its <samp class="firstterm">target</samp>. A <samp class="classname">Looper</samp> has a whole queue of <samp class="classname">Message</samp>s. Multiple <samp class="classname">Message</samp>s can reference the same target <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> ([Figure 25.5](#ch25s05.xhtml_fig_looper_and_handler "Figure 25.5  Looper, Handler, HandlerThread, and Messages")).

Multiple <samp class="classname">Handler</samp>s can be attached to one <samp class="classname">Looper</samp> ([Figure 25.6](#ch25s05.xhtml_fig_looper_and_multiple_handlers "Figure 25.6  Multiple Handlers, one Looper")). This means that your <samp class="classname">Handler</samp>’s <samp class="classname">Message</samp>s may be living side by side with another <samp class="classname">Handler</samp>’s messages.

**Figure 25.6  Multiple `Handler`s, one `Looper`**

![Multiple Handlers, one Looper](Images/looper_and_multiple_handlers.png)

### Using handlers

Usually, you do not set a message’s target <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> by hand. It is better to build the message by calling <samp class="methodname">Handler.obtainMessage(…)</samp>. You pass the other message fields into this function, and it automatically sets the target to the <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> object the function was called on for you.

<samp class="methodname">Handler.obtainMessage(…)</samp> pulls from a common recycling pool to avoid creating new <samp class="classname">Message</samp> objects, so it is also more efficient than creating new instances.

Once you have obtained a <samp class="classname">Message</samp>, you call <samp class="methodname">sendToTarget()</samp> to send the <samp class="classname">Message</samp> to its <samp class="classname">Handler</samp>. The <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> will then put the <samp class="classname">Message</samp> on the end of <samp class="classname">Looper</samp>’s message queue.

In this case, you are going to obtain a message and send it to its target within the implementation of <samp class="methodname">queueThumbnail()</samp>. The message’s <samp class="varname">what</samp> will be a constant defined as `MESSAGE_DOWNLOAD`. The message’s <samp class="varname">obj</samp> will be an object of type <samp class="type">T</samp>, which will be used to identify the download. In this case, <samp class="varname">obj</samp> will be the <samp class="classname">PhotoHolder</samp> that the adapter passed in to <samp class="methodname">queueThumbnail()</samp>.

When the looper pulls a <samp class="classname">Message</samp> from the queue, it gives the message to the message’s target <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> to handle. Typically, the message is handled in the target’s implementation of <samp class="methodname">Handler.handleMessage(…)</samp>.

[Figure 25.7](#ch25s05.xhtml_fig_posting_a_message "Figure 25.7  Creating a Message and sending it") shows the object relationships involved.

**Figure 25.7  Creating a `Message` and sending it**

![Creating a Message and sending it](Images/posting_a_message.png)

In this case, your implementation of <samp class="methodname">handleMessage(…)</samp> will use <samp class="classname">FlickrFetchr</samp> to download bytes from the URL and then turn those bytes into a bitmap.

First, add the constant and properties shown in [Listing 25.13](#ch25s05.xhtml_pl_pg_thumbnaildownloader_message_vars "Listing 25.13  Adding a constant and properties (ThumbnailDownloader.kt)").

**Listing 25.13  Adding a constant and properties (`ThumbnailDownloader.kt`)**

```
private const val TAG = "ThumbnailDownloader"
private const val MESSAGE_DOWNLOAD = 0

class ThumbnailDownloader<in T>
    : HandlerThread(TAG), LifecycleObserver {

    private var hasQuit = false
    private lateinit var requestHandler: Handler
    private val requestMap = ConcurrentHashMap<T, String>()
    private val flickrFetchr = FlickrFetchr()
    ...
}
```

<samp class="varname">MESSAGE_DOWNLOAD</samp> will be used to identify messages as download requests. (<samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> will set this as the `what` on any new download messages it creates.)

The newly added <samp class="varname">requestHandler</samp> will store a reference to the <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> responsible for queueing download requests as messages onto the <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> background thread. This handler will also be in charge of processing download request messages when they are pulled off the queue.

The <samp class="varname">requestMap</samp> property is a <samp class="classname">ConcurrentHashMap</samp>, a thread-safe version of <samp class="classname">HashMap</samp>. Here, using a download request’s identifying object of type <samp class="type">T</samp> as a key, you can store and retrieve the URL associated with a particular request. (In this case, the identifying object is a <samp class="classname">PhotoHolder</samp>, so the request response can be easily routed back to the UI element where the downloaded image should be placed.)

The `flickrFetchr` property stores a reference to a <samp class="classname">FlickrFetchr</samp> instance. This way all of the Retrofit setup code will only execute once during the lifetime of the thread. (Creating and configuring a new Retrofit instance every time you make a web request can slow your app down, especially if you are doing many requests in rapid succession.)

Next, add code to <samp class="methodname">queueThumbnail(…)</samp> to update <samp class="varname">requestMap</samp> and to post a new message to the background thread’s message queue.

**Listing 25.14  Obtaining and sending a message (`ThumbnailDownloader.kt`)**

```
class ThumbnailDownloader<in T>
    : HandlerThread(TAG), LifecycleObserver {
    ...
    fun queueThumbnail(target: T, url: String) {
        Log.i(TAG, "Got a URL: $url")
        requestMap[target] = url
        requestHandler.obtainMessage(MESSAGE_DOWNLOAD, target)
            .sendToTarget()
    }
}
```

You obtain a message directly from <samp class="varname">requestHandler</samp>, which automatically sets the new <samp class="classname">Message</samp> object’s <samp class="varname">target</samp> field to <samp class="varname">requestHandler</samp>. This means <samp class="varname">requestHandler</samp> will be in charge of processing the message when it is pulled off the message queue. The message’s <samp class="varname">what</samp> field is set to <samp class="varname">MESSAGE_DOWNLOAD</samp>. Its <samp class="varname">obj</samp> field is set to the `T target` value (a <samp class="classname">PhotoHolder</samp>, in this case) that is passed to <samp class="methodname">queueThumbnail(…)</samp>.

The new message represents a download request for the specified <samp class="varname">T target</samp> (a <samp class="classname">PhotoHolder</samp> from the <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp>). Recall that <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp>’s adapter implementation in <samp class="classname">PhotoGalleryFragment</samp> calls <samp class="methodname">queueThumbnail(…)</samp> from <samp class="methodname">onBindViewHolder(…)</samp>, passing along the <samp class="classname">PhotoHolder</samp> the image is being downloaded for and the URL location of the image to download.

Notice that the message itself does not include the URL. Instead, you update <samp class="varname">requestMap</samp> with a mapping between the request identifier (<samp class="classname">PhotoHolder</samp>) and the URL for the request. Later you will pull the URL from <samp class="varname">requestMap</samp> to ensure that you are always downloading the most recently requested URL for a given <samp class="classname">PhotoHolder</samp> instance. (This is important because <samp class="classname">ViewHolder</samp> objects in <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp>s are recycled and reused.)

Finally, initialize <samp class="varname">requestHandler</samp> and define what that <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> will do when downloaded messages are pulled off the queue and passed to it.

**Listing 25.15  Handling a message (`ThumbnailDownloader.kt`)**

```
class ThumbnailDownloader<in T>
    : HandlerThread(TAG), LifecycleObserver {
    ...
    private val requestMap = ConcurrentHashMap<T, String>()
    private val flickrFetchr = FlickrFetchr()

    @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")
    @SuppressLint("HandlerLeak")
    override fun onLooperPrepared() {
        requestHandler = object : Handler() {
            override fun handleMessage(msg: Message) {
                if (msg.what == MESSAGE_DOWNLOAD) {
                    val target = msg.obj as T
                    Log.i(TAG, "Got a request for URL: ${requestMap[target]}")
                    handleRequest(target)
                }
            }
        }
    }
    ...
    fun queueThumbnail(target: T, url: String) {
        ...
    }

    private fun handleRequest(target: T) {
        val url = requestMap[target] ?: return
        val bitmap = flickrFetchr.fetchPhoto(url) ?: return
    }
}
```

When importing <samp class="classname">Message</samp>, make sure to select `android.os.Message` from the options presented.

You implemented <samp class="methodname">Handler.handleMessage(…)</samp> in your <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> subclass within <samp class="methodname">onLooperPrepared()</samp>. <samp class="methodname">HandlerThread.onLooperPrepared()</samp> is called before the <samp class="classname">Looper</samp> checks the queue for the first time. This makes it a good place to create your <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> implementation.

Within <samp class="methodname">Handler.handleMessage(…)</samp>, you check the message type, retrieve the <samp class="varname">obj</samp> value (which will be of type <samp class="type">T</samp> and serves as the identifier for the request), and then pass it to <samp class="methodname">handleRequest(…)</samp>. (Recall that <samp class="methodname">Handler.handleMessage(…)</samp> will get called when a download message is pulled off the queue and ready to be processed.)

The <samp class="methodname">handleRequest()</samp> function is a helper function where the downloading happens. Here you check for the existence of a URL. Then you pass the URL to the <samp class="methodname">FlickrFetchr.fetchPhoto(…)</samp> function that you created with such foresight at the beginning of this chapter.

The `@Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")` annotation tells the Lint checker that you are well aware that you are casting `msg.obj` to type `T` without first checking whether `msg.obj` is indeed of type `T`. This is OK for now because you are the only developer dealing with your PhotoGallery code. You control messages added to the queue, and you know that at this point all the messages you queue have their `obj` field set to a <samp class="classname">PhotoHolder</samp> instance (which matches the `T` specified on <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp>).

The way you create the <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> implementation above technically creates an inner class. Inner classes hold a reference to their outer class (<samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> in this case), which can in turn cause the outer class to leak if the lifetime of the inner class is longer than the intended lifetime of the outer class.

This is only problematic if your handler is attached to the main thread’s looper. You suppress a <samp class="classname">HandlerLeak</samp> warning using `@SuppressLint("HandlerLeak")`, since the handler you create is attached to the looper of a background thread. If the handler were instead attached to the main thread’s looper, it might not be garbage-collected. If it were to leak, since it also holds a reference to the <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp>, your app would leak the <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> instance as well.

In general, you should only suppress Lint warnings if you truly understand the warning and why suppressing it in the given scenario is safe.

Run PhotoGallery and check Logcat for your confirming log statements.

Of course, the request will not be completely handled until you set the bitmap on the <samp class="classname">PhotoHolder</samp> that originally came from <samp class="classname">PhotoAdapter</samp>. However, that is UI work, so it must be done on the main thread.

Everything you have seen so far uses handlers and messages on a single thread – <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> putting messages in <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp>’s own inbox. In the next section, you will see how <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> can use a <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> to post requests to a separate thread (namely, the main thread).

### Passing handlers

So far you are able to schedule work on the background thread from the main thread using <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp>’s <samp class="varname">requestHandler</samp>. This flow is shown in [Figure 25.8](#ch25s05.xhtml_fig_handler_passing_1 "Figure 25.8  Scheduling work on ThumbnailDownloader from the main thread").

**Figure 25.8  Scheduling work on `ThumbnailDownloader` from the main thread**

![Scheduling work on ThumbnailDownloader from the main thread](Images/handler_passing_1.png)

You can also schedule work on the main thread from the background thread using a <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> attached to the main thread. This flow looks like [Figure 25.9](#ch25s05.xhtml_fig_handler_passing_2 "Figure 25.9  Scheduling work on the main thread from ThumbnailDownloader’s thread").

**Figure 25.9  Scheduling work on the main thread from `ThumbnailDownloader`’s thread**

![Scheduling work on the main thread from ThumbnailDownloader’s thread](Images/handler_passing_2.png)

The main thread is a message loop with handlers and a <samp class="classname">Looper</samp>. When you create a <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> in the main thread, it will be associated with the main thread’s <samp class="classname">Looper</samp>. You can then pass that <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> to another thread. The passed <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> maintains its loyalty to the <samp class="classname">Looper</samp> of the thread that created it. Any messages the <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> is responsible for will be handled on the main thread’s queue.

In <samp class="filename">ThumbnailDownloader.kt</samp>, add the <samp class="varname">responseHandler</samp> property seen above to hold a <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> passed from the main thread. Then replace the constructor with one that accepts a <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> (which will be stored in <samp class="varname">responseHandler</samp>) and a function type that will be used as a callback to communicate the responses (downloaded images) with the requester (the main thread).

**Listing 25.16  Adding the `responseHandler` (`ThumbnailDownloader.kt`)**

```
class ThumbnailDownloader<in T>(
    private val responseHandler: Handler,
    private val onThumbnailDownloaded: (T, Bitmap) -> Unit
) : HandlerThread(TAG), LifecycleObserver {
    ...
}
```

The function type property defined in your new constructor will eventually be called when an image has been fully downloaded and is ready to be added to the UI. Using this listener delegates the responsibility of what to do with the downloaded image to a class other than <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> (in this case, to <samp class="classname">PhotoGalleryFragment</samp>). Doing so separates the downloading task from the UI updating task (putting the images into <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp>s), so that <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> could be used for downloading into other kinds of <samp class="classname">View</samp> objects as needed.

Next, modify <samp class="classname">PhotoGalleryFragment</samp> to pass a <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> attached to the main thread to <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp>. Also, pass an anonymous function to handle the downloaded image once it is complete.

**Listing 25.17  Hooking up to response `Handler` (`PhotoGalleryFragment.kt`)**

```
class PhotoGalleryFragment : Fragment() {
    ...
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        ...
        thumbnailDownloader = ThumbnailDownloader()
        val responseHandler = Handler()
        thumbnailDownloader =
                ThumbnailDownloader(responseHandler) { photoHolder, bitmap ->
                    val drawable = BitmapDrawable(resources, bitmap)
                    photoHolder.bindDrawable(drawable)
                }
        lifecycle.addObserver(thumbnailDownloader)
    }
    ...
}
```

Remember that by default, the <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> will attach itself to the <samp class="classname">Looper</samp> for the current thread. Because this <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> is created in <samp class="methodname">onCreate(…)</samp>, it will be attached to the main thread’s <samp class="classname">Looper</samp>.

Now <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> has access via <samp class="varname">responseHandler</samp> to a <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> that is tied to the main thread’s <samp class="classname">Looper</samp>. It also has your function type implementation to do the UI work with the returning <samp class="classname">Bitmap</samp>s. Specifically, the function passed to the <samp class="methodname">onThumbnailDownloaded</samp> higher-order function sets the <samp class="methodname">Drawable</samp> of the originally requested <samp class="methodname">PhotoHolder</samp> to the newly downloaded <samp class="methodname">Bitmap</samp>.

You could send a custom <samp class="classname">Message</samp> back to the main thread requesting to add the image to the UI, similar to how you queued a request on the background thread to download the image. However, this would require another subclass of <samp class="classname">Handler</samp>, with an override of <samp class="methodname">handleMessage(…)</samp>.

Instead, use another handy <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> function – <samp class="methodname">post(Runnable)</samp>.

<samp class="methodname">Handler.post(Runnable)</samp> is a convenience function for posting <samp class="classname">Message</samp>s that look like this:

```
 var myRunnable: Runnable = object : Runnable {
        override fun run() {
            // Your code here
        }
    }
    var msg: Message = Message.obtain(someHandler, myRunnable)
    // Sets msg.callback to myRunnable
```

When a <samp class="classname">Message</samp> has its <samp class="varname">callback</samp> field set, it is not routed to its <samp class="varname">target</samp> <samp class="classname">Handler</samp> when pulled off the message queue. Instead, the <samp class="methodname">run()</samp> function of the <samp class="classname">Runnable</samp> stored in <samp class="varname">callback</samp> is executed directly.

In <samp class="methodname">ThumbnailDownloader.handleRequest()</samp>, post a <samp class="classname">Runnable</samp> to the main thread’s queue through <samp class="varname">responseHandler</samp> ([Listing 25.18](#ch25s05.xhtml_pl_pg_downloading_and_displaying "Listing 25.18  Downloading and displaying images (ThumbnailDownloader.kt)")).

**Listing 25.18  Downloading and displaying images (`ThumbnailDownloader.kt`)**

```
class ThumbnailDownloader<in T>(
    private val responseHandler: Handler,
    private val onThumbnailDownloaded: (T, Bitmap) -> Unit
) : HandlerThread(TAG), LifecycleObserver {
    ...
    private fun handleRequest(target: T) {
        val url = requestMap[target] ?: return
        val bitmap = flickrFetchr.fetchPhoto(url) ?: return

        responseHandler.post(Runnable {
            if (requestMap[target] != url || hasQuit) {
                return@Runnable
            }

            requestMap.remove(target)
            onThumbnailDownloaded(target, bitmap)
        })
    }
}
```

Because <samp class="varname">responseHandler</samp> is associated with the main thread’s <samp class="classname">Looper</samp>, all of the code inside of <samp class="classname">Runnable</samp>’s <samp class="methodname">run()</samp> will be executed on the main thread.

So what does this code do? First, you double-check the `requestMap`. This is necessary because the <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> recycles its views. By the time <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> finishes downloading the <samp class="classname">Bitmap</samp>, <samp class="classname">RecyclerView</samp> may have recycled the <samp class="classname">PhotoHolder</samp> and requested a different URL for it. This check ensures that each <samp class="classname">PhotoHolder</samp> gets the correct image, even if another request has been made in the meantime.

Next, you check `hasQuit`. If <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> has already quit, it may be unsafe to run any callbacks.

Finally, you remove the <samp class="classname">PhotoHolder</samp>-URL mapping from the `requestMap` and set the bitmap on the target <samp class="classname">PhotoHolder</samp>.

## Listening to the View Lifecycle

Before running PhotoGallery and seeing your hard-won images, there is one last danger you need to account for. If the user rotates the screen, <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> may be hanging on to invalid <samp class="classname">PhotoHolder</samp>s. Your app could crash if <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> tries to send a bitmap to a <samp class="classname">PhotoHolder</samp> that was part of a view that was destroyed across rotation.

Fix this leak by clearing all the requests out of your queue when the fragment’s view is destroyed. To do this, <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> needs to know about the fragment’s view lifecycle. (Recall that the lifecycles for the fragment and its view diverge, since you are retaining the fragment: The view will be destroyed across rotation, but the fragment instance itself will not.)

First, refactor your existing fragment lifecycle observer code to make room for a second lifecycle observer implementation.

**Listing 25.19  Refactoring your fragment lifecycle observer (`ThumbnailDownloader.kt`)**

```
class ThumbnailDownloader<in T>(
    private val responseHandler: Handler,
    private val onThumbnailDownloaded: (T, Bitmap) -> Unit
) : HandlerThread(TAG), LifecycleObserver {

    val fragmentLifecycleObserver: LifecycleObserver =
        object : LifecycleObserver {

            @OnLifecycleEvent(Lifecycle.Event.ON_CREATE)
            fun setup() {
                Log.i(TAG, "Starting background thread")
                start()
                looper
            }

            @OnLifecycleEvent(Lifecycle.Event.ON_DESTROY)
            fun tearDown() {
                Log.i(TAG, "Destroying background thread")
                quit()
            }
        }

    private var hasQuit = false
    ...
    @OnLifecycleEvent(Lifecycle.Event.ON_CREATE)
    fun setup() {
        start()
        looper
    }

    @OnLifecycleEvent(Lifecycle.Event.ON_DESTROY)
    fun tearDown() {
        Log.i(TAG, "Background thread destroyed")
        quit()
    }
    ...
}
```

Next, define a new observer that will eventually listen to lifecycle callbacks from the fragment’s view.

**Listing 25.20  Adding a view lifecycle observer (`ThumbnailDownloader.kt`)**

```
class ThumbnailDownloader<in T>(
    private val responseHandler: Handler,
    private val onThumbnailDownloaded: (T, Bitmap) -> Unit
) : HandlerThread(TAG) {

    val fragmentLifecycleObserver: LifecycleObserver =
        object : LifecycleObserver {
        ...
    }

    val viewLifecycleObserver: LifecycleObserver =
        object : LifecycleObserver {

            @OnLifecycleEvent(Lifecycle.Event.ON_DESTROY)
            fun clearQueue() {
                Log.i(TAG, "Clearing all requests from queue")
                requestHandler.removeMessages(MESSAGE_DOWNLOAD)
                requestMap.clear()
            }
        }
    ...
}
```

When observing a fragment’s view lifecycle, `Lifecycle.Event.ON_DESTROY` maps to <samp class="function">Fragment.onDestroyView()</samp>. (To learn how the other <samp class="classname">Lifecycle.Event</samp> constants map to the fragment’s lifecycle callbacks when you observe the fragment’s view lifecycle, see <samp class="methodname">getViewLifecycleOwner</samp> in the API reference for <samp class="classname">Fragment</samp> at [<samp class="uri">developer.android.com/​reference/​kotlin/​androidx/​fragment/​app/​Fragment</samp>](https://developer.android.com/reference/kotlin/androidx/fragment/app/Fragment).)

Now update <samp class="classname">PhotoGalleryFragment</samp> to register the refactored fragment observer. Also, register the newly added lifecycle observer to listen for the fragment’s view lifecycle.

**Listing 25.21  Registering the view lifecycle observer (`PhotoGalleryFragment.kt`)**

```
class PhotoGalleryFragment : Fragment() {
    ...
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        ...
        thumbnailDownloader =
            ThumbnailDownloader(responseHandler) {
            ...
        }
        lifecycle.addObserver(thumbnailDownloader.fragmentLifecycleObserver)
    }

    override fun onCreateView(
            inflater: LayoutInflater,
            container: ViewGroup?,
            savedInstanceState: Bundle?
    ): View {
        viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycle.addObserver(
            thumbnailDownloader.viewLifecycleObserver
        )
        ...
    }
    ...
}
```

You can safely observe the view lifecycle in <samp class="methodname">Fragment.onCreateView(…)</samp> so long as you return a non-null view at the end of the <samp class="methodname">onCreateView(…)</samp> function. See [the section called *Challenge: Observing View LifecycleOwner LiveData*](../Text/ch25s10.xhtml "Challenge: Observing View LifecycleOwner LiveData") near the end of this chapter to learn more about observing `viewLifecycleOwner`, which offers more flexibility in configuring the view lifecycle observation.

Finally, unregister `thumbnailDownloader` as a fragment view lifecycle observer in <samp class="methodname">Fragment.onDestroyView()</samp>. Update the existing code that unregisters `thumbnailDownloader` as a fragment lifecycle observer to reflect your recent refactor.

**Listing 25.22  Unregistering the view lifecycle observer (`PhotoGalleryFragment.kt`)**

```
class PhotoGalleryFragment : Fragment() {
    ...
    override fun onDestroyView() {
        super.onDestroyView()
        viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycle.removeObserver(
            thumbnailDownloader.viewLifecycleObserver
        )
    }

    override fun onDestroy() {
        super.onDestroy()
        lifecycle.removeObserver(
            thumbnailDownloader.fragmentLifecycleObserver
        )
    }
    ...
}
```

As with the fragment `lifecycle` observers, you do not have to explicitly unregister fragment `viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycle` observers. The fragment’s view lifecycle registry, which keeps track of all of the view lifecycle observers, gets nulled out when the fragment’s view is destroyed. However, just as before, we prefer to explicitly unregister observers rather than rely on garbage collection.

With that, your work for this chapter is complete. Run PhotoGallery. Scroll around to see images dynamically loading ([Figure 25.10](#ch25s06.xhtml_ss_pg_handlers_end_result "Figure 25.10  Images on display")).

**Figure 25.10  Images on display**

![Images on display](Images/photogallery_handler_final_product.png)

PhotoGallery has achieved its basic goal of displaying images from Flickr. In the next few chapters, you will add more functionality, like searching for photos and opening each photo’s Flickr page in a web view.

## Retained Fragments

By default, the retainInstance property of a fragment is `false`. This means it is not retained but is destroyed and re-created on rotation along with the activity that hosts it. Calling <samp class="methodname">setRetainInstance(true)</samp> retains the fragment. When a fragment is retained, the fragment is not destroyed with the activity. Instead, it is preserved and passed along intact to the new activity.

When you retain a fragment, you can count on all of its instance variables to keep the same values. When you reach for them, they are simply there.

### Rotation and retained fragments

Let’s take a closer look at how retained fragments work. Retained fragments take advantage of the fact that a fragment’s view can be destroyed and re-created without having to destroy the fragment itself.

During a configuration change, the <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> first destroys the views of the fragments in its list. Fragment views always get destroyed and re-created on a configuration change for the same reasons that activity views are destroyed and re-created: If you have a new configuration, then you might need new resources. Just in case better matching resources are now available, you rebuild the view from scratch.

Next, the <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> checks the retainInstance property of each fragment. If it is `false`, which it is by default, then the <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> destroys the fragment instance. The fragment and its view will be re-created by the new <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> of the new activity “on the other side” ([Figure 25.11](#ch25s07.xhtml_fig_rotation_default_with_fm "Figure 25.11  Default rotation with a UI fragment")).

**Figure 25.11  Default rotation with a UI fragment**

![Default rotation with a UI fragment](Images/rotation_default_with_fm.png)

On the other hand, if retainInstance is `true`, then the fragment’s view is destroyed, but the fragment itself is not. When the new activity is created, the new <samp class="classname">FragmentManager</samp> finds the retained fragment and re-creates its view ([Figure 25.12](#ch25s07.xhtml_fig_rotation_retained_with_fm "Figure 25.12  Rotation with a retained UI fragment")).

**Figure 25.12  Rotation with a retained UI fragment**

![Rotation with a retained UI fragment](Images/rotation_retained_with_fm.png)

A retained fragment is not destroyed, but it is <samp class="firstterm">detached</samp> from the dying activity. This puts the fragment in a retained state. The fragment still exists, but it is not hosted by any activity ([Figure 25.13](#ch25s07.xhtml_fragment_state_diagram_retain "Figure 25.13  Fragment lifecycle")).

**Figure 25.13  Fragment lifecycle**

![Fragment lifecycle](Images/fragment_lifecycle.png)

The retained state is entered when two conditions are met:

*   <samp class="methodname">setRetainInstance(true)</samp> has been called on the fragment

*   the hosting activity is being destroyed for a configuration change (typically rotation)

A fragment is only in the retained state for an extremely brief interval – the time between being detached from the old activity and being reattached to the new activity that is immediately created.

### Whether to retain

Retained fragments: pretty nifty, right? Yes! They are indeed nifty. They appear to solve all the problems that pop up from activities and fragments being destroyed on rotation. When the device configuration changes, you get the most appropriate resources by creating a brand-new view, and you have an easy way to retain data and objects.

You may wonder why you would not retain every fragment or why fragments are not retained by default. In general, we do not recommend using this mechanism unless you absolutely need to, for a few reasons.

The first reason is simply that retained fragments are more complicated than unretained fragments. When something goes wrong with them, it takes longer to get to the bottom of what went wrong. Programs are always more complicated than you want them to be, so if you can get by without this complication, you are better off.

The second reason is that fragments that handle rotation using saved instance state handle all lifecycle situations, but retained fragments only handle the case when an activity is destroyed for a configuration change. If your activity is destroyed because the OS needs to reclaim memory, then all your retained fragments are destroyed, too, which may mean that you lose some data.

The third reason is that the <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> class replaces the need for retained fragments in most cases. Use a <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> instead of a retained fragment to persist UI-related state across a configuration change. <samp class="classname">ViewModel</samp> gives the same benefit of retained state across a configuration change without the drawbacks of introducing a more complicated lifecycle for your fragment.

## For the More Curious: Solving the Image Downloading Problem

This book is here to teach you mostly about the tools in the standard Android library. If you are open to using more third-party libraries (in addition to Retrofit and the others we have introduced), there are a few libraries that can save you a whole lot of time in various scenarios, including the image downloading work you implemented in PhotoGallery.

Admittedly, the solution you implemented in this chapter is far from perfect. And when you start to need caching, transformations, and better performance, it is natural to ask whether someone else has solved this problem before you. The answer is yes: Someone has. There are several libraries available that solve the image-loading problem. We currently use Picasso ([<samp class="uri">square.github.io/​picasso</samp>](https://square.github.io/picasso/)) for image loading in our production applications.

Picasso lets you do everything from this chapter with just a few function calls:

```
 private class PhotoHolder(private val itemImageView: ImageView)
        : RecyclerView.ViewHolder(itemView) {
           ...
           fun bindGalleryItem(galleryItem: GalleryItem) {
               Picasso.get()
                      .load(galleryItem.url)
                      .placeholder(R.drawable.bill_up_close)
                      .into(itemImageView)
           }
          ...
    }
```

The fluent interface requires you get an instance of Picasso using <samp class="methodname">get()</samp>. You can specify the URL of the image to download using <samp class="methodname">load(String)</samp> and the <samp class="classname">ImageView</samp> object to load the result into using <samp class="methodname">into(ImageView)</samp>. There are many other configurable options, such as specifying an image to display until the requested image is fully downloaded (using <samp class="methodname">placeholder(Int)</samp> or <samp class="methodname">placeholder(drawable)</samp>).

In <samp class="methodname">PhotoAdapter.onBindViewHolder(…)</samp>, you would replace the existing code with a call through to the new <samp class="methodname">bindGalleryItem(…)</samp> function.

Picasso does all of the work of <samp class="methodname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> (along with the <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader.ThumbnailDownloadListener<T></samp> callback) and the image-related work of <samp class="classname">FlickrFetchr</samp>. This means you could remove <samp class="classname">ThumbnailDownloader</samp> if you used Picasso (you would still need <samp class="classname">FlickrFetchr</samp> for downloading the JSON data). In addition to simplifying your code, Picasso supports more advanced features such as image transformations and disk caching with minimal effort on your part.

You can add Picasso to your project as a library dependency, just as you have done for other dependencies (like RecyclerView).
